This is, in my opinion, the best installment in the Far Cry series. So let me start with the bad-
-The missions can get repetitive, especially during prolonged play.
-The music is one tier above stock music. I wish it had more nuance, more variation, or at least more than a handful of the same tracks on repeat. I turned it off, personally.
-In vanilla, the enemies can be bulletspongey- but there are mods out there to fix that issue, and they're not difficult to install.
-In vanilla, the colors can be a bit washed out. Plenty of SweetFX and other mods come in handy here, and without the desaturation, the game looks much better.
-The voice acting for everybody but the three main characters and the combatant enemies is phoned in- horrible accents,  people talking like English is their second language in real life (maybe it was intentional???) and generally just sounding monotone, rushed, and bored, like the best they could come up with for voice acting talent for the buddies was interns and script monkeys, which, knowing full well the quality of the game that preceded this entry, could have very well been the case.
-More of a personal gripe, but I wish I had a way to turn up the sounds of gunshots/explosions. I can adjust the "master" volume, but apart from that the only other option is to turn on/off the music.
With that out of the way, let's talk about the good.
-The way the game handles lighting, shadows, foliage, and fire is phenomenal, especially if you consider that this game was released back when Bush Jr. was still in office.
-The gunplay, in terms of sound and recoil apart from the sponginess, is great. I play it with mods myself, and that takes what was good and makes it absolutely perfect.
-Due to the extremely limited system for fast traveling, the player is forced to explore, by foot, boat, or automobile, a diverse, hostile, atmospheric, and at times, breathtakingly beautiful rendition of a fictional, unnamed central african country. This is how fast travel ought to be in every videogame- the problem is, you'd actually have to make the game fun to explore, which, luckily, this game excells at.
-The game is brave enough to explore at least a few of the darker topics regarding war, that being the execution of suspected political dissidents, international gun-running, and the use of PMCs between rival factions for dominance, which lends to it's immersion and worldbuilding. It's dissapointing there was no more narrative focus on such ideas, or others- it's darkness and moral ambiguity is what adds punch to the otherwise hit or miss plot. The new games are fun for their own reasons, but they're absolutely goofy and whimsical by comparison- they feel like murder playgrounds rather than life or death warzones, which, while entertaining, is dissapointing when you realize what they could have achieved if they had built on the ideas of this game instead of shirking them.
TL;DR- A handful of personal gripes aside, I love this game, and I think that, with or without mods, it is the best game in the series by far. If you're looking to buy a Far Cry game and you're new to the series, look no further- just bear in mind that this is vastly, vastly different from the rest of the series.

While the world was ogling over first-person shooters like Doom 3, Half Life 2 and even Unreal Tournament 2004 for which, incidentally, all developed by famous companies like id Software, Valve and Epic Games respectively, straight out of left field arrived a FPS game named Far Cry from Crytek and the net result was a brilliant display of technical prowess that requires an equally powerful PC to run it. However, as good as it sounds, it has its flaws like a pretty lame storyline as the game felt like a tech demo – that is, they have a great engine to toy with however needs a purpose to play the game; a.k.a. plot / storyline.
Why I’m giving a detailed opening about Far Cry’s first game is because Far Cry 2 (and thus forms the bases of this review), as good as it sounds with its visuals with plenty of explosions (if you manage to see the promos / trailers and all that wonderful stuff), it suffers from the same fate as in Far Cry however to somewhat a lessor extend. It also derived from the same gaming engine yet heavily modified Dunia Engine, the visuals certainly meet up to the awesome standards with brilliant lighting effects, beautifully rendered weather patterns and even has fire physics that’s simply rivals the real thing. Yet there are elements of improvement needed to bump this game from simply good to great.
According to an interview with Clint Hocking for Rock Paper Shotgun, Clint explained that to fully appreciate this game can take the player 50 plus hours to complete it. For me, arguably being the world’s slowest gamer, took me just shy of 100 hours to finish it; and that’s including locating every diamond, unlocking every safehouse, locating all the buddies…basically everything that you can possibly do in that game. However, it is a bit of a rinse, repeat type of gameplay for which is a shame (as explained before).

Make the game more believable instead of relying on graphics to tell the story, for which graphics, in itself, is a good thing however not in isolation though. Overall, it’s a good game to play and explore however there’s still a lot more room for improvement.

I really wanted to enjoy this game as I've always been a huge fan of the flight sims that straddle the line between arcade and realism.  But after the fourth time I had to reload one of the first few mission because of gameplay bugs, I gave up.  The first time, it gives me the conversation text as I'm lifting off, but doesn't mark my objective.  The second time it didn't give me even the conversation text.  The third time it crashed to the desktop.  The fourth time it seemed like everything was going to work, but then the target I was supposed to intercept shot away from me at a speed I couldn't match and then just kept running.  I chased him at max speed for roughly five minutes before I quit and made use of steam's new refund policy.
Also, having the overdrive or afterburner (or whatever it is called) just being the last 5% or so of the thrust throttle is very poor design.  Adjusting the throttle on a Logitech Extreme 3D Pro Joystick to the maximum speed without also hitting the afterburner is a headache of micro adjustments. Oh boy, where to begin....
If you want the short version - the game is just not fun.
If you want the long version - read on!
So to start with, here are the pros of the game:
+ Interesting premise
+ The characters seem funny enough at times
+ It's nice to see the devs attempt to emulate Crimson Skies type games.
And here are the cons:
- No tutorial what's so ever, the game is not hard to figure out, but it would have been nice if they included one.
- The mission pacing is awful, the first 3-4 missions last for about two minutes and just make you fly forward requiring minimal input from your end. They could have made them in to a single mission and it would have benefited the game.
- The flight model is arcade, but not the fun type of arcade like Ace Combat. The gravity doesn't seem to affect your plane, it flies the same no matter which direction you chose, be that up or down and the rudders rubberband like crazy. It will swing you back to the direction you came from the moment you release the turn button. I would also like to point out that it feels like you are flying though molasses instead of air.
- The environments look extremely bland and the trees flicker like crazy when you fly over them, the planes look nice, but everything else looks like an late Xbox / early360 game.
- The performance is spotty at best, I was getting frame drops from 80 to 20 while nothing was happening on the screen and it doesn't look like a game that should ever drop below 60 on a 290X even on the highest settings.
- The menus look like they are placeholder, especially the options screen and the mission failure one.
- And the main con of all that just made me quit for good? It just wasn't fun. I love flight game like the Crimson Sky, Ace Combat, Blazing Angels, Sky Crawlers, etc, and this is a disgrace compared to all of them.
I do not recommend this game unless you find it on sale.

Now that it's out of early access... It looked like a great game, it has a lot of potential, but the control support is awful. This is, without any doubt, the worst controlling game of any type or genre, that I've ever played since 1995.  Really really really reeeeaaaallly awful. With a 360 controller, the handling ranges from pretty bad to terrible. With a flight stick... well, it just doesn't map functionally onto a stick, so forget about it. With the keyboard it's.... Jesus, it's real bad.
Controls are a crucial part of any flight sim/arcade game and the control support isn't anywhere near being good enough to recommend.

Oh my...  This game is excellent.  It's not easy at all, even though it doesn't model planes realistically.  Any comparisons made to Crimson Skies are pretty accurate.  I'd say the flight model is similar to War Thunder on "arcade" but the planes are considerably less maneuverable.  Considering you're flying a twin engine cargo plane, that's expected.
The dialogue that strings the missions together is funny, brief, and to the point.  "Go blow up the thing."  There are bombs, rockets, torpedoes, and a variety of cannons that get strapped on the planes.  Thankfully the missions do have checkpoints, and restarting a mission after failing is ZERO load time.   I'm playing with a Logitech 3D Pro stick and it works perfectly after button mapping.  The game is set up for a 360 gamepad by default.  It also supports mouse control BUT that isn't quite working just yet.   Views are cockpit, 3rd person, and no-cockpit gunsight views.  Hold a key/button to momentarily padlock the current enemy, so you don't get lost in all the chaos.
There's multiplayer, and even a dedicated server you can download.  I played some skirmish with the AI, and had them turned up a difficulty notch plus had too many of them fighting me, and I can attest the my end was brutal and swift.  :-)  The only thing I really feel absent is a nice hammy voiceover of the character dialogue.  The voice work in Crimson Skies was superb and really brought the game to life.  Reading the text balloons just isn't the same.  A pretty small complaint considering how much goodness is going on here for $12.

I didn't have any expectations when I first played this, and since it was on a sale I decided to try it. And I got a lot of enjoyment from this game with the fun gameplay, ridiculous/cute story and cute artstyle.
So now I'll breakdown my points in this review
Gameplay
The gameplay is very simplistic and very typical when it comes to platform games, the only parts that differ from most of them is that you can hover for some seconds before you get tired and using your breath to destroy the enemies (both which have been done before, but it works and makes sense considering that you're a dragon).
It's solid and works well, and some of the ways on how you get to the items can be interesting to do.
Another part of the game consists on leveling up your stats, which are done my getting money and using it to get better skills or by finding the items that I've previously mentioned.
And the boss battles are relatively easy, except the final one if you don't have the necesary stats.
Controls
The controls are very solid and you won't have any problems by controling the dragon. There's no delay in any action and they're very intuitive, although there was this moment when i restarted a stage because i wanted to get an item when suddenly in one of these restarts my character didn't moved, but that's a very rare occurence.
(I used an xbox 360 controller for this game, I don't know if other controllers will do the trick)
Story
The story consists on the king kidnapping your girlfirend while you were watching TV, a very simple one. But one of the point that make me like the game consisted on the humor, which is very quirky and cute. A laughed a lot at the amount of ridiculous situations and jokes that the game presented.
They mostly consisdt on the situation that they're on, but they're well executed. And it also helps that when the dragon talks it consists on giberish that only a few of them understand.
Graphics
Some might not like the crayon style of the game, but it's one that adds cuteness and differs itself from the other generic "retro" indie games that appear quite a lot in steam. Even though I personally prefer another type of style this one seems very pleasant to look at and does the job in this game.
Soundtrack
IMO not the best since it's generic and while right now I can remember some songs I will forget them in a couple of days, but it does the trick and helps with he situation and the mood of them is compatible with the theme of the game.
Overall
The game is good and you'll have a fun time with the humor and the style of game, with a solid gameplay and good level design it will be a game that you'll mostly complete in 2-4 hours (or more if you want to get the items). Definetly recommended if it's on sale since it's very cheap.

Even though I recommend this game, I must admit it's not an easy sell.
First of all, the game is indeed charming thanks to an audiovisual retro shape and colors that match the jazzy soundtrack.
The game itself, however, is hard in a way that seems more like cheating.
As a guy who can only walk and slash, you must be really careful and precise regarding your actions, just like in an old-school NES Double Dragon or Final Fight game. However, not only is this game old-school simple and hard, it's also devoid of visual cues and an interface elements that could help you understand the game's state, where you can go to, and avoid mistakes.
For example, whenever you reach a door or edge of the screen, you may end up in another area. However, it's never clear which doors are open or closed and which edges connect to some other area. Additionally, you may end up in another region simply by slightly hitting a door while fighting. It would've been better to just have a button to open a door when available.
Similarly, it's not clear which items you can interact with, and they don't seem to improve the game that much.
One might argue that all this is deliberate, but I don't think it plays to the game's advantage. It just makes things confusing. Also, some bugs occur randomly that allow you go to outside the borders of the stage or paralyze enemies.
I'm ok with the difficulty since each area is a checkpoint, and it's not a bad concept. However, most of the time I overcame a challenge I felt more like luck rather than skill, either because an enemy moved differently from last time or because of some bug.
Still, I must say I'm glad I played it. The game's definitely unique and charming, and it's not expensive. And the music's amazing!

If you liked Crimson Skies or Wings of War, this game is right up your alley. I'm a life-long flight sim player who enjoys both simulations and arcade flight games, and this game has the special sauce.
- Fun, varied missions.
- Pretty, retro graphics in a beautiful tropical environment
- Accessible yet realistic-ish flight model (as far as arcade flying goes)

A very imaginative and streamlined take on a flight action game that doesn't overcomplicate itself so much that it's inaccessible, yet doesn't feel too mechanical and arcadey.
Pros:
-beautiful stylized environments
-unique and fun to fly aircraft
-decent flight model
-amusing writing
-decently varied campaign missions
-AI is clever enough to use the aircraft's advantages, but not exploitative of the mechanics, which means fights are always winnable if not always easy
-the boost mechanic is a neat idea that prevents fights from descending into two planes just flying in circles
Cons:
-tends to be on the buggy side, with the occasional invisible plane popping up
-only a few aircraft have cockpits modeled, and flying from external view makes the game way too easy, in my opinion
-frame rate tends to chug a lot, especially close to the ground
-missions tend to be combat-oriented in the campaign, which means the player doesn't really get to explore and admire the scenery
-loading times are rather long for such a light game (only about a 1 GB install)

BOMB allows you to live out your Porco Rosso fantasies such as verbally abusing your companions and engaging in nail biting aerial combat. This game is FUN.
Although it might not be a 100% accurate sim experience it is a nice break from the stress of DCS World/IL2 mechanics,  and does not require an expensive Track IR and joystick setup (although joystick is recommended because mouse controls are a bit wonky right now).
There are 3 views, pretty classic, 3rd person, cockpit (my personal favorite) and 1stperson no cockpit (why people fly like this i have no idea) Cockpit features lots of gauges and doohickys, all of which seem to function. Cockpits are also unique for each flyable plane, which seems obvious but is lacking in some other flight games.
It features believable planes that are a cool mix of prop and jet/rocket fighters. You can usually guess which realworld aircraft inspired them by how they handle. Weapons usually consist of your stock machine guns and your choice of cannons/flak guns and other options.
The game features multiplayer but i have not yet tried it, I think ill stick with the story for now.
One last note, the support is awesome. Email with an issue and you can expect a quick reply and fix within days. They're helpful and courteous, and even though my specific issue has yet to be solved they told be to expect a fix in the next patch. Worth a buy for this alone.
My only negatives are that mouse control and optimization could use some work (both are being worked on by the development team)
And that I would like to see more planes added (but to be honest, my ideal flight game features hundreds of unique planes, so take that with a grain of salt)
Happy Flying!

I can't figure out how this one slipped by my radar, but I was pleasantly surprised when I tried it out. The flying places itself nicely between arcady flyers such as Ace Combat and more advanced games such as the IL2 series. Although not required, a decent joystick setup makes this game a joy to fly, and it even supports TrackIR for those who are serious about their flight simulators (Oculus Rift support was added recently as well).
The aerial combat is reasonably plausible, and a working knowledge of advanced combat maneuvers will come in handy as the AI seems to be subject to the same rules of physics as the player. The storyline gives a bit of background to the fuss and although not perfect, it does the job reasonably well.
The missions are varied and there are actually some flying challenges in there (tricky landings) that is fun to pull off. The views are almost on par with what one would expect from a flightsim, and I primarly fly from the cockpit view with TrackIR. BOMB reminds a lot of the old Microsoft title Crimson Skies, and although this is a much smaller developer, the visuals are very pleasing and very functional.
If you are not into flying games or flight simulators this game is probably not for you, but I can highly recommend this to any flightsimmer that enjoys "seat-of-pants" flying. I really hope the game does well and that the developer has a passion for this type of game. With the current graphics engine and development skills, if applied correctly, this is perhaps an outfit that can bring us the next iteration of Origin's Strike Commander (one can dream, right?). Good luck to La Moustace Studio!

Playing Far Cry 2 - with the intent to finish it - is a chore at best.
While there are several positives about the game (all of which can be counted on two-hands' worth of fingers), the negatives of this game greatly diminish any ounce of joy that might have arisen from the game - it just had to be done right, and it really wasn't. To be clear, no game is perfect; I have played more video games than I care to count (and always play to completion), and the first thing I noticed about this game is that the terrible things about Far Cry that seem to sap away all fun and happiness are simple, blatant, obvious mistakes that are the result of poor attention to any detail regarding the game beyond the surface value. If you have ever attempted to try a new candy based solely on the look of the wrapper and the candy's name, and then tasted it only to find that it is terrible in every way yet you finish it simply because you bought it and don't want to waste the money you spent, then you know what it feels like to buy and play and (possibly) finish Far Cry 2.
There are several things I'll talk about in detail (which I don't do often with my reviews) but my demeaning temperment toward FC2 should be justified. The aforementioned topics will be as follows: gameplay, story, graphics and atmosphere, and replayability.
GAMEPLAY: I like to sum it up in one word: redundnant. Far Cry 2's most significant weakness is that the entirety of the game is the EXACT...SAME.....THING! And no I don't mean in the sense of a Tom Clancy game where it's "repetitive" because you found an easy way to beat missions with ease [See bottom of review to see what I am talking about] but in the sense that the entire game is the exact same style of gameplay whether or not you are doing a mission. This is so much so, that the player constantly is trying to actually AVOID the action, not for the sake of survival, but because the combat in this game is stupid, counter-productive (it is not rewarding whatsoever), and just frustrating. The enemy use rusted, dirty weapons to kill you -
which, by the way, they never jam on the enemy - and their accuracy is incredible. The bad guys can hit you accurately through any object or sprite or terrain that allows bullet penetration. And yes, that includes opaque, solid walls. It also includes those lush, green trees that they are able to hit you through. The AI in FC2 is laughable and even annoying. Oh, I actually mean lack of AI. In Far Cry 2, the redundancy is consistent from the second the game begins all the way to the end. Tactis and general combat approach do not change at all. The only variation is the weapons that are unlocked - and I mean it wholeheartedly when I say that unlocking new weapons and using them is the ONLY satisfaction in all of Far Cry 2. Trust me. There is NO variation regarding the missons as they are all practically the same. None of them are special in the sense that they differ from minute-to-minute interactions with the enemy. In other words, the missons have the exact same tone as the game does when you are not even doing a mission. As far as the terrain goes, the missions are repetitive in that sense because the terrain itself does not vary anywhere past the three "variations"; desert, savannah, and jungle
STORY: Story? What story? Oh, you mean the UFLL and APR fighting each other over a fictional piece of African real estate? Hmm, that actually sounds cool. So in Far Cry 2, let's choose a side! Psyche! It actually doesn't matter who you do missions for because you are no one's side. The story in this game is so outstandingly bland that it actually hurts whenever I get a mission from whichever side because I just really do not care about "who shot who", "who is where", "this guy is here and I want you to kill him because of this...", blah blah blah. The player is in it for the diamonds. Nothing else. The story is not only obsolete the ENTIRE REST OF THE GAME but it simply...does not exist at all. In other more simple terms, outside of the tiny rooms where the only NPC's with names throw diamonds at you so you'll do their dirty work, there is no evidence at all that there is even a story. None. There are subtle "hints" at things (if you are kind enough to credit them as such) but that is simply because you know the boring gist of the game: two African militant organizations want the other dead. What they want, and why? Who knows. The game indicates that some American arms dealer armed both sides for profit and he's wanted. Why he did it? Why he won't kill you - even after blaming you for helping both sides - is a mystery. It seems cool at first that he wants you alive, until he starts to critisize your progress with either faction, which just means that not even the Jackal knows what he wants. In the end, the story is so ridiculously invisible to the game that it makes no difference who you help or how you do it.
(There are a couple missions where you have to "choose" who to kill, and me just not caring or feeling like there would be any consequence to either choice, just go with whatever is more convenient. And of course, it turns out that it really doesn't matter what you choose.)
GRAPHICS and ATMOSPHERE: To the game's credit, Far Cry 2 does actually look really good. The graphics and detail are really pretty and the shading, godreys, mist, fog, and weather (although rare), add to the idea that you are in the wild. Again, this is one of the very few good things about FC2. And of course, there is a dirty side to this seemingly clean penny: the maneuverability in this "open world" game is laughable. FC2 seems to be an open world game, but it is actually incredibly linear. In fact it is so linear that the player's approaches to certain missions based on what you are doing (mainly one of three things: killing someone, blowing something up, or travelling) tend to be the same thing. Think I'm full of it? Try me...no matter what mission you get, if it is in a certain area, you WILL take the SAME ROUTE, probably in the SAME VEHICLE, you will encounter the SAME ENEMY FORCES in the SAME SPOTS, and YOU WILL DO WHATEVER YOU CAN TO AVOID THESE AREAS because the combat with a dumb but dead-accurate AI is so frustrating and a waste of time that it just kills whatever excitement you may have had when the mission started.
(Also, let me just say that I believe wholly that it is absolutely terrible gameplay to think you are adding to the action and danger of a game by allowing the enemies who were just killed by the player to respawn after travelling no more than 20 meters outside of that area. I mean, literally clearing an outpost top to bottom, turning around to hit a safe house in order to utitlize weapons crates or get ammo, and then turn around only to find that the outpost is fully-manned..)
REPLAYABILITY: None. I cannot even argue in favor of PLAYABILITY. If you ever happen to finish the game, never play it again.
RATINGS
STORY: 10/100
GAMEPLAY: 45/100
ATMOSPHERE/GRAPHICS: 65/100
MECHANICS: 40/100
GENRE SIGNIFICANCE: 35/100
OVERALL: 40/100
(Note: "Redundancy referring to 'Tom Clancy games' - Example:  in Splinter Cell 1, turn off light and sneak up on guard as he turns it on, grab player, repeat. Throw object, sneak up on enemy and grab as he stupidly investigates the noise in complete darkness. In Splinter Cell 3,  whistle then circumnavigate to grab enemy and knock him out in the shadows. This type of repetition is called "consistency", and it is the result of creating the same mission without changing the gameplay tone or tactics behind the progression. The missions DO change in these types of games and the environment in which they are completed changes, allowing for easy identification and differentiation when addressing the game. Players may also approach various missions based on the environment.)

It's been a lot of years since I've bought and played it but, surprisingly, it only gets better with time.
Sure, there are both pros and cons but getting it all together - the cons are not that bad.
First of all, the concept of open world is simple and it's working just as it should: you have a big map - you explore it pretty much as you wish with little restrictions. And what is even better - as soon as you start to get bored with the first map - the second one comes right away offering ne possibilities!
Second one - the gameplay. It's...complicated. Constantly respawning enemies that are enemies just to you and cannot fight between themselves is sometimes not okay but maybe it was just a bit difficult to get working at that time, I have no idea. All in all - just adds up some anarchist chaos as a part of "wild" Africa ( at least for me ).
Third - weapons. There are a lot, pretty much all of them can be put to good use, they are fun and number of different combinations is huge. It would actually be better to spend a few hours "grinding" some diamonds for guns and gear but it will definitey be worth it ( equipping two separate grenade launchers and a rocket launcher with loads of spare ammo just cannot be boring, heh ). Just FYI, better google the diamond maps to ease the process and get to the fun part quicker.
Fourth - graphics. Surprisingly, it has aged very well and even by the end of 2017 you cannot say that it looks bad. It is definitely more than decent. And will say no more as this can be a forever-long discussion.
So, to wrap this up - game is more than good, worth the time and money and can provide you with lots of fun. Try it out to see how it was like in 2007 if you haven't caght the time or just simply forgot about it. It is realy cheap now, especially with the constant sales, so shouldn't be that much of a burden to your wallet.
P.S.: not touching the storyline or multiplayer parts as those are, well, not very important.

I am recommending this game... but only barely.
I like word games. I especially like unorthodox word games. Lexica is a great idea for a word game. It creates some very interesting puzzles.
However, there is one caveat. I'm of the opinion that the puzzle should be "how do I slide these letters to make criss-crossing words", not "how good am I at remembering obscure words that I'd only ever use in Scrabble". For example, the first puzzle in the "Hard" category used the word "AWN". Are you familiar with this word? I sure wasn't. I had to look it up. It's a slender bristle that is a part of certain grasses.  Yeah, so obvious, right?
If you're okay being frustrated with the occasional obscure word to enjoy the clever puzzle, then this game is for you. If you needed a dictionary to look up "caveat", you'll probably be pulling your hair out with this one.

This game is a decent idea but has a large flaw. Here is why the game doesn't work.
The puzzles are designed on giving you an easy letter placement early on and using logic to attempt to solve the rest of it. The problem comes when they throw in an obscure word. If you don't know one of the words in the puzzle, you will never think of it as the proper solution and you can't use it as context to figure out the rest of the puzzle aside from trial and error.
Example: One of the easy packs started off by giving you an easy tile lay of "X". It ended a 4 letter word. I could not figure out the 4 letter word that it made. I attempted to solve the rest of the puzzle first by trial and error, and this would have been extremely tedious if I was on a harder difficulty. I first encountered an early build of Inversus at Bit Bash 2015, and was instantly impressed. At the time, there was just multiplayer mode and only about 7 or so stages, but it was already apparent that this was something special. The core mechanics were quite simple, but allowed for impressive strategic depth, intertwining shooting with territory control. Think Othello mixed with a competitive top-down shooter.
Since then, the developer has added about another 20 multiplayer stages, online play, a single-player arcade mode with 7 stages, and numerous unlockables, turning what was a promising demo into a quite compelling game.
Unfortunately, matchmaking appears quite sparse at the moment, but if you have friends to play with, Inversus comes highly recommended.

Inversus is a fantastic combination of deceptively simple gameplay with great strategic depth. I'm a big Geometry Wars fan, and this game doesn't feel like a replacement or a successor so much as a competitive compliment. There are two modes: verus and arcade. Arcade has you unlock levels one at a time, which is sometimes necessary for some of the more brain-bending levels, but just a little bit slower than I'd like. Versus is where the game really shines, though, if you can find a match.
There are some maps in Inversus that wrap around themselves, so your ship and enemy ships are repeated throughout the screen. This is a very interesting aspect of the game and adds a lot of strategic depth. You may be focused on your ship on one side of the screen, but since the level might wrap around, an enemy could fire and have the bullet hit you from where you weren't looking. In versus mode especially, this builds into a large element of mindgames, positioning and fighting for the timing of powerups.
When I have been able to connect to a match online, it's been very fun. The netcode is superb, everything is quite responsive, the gameplay is quick but very thoughtful. The only issue is that no one seems to be playing it online. The game works just as well as a multiplayer couch game, though.
The game has a lot of promise and is immensely fun to play with others. I feel like the full game price is worth the quality of the gameplay, but some frugal players might be turned away until a sale.

I can't  help but feel disappointed in samurai_jazz. The game starts out strong with an 8-bit film noir meets samurai art style and jazzy soundtrack that work well together to create an atmospheric vibe few games manage to pull off. The game's "tutorial" is comprised of a few of short messages graphitied on the walls and sides of buildings, and after learning the basic moveset I felt as though the combat system, which depends on proper positioning and timing, was both complex and deep.
Unfortunately, player mobility is poorly implemented in this game. Getting the player character into the right position and facing the right direction is no easy task, and since combat relys so heavily on player position and facing - you can only attack or block in the direction you are facing - the hampered mobility lead to a number of deaths that felt more like the game's fault than my own.
To add insult to injury, not only are samurai_jazz's enemies more mobile than the player, easily able to flank the player when engaging with multiple enemies, but the game's enemy placement seems to be designed around the player's hampered movement. I lost count of the number of times I entered a room only to be immediately ambushed by 3 or more enemies moving in from different directions, often with my character facing away from all of them and open to attack. If I moved to block or attack one of them, the other two would attack from the sides and kill me. More often than not, the solution to one of these ambushes was to run around avoiding the enemies until I could get into a more favorable position.
Many of the reviews here speak of the game's "challenge," but since the game's challenge depends on enemy placement and the player's hampered mobility, samurai_jazz feels less like a skill based game than a luck based one. The afforementioned entryway ambushes comprize most of the game's difficulty, but after they are taken care of, clearing out the remaining enemies in a room is fairly trivial as most of them attack one or two at a time, coming from the same direction, which makes them easy to block or kill.
The game's story is also lacking. The opening scene shows a samurai comitting harakiri (ritual suicide), after which the player character awakens from sleep. Given the film noir atmosphere, I expected to learn why this samurai decided to kill himself through the course of the game. Instead I was treated to a series of MacGuffin hunts straight out of a point and click adventure game, where I fetched cigarettes and bubble gum for strangers so they could let me pass through to the next alleyway. Why I wanted to get to the next allyway, I don't know. The game never bothers telling you why you're doing what you're doing.
The "story" culminates in an ending that has me thinking that this entire game was a troll. The ending felt as though the developer was brandishing a middle finger squarly in the face of any players masochistic enough to make their way through to the end of samurai_jazz. After all those BS deaths, hours spent wrestling with the controlls, and having to fetch cigarettes for the umpteenth time, the developers still manage to shout one last "FU" to the play at the very end. I won't spoil it for you, but someone posted a video of it if you're interested and want to save yourself a few hours of playing a bad game.

This is one of the worst games I've recently played. On almost every level is does something very obviously wrong!
I had my eye on Blaze Epic for a while, seeing that he released quite a lot of games following a similar vibe. I was interested, so I recently bought them all in a bundle. I started from the beginning: samurai_jazz.
The concept is appealing to me. It reminds of older animes like Cowboy Bebop, marked the its jazz soundtrack and a very distinct "samurai" character. So yeah, I was eager to try it!
Unfortunately, it is very, VERY primitive, and has some issues that just show how amateur the developer was -- and hurts the game a lot.
I didn't finish the game. I pulled my way through the first 3 chapters, but quit at the 4th (out of five) out of principle. I'll get into it later.
It follows many oldschool approaches: respawning enemies when you leave rooms, very basic controls, small levels/rooms, etc.
The enemies also have distinct patterns of attack, and they're easily identifiable, which is good.
The first thing that's awful is how the game controls. Dear God... Everything is so sticky!
For example, when you collide with something, you can move. You need to stop pressing everything, and then move only in the opposite direction. You know, in a standard game, if you moved diagonally against a vertical wall, the character should still be able to slide up/down the wall, right? In a way, going around the obstacle. I hope the point is clear. In this game, you're just stuck. It's infuriating, and one of the most basic movement concepts one should learn...
Then, there's the restart. When you die, you usually restart right at the top of the room. The problem is this -- you need to press a button to restart. Then, you need to press whatever button again to start moving. It's a big freakin' deal, since enemies are always very close to you. The game doesn't register is a button is
, only if it was pressed at that moment. It would be good, for example, if I pressed the right arrow to restart, and the character moved to the right when the game began. Nope. It's a big annoyance, believe me.
As I mentioned, enemies start very close to you. They also 1 hit you. And they're also grouped in a very punishing manner, often makign death unavoidable until you managed to get them stuck.
I don't want to go in detail into the combat. It is fairly cool, though. It's about having a stance to defend while you're standing still, and attacking when the time is right. Positioning is also important. But, since the controls are awful, I couldn't enjoy it at all.
I didn't enjoy the music, and graphically, it isn't anything good either. It's bland and not polished at all.
The story could be good, as the game goes for an interestingly cinematic style, especially in its framing. I like what it's trying to do. On the other hand, the whole game consists of getting "bubble gum" and "cigarettes" to random guys for them to let you pass. This, after you slaughter about 50 of them. But these, for some reason, you don't... Not welcome.
Finally, the level design. This is was made me quit. Every level is just a big trap to keep you going. It's the whole "time for money" deal. The levels are designed in the worst way possible. You backtrack constantly, through room after room of respawnable enemies... And the combat is incredibly fragile, leading to immense frustrating.
This isn't all, though. The game has some sections reliant on you getting through spike that go up and down. The player has to find the safe place to stand. Cool. Except -- oh, wait, there are invisible traps! Restart...
Wait, wait, one final thing. This is where I quite, this is good. There's a room full of enemies, with 3 switches. After you kill all of the enemies (after several restarts), you press a switch. Oops, spikes come from below you, dead! Restart the room full of enemies. What happened? Oh, yeah, you need to choose the correct switch not to die. They're all identical, so good luck.
It's pure trial and error in the worst way possible. I didn't find it fun in any way.
So there you go. This is one of the most frustrated reviews I've written, I hope it reflects what kind of game it is.
Hopefully, his other games are better than this! I'm not that eager anymore, though...

Pros
-Story grounded in realism unlike future titles
-Realistic game mechanics implemented to add tension and spice up gameplay
-Typical expansive landscape looking stunning for its time and still holding up now
-Interesting dynamic array of missions and side mission, nowhere as near generic ubisoft copy and paste missions as future titles and other ubisoft games
-Personally I find the gameplay hard but rewarding however this depends on whether you like a challenge
Cons
-AI is very dumb and generally at times tend to rush you giving you little sense of strategy
-Stealth system exists but is not as refined as Far Cry 3 and without alot of time put into the game knowing whether you're going to be detected amounts to guessing
-Lack of customisability for your weapons
-Fast travel exists but is nowhere near as prevalent as it should be. If fast travel existed from safehouse to safehouse then i'd have no problem however the bus system makes it pointless at times
-The revive system is an interesting concept but it does not work well and at times results in death rendering it pointless
-No skill tree leading to no personal development and so no incentive to do missions outside of the main story
Verdict:
Despite its flaws this is my favourite far cry game due to its grounding in reality. And though unrefined it still has that fun far cry gameplay that keeps me playing the new titles. I find it heartbreaking that they took a departure from this gritty realistic themed FPS and made it less serious and more of a rambo fantasy simulator. I accept that the newer games refinded the gameplay of Far cry to perfection however on the way they dropped some quirky but interesting mechanics because they were too much of a departure from the norm. If there was ever a remake that i want it would be this game. Same story same missions. However More weapons, weapon customisability, a skill tree and XP, the modern far cry stealth mechanics, the modern fast travel system. I personally wouldn't even mind the revive system still being in the game. I think to fix it you'd have to be pulled away to a location in which it is certain that you aren't in combat and not too far away. Then when you go back into the area the guards could be on alert but not directly engaging you yet.
TLDR
Best Far Cry IMO Some mechanics underdeveloped however still great game
Rating: 8/10  but 10/10 if i got that remake

If you get stuck, here's some things that I used to quickly get through potentially frustrating things.
-Doing the B version of missions, the buddy option, upgrades your save huts. Do them until you get a car with a machine gun on the roof. Don't do the B missions after for speed.
-When you know a checkpoint is coming check the map to see what direction you want to go and then drive straight through the checkpoints without stopping, no fighting. They will follow you a lot but not always. Drive some ways away and get on the mounted gun and mow them down from a distance.
-Shut off your headlights at night. It took me a while to know this was possible.
-Don't do any malaria runs until your last pill is gone. When you have none left your next mission is for pills. It didn't really cause me much bother.
-Don't hunt for diamonds. Pick your weapons ahead of time and mission rewards will give you enough payment for the main guns you need and then some extra.
-Bases that aren't part of missions will be later, so don't bother clearing them until the game directs you to.
Doing these things, I played a mainline run through FC2 in 16 hours.  If you are enjoying yourself, hunting for diamonds is pretty fun and you can earn all the guns to try different play-styles.  The B version of missions lets you see more of the forts and bases in the world, so if you want more places to explore while moving the story forward take those options.

This is a story for massive manly men who like nothing more than drinking beer and shagging all those there birds… that is to say there barely is a story…
You are an undercover CIA operative sent into a war-torn state in Africa to kill “The Jackal”, a legendary arms dealer currently supplying arms and ammunition to two warring factions whom will stop at nothing to bring this nation into their ideals.
To get to “The Jackal” you must basically do a tonne of random jobs until you can finally confront him… that’s it… so if you’re here for story then… :/
Since the story’s basically non-existent let’s judge it on its gameplay. This is a game with a brutal world where very nearly everyone will stop at nothing to remorselessly hound you to your demise. Your weapons can backfire, jam, break; your friends can permanently die, or go missing with no way of finding them; even if you decide to help a faction its members will still shoot you on sight… oh, and you’re also slowly dying from malaria and will need to constantly keep medication handy.
This is a game with an incredible survivalist feel, like Rambo but without being impervious to bullets… you’re impervious to nothing in this game.
One last note; this game is very immersive and organic, no pre-animated take downs, no railroading you into playing it one way. If you want to attack a village full of enemy combatants for example you simply have a decent number of tools and your own imagination to develop your own strategies.

To first word that pops up in my mind when thinking of Far Cry 2 is: pain. And oh boy... you're in for a world of pain. Not the kind that makes you want to gouge your eyes out because of all the unfathomable, unbelieveable over-the-top immerssion breaking design horrors you witnessed, but the good kind of pain. The kind that makes you proud to have achieved something. Or was it something? Even surviving can feel like an achievement in this game. You know the story: you get dumped into the mids of an Unnamed African Country gone haywire. You struggle to get your first gun, just for it to explode in your hands in the middle of an intense firefight. You struggle to get to safety, only to get a fit of malaria and from then onwards it all goes FUBAR for you. Perhaps you manage to survive. Perhaps your buddy saves you, before he catches a bullet and does the dirt nap. Most likely, however, you will die.
This game will punish you even when you're not messing up. And I love it. The Unnamed African Country is still one of the best settings created for a first person shooter, and it's a world that actually entices you to explore every nook and cranny. I wish there were more games featuring this setting. Alas... Far Cry 2 was also one of the first games that actually made me care whether my buddies survived (usually they didn't). The buddy system was a pretty neat way to give you a second try if your tactic didn't work out. And in Far Cry 2 a lot of your tactics will go south.
Sure the mechanics in this game are a bit dated for todays standards: checkpoints will respawn with enemies the moment you turn your back to them (there is a lot of checkpoints), the a.i. is pretty dumb (360 noscoping you one moment, oblivious to you the other moment), malaria is juist a nuisance and the ending might feel a bit rushed. But I'm willing to forgive Far Cry all those flaws, because between those few flaws the action and the immersion kicks♥♥♥♥♥ There is just no feeling like watching your perfectly staged ambush turn out exactly right—probably, because usually they don't work out that well.
Far Cry 2 is a game that turns boys into men and as such it is a true gem. An unpolished blood diamond, but a gem nontheless.

I bet this game could be better, but it just feels incomplete. I am going to list the problems with the game, in hopes you can decide if you want to buy the game yourself.
The amount of content (or lack thereof) should make this game about $9, give or take, but currently the game is at $16.99. If you are going to buy this game, I suggest you buy it on sale, or spend your money elsewhere. If you are concerned with my game hours (or lack thereof), I have played and have completed the Junk Jack X mobile app, and while playing the steam version, have noticed the same issues. But, the (Apple) app is priced at $4.99 (Google play is priced at $6.99), while the steam is more then 3x that price, and no additional content worth that price.
The combat in this game feels vary clunky. I think they were going for a sort of Minecrafty sort of approach where they only made combat half decent, to not distract the player form the main game, but to be used as a sort of novelty. The problem with the "novelty combat" approach is how it deals with armor and tools:
Similar to the weapons and the armor (I can see a pattern growing), the monsters have lots of variety, but unlike the weapons, the monsters can significant differences depending on the type and the planet they are from. But some (and the game itself) may argue that the point of the game is building, Mining, taming etc, so let's talk about that.
The biggest problem with building is how your character is 1 block tall. In other sandbox games, they have the character 2, 3, and even 4 blocks tall, but in Junk Jack, they decided to shake things up (and not in a good way). The taller the character, the more detail you can fit in a small space, allowing more creative freedom, but in Junk Jack, the character’s shortness makes detailed builds massive in comparison, encouraging ether massive, unwieldy builds, or small, boring builds. It is also annoying how there are lots of furniture that you may find underground, but when you break them, no item drops. This is unfortunate, because if they were obtainable, or they became craftable, you could have much more detailed and creative builds.
Arguably the best thing Junk Jack is the Mining. Each planet has different caves and ores to mine, and the micro-biomes and buildings can be a breath of fresh air. The variety of mobs truly shines in the caves, and it is cool to find the monsters matching with the surrounding environment. Your character being one block tall is perfect for easy and non-tedious mining (Which I think was the reason they did it in the first place). Overall, I think mining was (and should be) the focus of the game, but they later decided to say the game's focus was building for some reason.

Other that that, well, that’s it. I hope in the future, they add more use for tamed animals, but in the meantime, there not that useful.
Junk Jack’s platforming is one of the worst offenders. The character is too slow, and falls so fast, that it feels awkward, like the gravity is super strong, but you can still jump high. The character sticks to ladders like super-glue, and the speed that you fall in water, and the slowness you swim, makes you feel like a rock. It’s nice that you don’t skid on surfaces, and fall of ladders, but I think they overdid it.
Junk Jack has 12 different planets, each having their own ores, biomes, flora, fauna, blocks, backgrounds, and more. The planets are the biggest breath of fresh air, because there is both quantity and quality, the glorious balance that Junk Jack has so much trouble dealing with. To get to a portal, you need to go to hell and back and waste hours searching for just
of THREE portal pieces required to go to the next progression phase (not to mention how the dam portal doesn’t even look good). Some planets have special weather, but they don't affect the player, except for the acid rain of Xeno. It is also important to mention how each world is procedurally generated, but there are almost never any landmarks, mountains, or monuments to remember, so if you make two of the same planet, they will look the same.

Sure, there's "Lots of loot to collect!" but most of it is ether meaningless, too tedious to collect to be useful, or Just filler. INVERSUS feels like the marriage of Geometry Wars and Othello/Reversi. Originally forming out of a game jam, it's concept is super simple to understand but quickly gets hard to master and it provides all the basis for an addictive score attack title.
The concept is simple. You're a square that's trying to take out other squares, which have varying behaviours and capabilities. Some will try to swarm you, others will shoot at you, some have shields. You have limited ammo that charges over time, plus you can also pick up a certain amount of it from enemies you've taken out. You can only travel on white squares and shooting black squares will turn them white and the enemies can turn them black. You can only shoot in four directions but you can charge a shot that will shoot out on three rows instead of one. If you take out enemies that are close to each other, they will cause a chain explosion that will give you more points, plus there's a multiplier that increases over time. If you're really good, you can also disrupt or even parry shots from enemies back towards them. All of this is done in the interest of score.
The arcade mode can be played alone or with another local player in co-op. There's also a local or online competitive mode where you are aiming to take out the other player in a duel, alone or in teams. The online play actually works quite well but unfortunately, when I researched this, there were very few people playing online and it was hard to find a match. However, you can play single player arcade mode while waiting which is a very nice touch. There are a handful of arcade and competitive levels that you unlock over time, plus there's a progression system that can get you other cosmetic unlocks as well.
INVERSUS has a simple but effective art style and a great, beaty electronic soundtrack that helps keep you pumped as you play. There's also no load times and it's quick to get into a game and to start a new one after a game over.
INVERSUS is designed to be played repeatedly and I can certainly see myself doing that. I think a lot of people are going to find the $15 price point a bit steep given the limited numbers of levels and (at least at time of writing), almost non-existent online player base. I can certainly appreciate that but even if I hadn't gotten review code for this, I would have gotten $15 of fun out of it, especially if I got some local players together. I'm a sucker for a good score attack though. INVERSUS is a really cool idea that could maybe use a touch more content but is a great new spin on a tried and tested idea that I enjoy.

This game is superb if you belong to the group of people who are looking for games that are experiences far away from the mainstream. This game certainly belongs in that group.
The core mechanic of this game is a sound recorder that picks up on voices from the other side. When you talk to these voices the recordings need to be analyzed and played forwards and backwards at different speeds. Only that way can you understand what a spirit is trying to tell you. This way you will also piece together the mystery of the pace you are exploring. It's a very unique gameplay mechanic and lends itself to a lot of interesting plot development.
It is created by basically one person alone so please keep that in mind and maaaaybe try the demo first?
Because of this a few things might throw you off. First and foremost - the graphics. This game looks like a PS2 game. And not a good one at that. Keeping in mind, though, how much content there is in the final product that is still impressive. The controls are very basic as well. The game basically uses Unity's standard FPS controller in the first iteration - which means no headbobbing, running or ducking. Or in other words: controls are not bad but feel a little like wolfenstein. From 1992. Sounds can sometimes also be a little repetetive. But look beyond that and you get a psychological horror experience that is eerie, chilling and creates atmosphere without ever falling back into cheap scares.
The best I can compare it to is finding and reading an independent comic by a local artist. Someone who self-publishes only a very small amount of his comics  and sells most of it on conventions, local comicbook stores or his own website. That small thing that would not be picked up by a large publisher which still ends up the thing that you read and fall in love with for all the right reasons despite not being printed in fukll color or on glossy paper.
The game certainly is very rough around the edges and definetely not for mainstream players BUT If you are the kind of person who can appreciate a rough gem with atmosphere over the usual jumpscares: What are you waiting for?

Sylvio is a game that tries to cover a lot of bases. However this does lead to a game that comes with some issues as a result of this. So It has point and click, fps, open world exploration and jumping puzzles. And of course the EVP mechanic in which you use a tape recorder to decode messages from the dead. The game also deos not do much in the way of hand holding either.
However it is fair to say that other than the EVP mechanic, the other elements are somewhat rough around the egdes. And there is also some bugs and glitches thrown in as well. For example the shooting mechanic is over complicated with two tyoes of ammo, but no way to switch directly between them, as well as the pressure in your gun effecting its range and accuracy. Add to that even when you get a clear hit on your target, the game may not register the hit.
Jumping can be floaty and impresice, and sometimes you can jump into areas that will freeze your character in place forcing you to restart.
On the plus side, the game is a decent length, the EVP mechanic interesting and the voice acting and audio in general is good. So all in all this is really a diamond in the rough. However it will not be for everyone, and if you like a more polished experience then look elsewhere.

This is a rare kind of horror game which manages to be really unsettling without resorting to any jump scares.
You walk an abandoned family park and record ghost voices, then analyse these recordings in search for any clues. You do it by playing the recording slower, faster, backwards etc. It's an interesting and unique mechanics - and certainly a very strong point of this game. The recordings might seem random and chaotic at first, but fortunately you can return to your notes later (no need to listen to them all again - good!) and a bigger, unnerving picture starts to emerge.
Sylvio is also a very crude game in places: it has some collision problems, very uneven visuals (ranging from average to very bad). To make things worse, it employs a "videogame-logic" to many puzzles, forces you to go through a few abysmal jumping-and-walking-on-ledges puzzles.
Be prepared to persevere through these, but don't be turned off! The good things about Sylvio certainly outweigh the bad.
The game is strangely quiet - starting from the protagonist's voice. And by "quiet" I don't mean that there's no sound! The sound part is actually great and builds most of Sylvio's atmosphere. When nobody screams, even a small whisper can make you shiver.
If you like horror games, this one's very unique and strange. I want more games that are so courageous!
And if you don't like horror games, give it a shot as well. Nothing will jump on you nor eat your brains out - and you'll get to uncover an unsettling story.

MoW Face Off XL is a huge leap in multiplayer strategy card games. Players take control of huge armies and super battle powers and must defeat the other in a ruthless one on one match up. Players can build decks carrying the most amazing fantasy armies from all over the world.
This game has a lot of content ready to be won and collected without any waiting time! Gone are the days where an upgrade makes you wait before you use it.
Face Off XL has a rich multiplayer base and the Arena mode stands out in this regard. Players can choose 30 of the most powerful cards irrespective of their ladder position and play in their full skill capacity. Either win 12 games or lose 3, there is a guaranteed reward that helps one in the ladder PvP games.
PvP feature is very efficient in matching up players and completely lets the player depend on the skill and not much on the cards that he or she owns. There is immense content in the game and one can never truly finish the game due to this. The Ladder system has leagues and each league lets players match up to their respective fair opponents.
The community reach is excellent with the developers themselves reaching out constantly to the gamers and trying to improve the game, as well as events to keep the players motivated. There are regular give aways and tournaments one can participate to win good amount of in game rewards.
The Products on sale in the store are very low priced and are extreme value. Especially the special card backs stand out as truly unique artworks. The store lets one purchase more cards and booster packs with in game gold and therefore the game rewards focus on the skills of the player and always get the player try harder to climb the positions.
Overall, March of War Face Off XL and the series, is a great online game for anyone wanting to have great fun in a little time as well as someone who wants to build a brag tower of their skills, the game has something for everyone. The game is constatnly updated and new features and factons or cards are added and threfore the interest of a player is always kept on the edge. The game can also be taken anywhere on a Tab or a phone or even call friends to join steam and recruit them! Face Off is available on Steam, Android and Linux.

Pandora Directive isn't the most beautiful game. It's got clunky controls, and graphics fighting against Namco Museum on my PS1. But it's got one thing that not even modern games have. An immersive story. After about 10 minutes of figuring out the controlls, I was hooked again. I was too young to be able to get past the first few puzzels in 97, but now I can fully understand the complexity of the story and the true power an adventure game has in story telling.
It's a gripping narrative which is not only brooding but overlayed of two seemingly not-crossible genres, noire and science fiction. It gives you exactly what you ask for out of the crossing between the two, and does not dissapoint. Characters, albeit primitive in design, are complex. Characters change when connecting plot points together, something that video games as a whole have not been able to since preserve, which is a major tennant of any American film. It features both conspiracies and science in the same breath, and does not overstep the boundraies of which the game lays. It is firmly rooted and knows what it wants to deliver in terms of story, and does so devistatingly well.
It's never a race of who has the better graphics, but who can convey the best story, and Tex Murphy is top gun in my book.

Samurai_Jazz is an action/adventure beat 'em up heavily inspired by NES games. Way more so than most retro games, in fact, down to the obtuse game design. The game pegs itself as a hack 'n slash noir, and I do love the idea of a noir samurai, but the story is entirely incomprehensible. I'm not meaning to say that it's convoluted, just that it's impossible to actually see. Your character makes vague references on occasion, and at the end of the game you fight an evil version of yourself. There's no direct statement as to what's going on or what you're doing, and it feels like a game poorly translated from another language. I supposed that adds to the retro, though.
The game design fairs a lot better than the narrative, setting up each room of enemies as a puzzle. Which enemy needs taken out first, what's the most efficient way to kill them all without getting cut down yourself? The game forces you to ask these questions the more you get into the game. This is only aided with the game's block mechanic, which allows you to strafe and parry at the cost of your movement speed. Combat requires immensely fast reflexes and an analytical mind. You will die, a lot.
The design also suffers from some noticeable setbacks, however, such as an inconsitent design for the most basic enemy: the samurai. They sometimes block your attacks, and sometimes don't. There's no rhyme or reason as to when they do block, and I've tried relentlessly to find an exploit. The only safe means to attack them appears to be parrying back and forth until they give in, but this isn't ideal when many of the rooms require you to destroy samurai quickly, lest you be destroyed by other enemies. It's also very easy to exploit the AI's field of vision, allowing you to lure out enemies one at a time, when they're meant to be faced as a group.
Even considering all of that, I think Samurai_Jazz is worth a look, especially considering its price. It nails the retro game feel far better than plenty of other games I've played. I definitely felt like I was sitting down and pouring my afternoon into an old, obtuse NES game, for better or worse.

You can't break a man the way you break a dog, or a horse.
The harder you beat a man, the taller he stands. To break a man's will, to break his spirit, you have to break his mind. Men have this idea that we can fight with dignity, that there's a proper way to kill someone. It's absurd, its anesthetic, we need it to endure the bloody horror of murder. You must destroy that idea. Show them what a messy, terrible, thing it is to kill a man, and then show them that you relish in it. Shoot to wound, and then execute the wounded, burn them, take them in close combat. Destroy their preconceptions of what a man is and you become their personal monster. When they fear you, you become stronger, you become better. But let's never forget, it's a display, it's a posture, like a lions roar, or a gorilla thumping at his chest. If you lose yourself in the display, if you succumb to the horror, then you become the monster. You become reduced, not more than a man, but less.
And it could be fatal.

Word game similar to scrabble, but the tiles are limited to certain locations. You have to figure out how to use all of the tiles to form words (similar to a crossword puzzle in this aspect). Worthwhile purchase in my opinion because word games are great.

There isn't much can be said about the game's visuals asides from that they're simplicity. Pretty much the same thing can be said about the game's audio. The visual and audio can be adjusted in the game's option menu.
There are three different game difficulty modes to choose from: Easy, Medium and Hard.
The game plays like a crossword, sudoku and scrabble puzzles. The goal of this game is to figure out where all the letters fit properly so that they spell out the correct word. This isn't a race against the clock even though there is a timer. It's there to show how long it took to solve the puzzle completely.

I love words, but am often frustrated by word puzzles as they are generally dependant on what is assumed to be common knowledge. With something like a crossword, if you do not know the word you cannot solve the puzzle. Lexica is a bit different because it presents you with all the letters you need to solve for the words. All the information is there; you just need to put it in the right place. Some of the mid-game puzzles I found to be much more difficult to solve than the late-game puzzles. Despite this odd difficuly curve, this is easily the most enjoyable word puzzle I've encountered.
Edit: I started to play this game with others and would sometimes return to my laptop to find several new puzzles completed.

Lexica serves as a fun, challenging, but casual puzzle game. It acts as a practice for scrabble (or crossword puzzles) without any scoring (except the time taken). There is only one correct solution and finding it is done by rearranging letter tiles that either move horizontally or vertically.
When you have an almost correct placement of the letters it sometimes proves frustrating to overcome that mental hurdle and find different words.
My time spent in game is a smidge inflated - I occasionally left the game unattended (even overnight).
Pros
+ Fun, challenging word puzzle game
+ Simple mechanics make it easy to learn
+ Cheap when on sale (less than $1 I think)
Cons
- There doesn't seem to be an easy way to review completed puzzles. Often there is one last word that can be weird that is found by trial-and-error. It would be nice if the game gave you a chance to learn some of these words.
- A hover over definitions of some of the exotic words would be nice.
A great deal when on sale. There should be more SIMPLE and cheap puzzle games on Steam.

INVERSUS
Arcade Singleplayer & Multiplayer
Hypersect
Hypersect
is an arcade singleplayer and multiplayer game developed and published by Hypersect.
The game uses black and white to identify the different blocks and characters. While it looks very simple, the highlight of the game is the design of the areas: the first ones you unlock are very standard, but later on you will also play in arenas where you are reflected multiple times, and this really messes with your mind. It's a simple gimmick that works very well, leading to some very fun fights with your friends since everyone is looking at a different part of the screen.
In Versus mode (which can be played locally or online), there are two teams of either one or two players each: Black and White. The Black team can only move in white squares, and the White team can only move in black squares. To win, you have to hit your opponent once by shooting at him. This is very easy to understand, but very hard to master.
If you want to improve your skills and speed, you can play Arcade mode, where you must survive endless waves or red players who spawn blocks of your different colors.
Arcade mode is very hard, starting out slow with just a few enemies, but quickly speeding things up until you are overwhelmed by them. Since you die in just one hit, playing Versus mode is very intense, however it is always fun and fair.
The techno soundtrack is very good, and the sound effects of the shooting are soft, so they don't annoy you constantly.
The game has high replayability thanks to multiple maps, Steam achievements, and multiplayer. Highly recommended as a party game when you have three friends over.
Overall, if you like simple arcade games to play with friends both locally and offline, I highly recommend you play INVERSUS. The price might be a little too high right now, so I recommend you wait for it to be at 10$ to get your money's worth.

This game is what arcade games strive to be: easy to learn, but difficult to master.  This super simple eight button control setup takes seconds for any veteran game to figure out and even someone new to games should be able to understand it in under a minute.  Four buttons to move, four buttons to shoot.  What could be easier?  While each map starts out nice and easy with some slow enemies that aren't very harmful, the pace picks up fairly quickly, introducing faster and more complicated enemies.  With the chain-combo and hit streak mechanics, this is both a blessing and a curse.  The game rewards you for pulling off risky maneuvers, but itsn't going to hand you lots of  opportunities for easy points.  I keep finding myself backing into a corner trying to lure large groups of basic enemies together to get one large combo just to get hit from behind by a newly-spawned enemy from a spot I just wasn't paying enough attention to.  After that, I have to fight to take back any chunk of the map I can so that I'm not locked into a tiny space and picked off easily by even the most basic enemies.
Playing enough arcade mode on a given map will unlock a new map to enjoy and spice up your experience.  The different shapes and spawn points of the map add a lot of variety to the gameplay, though I doubt anyone has played quite the same game twice on any given map.  There are also two distinct game modes.  You can face off against the waves of computer-controlled enemies or compete in a one-on-one or two-on-two deathmatch to prove who really has the faster reflexes and more refined control.  Of course, we can't forget to mention that you don't have to face the horde alone.  Break out the second controller and bring your friend into the fray with you in local or online co-op arcade mode.
As with any true arcade game, there are leaderboards for each map to see how your skills stack up against the rest with a convenient filter to show either the world rankings or just your friends.  The desire to climb the leaderboard and prove your skill to the world is as strong with this game as any other I've played; perhaps even stronger.  I very strongly considered allowing myself to be late to work because I thought I might be able to beat a score higher than my own.
More important than anything else, though, is that this game is a lot of fun.  What more can you ask for?
The game is really fun and addictive! Definitely a good buy if you like this sort of arcade game. Reminds me of resogun.

Sylvio is probably one of the most creative, atmospheric and underrated horror game that I have played. A unique horror title that follows a different formula, with no cheap tricks or jumpscares. Recording ghosts sounds can be a very tense and rewarding experierence. A must buy for horror game fans.
Also check out the sequel!

TLDR: Sylvio is a diamond in the rough. It successfully manages to separate itself from the plethora of underdeveloped indie horror games on the market. Indeed, it is lacking in the visual department, but it more than makes up for that with it's genuinely innovate gameplay mechanics. If you are looking for a light horror game or some mysterious adventure then you should really give Sylvio a go.
Sylvio is a 1st person horror adevnture game. You are Juliette Waters, exploring a dilapidated family theme park, armed with a microphone and a blunderbuss that can shoot anything you pick off the ground. You can explore the large levels, picking up audio samples with your microphone and decoding them to reveal clues. This is an interesting game progression mechanic that works very well. The levels are large and open ended, and you're sometimes able to drive your car around.
- This is an indie horror game made in Unity, so that may put some people off. Unfortunately the visuals won't do it much justice; the graphics look dated by almost a decade. On the contrary, the game manages to pull off an atmospheric and creepy aesthetic which is enough to immerse you. And since the game is so dark and sombre, the lack of graphical detail isn't a big issue. The lighting with the torch is decent, but just don't expect any dynamic shadows.
- The voice actor for the protagonist is a bit of a mixed bag. While the voice acting quality is alright, it definitely lacks emotion and enthusiasm. One time in the game you suddenly fall through a hole in the ground, which is quite frightful. In response, the protagonst humorously proclaims "I'm not getting back out that way," in a quiet whisper. Every line the protagonist speaks is quiet and sometimes difficult to hear, so thank goodness for subtitles. The music is definitely a positive aspect, and it's got a sort of 80's horror vibe going for it, with nice electric synth sounds.
- This game is certainly very interesting. Each enemy you 'kill' actually helps you progess in the game. Sylvio's staple mecahnic is recording and deciphering audio using the EVP recording equipment. EVP stands for electronic voice phenomena, which are voices of spirits recorded electronically (and there's even
Using the micropone, you can pick up bits of audio after killing the creatures, or just around the place randomly. You can then playback the audio using the EVP to reveal a message, but you will also be able to find hidden messages by playing the audio in reverse and/or at different speeds. After successfully revealing the hidden messages, certain items or locations of interest will be highlighted. This is a really interesting mechanic for a horror game and it works quite well.
For those of you looking for a scary horror game, you may be dissapointed to hear that this game is not very scary, barely at all. The game fits better into the 'adventure' genre, as you will be exploring locations, picking up items and using them to progress. Instead of relying on cheap horror tactics, this game's eeriness and intriguing story is what will be haunting you.
- the story is slow and unravels as you play, and you can find audio tapes that also reveal some lore. The game's story might be slow, but it definitely does not fall into cliché horror tropes. Progressing the story involves holding seances to acquire information, and the EVP equipment can also be used to reveal extra hidden messages.
- The game runs on the Unity engine, which I have had quite a negative experience with. However, this game is indeed very well optimised and I didn't experience any stuttering or framerate drops.
- Sylvio makes some unusual control binding decisions, but it's easy to adapt to and the game is fairly simple overall. Using the EVP equipment is as easy as pressing the arrow keys. However, there is an odd lack of mouse support for the menus, and the in-game help guide is quite awkward to navigate.
- The game isn't really long, and can be completed in under 10 hours. But you'll probably be wanting to come back for more and finding all the secrets and recording every voice, as it's a worthwhile and fun experience.
- None
- The game has received quite a bit of updates, and has even been remastered during it's time on Steam. However, the developer hasn't responded in the forums in over a year.
I would say that if you get this discounted for under $10, then it's a very worthwhile experience for any fans of adventure or horror.
Sylvio is a very unique horror game and I'd definitely recommend it if your even the slightest fan of horror or mystery. It's likely unlike anything you'd ever played before.
I give this game a 7/10 - an innovative indie horror game with lack of polish
