Sure, it's early access - and we make allowances for that, but from a game play viewpoint, the game has the excitement and personality of a wet dishrag.
Its easthetic is well executed and clean, but doesn't deviate from "oh, retro". It doesn't look bad, and you're never confused about things, and the various tilesets are decenty varied and with a clean animation quality, but if you put it against 10 other retro style games I'd be hard pressed to find a something to point out as exceptional about it, its safe and clean in a market saturated with it.
Its randomised levels and rogue like progression are basic and provide very little variety or emergent gameplay besides the basics, and while different mobs spawn everywhere you have no need to adapt or alter your tactics or think ahead... it's all identical "hold down left mouse button and wait"
When most your game consists out of "Hold down LMB and wait" in terms of combat or tactical complexity, in a game where combat is 95% of the gameplay - that is a massive issue and needs to be adressed from the ground up. This games combat, progression and itemisation / character building is so very bland, it might as well not exist.
Which isn't to say this game doesn't have potential, as from a technical perspective this is one of the most stable and technicly competent titles to come into early access in ages. It runs smooth, clean and performs fine.
..It's just that the combat mechanics puts you to sleep.

Guilty Gear Isuka is... difficult to recommend. On one hand, Guilty Gear will always be a great fighting game even with a few detriments, and the soundtrack is arguably worth the price alone. On the other, besides the unique soundtrack, this particular version of Guilty Gear is pretty much pointless to have now that there are others on Steam. It's really just Guilty Gear, with a more novel than truly enjoyable four-player gimmick (that I will admit I never played with four people) that's bogged down by a flawed (though necessary) change, namely the need to press a button to turn around. There is a beat-'em-up styled mode along with it, but again, it feels more novel than fun, never really feeling fleshed out to something good. Even the new characters aren't worth it alone, with A.B.A. being in a standard Guilty Gear game now, and Robo Ky Mk. 2 feeling more like a gimmick than a character. The included soundtrack isn't even the full one, missing songs like A.B.A.'s theme (which is my favorite track, so that's a downer). I just can't recommend it unless you really want all the Guilty Gears on Steam, you don't mind an incomplete soundtrack, and it's on a decent sale. Otherwise, go with one of the X2s that are available, or Xrd -SIGN- now that it's here too.

The biggest problem with Junk Jack is that while the game has much to offer, an enourmitude of it requires hours of play to access yet the play before that is fraught with monotony and simply being basic.
Junk Jack is a Terraria-like 2D sandbox game made by the PixBits, Italian game developers Jacopo Santoni and Silvio Eusebio. Work on the original version of Junk Jack started in Spring of 2011 on mobile, when the PIxBits, having met in Minecraft, decided to work to fix the status quo of what was currently a lack of Minecraft like games on iOS (They didn't learn of Terraria until months later, though the game has taken a fair amount of inspiration from Terraria since then and the steam version has a splash that jokingly refers to the game as "Another Terraria Clone"). It was released on iOS in November 2011, though the initial release was kinda crash-prone. It took them a couple of months and updates to finally bring the game to stability. The original game continued to be updated through February 2013, adding features such as farming and archery to the game. I can state unequivocally that Junk Jack was the best Minecraft-style game on iOS during that time period. In August 2013 they released a sequel, Junk Jack X onto the appstore (ostensibly because they wanted to preserve the ability for low spec iPods and iPhones to play the original game). X added four new planets, water, and revamped graphics. In my opinion Junk Jack(x) still has the best art style in the open world block sandbox genre. Updates since then to the game have added seven more planets, a plant splicing system, a complex potion brewing system, and an electronics/wiring system, among other things, and the game remains the best sandbox game on iOS, mainly due to it having been designed for mobile and thus avoiding the clunkyness of Terraria iOS. (As an aside, though there is no crossplatform play, you can transfer worlds from iOS to PC and visa versa if you have the know-how)
This version of Junk Jack suffers from two broad problems: this is a pc port of an ios game, and the game takes hours of play to really get into.
The first part renders the game worse to play than the iOS version. Essentially, the controls have been Terraria'ized. That's good. The combat system has however been overhauled, for the worse in my opinion. On iOS, you tap on enemies within range to kill them. Swords don't need to make contact with the enemy or anything. On PC, like Terraria, melee weapons must make contact with the enemy to do damage. Keep in mind that blocks in Junk Jack are very large (character is less than one block large, compared to two blocks wide and three blocks tall in Terraria) and enemies are small relative to blocks when compared to Terraria. This makes killing enemies without taking damage very, very difficult. To worsen things, in order to get much in the way of good loot you need to have your game difficulty turned up, which makes the game even more difficult to play. While this doesn't positively impact planet progression, it does slow down the game. The other problem from iOS is that this game was clearly made for iOS. The blocks are beautiful, but they're also large, which can have other problems in addition to its implications in combat. You may find it harder to build because each block takes up so much space.
(I should get this out of the way now, the way planet progression works is that there's five tiers of planets. On each tier, you can find chests containing portal pieces to worlds on the next tier; assemble 3 of them in a triangle to create a portal)
The other problem is that the game takes a long time to get into. The first planet, Terra, is by far the most boring, and ores are fairly rare on it, ostensibly for game balance to make the other planets worthwhile. The next set of planets isn't very vibrant, containing an egyptian themed world and a graveyard themed world. Thus, it isn't until the third tier of worlds and at a minimum 3 hours of gameplay and most probably more that you really get some interesting vibrant worlds (and tools that aren't bad; later planets have better ores). Other mechanics are similarly locked away. The most egregious is probably the electronic wiring system, which requires getting to a very specific 5th tier world Lilith in order to access, which takes at a minimum 10 hours of gameplay and probably more.
In terms of content, the game has it in droves. 12 planets, dozens of different plants, animals, enemies, blocks, etc. Looking at fishing alone, there are something like 120 different cosmetic fish for you to find and store in an aquarium or whatever you choose to do with them. There could be something to be said in terms of quality over quantity here; those 120 fish are all well and good (and the graphics artist isn't very much involved in the actual game features anyway so they can be cranked out) but the core gameplay of the game itself leaves something to be desired so those fish aren't doing all that much for the gameplay.
Where Junk Jack really shines is in the building department. The immense quantity of options means that you have tremendous freedom in customizing the look of your place; since you have upwards of 12 planets to choose from once you've unlocked them all you even have a lot of choice in the backdrop to your place. The art style of the game is absolutely gorgeous; I don't see how one could criticize the game here. If you like to build, then Junk Jack is the game for you.
The 12 planets also give the game a lot of content in the exploration aspect, although this is marred by the combat system making exploration with meaningful opposition frustrating.
As a note, some have complained that you can't use the portals to other worlds in multiplayer; this is half true. You can't use portals while another player is in your world, but there's nothing stopping them from exiting, waiting for you to enter the portal, and re-entering into the new world.
The game's tutorial is all text and image based, and while comprehensive, it probably puts too much faith in the patience of gamers. If you have any questions, hit up the unoffical Junk Jack discord here:
In summary, Junk Jack is a quality, if somewhat flawed game. It is unsurpassed in the art department, and is excellent for building and decent for exploration, marred by a poor combat system and some giveaways of its heritage as an iOS game. If looking for action and combat, Terraria is a better game than this. If exploring new worlds and building grand structures is more your forte, then Junk Jack will fit your needs fine.
In the interest of transparency, I am a moderator on the official Junk Jack forums and the administrator of the unofficial discord server linked above, and participated in the beta tests for Junk Jack X on iOS and the steam version of Junk Jack on here, which is how I got the steam version for free. Nonetheless I have tried my best to be objective and fair in this review.

I hope future iterations will also have it. Even if I have to pay an extra fee.
> Fill tool has fill canvas, alpha and its invert version. I haven't seen any option to manually fill specific parts of the layer only (For example, if I have a lineart where I want the top to be orange and the bottom to be be blue outlines like other art programs). I'm assuming it's not in.
Now that I have said all my gripes I will now spaz out as to why this program has so much promise and why I want to recommend it.
> The UI feels soooo good to draw in. It's also so nice to navigate. It is unnatural at first but it's easily fixable. The UI is also dockable and adjustable so I can do whatever workspace I want in it.
> All Basic shape options are in. That's good!
> The default brushes themselves are nice, especially when pen tips are all the types I like as well. I have no complaints. Especially when used with the Controller Editor. The ability to use gradient as a brush color is a super nice touch as well. The brush blending options (Normal, Multiply, Additive and Subtract) are a nice welcome. Now all I need is Color Dodge and my life is complete haha.
> The Controller Editor is unique and fun to use. It's almost like designed for a game engine, Adobe After Effects or Toon Boom's animation options that I'm super familiar with. I still have to create more brushes but so far I am liking it and I think it's easily one of the strengths of the program.
> The line options. Making background layouts in this program fits my workflow much better. Shift using a brush is great because it shows a wheel to show what angle you are in and helps me alot to be accurate. My space perception is horrible so this helps me a LOT. It also can be adjusted to detect pressure sensitivity or static. This is great.
> The Smoothing. I never liked using these because I am confident of with my strokes, but the way the smoothing actually helps me and doesn't feel intrusive is great. Especially the way it adjusts. It's like a better version of Flash curved line.
> The ability to put an image for referencing/tracing over sketches without having to add a new layer is GREAT. I love it. Thank you for that :)
Do I recommend this? Well it depends.
Personally, I don't see this working for any final work. I recommend it for experimental sketching or concepts. It's fun to use, great feel and has enough tools. However, compared to Photoshop especially it's blending layers, it might be lacking. Especially if you're the type to put in pictures and abuse its blending modes to get an idea for a compositional piece. The lack of documentation is very offputting but if you're used to tinkering other softwares, this isn't going to be hard to understand.
But yes, I do recommend it. I can't wait for future updates and a better documentation. I will adjust this review if an update happens.

This game was provided to me by the developer. When I first read about it I was super excited, boy was I disappointed.
Now, let's not get this confused; this game has a TON of potential. The atmosphere and setting are on point. I am not a big jump scare person, not that I don't like them, they just do almost nothing for me. If a game is to get under my skin, it's going to do it with sound. This game has that nailed. The random heavy breathing, the eerie talking, all the subtle sounds are incredible and unnerving. So well done.
Where the game fell flat for me was in the gameplay itself. Moving was often sluggish feeling, almost laggy. My computer can run a lot of games at the highest of graphical settings so there was no reason for this. When I sprinted the game felt fine, but the walking was just .... I don't know, muddy? Also, there were challenges that I had no idea why I was even doing them. They were just there, so I started doing them.. without any direction from the game or any feedback that I was doing exactly what I needed to. These things need to be sorted out.
Now.... let's talk about the main procrastinator. The "monster". Interesting design, though not frightening at all. Is he supposed to be as unintelligent as he is? I mean, he is 3 feet over my cover, I can see all of him and he can't see me? And why does he make that noise? It's not scary, it's nearly gratingly annoying.
Like I said, this game has a ton of potential and I'd love to revisit it if these things are ironed out. As it stands right now, I simply have no interest. I hope this gets the fixes it needs.

It's a very unorthadox combination of a crossword puzzle and sudoku.
The reason why I can't recommend it is because of three main things:
1) It uses several word spellings that are rarely seen in the USA (ex: miaow). I think there's a localization issue that needs to be addressed.
2) Several words I've seen aren't completely obvious. I understand that this is a puzzle and it shouldn't be handed to you, but nothing prepared me for some of the solutions, where some words sound like something straight out of a NYT newspaper.
3) Unlike Sudoku, there is no flow to finding a solution - a lot of it is guess and check. Puzzles that have no flow aren't good puzzles - they're guessing machines. In sudoku, there are a few numbers given at the start of a puzzle, and that's what a game like this would have needed to be successful.
There is no wrong game on Steam, but this idea had more potential than what was actually delivered.

First silly question:  Is this a cheap Amnesia: The Dark Descent knock-off?  Yes.  I'm also told that it's a port of a mobile game, renamed for Steam because it originally had the word "Slenderman" in the title (why is anyone's guess, as there's not a Slender in sight).  Next silly question:  Is it anywhere near as GOOD as Amnesia: The Dark Descent?  No.  Of course not, you preposterous excuse for a human being.  The good news, however, is that it's not as bad as it could have been, given what I've just stated.  Alas, this ain't exactly the second coming of Frictional...
Something which this game does a mostly decent job of emulating is Amnesia's ATMOSPHERE.  The visuals are nice enough, all things considered, and the sound is pretty effective apart from the occasional jarring moment of abruptness, when a ghoulie departs the area you're in with all the subtle smoothness of someone pressing the stop button on an old cassette walkman.  There's also some - emphasis on SOME - reasonably half-decent puzzles to be found in the game's three to five hour playing time, and the story is...well, alright, even if the ending brings new meaning and depth to the word "unsatisfying" ("To be continued"...yeah, right, sure...we'll all hold our collective breaths for that one).

So what does the game do not-quite-so-well?  Well, for a "stealth horror" game, the actual stealth mechanics are kinda dodgy to say the least.  Many is the time that I crouched in a corner, with my lantern off, assuming that the ghostie chasing me surely couldn't see me behind this pillar and...nope.  He found me.  See, the early part of the game, at least, works off pre-designated hiding places, clearly indicated to you by a closed eye symbol which appears on-screen, and you just have to trust the logic of said hiding places...even when they seem way more out in the open than other places which would appear, to the logical mind at least, to be more sure-fire safe-spots.  The second half of the game raises the bar of stupidity some more by removing the closed eye symbol altogether, and replacing it with some incomprehensible gobbledygook written on a scroll about hiding in a particular area of the tunnels or some-such...a message which I clearly had little chance of making heads or tails of, given that the only language I'm currently fluent in is English.  (Google Translate really does need to be taken off the internet altogether, as it evidently does more harm than good.)

Then there's the completely illogical back-tracking.  Oh yes, you're gonna love the back-tracking.  Remember the holy water you forgot to pick up in that area way, way back...the area which you've already combed from top-to-bottom five times already?  Nah, me neither.  But there it was, just like the ritual knives I couldn't pick up the first time, and so on and so forth.  I guess it's a "realistic" change from the usual video game antics in which you pick up almost everything in sight, somehow just KNOWING you're gonna need it later on.  So in the interests of grittiness, Underdread makes you wait for a journal entry telling you to go look for said object...before promptly saving you the hassle of spending another ten minutes searching areas you've already been by letting you PRESS A TIP BUTTON which generates a magical blue light which leads you straight to the object in question.  What was that I was just saying about realism?  Oh well.  They tried, I guess.  And it did save them the bother of having to, y'know, make more maps than was absolutely necessary to pad the game out to a vaguely reasonable length.

Oh, and to add to the aggravation of the ceaseless back-tracking, they of course had to put a "stamina meter" in to ensure that you can only sprint for so long before you have to walk for a while.  You can, on the other hand, sprint while CROUCHING, so maybe some of you may consider that something of a novelty and/or consolation.  Me, I just thought it was kinda silly, and could only imagine how unintentionally creepy my character must look WADDLING along at that speed...

To anyone else, seriously:  What the ♥♥♥♥ is wrong with you people?!  Amnesia: The Dark Descent.  Buy it now.  And everything else in the Frictional catalogue, for that matter.  And Outlast, while we're at it.  And Alien: Isolation.  And Among the Sleep.  In short, there's a veritable♥♥♥♥♥♥TONNE of "stealth horror" games out there which you should play before you bother with this one.  Go play those instead, and I don't want to see you back on this wretched excuse for a Store page until you've bought and played all the games I just mentioned.

I do enjoy this game as it merges two of my favorite puzzle games in one. Unique.

What is Lexica?
Lexica is a puzzle game where you have a set number of letters that each slide in one direction from a side of a crossword puzzle like box into the fields designated for them. So the letters to the left and right will only fit into the rank they are at, while the letters to the top and bottom will only fit into the file they are at.
The difficulty in the game stems entirely from trying to find out what words you need to create. Since the game has three difficulties and is entirely in English, a good knowledge of English language is recommended to play this, otherwise you will spend a lot of time trying to figure out words since usually there would be several ways to fit all letters into all places, but only one where all designated ranks and files will contain English words.
There is a total of 96 puzzles, divided into eight "puzzle packs", per difficulty - easy, intermediate and hard -, making a total of 288 puzzles in 36 packs. Since the only requirement for achievements is to complete all puzzles, 100p are definitely possible for everyone, although they will go a lot faster if he knows English language well and has a bit of geometrical thinking.
The sound is nothing special, I usually have it off and music playing instead. The graphics are good enough, as you can see on the official screenshots. Overall the gameplay is the only selling point of this. For me, at a good but not perfect English level, the harder levels seem crazy at first view, but the easy ones are fine.
The one thing that I really dislike is that only certain letters are used for achievements. Here I would have liked to have 26 achievements with one letter for each one, like in Lyne where you eventually can use them to spell out words on your Steam profile (achievement showcase).
Recommended:
For linguistic puzzle fans
(Note that at the time of writing this review, on 14 December 2014, the game is 90p off, at this price you definitely should get it!)

UnderDread:
~~~~~~~~~~
Absolutely buggered with your long journey (who can blame you travelling in the 18th century in a caravan), you and your daughter end up in a small inn. A good night’s sleep is probably a good remedy. As you wake up, your daughter is missing! In a panic, you go out for information and you will quickly find out that several children were missing from this village. Fortunately for you, a detective managed to rescue several children and he is on a lead to an old and enigmatic castle. You decide to try to catch up with him with the aim of saving your daughter!
UnderDread is an adventure / horror game set in a scary yet intriguing castle. Armed with a lantern, you will make your way through this very spooky castle to save your daughter. As you follow the footsteps of a detective, you will find scrolls lying around which will give you hints of what to do and what to look for within the level. Make sure you check all chests, desks and closets as they might hold ancient coins, scroll and letters. You will not get much action in this game but you will need a fair bit of stealth and puzzle-solving ability in order to move forward in the story.
The aspect of fear is very well portrayed in this game and you will encounter interesting and well-designed enemies through this ancient castle. Spooky sounds will float here and there and you will get the occasional weird visions too, which will make you sit on the edge of your comfy chair! Great atmosphere, in other words!
Graphically, this game looks great and the music fits the atmosphere really well. Mouse and keyboard in regards to the controls but they could have been smoother in my opinion.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Good graphics
-	Creepy atmosphere
-	Interesting Story
-	Trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Controls should have been smoother
-	No achievements
UnderDread is an interesting and well done horror game. Deserves to be find its way into your game library.

I wanted so bad to keep playing, and to love it, but I couldn't. Of course, the story is just uninteresting, that's not what your here for. But there's just SO MANY annoying bits. I was nearly falling asleep driving everywhere, or being left to walk as slow as you do. The stealth is just bloody broken. The guns get real boring real fast, and jamming is more annoying than challenging. The enemy AI is kinda impressive, but by today's standards isn't much. It's like this game doesn't want you to like it; you have to constantly stock on malaria pills, your weapons jam after a short time of using them, mission objectives are usually on the other side of the map, and every outpost you cleared out along the way will have reset by the time you get back to them.
At the same time, this is one of the most wonderful games I've ever played. Its tone is hidden by quick-talking characters and the ability to skip almost every mission conversation, but this game isn't afraid to go dark. No character, including the player himself, finishes the story without blood on his hands. Enemies (whose faction is always indecipherable) will be begging for their lives as you finish them off. Every alliance is founded on pillars of sand.
Most people wouldn't be able to finish this game: a first-time playthrough will probably rack up to close to 20 hours if you take your time. These 20 hours can be seen to be incredibly repetitive and increasingly frustrating as the game's quirks quickly turn into barriers. If you can get past, or at least shelf, the glaring problems with Far Cry 2, you'll find a satisfying, unique shooter, and a story that doesn't pull its punches.

You know the biggest difference between this game and "open-world" games from, let's say, Bethesda?
There, they copy-paste and slightly rearrange the same prefabs, to create 150 variations of essentially the same few locations, with the same basic elements, same enemies etc., and ask you to believe that this is worth $60. You see a glowing and blinking nuclear reactor, and you know that it's exactly the same as other 20 reactors you've already looted. It will give you an item, and that's it. Nothing to look forward to.
Here, you can click on a foot locker you already looted and get a unique experience, because some guy with a really nice sense of humor spent some time on writing a unique joke just_for_this_one_object, just in case you'll click on it again after you've already looted it. You see a paper bag that looks identical to a few other ones you've seen in other places, and you look forward to the dialogue you'll click through because you know it's going to be unique and hilarious. You shiver in anticipation a little bit before interacting with any unfamiliar object, character or even an element of the background, because you know they will most likely do something that will make you, as a player, a little bit happier.
And this is definitely something worth paying for.

I think my opinion of the game will chime or resonate with alot of the other reviews for this game when I say that the game has a lot of potential but is delving into a very competitive market for pubg-like battle royale games. The idea of a more futuristic BR game is a cool concept however I feel that with BR games, similiar to PUBG or FORTNITE BR, the game requires that feeling of scale. The feeling that world itself is much bigger than the player, the daunting fact that you are not alone in the huge world, and even worse, you have no idea where anyone is.
It useful to put bots into the game, since the game isnt as well known or popular as your mainstream BR games like PUBG, so that at least we can get a feel for combat. The combat itself isnt bad however I feel the use of more text aids for visual aids to let the player know: "hey if you stay in this area, you're gonna die." it took me a few rounds to realise the flashing area was bad jujus.
I liked the idea of indoor and outdoor style of play, indoor combat feels very different from outdoor combat, and it gives me a sense of hunger games with the random turrets that try to kill you in the environment. So the player isn't just fighting others, but the map itself is trying to actively kill everyone. I really like that concept and I think they can really make this game shine in that particular area that no other BR games has really explored. The idea of a PVP/E BR game is really exciting to me.
UNR:BR is a futuristic BR arena style shooter that only allows the player to fight from a 3rd person perspective. The guns, armour and environments are impressive and fit the sci-fi genre. However some of the effects on the guns, specifically sound fx and the sfx of certain guns, arent very impressive and would require a bit of a patch up in terms of sound quality and visual quality.
The price of the game is very fitting for the content that it has, and unlike most early access games, does not try to rip you off from the get go. It is still an early access game, and in saying that, it still holds the possibility for greatness. My advice to the developer would be to go away and review many of these user reviews and prioritize the major points that commonly occur between reviews.
Also please change the text the lobby to something more futurstic, that felt like a sloppy job.

FULL REVIEW:
Until none remain is a futuristic multiplayer third person shooter in a Battle Royale or Last Man Standing format.
It also has a VR Version of the game that is sold separately when purchasing.
Disclaimers: This is my first playthrough / review on an early access game this game may change and this review is only a review on the version that the game is currently on, I did not buy this game, I was given it by the developer.
Alright, up straight im going to say that I can definitely see the potential in this game, it has the building blocks there. I think its biggest issue right now is its player base, the game you’ve been seeing is purely against bots, I can appreciate the fact they’ve even bothered to put bots in, but my suggestion for this is to increase the amount of bots that way the game is more challenging.
Now let's talk sound design, I love it. Some guns are a little weird but for the most part I think the developer has done a good job, my only suggestion is to make footsteps quiet when in crouching mode.
The graphics are well done, nothing is particularly ugly, sometimes it feels a little bland but I believe that's just from me having nothing else to look at, the game runs well on my computer which is an i7 6700k , GTX 1080 and 32GBs of RAM.
The tutorial is appreciated.
All in all, this game is trying to get players in a market that already has dominating forces, I believe its twist is strong enough to warrent playing it, im just not sure I would pay asking rate to play this game at its current stage with its current playerbase, but I wont strike the developers down because they dont have a player base, im giving it a solid 3 out of 5, thus an “Average” score.
My suggestions to the developers:
Grow the playerbase. (Maybe free weekends?)
Make crouching more stealthy.
Thank you all for watching and thanks to the developer for providing the game key.

*Note: This game is still very young and in Early Access; I may change this review in the future.*
D.W.S. said they expect the game to leave Early Access in the first half of 2018. It surely needs a few tweaks, together with more content, player stats, leaderboards, more maps (which will be added when the time comes). I would also like to see a 1st person match option. If more people from several places eventually join this game, I think there can be a chance of having servers not limited only to US East (not a problem for me though, still able to play without any lag).
**Pros:**
- Solid gameplay
- It runs smooth
- Easy to learn (even without the tutorial - which I actually suggest you to follow, at least to get used to the controls)
- Good for whoever doesn't have much time to spend with games, as the matches are not very long
- Graphics are ok, and it's easy to see the environment elements and enemies
- Guns and grenades are easy to deal with
- The character's movement looks good
- It can be more fun once more people come to play this game
- Reasonable price
- It has a VR version, even cheaper than the main game
- It resembles Empyrion: Galactic Survival (even the graphics), but in a battle royale version
**Cons**
- Very, very little player base right now; young game, hope it gets more known and people get curious about trying it
- Indoor map is small and you'll reach the center quickly
- I'm not a fan of the inventory interface
- Some rooms have too much loot; it could be more scattered through the map

VIDEOBALL's really good.
This game's simple mechanics provide a lot of emergent depth. As you get more familiar with the game, you begin to fully understand and appreciate all the four different charge levels for shots.
This game makes you feel good: scoring a touchdown, aiming a level two triangle perfectly so it can push the ball across the court, being advantageously blasted by an opponent into a better position, reversing a level three shot, etc. You're bound to encounter countless feel-good moments in every single game.
This game's at its best as a local multiplayer game, where you can sit down with some buds and play the game latency-free. However, there is an online mode. Although you're unlikely to find an open random lobby, you definitely can play online if you coordinate with the friendly folks in the official Discord server, where people are setting up ranked matches throughout the day. Or you could play with your friends online of course. It's unfortunate you can't just pop in a game, but it's not too inconvenient to coordinate.
There can be some latency online for everyone who isn't the host, but it's not unbearable for me usually and I still have fun.
If you're into competitive games and you have friends to play with or are willing to join the Discord server, you should consider buying this game.
Also you should play with a controller.

Hello everybody, End World Gaming here to share my thoughts on ICEBOX: Speedgunner.
ICEBOX is a fast paced speedrunning game with run and gun mechanics mixed in.
The game has you escaping from a virtual prison known as the ICEBOX. With the aid of an unnamed woman, you'll have to make your way to the exit in the fastest time possible without dying along the way.
There a lot of different game modes including a 21 level Campaign, Daily/Monthly challenges, Marathons, various Quick Games and 20 New Game+ levels. This (And the leaderboards for each) makes for a lot of replay value, even though the levels go by pretty quickly.
The game also allows you to slow down time for a short duration. While in slow motion you take no damage, and  move/jump longer distances. So, if you jump off a ledge on accident you can slow down time, jump a few times and land back on the platform so you can continue.
Overall, I had quite a bit of fun with ICEBOX Speedgunner. I found it to be pretty addicting but the campaign flew right by due to the relative shortness of the levels. Still, they were a lot of fun to play through and the other game modes proved to be quite fun as well. If you’re into speedrunning games and are looking for something unique then ICEBOX Speedgunner might be a good choice.
If you'd like to see the score I gave the game be sure to check out the full review here:
Satisfying, fast and fun!

Slick, fast paced and addictive. The speed running element of Icebox is fantastic, and it's very difficult to put down, once you decide to climb that leaderboard. There is also an option to play the campaign end to end without a loading screen, a challenge I haven't taken on yet but am super keen to investigate.

Having a blast, I totally recommend it!

You don't have to be a fighting game master to learn how to play Melty Blood if you know the basics. Charge up your magic gauge, do a quarter circle + C for a special, and beat 'em up with your expert combos.
Melty Blood is a fighting game like any other, but with some unique elements that make it stand out from the rest.
As you can probably tell by reading the description, there's 31 characters to choose from (Or you can cheat and play as the boss) and 3 styles for each character.
Some unique elements that separate it from the other fighting games:
- Styles change how your characters play, Cresent Moon is high speed and low attack for comboing, Half Moon is easy modo, and Full Moon is high attack and low speed.
- EX Sheilding, which allows you to counter an attack by pressing D at the right time or perfect shield it.
- Dedicated dash button if you play on a controller.
- Charge up your special gauge (known as the Magic Circuit in MB) if you pick Full Moon Style
- specials are pretty simple to execute
- 30 or so palettes for each character
- It's has the same 480p resolution that it had 10 years ago, but at least now it has command tips on the side of the screen.
- Some stages STILL aren't playable in Multiplayer, but there's a mod that enables them.

*SPOILER FREE REVIEW*
As a huge fan of pixel horror RPGs, I was very happy to see Mad Father on here; I've watched people play it before and enjoyed it enough that I wanted to have a go myself, and it did not disappoint!
Technically speaking, the controls are very simple and the game is easy to navigate.  I do have to say, however, that I wouldn't recommend expanding the screen size despite the relatively small window it opens in, as the visuals get VERY fuzzy and distorted.  It simply wasn't made for the fullscreen experience.  However, unless you're overly finicky about something like that, I can promise you that the smaller game screen does not affect your enjoyment of the game.  It's a minor detail that is very easily forgotten about once you start playing.
Concerning the plot, I think it's a great story that isn't too complicated, but it doesn't stop the revelations from being exciting and the intentions of the villain from being disturbing.  The fact that I'd already seen the entire game before and knew how it ended made no difference to how much I enjoyed it playing it myself, and I really did.  I like the level of challenge in that it was relatively easy to figure out what to do next without getting stuck and having to look it up.  The horror aspect of the game is well done in that it doesn't rely on sudden jumpscares or loud noises, but is more subtle in the way it creeps you out.  It's in the way something looks or moves.  There were some great moments that made me gasp that were simply something in the background moving for a second, or something appearing that wasn't there before.  This isn't a plot spoiler, but as an example of such, I love the moment you leave the kitchen while the rabid dog is still in it for the first time, and just as you activate the door, the dog suddenly flies across the room running so fast and is right behind you as the visual cuts to black.  There wasn't even a noise that came with it, but I genuinely freaked out for a second cos it was unexpected and very sneaky!  There are a lot of great moments like that that keep you on your toes.  I also really appreciate the game's very sparse use of voices and speech, as pretty much the only voice you will hear throughout the game is the protagonist's little gasps, unsure noises and screams, and then the odd monster groan.  Hardly any other characters are voiced, which means that when you do suddenly hear a voice out of the blue, it has that much more impact.  Again, I'm not going to spoil, because this one does involve a MASSIVE plot point, but there's a hugely important character that never speaks aloud until a certain moment, and when they do, it's the most creepy, malicious sounding voice of the whole game, yet almost an intimate murmur-in-your-ear in the way it's delivered... it gave me a full body shiver because it was so creepy!
The plot was decently paced and the game felt like the right length for the story, not too long or short.  The twists are, while potentially easy to spot in advance, very enjoyable and you really get a feel of being that protagonist trapped in a horrible situation where you just want the people you love to be alive and happy and all get along, but it just doesn't seem like it's able to work out that way, forcing you to make very tough decisions and choose between people you'd rather not.  There are several endings to achieve, and the 'true' ending definitely has a sinister twist to it that you really don't expect after going through what you went through.  There is also a very cleverly written and very mysterious character that I still don't believe anyone truly understands.  Once you play it, you'll know exactly who I'm talking about.
He appears friendly and helps the protagonist, yet he then goes on to do certain things behind her back that contradict that, and his true intentions are never revealed, leaving him to perpetually walk the line between good and evil without you ever understanding who he is and what he's trying to achieve.  I felt loyal to him one moment and scared of him the next, and I love his character because he infuriates me!  I want to know!
One last thing that's important to say; Mad Father was being sold at Halloween in the Bloodsoaked Bundle with the game Misao.  They might not be bundled anymore, but once you've played Mad Father, I still highly recommend you play Misao because...  in the least spoilery way possible, there's a continuation.  The actual main games seem completely unrelated to each other, but let's just say there are characters and themes that are related to Mad Father that appear unexpectedly with no warning in Misao.  If you weren't familiar with Mad Father, you wouldn't even realise.  In the small moments that they do appear, they give you extra information on the more mysterious and unresolved elements of Mad Father that, while not providing a definitive answer, set a lot of possibilities running through your head.  I very much like that sneaky little extra.  Do try it for yourself.
Right, I've rambled enough!  Short version: Mad Father is one of my very favourite games of this genre and you should definitely give it a go.  Interesting plot, creepy villain, drama and deceit, running for your life, and mysteries that never quite get an answer...  also, who doesn't love a good chainsaw?

A crossword puzzle game - you might think "Wow, Really". It is. No story, no gameplay to talk about, just brooding over riddles and try to figure them out - some are quite a challenge, others are very easy. The game itself can turn into an addiction, because you will come back for more riddles.
Of course, there will be people that are missing the great artworks, or depth of other games, but with riddles you don't need any great art, sound or even story to tell - and it still can be challenging, and bring a lot of joy in completing a given puzzle.
If you like puzzles or riddles, this game is for you - but don't expect rocket science.

Lexica is similar to a crossword puzzle but with a twist. You have letters above, below and to the sides of the puzzle. You then slide those letters into place. Top and bottom letters slide only up and down. Side letters only move left and right. You will slide these letters making words. It will end up like a completed crossword puzzles. So the first letter of a word might have a choice of F L A P. The second letter might have A R. The third letter of the same word might have R U T. The words you're assembling intersect with other words so competing one word will lead to a basis for other words. It is a great system. Words everywhere from far, sop and dot to impact, craven and scruff.
There are a lot of puzzles here, over two hundred. Each subjugated to puzzle packs of 9 puzzles in three difficulties. You can play any puzzle at any time. When you play a puzzle it starts a timer to determine how long it takes you. You can go to the next puzzle or back to the menu, but Lexica saves your game and remembers your time. When you return to the puzzle, your time is still there.
This is a difficult game. The first nine puzzles are easy enough, but even on easy, the game cranks up the challenge. This game could still be for you. It is a good coffee break game that you can complete a puzzle or so in 15 minutes. It is a great game for people with a big vocabulary, but you'll never have words more than six letters long.
The game doesn't grade you except for your overall skill rating in the stats. It doesn't feel like completing a puzzle is an achievement. Its just onto the next puzzle. The game keeps going progressing in challenge with no easy puzzles between to give your brain a break. The challenge and tedium begin to outweigh the fun and joy of solving a puzzle. There is no reward like unlocking new puzzles when you already have over 200 to play at once. In fact the game takes away puzzles. When the puzzle is complete, YOU CAN NEVER REPLAY THAT PUZZLE. So its gone. You can see its time, but that is all.
I like the game, its a great system. I felt it is more difficult than fun. That doesn't mean you can't have fun with it. If you need to keep your vocabulary sharp or if you need a fresh take on crossword puzzles, this could be the game for you.

Do you like dragons? Do you enjoy hand drawn animation? Are games based on a labor of love your thing? Then look no further than DRAGON: A Game About a Dragon. This game, while not perfect, is a real gem, it comes highly recomended*.
Note the * - the first time I installed this game, it crashed constantly. Re-installing it fixed this issue for me; however, your mileage may vary.
As far as games go, this one's a real charmer. Lovingly hand-illustrated drawings done in crayon, the visual aesthetic is not unlike that of a children's book. This, combined with the tongue-in-cheek humor sets a whimsical tone for a very casual, pick up and play experience that anyone can enjoy.
While the game mostly progresses in a linear fashion, the player is able to go through the game at their pace. While this game is 2D platformer, it has both "Metroidvania" and RPG element infused within it. Basically, what this means is that the player is always given an option to set their own difficulty levels. For example, if you're having trouble with a boss, go back and explore the levels to find any hidden treasures / upgrades you may have missed and level up. Or, if the player is wanting more of a challenge, they are able to face any of the enemies head on.
This is my first review of a game - numerical values / scores are arbritrary, so I'll simply post my final verdict on it.
I'm glad I gave it a second chance, as the lovely visuals, charming music, and wonderful world and characters have won me over. Also, you get to play as a dragon, which is always good times. Is it for everyone? Of course not, but then no game truly is.  Is it good value for the $5.99 pricetag? Absolutely. There's a lot of game in DRAGON, and even more love.
FINAL VERDICT: If you like dragons, hand-drawn 2D platformers, and adjustable gameplay, go pick it up.

DRAGON: A Game About a Dragon is a small 2D light-RPG based game, in which you play as the dragon in an attempt to rescue your girlfriend (who is the Kings daughter)!
Controls; 9/10 Very simple controls that allow for both keyboard and controller, can be customized in the options menu. The only problem I had was that at times the controls would stop responding, which is only a problem while going for some achivments (Boss fights without taking damage).
Music; 8/10 Great little sound track with a nice blend of music, can be a bit repetitive after a while. I wish they made it available for purchase!
Graphics; 8.5/10 Hand drawn graphics are easy on the eyes, its like looking into a coloring book.
Story; 6/10 Basic level of in depth of characters, most of the 'enemy' figures are actually friends with you. I felt that there was a lack in detail, but other then that its ok. Story was simple and to the point.
Gameplay; 8/10 Gameplay was enjoyable, with unique level design and enemy type, however there was a large lack of melee based enemies, most were ranged. Boss fights are simple if you learn the patterns, but are random in attacks. Also lots of easter-eggs within the game itself.
Replayability; 3/10 Once you beat the game and seen both endings, there is little else to do other than achivments.
In the end it only took me about 2.5 hours to beat the game start to finish, and get 12/15 of the achivments, so if you wanted you could try to get a refund for the game if you did a speed run, but I don't think I will, for some reason it has a nice charming feeling for a game of its size.
Overall Ranking; 7/10 Above Average.

This is a game which is firmly mediocre but shoots for the stars. A lot of really neat ideas are in here, but the execution is lacking. Or horrendously buggy. One of those two. DO NOT assume I am calling the game crap, but I don't really recommend it in the state that it was in as I played it.
The hand-drawn/crayon-style art is really, really inconsistent. On some stages (the air force base comes to mind), the whole thing gels really well and you get a unique appearance that I can't think of a good comparison for. On others (pretty much any kind of indoor stage), it is horrendous as at least one layer of scrolling is nothing but [solid color on uneven construction paper scan]. The sprites themselves don't seem to follow any real guidelines either, and in a few cases it's really challenging to determine what's foreground, enemy, or just random detail.
I'm gonna spin out of that into what is probably one of the game's worst levels, spent climbing a massive tree. It's the perfect example of the game's myriad flaws in one place: Ranged enemies can fire at you from offscreen with no visual cue to their existence, with you having absolutely no way to know they exist until an arrow/cymbal/etc. flies into you mid-leap. Incredibly tight platforming with controls not meant for it (one in particular is either something I was either doing wrong, or demanded surprising precision from you for a game with such floatiness of movement). Enemies who have suspiciously large hitboxes, resulting in cheap hits when you try getting near to attack them*. Objects which appear to be part of the background, but in fact cause damage on contact.
Even if you want to tell me I screwed up in that one, it doesn't change that the game IS poorly coded. A game with such minimal specs as this should not be having random moments of slowdown/lag on my computer. At least once, I fell through a level into the void, but did not die, leaving me to have to force-quit the game and restart, as there's no "exit level" function. The final boss is a real mess, with at least one attack being wildly inconsistent as to whether or not you can dodge it or not**, then proceeding to kill him left a booming laser sound effect playing over the entire ending, THEN the game crashed mid-credits.
Design-wise, it's also got some problems. More than once an enemy did a perfect 180 into attacking me with no tell, sometimes flipping themselves around (and bringing the already-in-progress attack) to hit me when I tried leaping past. I don't know if some animations have bugged frames, but at least a few times I just had projectiles spawn in my skull all of a sudden. Most, but not all, enemies end up in a stun animation when you attack them, leading the ones that can still move/strike you while flashing to be real nasty tricks the first time they appear. Basically, it's that inconsistency at work again - you think you know the rules it plays by until you suddenly don't.
I get it and all, the game is basically one dude's passion project with some help from friends, but it doesn't excuse the game just having huge problems. Wait for a sale, wait for a patch, just... yeah. I do not advise leaping on this game.
* In the game's defense, I probably should have used the breath weapons more around these jerks, except for the fact that more than a few enemies would just seem to be immune to them. Which was also a crapshoot.
** This is not hyperbole. Said attack is a left-to-right sky laser which you are supposed to be able to shut down by shooting a target in time. The problem is that even if you do so before the laser even shows up, the speed at which it vanishes is inconsistent as all get out, and sometimes it will vanish after covering every single inhabitable part of the screen - meaning you are guaranteed to take a hit. Someone else on the game's forums mentioned this being an issue for them too, giving me proof that at least some of this is a known quantity.

I had never played any of the Far Cry games, so when Far Cry 1 through 3 were on sale on Steam I bought them in August 2016.  I play a LOT of retro games, so I am forgiving on antiquated interfaces, and even more forgiving on outdated graphics.  With this in mind, I found Far Cry 1 to be incredibly underwhelming.  Trust me when I tell you that I am well aware of and a frequent purveyor of the phrase "For it's time, it was amazing."  With Far Cry 1, however, I did not feel this way with the exception of two details: 1) It had an open-world angle to it, and 2) the graphics, for it's time, were really good.  With that said, to me it still felt like just-another-first-person-shooter.
So when I decided a year later to play Far Cry 2, I wasn't really sure what to expect.  I've read numerous claims that "It's the best in the serious," yada-yada... but as an incredibly picky gamer, I've learned that you can't really trust anyone's opinion but your own.  With THAT being said, I found this game, even being nine years old, to be nothing short of excellent.  The only detriments to the game are the sped-up voice clips (to save disk space) and the AI being able to see and shoot you through all manner of cover (grass, metal sheets, you name it; though it's not QUITE as bad as Far Cry 1 was for this).  The music was great (if you appreciate styles like African-Tribal, as I do), the graphics hold up, the gun play is fun (this coming from a guy who doesn't really like gun play, but more of a Serious Sam/Killing Floor/Left 4 Dead shooting hordes of ♥♥♥♥♥es that run at you type of gamer), and the way that you weave your own web in the story to a very satisfying extent is fantastic.  What an extraordinary game. In my opinion it COMPLETELY blows Far Cry 1 out of the water; it's not even comparable.
On to Far Cry 3... whenever I get back in the mood for another Far Cry game. :)

The Good:

The Bad:

- Enemy camps respawn way to fast!
The Verdict:
For those interested, this was the far cry game in the series that started the trend of how the far cry games play now. You are a dude the arrives in africa and is sent there to kill someone. As you explore and do quests for people you get more and more diamonds to unlock weapons at your safe houses. And when focusing on this the game is fun.
Where the game really lets me down is when you spend 5-10 minutes clearing out a camp of enemies, go past it, and then turn around 2 minutes later after getting the thing for a quest only to find all of the enemies there ALIVE that you had just killed. Now this wouldn't be any issue if you could just drive by them (and honestly sometimes you do get luck and can do that) but more often than not, they shoot your car a few times and you are forced to stop and fight them.
To keep it short - there is a good 6-7 hours worth of game here, and it's fun. But everything you do takes twice as long, because you have to fight a bunch of dudes on the way to your objective, and fight the EXACT SAME dudes on the way back. There is a reason that in the sequals to this game they added camp liberations to remove all bad guys for good etc.
That all being said though, this game is fun, I recommend it. But don't be surprised when you get frustrated having to kill the same enemies twice over and over again.

I’m always a little wary of the indie horror games that get unleashed onto Steam. They have a habit of either being hype machines that fail to live up to the billing or they’re utter garbage that gain notoriety for just how bad they are. Some would argue that its because its generally fairly inexpensive to create cheap jump scares in games and that’s ultimately what you end up getting – a game loaded with cheap jump scares. Very rarely do you find an indie horror game that is worth its weight in gold or in our case the time spent playing the game. And so it was with trepidation that I loaded up UnderDread Bigzur Games’s debut Steam release even though at time of playing the game had a positive review score with the 17 published reviews (14-3).
In doing research for the game I discovered that this game was titled Slender Man Origins 2 Saga but was changed to UnderDread for its Steam release so as to not get caught up in any copyright arguments with Slender: The Arrival which of course features the now famous Slenderman. The title was highly rated on the various app stores with most finding the game to be rather impressive. However, as we all know phone to Steam ports often go awry so until one reports on it you may never know. As others have already done so and I can confirm the game plays comfortably well on Steam and works as fully intended.
The game has you adventuring through a horror filled ancient castle. Throughout your journey you will solve a lot of puzzles and avoid the standard ghouls, goblins and associated horrors that one would find in a haunted castle. The objective is to find your daughter who was kidnapped from the inn you were staying at. A strong bonus from my vantage point is that all of the puzzles and the horrors fit within the story being told. There doesn’t appear to be many, if any, occasions where I wondered why a particular game design choice was made when perhaps a better – and more obvious – one would have worked better. The puzzles are enjoyable and the supernatural enemies well designed. I particularly enjoyed the relatively simple but well executed stealth mechanic where you could hide from the enemies by crouching and hiding behind walls, etc. while with a key press you could dispel the enemy for a short time to enable you to complete the task at hand.
The atmosphere of the game is fantastic and arguably the game’s greatest highlight. It enables a good level of immersion that is only ever broken when you need to use the hint system. This is aided by a good choice of soundtrack and solid, albeit unspectacular, visuals. All in all the developers did a solid job in this area of the game – one of the most important for a horror game. Furthermore, they really didn’t go with the cheap tricks that lesser horror titles do.
There is a hint system within the game that works rather well and allows you to progress through the game when you become stuck. I do believe that there may be some sort of timer in some of the areas of the game on the system so that it doesn’t get abused as there were a couple of areas where I wasn’t receiving a hint when I called for one shortly after using.
I wish that there was greater controller support for the game. There is no reason why the game lacks full controller support but it does. I am fine using keyboard and mouse for games but I do prefer controller. I’m far from a console peasant either for those of you reading from /r/PCMasterRace – I just find that for non-precision games my enjoyment factor increases. I have noticed a lot of complaints about the head weaving. I never really had that as a personal problem but if it was at all possible perhaps in a later update make that an option that players who do suffer from motion sickness can turn off. I’d also like to see the devs add Steam achievements and trading cards. These four factors would improve the game and/or the amount of people who would purchase the game substantially.
UnderDread was a pleasant surprise. I went into the game not expecting a lot and received much more than I bargained for. A very solid indie horror title.

This title was originally released for the phone under the title Slender Man Origins 2 saga, originally released for phones, although with that said the original game was highly rated and I don't personally think the developers did it intentionally to mislead people but rather to avoid any conflicts with Slenderman copyright.  With that said, the game is really good with the updates and changes made from the original game are pretty good, or so I've heard as I never originally played the phone game.  The only addition that would have been nice is controller support (the game allows you to move back and forth with a controller but everything else is disabled.
The game starts off with hand drawn images giving you the basics of the story, you're daughter has gone missing during the night, after asking the locals,  you discover that other children have gone missing as well, a detective is currently investigating the disappearances and has in fact brought several of the children home.  So after searching and failing to discover anything you set out for an isolated castle which is where the Detective was heading the night before.  After getting to the castle you discover something is quite amiss about the large foreboding structure.  The need to discover what happened to your daughter outweighs any fear you may have and you trounce into the castle armed with a trusty lantern.
The game plays a lot like other games in this genre, you search for items, and use those items to delve deeper into the castle. Aside from searching for items and the spooky atmosphere you discover numerous monsters ready to eat, abuse or generally do unmentionable things to your vulnerable body.  When monsters are nearby you're required to hide and wait for them to leave, or use a ward to send them away.  Furthermore you're able to use hints to help with your current missions, the hints come in handy for users who aren't used to playing old school games that didn't hold your hand..  (major plus IMO, as most games these days hold your hands, this one doesn't do that, but offers you a way to help yourself out on those really tough missions).  As well as finding items to help get deeper into the castle you can pick up notes and pages which help out with information about getting further and giving a general background on the castle and expanding the story-line.
Pro's
Great Atmosphere,
Eerie Music,
Interesting Story, (albeit kind of cliche)
Decent character models and graphics
con's
Lack of controller support (not a big deal but meh, I love me some controllers and see the basics of them are there)
Sluggish controls
Head bobbing  (this is again a personal preference.)
So overall:  I'd recommend this game if you're a fan of hide and glide gameplay (yeah I termed these types of game hide and glide... I'm bringing it back.. err well starting it up.), I'd give it a very solid 8 out of 10, that score would go up by a half a point if controller support and achievements were added.

is indeed a re-titled re-release of 2015's mobile horror
, the only changes being some minor bug fixes and the removal of in-app purchases, but don't let that dissuade you in and of itself. The Slender Man intellectual property banhammer is swung hard at everything from movies to books these days so the developers weren't exactly left with much wiggling room in that respect.
As it stands,
is a solid title; perhaps a little expensive for what it actually is considering the original's going for less than £1 on Google Play at the minute but still charmingly spooky in its atmospherics and inventively expansive in contributing to the Slender Man mythology.
You play a father searching an isolated castle for his kidnapped daughter, as well as stone keys, ancient coins, holy water, daggers, potions, switches, planks of wood and anything else the game can conceivably force you to hunt down as you are stalked by various monsters from which you must hide like a coward. Some aid is offered in the form of Tip Scrolls that will lead you to your next available item and Shields that banish your supernatural adversaries for a spell. It's simple but becomes repetitive quickly as you're forced to backtrack large distances in the name of guesswork. The holy water quest in particular exhaustingly drags you back to the start of the chapter without giving you any indication of just how much of the bloody stuff you're supposed to be looking for. The only way you'll know is to head back to where you're supposed to be using it to be met with a 'Not enough yet, bucko!' taunt. I fail to see what harm a counter or track would have done to combat the sluggish recharging of the sprint meter there.
Thankfully,
abandons most of its scavenger hunting just over halfway through. There's just enough gloss and plot to keep it interesting throughout and some of the enemy designs are lovely, particularly the portable corridor of vengeful corpses that stalks the tunnels under the castle. Worth a go but maybe wait for a sale.

Until None Remain is a battle royale game in a sci-fi setting. The premise is simple like with any other BR game:
Be the Last Man Standing. So what's different from other games in the genre.. well the futuristing setting is a warm welcome.
Also matches last no more then 10 mins which makes it pretty fast paced.
Soon as you drop into the arena it's of course best to quickly find a weapon, but there's more to explore and loot like energy shields, armor (which stays on you the entire match) and even jetpacks that give you some flight capabilities or a hoverbike for faster transportation.
One of the things that's a big plus is that if there are not enough players the match will feature Bots. Truth be told Bots are not as smart as players but it keeps the game going so you don't have to wait and wait till all slots are filled.
The devs seem really dedicated to this project (there's already a VR version released as well) with constant updates.
Some flaws imo at the time of writing:
- The animations for picking up stuff are a bit slow/clunky especially for a fast paced game
- The maps could use some work to be more interesting (they seem a bit bland)

An enjoyable game that I originally played on the PS2, The Bards Tale takes place in your general fantasy world filled with various monsters and spell casters. However, it isn't the world that grabs my attention the most, rather it's the characters and their dialogue that interests me the most; all the dialogue feels interesting and most of it is quite witty and laced with appropriate amount of satire.
The main source of this enjoyment comes from our titular character: The Bard. He's no hero or noble knight, but he's a joy to play as for his banter that even when you're trying to be nice sounds a little sarcastic. You can customize him in a fairly diverse system, allocating stats and skills that will allow you to use various weapons and fighting styles to defeat your enemies as well as songs that summon various companions meant for offense, defense, or utility.
The story is intentionally generic but never dull and the combat can be a bit difficult, but with enough time and a little bit of luck you can pull through. Overall this is a fun game for me and while it's no masterpiece, it's definitely a good game for fans of fantasy games who enjoy a bit of dry wit.

I specifically wanted to make something entirely fake-looking, and honestly Photoshop was not random enough in it's brush strokes. With Black Ink I can make really, REALLY digital-looking art from scratch. Right now Black Ink is pretty bare, with a lot of basic fuctionality missing (such as shapes and color swatch sets), but there's enough there so that if you want to straight up paint this program can do a lot.
However, my biggest wish right now is for more customized brushes. The community has made a few neat ones, available at Bleank's forums, but it's nowhere near enough. This program's uses math-based brush work, meaning you can go completely nuts with a stroke's parameters, as shown in official YouTube tutorials and the trailers. Dozens of "controllers" and numerous options for each create a staggering suite of options. I was simultaneously blown away and shockingly overwhelmed. Having brush sets (a feature not in the program, at least for now) with even a handful of similar, crazy brushes would make this program easier for people like me, who don't want to spend hours making their own perfect group.
On a side note, because Black Ink is GPU-based, it cranks my computer barely less than the Witcher 3 at near-max settings. Not a huge deal, but worth noting for those with mid-range or lower video cards.
All in all, this program is absolutely amazing and is doing a better job for the ultra-digital look I want than Photoshop could ever attempt. I look forward to more updates, but even in a beta state I'll be using this program quite a bit.

may seem simplistic at first glance, but take a look at it, and you’re looking at a very good model for adapting the adrenaline-filled world that is
to Video Games.
Sportsssssssss
is a game that can be understood by the time you’re done with your first match.
is a game that has enough complexity to literally appear as it’s own, individual sport. Despite being confined to the contextual actions of the controller’s buttons and the code of it’s own engine, Videoball still plays like a emergent, energetic, and entertaining team-based sport.
This is how
works. You shoot triangles at these balls. Charge up your shots to shoot bigger triangles that have more strength. Push the balls to the enemy goal (like in Soccer/Football) to score points. Score Points to win. In execution, it just works. The game doesn’t feel convoluted or especially cluttered with it’s simplistic mechanics, rules, and map layouts, making it incredibly easy for anybody to pick up on the fly.
With the simple pick-up-n-play design,
becomes an absolute hit for parties and game nights. Practice isn’t required for people to play proficiently and it’s profile system allows for player statistics (goal tracking, amount of wins/loses, etc.). While it’s eSport appeal may not be as strong or nearly as successful as other games, it’ll definitely still be a stellar pick-up for someone wanting to bring some competition to their LAN Parties.
Oh, and it has online-multiplayer as well! Which is nice, but it’s all peer-to-peer, meaning there’s a good chance your experience with it will be an absolute mess regardless. It has leaderboards, 3v3 matches, and Team Matchmaking, so it isn’t just some cookie-cutter online experience. However, don’t rely on it for finding matches though, as the player count is unfortunately incredibly weak for the game at the time.
Those looking for some single-player action may also find themselves a bit on the short-end on the stick. However, there is Arcade Mode, which presents a series of challenges against unique bots that while don’t come close to capturing the thrill of the multiplayer matches, are OK and decent puzzle-like challenges. The bots included while are unique, often can be obnoxious with following simplistic patterns and behaviors that can be aggravating to counter alone.
It’s presentation is incredibly slick to top off the rest of the package, however. It’s minimalistic design carries on to it’s aesthetic of popping colors and simple visuals. The game itself evokes the unique humor and personality found in its trailers/promotional material, with it’s cheesy narrators and constant branding of itself as a digital entertainment sporting good. And also, it’s soundtrack is pretty decent, with coda providing incredibly energetic and enjoyable tracks to go along in the background.
The final package of
may be a bit lacking for those expecting a single-player experience, but for everyone looking for a fun local-multiplayer game, you are absolutely in luck!
is one of the most elegantly designed multiplayer games I’ve ever played, and you shouldn’t miss out on it if you frequent LAN Parties.

"Hunted: One Step Too Far" is a neat concept, with an all too familiar twist...
=====
Rather than my regular breakdown, I want to keep this simple and not give anything away, really, for those interested.
As a person who has partaken in Geocaching, and spent countless hours following clues, logging coordinates, and solving riddles to find the cache boxes, I found the concept of this game to be very intriguing. When I first played, I thought "Wow, this is really capturing the feel of going on a Geocache!" The main menu was well polished, and the opening cinematic gave a very good setup of the plot. The "tutorial-esque" area at the beginning was well done, and the atmosphere of being alone with nature, with only a primitive "guide" of sorts to show you the way to safety was a great touch.
Soon to follow those feelings, however, were feelings of disappointment as it began to devolve into cliche.
Asylums, crazed people with deranged motivations, and "take your eyes off them and they move!" mechanics...
I wasn't happy that it turned out this way.
It's a great looking game built on a fantastic concept, but it fell victim to going the "easy" route and following every other indie "horror" game out there.
=====
Do I recommend?
No, I can't.
They really botched what I feel was a great concept, with a fantastic setup, that could have been the type of game that makes a mark and holds its' own, but instead it cheaped out with run-of-the-mill tropes.
..It does make me want to go out Geocaching again though~ :)

Even if I knew nothing about the game, I would praise it.
Why?
Because it nails the perfect balance between a gloomy mystery and a dark horror atmosphere. It has a lot of suspense to offer, the world is clever designed, it seems bigger than it is (and it is actually quite huge for its scope), it offers quite some gameplay (could be more, though) and a really solid stability.
Throw in some really good and nasty surprises instead of cheap jump-scares and a good sound production, and you have a convincing little Indie horror experience better than many competitors.
However, as I am the developer of Father's Island
I know the limitations of GameGuru very well - and "Hunted" is in my eyes nothing less than a shiny masterpiece of GameGuru-driven game development.
It doesn't only dodge and evade cleverly the usual limitations GG has in its current Beta state, no, it even turns some of them into an advantage while utilising all the good sides of GG perfectly.
Summary:
8/10 as an Indie Horror Experience
9/10 as a showcase for GG game development.

A simple puzzle game where you are given the letters to fit into a grid, then you slot them in to make words.
Positives:
- Easy to understand.
- Hundreds of puzzles.
- Difficulty levels.
Negatives:
- Some general polish issues, such as low quality text displaying, text appearing behind objects and icons being slightly misaligned.
- No way to see or replay a puzzle.
- Every puzzle in the game is the same size, despite the choice of difficulty. The difficulty only affects how many spaces are filled and how obscure the words are. Consequently you never get a word that is longer than six letters, even on the highest difficulty.
- The stats screen shows your fastest completion time, but presumably for everyone this is just one of the very easy tutorial puzzles, so this stat seems useless.
- The rating system is somewhat confusing. I'm rated as "Competent" on hard, despite completing zero hard puzzles.
- Doesn't appear to be a quick way to swap letters.
- No in-game way to reset all progress. This means no way to improve times and no way to let someone else play the game.
- Nothing extra in the game: No random mode. No daily challenge. No puzzle editor. No hint system.
- The clock at the top of the screen is constantly ticking, which stops the game being relaxing. The time has no effect on the game, other than the statistics screen.
- Limited amount of window-size options. No full screen.
- Definitions of the words would have been nice.
- One of the screenshots for the game shows the time saying "1:45 vs 1:45", but I don't see any functionality that allows this to happen.
Notes:
- The interface has a lot going on: shadows, 3d, lots of unnecessary lines, gradients, highlights. Nothing inherently wrong with this, but after playing aesthetically pleasing games like Hexcells and LYNE, this looks very busy.
- By the nature of the game, this would be extremely difficult for someone that was unsure about the English language.
Overall I like the puzzle concept and I hope the game gets a big improvement update or a sequel.

Not a big deal, you just close the window with the OS close button...just seems inelegant.  Also, no fullscreen mode, but then again this game really doesn't need that either.
The descriptive text says it's a combination of Sudoku and Scrabble; I guess, but the only thing that's like Sudoku is the fact that you've got a grid.  That's not a bad thing, it's just worth mentioning that there is nothing about this game that has to do with Sudoku's pattern recognition or arrangement logic; it's all just vocabulary.
On the plus side, when the real question comes up: Does this game justify its asking price ($5)?  Absolutely.  Obviously it's a mobile port, but that's perfectly fine for a game like this.  When I was a little over halfway through the Easy puzzle sets I felt like it was difficult, but not super hard.  You really do have to bring your vocabulary A game though.  I'm quite a literate English speaker (not bragging, it's relevant to this particular review) and even I was a little worried about Medium and Hard back then.  :)
Now that I've completed the rest of the game, I can confirm that it does get quite a bit harder.  Given a strong enough English vocabulary, it is possible to complete the game without breaking out a Scrabble dictionary, but only barely.  There were a few words even I didn't know (again, not bragging...just giving context), which I only ever "got" because I filled in enough perpendicular words to either make the word or form an educated guess based on conjugation norms.
So yes, at the end of the day I'd recommend this game; it's not the most robust word puzzle game you'll find, but if you like the gameplay (and the storefront images/video will tell you everything you need to know) then for the price you should definitely get your money's worth.
On a contrary note, I'd have to recommend that non-English speakers avoid this game unless/until they add user-generated content support (all the puzzle words are in English).

Very fun RPG. The humor is omnipresent and quite good, but what really makes the game fun is the variety in non-combat stuff. Various skills, stats, perks and items constantly present options, making them feel vibrant. There's 3 or more ways to resolve every step of the "main" quest and at least 2 for almost every notrivial sidequest. There's also creative puzzles, a battle reenactment minigame, several quests that affect the ending, and probably more I forgot.
And yes, everything in it is funny.
The combat system's not the greatest but not terrible, good enough to support the rest of the game. On the plus side the different party members and classes do feel different on a second playthrough, and there is a "hard mode" you can activate during the prologue. And replay value is unusually high for a game of this type since, as said above, there's many ways to resolve the main quest.
Overall, it's everything I'd hope for from an RPG spinoff of Kingdom of Loathing.
