Mad Father:
~~~~~~~~~

The Drevis residence is a majestic mansion located in Northern Germany. The exterior is absolutely breathtaking, the interior decoration would bring happiness to whoever lives there. But there is sadness in this place. Tomorrow is the anniversary of the passing of Aya’s mother. Before going to bed, she asked her father if he would celebrate and remember the good times they had together on the day of her death. After a positive response, she fell into a deep sleep until being awoken by terrible screams coming from the mansion basement. The basement is where her father is conducting unorthodox experiments!
Mad Father is an adventure/horror/puzzle game with a touch of Anime (cut scenes) where you play a young girl named Aya. She was very close to her mother and despite knowing (to a certain degree) that her dad was performing strange experiments in the basement, they vowed to each other to always support him no matter what happens. That night, the screams were so intense that she decided to check it out herself and in the process found out the true story of her mother’s death.
As Aya explores this vast mansion, she will discover items by searching inside cabinets and wardrobes and around other furniture. Make sure she examines everything, everywhere. Also, she will collect gems. Some of them will appear when she successfully completes puzzles (they are not too difficult, to be honest) and others will be hidden within the mansion.
Aya will meet interesting characters throughout this rich story but will also need to avoid some really scary people who will be chasing her; being caught is game over! So, if Aya happens to see a crow in a room, make sure she interacts with it to save her progress. The atmosphere of fear and of the unknown is great in Mad Father. On a couple of occasions, Aya will be caught, but she will be able to free herself with your help by pressing (using the arrows on your keyboard) as fast as possible the sequence which will appear on your screen.
I really like the pixel artwork and the Anime aspect of the cut scenes. The soundtrack really embellishes the acute atmosphere the game portrays - just marvellous! Control-wise they are responsive. The story is very good and will offer a few different endings, which is great.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Good pixel artwork
-	Good story
-	Good atmosphere
-	Achievements and trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	The game should have an option tab within the game menu
I enjoyed Mad Father from start to finish!  If you like Pixel artwork, horror and puzzle games. Then give this game a try, its fun!
8/10

I almost overlooked this game. The art style (Alice in Wonderland-esque Lolita) almost put me off, but I’m so very glad it didn’t. If you are unsure about small, indie Wolf RPG maker games, please give this one a shot.
The gameplay is fairly simple, puzzle-adventure stuff but I stayed for the story. At first glance the plot is pretty basic and within a few minutes of playing you find yourself making certain predictions about the path the narrative will take. But that was part of the charm – the game reveals a lot of information to you early on, leaving you to explore the rest of the game with that knowledge hanging over your head. With the majority of the big reveals out of the way, you are then allowed to learn more about the characters, discover their deeper motivations and histories, including some careful clues about the protagonist you might miss. Even seemingly minor characters like Maria end up becoming a complex issue for the protagonist.
The story is quite linear however, there are not many choices to make. All of the endings can be unlocked from the final scene so there’s no need to backtrack. The puzzles are easy, except for a few I found more difficult because my reflexes seize up when a murderous corpse-doll is running at me.
But what I really want to do is talk about the endings and the characters, so from here on out there will be
[spoilers]
…
…
This is a story about victims of abuse, and how the women in the Mad Father’s life use different strategies to survive in that kind of environment.
So let’s start from the beginning.
The Mad Father himself, Alfred Drevis, was a troubled boy who enjoyed killing animals for fun. His first victim was his mother. In an argument over his proclivity for sadism, he stabs her and fawns over how beautiful she looks in death. Obsessed with creating an eternal beauty, he conducts experiments to turn human remains into dolls. Your typical creepy psychopath type, he is the most underdeveloped character – but that’s okay. We don’t need him to be developed, he may give the game its title but this story is not really about him.
He murders his way across Europe and in a small German village attempts to murder a local woman, Monika, but for an unknown reason is unable to. It’s implied that she was exposed to horrific things growing up in her ex-cultist mansion, and that this has affected her view of affection. The religious cult sacrificed humans out of love for their deity, and when she was put in a similar position as a potential murder victim, she felt excited rather than afraid. This was how love looked like to her. She invited him to live with her in the mansion, and soon gave birth to Aya.
(It’s possible the father’s experiments on the sacred cult ground was what summoned Mr Ogre in the first place)
She never showed sadistic traits herself, but she nurtures and cares for the sadistic traits in others. Hence Aya, the player controlled character, begins to show signs of cruelty. She kills cats. Her mother catches her a rat to play with, with the words “I could have cried from delight. To think she enjoys it so. Perhaps she resembles her father in curiosity? I look forward to seeing her mature.” Implying Aya did not treat the unfortunate rat well. Aya mistreats her pet rabbit Snowball, cutting its leg with a chainsaw and (as snowball is cloned whenever it gets hurt) judging by the number of dead Snowballs in jars, she has done it many times. She is all kept from the player, Aya even lies to her father and to the player at the same time when in her flashback she says she’s worried about losing Snowball. It’s only in the true ending when she is an adult is the player invited to put two and two together.
(Adult Aya runs a small clinic in a forest, helping the poor get medical care for free. A young woman called Jean comes for treatment, and the two of them flirt heavily. Then Aya murders her. For me personally, having Aya grow up into a forest hermit lesbian serial killer is the best way this game could have ended.)
Aya is conflicted over her feelings for father’s assistant Maria, who he is also sleeping with. At first the game implies Maria could be the one trying to hurt her, but it turns out she cares deeply for both Aya and Monika and regrets any bad blood that rises up between them. She was rescued off the streets by the doctor as a potential victim, but she proved to be a useful assistant. He has no strong feelings for her, but her position is tenuous. She has cultivated a strong attraction to him for self-preservation. If she doesn’t like her job, she dies. So she likes her job. It is implied strongly at first that she could be a doll with her inhuman eyes, but this is a red herring. She may not be a physical doll but she is the complete puppet of the father.
The reveal at the end is that Monika was not really so jealous of Maria, and it was because the father wanted to turn Aya into his next doll that she put into motion the events of the story. And here’s the interesting part: In no ending is it possible to prevent Aya becoming a doll. The secret ending makes that clear – father’s work will go on, with or without Aya. she WILL be objectified, whether she likes it or not.
With this in mind all of the women, Aya, Maria, Monika, show different ways that people cope with abusive situations. This is also true of some of the test subjects like Ines, who was groomed to be Aya’s big sister until the doctor got bored of her. All of them are complex, no-one fits perfectly into a box. None of them are ‘evil’. If you read them all as merely a sadistic child, evil maid and scorned wife then you’re missing out. That’s maybe what made this game stand out for me in the end, all these characters are human and the player is not invited to make sweeping judgements about them.
The Mad Father, however, is an easy villain to hate.

I don't entirely know how to start this review other than saying, as a game, Far Cry 2 isn't my cup of tea. However, I'm still leaving a positive review for it. Why? I like it as an experience, not as a game. And I don't mean this in the pretentious way that people go about reviewing walking simulators simply because "it's pretty and you can explore and stuff". The entire reason I like this game for the experience you get is exactly because it isn't pretty. It's ugly, bogs you down, makes you feel like garbage for continuing if you even get slightly invested in the overall story. You can't trust anyone, and if you get too attached to any one person, the game crushes you more. Unlike Far Cry 2's successor, "Far Cry 3", or the way too stuck-up-its-own♥♥♥♥♥"Spec Ops: The Line", this game really shows just how dirty war (particularly civil war) and killing is, even without realistic gore or damage values. You do things that hurt innocent people either directly or indirectly just for money, etc. You aren't a hero, and the game hardly ever pays favor to the fantasy that you are. The only time I ever felt like some kind of "badass" is when I would perform finishers on wounded enemies with the machete, or finishers on people that were already surrendering, which are the closest you'll get to a "takedown kill" like you would get in the later Far Cry games. Yeah, the flashiest way of killing someone is when they're wounded and/or not trying/able to fight back. Something the game makes note of in a collectible recording is that there is no "proper" way of taking someone's life, and I'd say that the game demonstrates that. Speaking of killing, a particularly sobering moment for me was when I was sneaking around a guarded area by a riverside, and I silently killed a soldier. Another soldier found his body and told his closeby comrade: &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥ he got the new guy." The other soldier responded "TJ. His name was TJ..." The enemies interact with each other, and not in a "TANGO FOXTROT ON MY POSITION ENGAGE THE HOSTILE FALL BACK SUPPRESSING FIRE" type of way. It feels more natural. Some of them are still rookies, wanting to rush in at you when you've killed their friends halfway across their encampment, while another member of their squad will firmly tell them to stay put so they don't get flanked.They won't always just fall dead, stiffly ragdolled in a gamey sort of way when you've done a lot of damage to them. Sometimes they'll get knocked down and wounded, clutching their wound and saying how they've been hit or that they can't move. They're a bunch of disposable henchmen with not a lot of variety in their portrayal, sure, but they feel more real than in a lot of games I've played. Did I mention, too, that these enemies open fire on you regardless of who you're currently working for? You can be working for their boss, but because of selfishness, secrecy, and agendas from their bosses, they don't get told who's helping who so they automatically assume you to be an enemy when they spot you out in the wild or in their bases. The faction leaders are real jerks and will sacrifice whatever is necessary just to get ahead in the war and to take control. And naturally, an opportunistic mercenary like yourself will just take the job, no matter who it will affect. Really, the only times you do something good are when you complete underground missions (so you can get medication for your  malaria, of course), and in the end. I won't spoil the end though. As far as the gameplay goes, it's not exactly what you would expect from your typical FPS (or even Ubisoft game), especially more modern ones. There's no tagging enemies, no fast travel (beyond certain bus station spots on the map), nothing to indicate how close you are to being detected until people start moving towards you and lead starts flying. You don't run very fast (considering you have malaria), your weapons jam and break, health only regenerates to an extent and if you take a heavy blow, a syrette full of drugs won't cut it. You'll need to perform quick first aid (such as ripping a bullet out of your leg with pliers and a combat knife) to stabilize your wound or you're a goner. You need to have a suppressed weapon to kill enemies without detection because, well, hacking someone to death with a machete is pretty noisy when they're screaming... Basically it's a bit more realistic than your average shooter even though yourself and enemies can tank more than a few shots before going down. Maybe the more realistic, slow-paced, and dragged-out gameplay is why I'm not particularly fond of it as an FPS game, but like I said, as an experience, I thoroughly enjoyed it even though I felt like a jerk for the majority of it. All-in-all, I recommend it with a bit of caution. Just know what you're getting yourself into, basically.
Yes it's short, that doesn't mean it isn't a great experience. But yes, I do want more of the world, of the story, of the game.

I highly recommend this game if you're one of the following.
1. 2D Fighting game fan
2. Typemoon Fan
3. General Anime fan
I've played tons of fighting games but I'm in no way super competitive so I can't explain to you what this game has as far as mechanics over other titles. what I can tell you is that it's characters is highly diverse with even the silliest ones fitting well into the world. There is no story mode however the Arcade mode of the game will provide at least enough dialogue to get you invested in the fighter, their goals (or lack thereof), and a hint of the lore.
To add to that each character has three different styles. Crescent, Half, and Full moons. If you're a combo heavy player you'll enjoy Crescent Moon style. Full moon style gives you hard hits and decent damage at the sacrifice of usually being slight slower. Finally Half-Moon style cuts out a lot of the more complicate mechanics and usually gives your character a more vast move set that is a mix of the other two. This essentially gives the already sizable cast nearly triple the size as they can play like a totally different fighter depending on the style you pick
The music of the game is fairly well done with a mix of mellow and harder hitting tracks. Plenty of stages, and while this game is a bit old the sprite work is still hasn't aged a day.
The netplay has been solid for me so far. Haven't had trouble playing in over 4 man lobbies.  Honestly there isn't very many flaws I can personally come up with. It is, and has remained, one of my favorite 2d fighting games and I once again highly recommend it.

Act of War: Direct Action has got to be the absolute best Real Time Strategy (RTS) game I've ever played in my entire life - and I'm a HUGE fan of Command and Conquer. The entire franchise.
Act of War: Direct Action had elements I never saw in Command and Conquer. For example, entering buildings was new but you had to first destroy the building or clear the enemy out before re-capturing it. A lot of times once the enemy had it, you couldn't take it from them. Command and Conquer: Red Alert 2 is a good example. In Act of War: Direct Action, if an enemy has a building and you want it, you must send in your infantry to fight for it. Your infantry will garrison the building and fight indoors to wrest control over it. Usually whomever has the most units or highest ranking units wins and the survivors are placed outside to be captured or left for dead.
I forgot to mention one of the best features of the game! You can capture wounded enemy infantry or non-combatants like vehicle crews or pilots. On the map, the resource is oil. You will eventually run out of it and once you do, well, you're sort of stuck. You'll get no more money. At all. Unless you have a hospital handy and enough to train some infantry. Wound some enemies, destroy some vehicles, and capture the infantry. Each enemy you capture gives you immediate money plus $50 every ~30 seconds. Each hospital can hold 10 prisoners so that's $500 every ~30 seconds. You can have an unlimited amount of hospitals to gain more and more money.
Units also gain veterancy based on kills and captures. When they attain new veterancy, their health bar increases and they get a small surge of healing/repairing for a few seconds. They also become more deadly.
Not to mention that each faction of the 3 available is unique in its own way. I usually pick favourites in RTS games but not this one. I can't. I absolutely love all 3 factions for different playstyles.
Building in this game was interesting too. The buildings were awesome and the animations for each structure fit amazingly. Airdropping a vehicle? You can watch it do so at no additional cost to wait time - the animation IS part of the wait time. Works for all types of structures.
You could call in airstrikes which I thought was amazing, but could make a game very difficult. There were lots of upgrades, vehicles, and infantry. The game was amazing.
What made it the best for me was how everything reacted to each other. In other games like Command and Conquer, infantry inside of a building could make short work of a tank. In Act of War: Direct Action, a tank takes less damage from small arms fire and can punch holes in structures. If hit in the right spot, can wipe out a small group of garrisoned infantry. Most of the time the building catches fire and it varies in size and can sometimes envelope the entire screen, making it hard to see what's going on. What else? Infantry can be placed on top of buildings - on the roofs. It doesn't really provide any extra cover or other bonuses but it's awesome. Sometimes I like to airdrop mortars on top of structures - like banks - to rain hell on the enemy and protect them from enemy tanks.
I can easily say I put over 1,000 hours into this game during the years I owned it. Of course, I owned it on disc. I still do, actually. I still find it to be the absolute best RTS game out there, right next to Company of Heroes 2 presently for realism.
Pretty much just an expansion of all the above but with added features.

Otherwise, it's the exact same as above. I only recently bought High Treason a couple years ago but either way, it pretty much gives me Direct Action with more features so I'll play this one. :)
Act of War: Direct Action and Act of War: High Treason are two of the best RTS games out there. Definitely pick them up. Both of them. Play them. Enjoy them. They are classics and you will probably never find anything like this again in your life.

I'm afraid I cannot recommend this game, even at a highly discounted price. The game plays ok, but it is just not interesting or complex enough to merit attention as a puzzle platformer.
Here are my main gripes:
-Platforming: The basic platforming mechanics of the game are not fun. Movement/jumping is functional, but it is sluggish and just doesn't feel good. I was also annoyed by ocassional cheap deaths when trying to jump over raised spikes--the hitboxes felt too large.
-Level Design/Puzzles:The level designs/puzzles are mostly lacking in challenge or complexity. Oftentimes, you can immediately see what you need to do to finish a level. There is very little sense of satisfaction in completing a level--very few "aha!" moments.
-The "Zombie Mode" Mechanic: A new mechanic is added late in the game, but it unfortunately makes the level design issues even more pronounced. The zombie mechanic often forces you to wait for long stretches of time before you can complete the next step of a puzzle. This kills any sense of momentum, since you may know exactly what you need to do, but must wait to do it. This zombie mechanic is especially annoying on the last level of the main game, which is extremely tedious (rather than complex).
-Steam Workshop: While it is great that the game includes a level editor and Steam Workshop support, the implementation is cumbersome. I had to go to the forums to figure out how to load and play levels I'd subscribed to. It was not an intuitive process.

A short (2-ish hours) horror game made in WOLF RPG Editor, a free alternative to RPG Maker. At launch the game was very crash-prone and I would've been more hesitant to recommend, but it's been patched up since then and is working fine again, with my own problems running the game being solved by switching AppLocale to English.
It's very much in the style of games like Ib or The Witch's House, with a focus on being playable and completable by anyone, and it's got some nice variety for a short game, a great sense of atmosphere and dread, some very good use of free assets to strong effect (including lots of examinable details), and keeps your motivation to get to the end going until it's all over. It is probably a little too easy for some (as someone who is terrible at adventure games, though, it's nice to have puzzles I can solve by myself) but is a lot easier and more player-friendly than The Witch's House, and has some neat little character moments (even if it relies a lot on flashbacks). An easy recommendation if you like short-form games, and there's also incentive to play a second time for more details you missed the first time.

Yet another gem on Steam that unfortunately many would let slip by. Personally, I couldn't recommend it enough, due to the resonable pricetag for all what its worth as an experience.
The game, had one of the most original and unique plots I've ever come across in a top down RPG game. I personally was so engaged and moved by the storyline that I just couldn't find the leeway on leaving the game half way through without having curiousity lingering in my mind.
Consequently, I managed to finish the entire game in straight 5-7 hours, collecting all the achievements whilst emphasizing on the comprehension of dialogue and minor details to get the perfect grasp on what the game had offered and truly, it was worth it.
By the end of the game, my experience regarding the game was unsettling due to the disturbing plot and the many twists that it had as per the progression in game but regardless of that, they were part of the escapade which was, dare I say, amusing.
Mad Father, as the title goes by is a psychological horror that offers exceptional soundtracks for every scenario in the game, an atmospheric top down level design, minor puzzles, simple controls and grotesque material / content in compliance with an innovative yet captivating plot. It comprises of multiple endings for which the choice is to be made at the very end of the game for the subsequent ending.
A fine indie rpg,  purely a bang for the buck, twisted yet fascinating.

Far Cry 2 is definitely one of my absolute favourite games.
Playing it, you see Salva Kiir, Jonas Savimbe, Laurent Nkunda, all the bush generals you ever wanted to read about in the rival faction leadership. They feel like real African war lords, vying for a cut of the UAC. Their dialogue feels like it's explaining bush generals who knew they could never finish the war or they'd have to govern, which they'd have difficulty doing.
The war of the acronym groups feels like I'm reading about South Sudan or the CAR; never ending, always splintering groups bent on coming out on top.
And then there's the characters that humanise the game; the Underground shows how desperate people are to get out but can't pay, Reuben the struggling, starving, hounded journalist, who'll never get recognition for his work because he's just another African, worse still, a freelance journalist.
Your buddies seem to be a mix of desperate and fool hardy, stuck somewhere they can't get out, but seem to always be that tiny step ahead of death or worse. The fact that they can come to your aid and you can come to theirs adds such a fantastic dynamic. The story works well with them, especially near the end.
The biggest quibble I have with the game is the NATIONAL SPORT IN THE UAC IS DRIVING. IT NEVER ENDS. I wouldn't mind so much if there wasn't checkpoint after respawning checkpoint of NPCs to try and get through. You don't have a lot of option BUT kill them because they'll shoot up your car and injure you. It's a real pain. Good thing safehouses and arms dealers are plentiful (safehouses anyway).
Foilage makes it damn near impossible to see an enemy before they see you. I don't know how they did it, but every time you're in contact, it's generally not because you initiated it.
The ending is kinda weak, but I can live with that considering how fantastic the story is and how it fleshes itself out. I love this game, warts and all, it's just the warts are really irritating.

Decided I'd do my first review for a game. I'll break this up into segments on my opinions.
Story: 5/10
Choose one of several starting people (no impact I could see except which companions appear in each location.) You were chosen to come kill The Jackal (Essentially, your only bestie). Upon entering the game (with a lengthy driving sequence with a guy I kinda liked, now presumed dead.) You catch malaria.  Now, it's more about the journey, than the destination I think. It kinda leaves you to your own machinations on how to get to point A to B.
Gameplay:  6.5/10
Now, the gameplay is pretty good actually, I have quite a bit more hours on this game than steam lets on. The A.I is actually a bit tactical, and use the environment to their advantage just as you do. I love how you can set a massive fire to distract the enemy, pick them off silently, or go in guns a blazing. However, this game isn't without flaws.
For one the stealth system is a bit wonky. I could be crouched in front of an enemy if broad daylight and not be seen. But, behind a bush in the dead of the night "Enemy!" Now, this is a minor issue as it only happens on those rare occasions, however the stealth suit really helps.
Next, it would have to be the Malaria. It's an annoying occurrence. At first it presents a bit of challenge, blurring the screen, possibly passing out in the middle of battle. Yet as you begin to realise you can't counteract it in any meaningful way. It becomes annoying.  You could do several missions to get pills for the malaria, attempting to stockpile. That proves useless as the game deems when you run out, even if you just went and collected five  different bottles.
Now, this is just my own personal flavor. I don't enjoy the lack of allies. Yes, the companions you get are helpful (especially when you get gunned down, and they save your sorry butt.) However, outside the 'cease fire' zones, everything is out to kill you. Now, this provides a bit of challenge (and I loved it at the beginning). It really brought on this 'stranger in an unknown land' vibe. Though, you quickly realise, that with all the hostile checkpoints, and respawn timer/system in general. It becomes a major annoyance. (They will find you, and they will ram you.) Just felt odd coming back through a checkpoint you wiped out, only for all enemies to be back after two minutes.
This one doesn't count into the score I give it, but I wish the wildlife had a bit more purpose. Now, I understand (haven't played them) in the later ones they do. But, this isn't a big deal, it at the least adds to the immersion and atmosphere.
Sound: 7/10
The sounds are great. Mostly accurate at least from what I gained to listen from. Running or moving through grass/concrete/dirt areas sounded different, so did driving suprisingly. Fires sounded as if they were burning stuff, waves sounded pretty decent. I loved how the enemies would communicate with each other in order to (for better or worse) try and kill you. The explosions are pretty great! Loved setting the plants, and such on fire, because it seemed to spread pretty decently. I jumped a few times when I heard the bullets passing beside my characters head.
Overall: 7/10
This game is a bit of an old one. Not that old, and it still looks really great. You probably noticed that lack of graphics section. I choose to not really judge a game by looks. Finding some of my most favorite games to not actually look that impressive.
The game overall is very fun, and definitely worth the purchase price at this point in time.  While it does have its flaws (what game doesn't?). It adds a bit of fun in your spare time. Now, the game does get semi-repetitive, and I don't suspect it has any replay value. (Unless, you decide not to take the 'buddy' misions first time around.
They can change the quests up slightly.) You can play through this game as much as you want, and still get an experience. But, if you've played through it twice (doing the side missions, and main missions (with and without buddy missions). You've pretty much seen it all.
The story itself is decent. A story of sacrifice, betrayal, malaria, and your bestie Jackal.

Conclusion: For serious FPS gamers with a lot of free time.
If you hate minimaps, markers, pointers above enemies: this is your game!

ESL is a F2P that looks better with every update. It only launches successfully at best half the time. The other half of the time it freezes up. This is unacceptable.  More unacceptable still, the single player campaign is short and to add insult to injury the single player campaign is merely just training you for the tedious multiplayer.
On top of that they expect you to pay what amounts to nearly another $80 for another 2 single player campaigns that should have been free, each probably five hours in length.  It would have been more practical to charge for multiplayer then penalize people like me who were only ever going to be interested in single player.
Do I think Elder Scrolls Legends is worth $5.23 an hour?  No I don’t.  It’s not that fun.  Might as well go back to Skyrim. I’ve logged in 300+ hours and it only cost me $1.20! Multiplayer matches seem like too much RNG and too much hassle for me.  Even the story campaign felt subpar. Sure it was in the Elder Scrolls universe, but so was Daggerfall.
It’s quite honestly an embarrassment to the Skyrim brand.  I’ll still log in to get my daily rewards don’t get me wrong, I just don’t think the game is either functional or good value. Maybe if the purchasable single player campaigns were a little cheaper and a little lengthier and everything was included I might have dropped $10 on this game.
Might have. On the other hand, you could do worse.  Cheeky enough Elder Scrolls Online, if you want everything is about $105 plus another $250 for an annual membershipOr you could just save yourself $350 something dollars, buy the old Skyrim and the all the dlcs for about $80 and mod it to Oblivion unless you’re a rich prick or mentally deficient.
Elder Scrolls Legends feels like a cheap, cynical cash grab. Probably because that’s all it is.  If you’re into this sort of thing, Hearthstone and Heroes of Might & Magic are better. If you’re like me and you’re playing it purely for the single player I can honestly recommend Infinity Wars or Hand of Fate over this so-called ‘game’, good joke Bethesda, really.

A highly underrated classic from the PS2/Xbox Era of gaming, The Bard's Tale offers challenging combat along with hilarious dialogue that will keep you lauging through out the entire quest for Coin, Clevage and Song. The Combat system is fairly similar to what's seen in the Fable games and offers many different ways to dispose of various threats to The Bard, you can chose to use a Sword and Shield for a balance of attack and defense, dual weilding to increase your Damage output or Two Handed for similar results. Or you can use a Flail to execute an unblockable attack, or you can summon allies through various songs you'll find through out the land and have them take care of your light work.
The Songs that play through out the game are not only hilarious but also very catchy, you'll no doubt find yourself singing at least one of them at some point after playing. Though there isn't much in the way of background music, the amusing and witty banter between the Narrator (Voiced by the late and Great Tony Jay) and The Bard (Voiced by Cary Elwes) is more than enough to make up for it. The humor is enhanced more if you're familiar with the various scottish folklore that inspired many of the monsters you encounter through out the game,
Graphic wise The Bard's Tale sports standard PS2/Xbox quality while not the most spectacular graphics by today's standards, at the time of the game's release they're not hard on the eyes either. All in all I recomend playing through this game at least once, I guarantee you'll end up laughing out loud numerous times and singing along to the games catchy musical numbers.
This version also comes with the original Bard's Tale games so you can experience  the classic games in addition to this one.

What can I say about this game? Long story short, Stranded is a wasted opportunity. A promising game sunken by many avoidable flaws. Do I recommend this game at its current price? Nope. Despite my love for it, It's a bit overpriced. So why did I end up recommending it anyway? Despite its flaws, I truly enjoyed my (little) time spent playing it. It came as a part of a 2€ bundle, so it was definitely a deal. If you can get it on a heavy discount or in a bundle, then you should really give it a try.
So, what's Stranded about? Stranded is a point and click exploration game, without dialogues or texts. You are a lone astronaut, woken up from your cryostasis on an unknown world. Your ship is heavily damaged and you have to find a way to survive before its imminent destruction.
Pros:
-Beautiful pixel arts, if you're a fan of retro graphics you'll love it for sure.
-The landscapes are very bright and colorful, I enjoyed taking my time just exploring the planet.
-Outstanding soundtrack, very fitting and immersive. I really really loved it.
-I personally liked the ending, it totally caught me by surprise.
-Immersive atmosfere.
Cons:
-The game is pretty short. I usually don't care about games length, as long as the game itself provides meaningful contents. So in this case I'm not really bothered about it. I completed Stranded in 1 hour, but I took my sweet time wandering around and taking screenshots, so it probably can be finished in half and hour or so, I guess.
-There's no real interaction with your surroundings. During the first minutes I tried to click on everything, hoping there would have been some kind of reaction, but nothing happened.
-You basically have to explore the world and walk a lot. Not necessarily a con, I personally like exploration games. Too bad your character walks really slow, so if you're not into "walking simulator" games, you should probably skip this one as well.
-The point and click can be really frustrating: you have to click somewhere on the screen to move your character, but you have to wait till she's done walking before moving again. The fact that she walks that slow doesn't help at all, so better not click the wrong way.
Times like these I wish there were a "maybe" recommendation option. I personally loved this game and don't regret playing it at all, but at the same time I'm aware this is not a game for everyone.
In the end, I really wish this game could be improved. It has a lot of potential, and I feel bad about the negative reviews it gets (although I fully understand why). Nonetheless, I'm sure many people will enjoy it anyway despite its weak points.

Pros: Nice art and music. Atmosphere. Decent animation.
Cons: Artificially lengthened by slow walking speed and being unable to move directly from one side of the screen to another. You have to click multiple times, and you always stop at every waypoint. Probably from animation/engine difficulties. The trailer's a clue to the game play - half of the scenes have the player standing in the exact same position on every screen.
There are around five things that you can click on in the game that aren't just room transitions, and there's no feedback on what's clickable. You'd think that a point-and-click lets you interact more, but you quickly stop that. Because if you click in the wrong direction, you have to sit there and wait for the character to move. There's a little over a dozen screens, most of them being non-interactive - you just walk through them, half a minute each. If it wasn't for the interactions taking so frustratingly long, and having to do everything in the exact special order, this game could be finished in 5 minutes.
Verdict: Don't bother. It's over-hyped and over-priced. There's no dialog, and not enough interaction to justify that. No plot, no gameplay - just setting. I'm annoyed that they wasted my time to inflate the game length. It seems there was a grand vision involved to justify the "Adventure" tag that was promptly sent through the wood-chipper. Makes me feel bad because it had potential. As is, it's a slideshow with music. Caveat emptor.

Frontiers is a buggy, but immersive open-world RPG game made by one man, and I heartily recommend it if you want to feel like you're a part of the world you're exploring, and doing everything you can to unearth its secrets.
+ Graphics: Pretty good when everything is maxed.
+ Gameplay: Explore, and do everything with your own hands.
+ Audio: GREAT music, ambient sound, and sound effects.
+ Really good fasttravel system!
+ A ton of sights to see!
+ Engaging story
- Performance: Pretty bad when everything is maxed.
- Bugs: Bugs can be found easily in many areas.
- Bugs: No really, you've been warned.
- Fast travel will often kill you.
+/- Doesn't hold your hand at all.
+/- Requires a pretty decent GPU.
+/- Some of the sounds are louder than they should be.
You are a man whose uncle has according to the law, passed away, on a quest to honor his life by doing the chores he left behind in it, and potentially find him across the Rift on the way. The Rift is an aptly named place where everything stops in favor of a more molten theme. Many have tried to cross it, but any who have, have yet to come back. Your family has been trying for generations, with varying degrees of success, and Daniel has caught this wanderlust. Will you?
Welcome to FRONTIERS. a game about exploring new frontiers! I can definitely see the comparisons to Morrowind and Daggerfall here, and I'll add my own, this universe is strangely reminiscent of one of my favorite series as a kid: Deltora Quest. Everything has an ethereal sense of urgency and wonder and magic.
FRONTIERS sets a slow-paced lore-filled task of mainly exploring before you. You will wander from location to location, reading books, talking to inhabitants, burning firewood, ocassionaly fighting beast and man alike, and occasionaly partaking of food and drink. Skills may level through usage or by studying books, but skills take a backseat to your sightseeing, of which there is much to do. Every area feels unique, from the lay of the land, to the construction of the homes, to the color of the ground or sky or plants.
One thing this game doesn't do is hold your hand. I'm surprised the map even marks locations, or where you are currently, for that matter. You will be told to go places  without specific instructions on how to get there, or where specifically to go. You will be thrust into a world with little idea of how to interact with it. You will be tasked with surviving with no instruction on how to kill, what to kill with, or what all you can or can not eat. And for some people that's where all the fun comes from. You will be given basic instructions, though, such as that you need food, water, and to avoid the ocean. At one point I successfully asked for directions to a family friend. It's not all bad, just hit and miss. Depth is how I would sum up my experience.
All things said, it seems there's a lot beneath the surface here, with plenty of things to see.
The graphics in FRONTIER are beautiful, for a price. You will take quite a hit to performance for maxing them out, but they will look quite nice. There's a good sense of light and dark, and things look relatively realistic. Nights are nice and dark, and light sources aren't fountains of bloom. A lot of the models look fairly realistic, but the animations could use just a little work. I can't say too much about the graphics, because they need to be experienced through playing, and also, in order to play, I had to turn them down to late 90s level quality.
The audio in FRONTIERS is amazing. Everything and everywhere will have an exhuberant ambient sound to go with it that gives the game some real life. Some of it can be a little loud depending on the location, though, seeming a bit unrealistic. Each region has unique music, offering a nice thematic touch. The audio cues are nice, but the lack of any voice for the NPCs makes things feel slightly lonely after a while. Either way, what's there has heart and soul.
I heavily recommend experiencing this game for yourself, even if it can be quite buggy, and is definitely still a bit early in development. It's beautiful, vast, varied and feels like it has been imbued with the heart and soul of its creator.

I want to love this game, I really do.  The concept is great, the dev is passionate and invested in making it...
...but it's a hot mess.
It's loaded with game breaking bugs, AI pathfinding issues, the controls feel swimmy and loose, the menus are confusing and hard to navigate, combat is servicable at best.
It really feels like the dev should have started with a smalled area, gotten the engine hammered out and functional, then worried about story and content after.  As it stands, it's pretty unplayable, and despite several updates, not much ever really changes.
Getting the world working should be the priority before deciding how players should buy things.
All in all, worth a follow, and maybe a causious purchase to support the dev as he really does seem dedicated to making his game happen, but if you're looking for something to play, you may want to hold off.  Can't recommend it for now, but will keep checking back on it.

Please keep in mind, FRONTIERS is in the Early-Access Beta Stage. FRONTIERS, is a First Person perspective RPG, with low budget graphics. In it's early-access state, it still has bugs, but reminds me of Morrowwind a little. It has a vast map, full of varying landscapes, and Villages with NPC's. Collect resources and live off the land, Interact with NPC's, Explore and Discover ancient ruins, FRONTIERS is a complete open-world RPG.
I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoys open-world RPG's, but I will stress again that it is an Early-Access Beta, so it does have bugs, and the graphics are something you would expect of a game from 2002 - 2004, not 2015. This doesn't make it a bad game, but for some who are used to the hyper-realism of todays games, the point needs to be stressed. Given the game is being created by one person, I can only imagine what it could be if it had a full team of developers and the budget of an Elder Scrolls game. I think this game has a lot of potential and give it a thumbs up.

is a horror game made with Wolf RPG Editor (not RPG Maker!) that was originally released in 2012 as freeware. So is it worth buying when you can play it for free? I'd say yes! While there weren't a lot of changes from the free version, they're at least big enough to be worth paying for. You can check the first update for the full list of changes, but basically most of the graphics were updated, new scenes were added and some aspects of the gameplay were changed.
As for the game itself, it’s one of the better examples of its little sub-genre. The plot and characters aren’t super complex, but they do have a B-movie charm to them. The art is well drawn, and its huge character portraits set it apart from similar games. The puzzles are clever without being too difficult. It’s also an easy game to 100%, if you care about that.
Unfortunately, it’s on the short side; completing it takes around 2 - 3 hours, maybe 4 if you decide to get all of the achievements. While the Steam version used to have a lot of bugs the publisher, Playsim, has been diligent about fixing them. My only major complaint is that some of the sound effects are too loud, such as Aya's scream when you get a game over, but according to the updates this might have been fixed? I wouldn't turn your sound up all the way just in case.
Overall,
is definitely worth playing if you like indie horror games. You should also play
, which is by the same creator, if you haven't already. (It currently isn't on Steam but I would totally buy it if it were.)

Most people buying this game have been playing it and its predecessors for over a decade, either by importing it through some dodgy online shop, or through other less official means. It's good this game got its long overdue official localization.
If you're new to this game and wondering if you should buy it, it's a fairly easy game to pick up at any skill level or experience with fighting games in general. It's fairly well balanced and has a bunch of neat mechanics, which keeps it interesting at a higher skill level. Most of the special moves are fairly easy to execute, with the most difficult ones being a half circle on a controller/stick. The gameplay itself is fast paced compared to most others in the genre. There's a wide variety of characters to play with, and each character comes with three styles to experiment with. I'll spare you the details, but it should give you enough variation to keep the game fresh and fun for a long time.
The graphics might look a bit dated, but if you keep in mind that the original artwork for this game is older than a decade it's not really a surprise. That said, given the general style of the game it doesn't really get in the way, and it doesn't matter with the gameplay anyway. The music for most stages is very well done, and sometimes a little too catchy.
As for multiplayer... By default as it is, it's a good game for playing with a friend coming over, but the netcode for online play is abominable. Previous iterations of this game were often played using the help of an external tool called CCCaster, so I'm sure something similar will come out over time to make the experience more enjoyable. A bit of a shame the netcode didn't get an update, but I really wasn't expecting a major update to this particular age old problem.
On the downside, if you do play against someone over the internet, chances are they've been playing this game on and off for roughly 10 years, and have likely at some point tossed a few 100 yen coins into one of the machines still present in some of the arcade halls in Akihabara today.

I am certain that after excessive amounts of practice, it becomes possible, but I am not sure if the trouble is worth it. There are barely any sound effects of any kind. You will hear the occasional beeps and bloops every once in a while, but that is all besides the continuous uninspired music. The game does not give you any indication that you are actually running around and jumping. There is no feeling involved with the movement and game physics. It is as if you are gliding from place to place, then floating, gliding some more, all with odd physics that do not blend well with the game's setting or anything that makes any sense at all. Timing your glides and floats so that you land on the platforms requires mostly luck, as the controls are incredibly imprecise, and do not allow for the player to develop any real skills or techniques in order to accomplish each level rapidly and properly. inMomentum does not have any story or introduction as to why you are doing this gliding and floating around on platforms collecting orbs and doing time trials. There is no campaign of any kind to speak of, and the only aspect of the game that provides feelings of accomplishment are found in online leaderboards for the two limited game modes available. The game is so bare bones, in fact, that you will wonder if it was actually finished, and if the developer should actually be expecting money for it. inMomentum is a cheap, unfinished, unpolished, bore. Play it every once in a while for five to ten minutes at a time in order to maximize your fun with it.

I really enjoyed my time with this game, but now that I'm at the point where I'm no longer likely to spend any more time with it I find myself being disappointed.

Let me explain.

This game handles speed really well and pulling off a flawless run feels great. There's a decent amount of content to keep you occupied, and there are some pretty well designed levels that are fun to play over and over. The core mechanics feel solid and are satisfying. Basically, if you're into speedruning at all this should be right up your alley.

That being said there is certainly a huge lack of polish on this game. The game advertises multiple game modes but only one of them is worth playing. The difficulty modes are an interesting idea, but there certainly doesn't need to be as many of them as there are. Some levels are (while all beatable) clearly not designed for the hardest one. Additionally, its also impossible (from what I can see) to tell how many rockets you have left on the harder settings.

I really wish the devs stuck with this game a bit longer. While I am mostly satisfied with what I got, I can only imagine how great this game would have been with workshop support or even decent alternative game modes, but it looks like we wont be getting any of that. Overall it's still a good time, and worth a buy if its on sale.

An absorbing and atmospheric, if repetitive and drawn out shooter.
Pros:
- Has aged incredibly well graphically. The lighting can still take your breath away, and sometimes you can just feel the heat of the savannah pouring off the screen
- Weapons pack a punch with wide variety and immensely satisfying sound effects
- The game conveys a sense of collapse and decrepitude very well: things are worn out, rusted, breaking down, dirty, piles of garbage and decay litter the landscape, the characters are cynical, ruthless, amoral and opportunistic, and even the few safe zones feel like they're one step away from total war
- The open world allows a multitude of ways to approach missions, as well as chaos and mayhem to escalate in unpredictable ways completely organically, adding to the atmosphere of anarchy
- Good vehicle handling
- The minimalist story allows the player to advance at their own pace and get lost in the exploration without pressure
Cons:
- Very repetitive: all the missions save for the most important story ones are virtually identical, and the side missions are literally identical
- The aggressive AI can be downright silly at times. You'll often be forced to a quick firefight with an errant mercenary truck when you'd rather just be getting on with the mission
- Minimal story: if you're looking for emotional attachment or an amazing story, you won't find it here
- Drawn out: this could have easily been split into two different single player campaigns, or been a game and a DLC pack, but instead it's essentially the same campaign played twice in a row. And since the best weapons and more interesting environments are only available in the second half of the game, replaying the first half becomes a chore
- To get upgrades for the safe houses you need to do optional story mission objectives which do nothing but draw out their duration
- A bug prevents you from being able to listen to half of the Jackal's audio tapes, which is a big loss, considering he's the only interesting character (or even character per se) in the game
This is a game that puts gameplay and exploration ahead of story or complexity. If you don't mind that and a fair bit of repetition, I can recommend this game.

The Bard's Tale is a comedy based action/adventure with RPG elements.
The plot of the game is your sterotypical 'rescue the princess and live happily
ever after' story, but with a comedic twist.
Ironically, the game that centers around a Bard has a distinct lack
of music, which does take away from the atmosphere somewhat.
Despite this being a game from 2005, graphically it does a good job
of keeping up with the times. Visually the only issue I noticed was
as the game wasn't designed for 1920x1080, the overhead view was
lacking a bit in peripheral vision, making it difficult to see far ahead.
The level design does hint at its' age, and although it isn't bad,
and ties in well to the world map, it does harken back to ye old "05.
It does a good job of showing different atmospheres, but does get
repetitive as you travel between the main towers of the game.  That
combined with the limited combat makes for a stretched out feel, and
takes away from the enjoyment of gameplay.
The UI is well done, and every object in the game has the potential
for synergy with other objects.  One big plus is that unwanted loot
is automatically changed to money, eliminating the need for constant
return trips to merchants, or constant inventory management.  As a
self-admitted loot ♥♥♥♥♥, I found this to make the game stronger by
playing around its' limitatons.
Overall, this game is well balanced, has a strong and entertaining story,
and while it may not be 'game of the year', it's a fun experience that
I can happily recommend.

There are very few games I play through more than once.   There are even fewer RPGs.  This is one of them.  With the amazing vocal talents, excellent music, laugh-out-loud funny comments, asides, and conversations, this game will forever give me a smile.
As with the majority of RPGs, you're a low-level schmo who gets 'invited' to partake on an ever-expanding adventure where you ascend the level tree, getting bigger weapons, fighting bigger monsters, and eventually get the girl, and live happily ever after.  Except in this case, the game shows that things aren't quite peachy, and seem to go downhill, rather than up.
The game shows you the wonderful side-effects of your murderous misanthropy, as you gaily stab, shoot and zap your way across a beautiful scottish and norse-themed fantasy land... Whether you follow the plot, or try to deviate from it, the wonderful writing keeps you amused, and on your toes, guiding you in the right direction at all times.
There's a LOT in this game, although it sometimes doesn't feel that way.   The level-grinders will find a lot to keep them amused, the magic-lovers, the archers, the swordsmen, will all find that the balance is quite nice (although I think the bow may be slightly under-powered compared to the sword, but only by a fraction, and the ability to sit out of the action and pepper opponents with arrows is fun enough.).  I've played this through as both sword and bow, and both are very playable.
I can heartily recommend this to anyone who likes a good old-fashioned RPG, but wants something with its tongue firmly wedged in its cheek.    Wonderful on both PC and android, it's a great game for whiling away the hours.
The voice acting of the wonderful Tony Jay will forever be missed.  His voice lives on in all the games and TV media he did.  You should play this, just to hear his wry humour and phenomenal voice.
Thanks  InXile! You've made an old-fashioned RPGer very happy!

While I won't say this isn't a game, it is a completely vapid experience. By definition, games are an interactive medium. Thing is, this game loses nothing if you just watch a no-commentary Youtube play-through. Being in the driver's seat changes nothing in my opinion. You click around for a while, then it ends with the player having had no substantive part in the game other than getting the character from beginning to end. The "game" part of the game is slow and egregious, using a point-to-point movement system that is dated even by early AGI point and click games. The reason I bring it up is that it is the first thing you are presented with is the painfully slow game-play and it drags so much that even if there was a promise of an interesting story (which, in my opinion, there isn't) I found it impossible to connect with the game in any way because the constant busy work of clicking around the world pulled me out the experience.
The sound design, art and music are all fantastic. Truly outstanding for a game of this caliber, but it doesn't remotely excuse what a hollow experience this game is overall. Also, an eight dollar price-tag for this game is downright criminal consider the quality of the overall experience. I have no problem with a game being short as long as it's good but this game is not. In the face of simplistic, arduous game-play, the game's last possible sell was being interesting and I just didn't find that was the case. Maybe the story, mystery, and/or adventure will make/have made this a positive experience for you but it just didn't happen for me. I don't even think an involving story can't emerge in as minimalistic of a game as this is however I just found that, in this instance, there was nothing here for me; which is a shame considering how good all of the aesthetic parts of the game are.

Character is moving too slow, and controls in general feels odd. It's hard to imagine someone can produce, and have a courage to sell such half-baked product.
I wouldn't be angry if a game would be offered as what it is. But to mention Stanley Kubrick and a minimalist adventure game, for something that basically feels like very much unfinished, non-even-a-tech-demo of a game, it's just offensive. I have feeling something went very wrong at a very early stage of development and someone said: "can't we use just what we have and brand it as some fabulous Zen, minimalistic adventure game?" Sure, why not. It's not a question of money (I've paid something like 5eur + got it as a part of one bundle), it's a question of honesty. I felt cheated, and by the amount of negative reviews here, I see I'm not the only one.

After +13 years of waiting, its finally here. Considered one of the holy grails of fighters, Melty Blood: Actress Again Current Code has finally released in the States thanks in a big part to publisher Arc System Works. Melty Blood started originally as a doujin fighting game co-developed by  French-Bread, Ecole Software and Type-Moon, the very same Type-Moon thats behind the Fate/Stay Night visual novel series. Melty Blood is a follow up to Tsukihime which is another VN title made by Type-Moon. Its not necessarly to play Tsukihime first in order to enjoy Melty Blood, but it does help to get a better grasp of the overall lore and characters of the series. Melty Blood has gone through a number of itterations which leads into this latest version released on Steam. What stands out from other fighters is that despite the simple 5 button set up there's quite of bit of layers and complexity with its mechanics. 3 different fighting styles for each of the 31 character roster gives the potential of near limitless possibliies on finding your perfect fighter. This along with an online mode gives the potential for a thriving community.
Pros:
-A total of 31 characters, each with 3 optional fighting styels to choose from giving different results on how they play
-The music for the most part gives that supernatural vibe one would expect from Tsukihime
-The simple 5 button set up is easy to grasp, but the layers and complexity of the game's mechanics with their own risk/rewards and features makes for a much beefy fighter that even some of the more mainstream fighters today have yet to achieve
-The story mode, while straight forward, does in part make you feel as if one was playing a visual novel
-The online mode is simple fairly easy to navigate and does the job of getting a match going
Cons:
-The available modes offered is standard at best
-The online mode, while mostly fuctional, is something to be desired since this version of Melty Blood AACC doesnt use CCCaster, but a delay beased built.
-Being that this is a decade old game, there is some age shown in the visuals, especially some of the screen tearing during fights. It doesnt break the game but it is present even with your gpu's V-sync on.
-The game isn't quite newbie friendly for those looking for a simple fighter to jump into.
Vertict:
Thumbs up and an easy high reccomendation for experienced fighting fans especially for those who want a complete experience in their fighters (looking at you SF5). The online mode needs some tweeking and the screen tearing is at times annoying. Hopefully some of these issues will be addressed with patches. The $25 price point is a little high for a decade old fighter as Melty Blood, but there's nothing wrong waiting for a sale knocking it down to $20 or lower. Either way you're still getting a premium fighting game to add to your library.

Let me just start this off by saying that if you love Type-Moon, you should get this game. If you love fighters, you should get this game. There is a reason this series has been a staple of the Japanese fighting scene for well over 10 years.

This game unfortunately fell into a trap many artsy flash games fall into: artificial restriction of choice.
I can't explore beyond the tiny 10 or so screens they give me.
I can't attempt to interface with any of the ship's other systems.
I can't attempt to read or record a log from the ship.
I can't attempt to fix the ship.
I can't examine any of the plants or minerals on this strange, alien world.
I can't take off my helmet and test the hard way to see if the atmosphere is breatheable.
I can't kill myself by jumping over the cliff.
I can't talk.
I can't attack.
I can't even run.
My only options are slowly meander and eventually sleep.
This doesn't make sense, given the situation. I play a stranded space-faring survivalist, not a Roomba.
Again, this game reminds me of many FREE flash games I've played in the past. Artsy, ponderous, but ultimately not plausible or relatable given the narrow railroad the player is forced to travel.

First of all, I just want to say that I have played the original Mad Father and Misao games, and thoroughly enjoyed both. This developer has always impressed me with their ability to create interesting storylines that keep the player entertained.
The controls are simple, and gameplay is pretty straight-forward; there is nothing complex about it. The story and environment are why you want to play this game.
Now, with this simple, remastered version, there are many improved elements. Among these are improved visuals, new puzzle styles (the "correct sequence" method, instead of "button mashing" when being attacked), and, of course, some great, new character development. Each ending is unique, and provides a plot twist to the storyline, including the "If" ending.
Just like in the original version, you can unlock character art and tracks used in the game, which are always a nice little touch.
To put it simply, this game is a great buy. I am personally very thrilled it has reached Steam!

Act of War is one of the finest Real-Time-Strategy games in gaming history. Its graphics are superb even by modern standards, and the realistic US Army faction makes Act of War what many gamers wished CnC:Generals had been. The game plays very similarly to Generals, but lacks any generals themselves to add flavor to the skirmishes. The units don't have anything witty or neccessarily interesting to say; they instead respond in ways that you'd expect their real-life counterparts to respond. If you're a fan of RTS but want to play in a world which looks and sounds authentic as opposed to the sci-fi or cartoon representation of other RTS games, then AoW is exactly what you're after.
Despite its age, it works on modern machines, including Windows 10 and even NVIDIA mobile series graphics cards, which are notorious for their legacy incompatibility. If you're like me and more interested in playing skirmishes than the campaign, then Act of War: Direct Action is uneccesary because Act of War: High Treason is a standalone expansion pack which includes the full game. The only thing that DA has which HT doesn't is the DA campaign.
AoW is an amazing game, quite possibly the best RTS yet. It's a steal at three bucks. Buy it, play it, love it.

This quirky, yet highly involved, visual novel clawed its way into my heart with its dramatic flair, vibrant characters, and poignant storyline.
If you're even remotely interested in the title, give it a chance. It's pretty darn good.
One of the first things that stand out upon starting the game are its outlandish premise and slightly-subpar visuals. Don't get me wrong, most of the actual dedicated CGs and completion art is absolutely fantastic, but the standard character portraits are kind of lacking in comparison, which, coupled with the premise of the story may seem a little unpolished and be a turnoff for some. (Though, of course, the basis of dating dragons is also the main enticement of the game!)
However, the actual story itself more than makes up for these minor issues; it is an experience that not only tugs at the heartstrings but leaves the player thinking. The pacing and wording suffer from a modest amount of discomfort here and there, but the main humour, drama, and plot devices (as well as the "romance" sections) are blended together in a pleasing and familiar manner. There are much less dating-sim elements present in the game than the store page would have you believe (and a lot more drama instead); most of the possible romance scenes seem like natural extensions of the main storyline and serve to further worldbuilding and character development. In the same vein, the aforementioned scenes do not include any of the explicit "romance-reward" scenes one would expect to find in a run of the mill dating sim. Well, most of the romance options don't. (The ones that do are totally worth it, though.)
Not much else can be said about the storyline without potentially spoiling anything, so I will simply take the liberty of saying that it is, in short, really good. The emotion embedded in the plot, though not the absolute pinnacle of tragedy, is definitively touching and invested, and it is bested only by the drama and turmoil of the sci-fi elements of the plot. Oh, and of course, there are several secrets to be found as well, not just in the story, but also elswhere...
To conclude, if you are a dedicated fan of visual novels (or dragons), I would highly recommend picking up Angels with Scaly Wings. However, if you're looking for something romantically-focused, or a light, happy dating sim, this is not the VN for you. General playtime is around 10-15 hours, or a lot more, depending on how generously the player uses the skip function.
P.S. The soundtrack deserves a mention; it's rather pleasant, fits the atmosphere of scenes well, and I enjoyed it overall, but in my opinion, it's not anything exceptionally special.

Top-down view RPG-lite, more of an action-adventure, I suppose - one of those titles that focuses more on the characters and story rather than loot, combat, or game mechanics in general.
That is not to say it abandons game mechanics completely - just simplifies them compared to more mainstream RPGs (especially "western", as opposed to JRPGs).
However, in the story department - it excels, with witty, humorous writing (it's essentially a parody/spoof of fantasy RPG games) and superb voice acting (at least in English version). Well worth playing just for that! And you'd be surprised how much is based on real world mythology and places.
There are essentially two main characters in the game - the eponymous Bard, whose misadventures you follow and whom you control directly, and The Narrator, who holds the Bard in great contempt, never failing to throw in some sarcastic commentary. There's fourth wall to be broken for sure, and generally the game does instill this idea that it is a tale, sort of reenactment you're witnessing, rather than directly participating in, at least that's how it worked for me - I would place myself, perhaps paradoxically, more next to The Narrator, who's spinning the tale, rather than the Bard, who's living (reliving?) it.
The story mostly revolves around Bard being
Chosen One, enduring trials and tribulations to save a princess, although his motives are clear: coin and cleavage, and definitely
saving the world. Which rapidly enters worse and worse state. Which may or may not be related to Bard's questing around. Nothing really to dwell on much, you're here pretty much to enjoy the ride.
I finished it on hard difficulty, but I wouldn't really bother if I were you, it only serves as annoyance really rather than a proper challenge, and everything can be easily cheesed anyway, with you shooting offscreen enemies with bows, minmaxing dexterity and rhythm (as a bard, you can summon variety of allies and rhythm makes them stronger), so playing it easy just lets you enjoy the ride more.
If you're unaware, it's well worth pointing out that none other than Brian Fargo is behind this game, one of industry titans (does Fallout ring a bell? something he was personally responsible for, not mentioning other great titles he was more or less involved with, and most recently, Kickstarter backed great promises of Torment and Wasteland 2). You really should cast away any doubts with regard to writing quality this game has to offer (mind though, again, it's not a "serious" title, and not big one either, giving off somewhat indie, passion project vibe rather than triple-A vibe Interplay could muster and inXile not so much, at least until Kickstarter and ever growing technological advances.. but I digress; look the guy up on Wikipedia if you don't know who he is).

The Last Days Of Spring is a visual novel developed and published by Sapphire Dragon Productions. The title follows a group of high school seniors in their last week of school as they come to terms with questions about love, life and destiny. You take the role of Yuka Kishimoto, a brilliant student as she navigates across her final week as a high school student and sees her life come to a complete change. Yuka begins feeling the pressure as one stage of her life comes to an end just as the next is set to begin and, as the reader, you come along for the ride as she experiences the last days of her high school education.
This is a pleasant albeit quite short visual novel about teen life with some minor choices scattered throughout the storyline. One thing I really like about visual novels is the art which The Last Days Of Spring had on the characters but for the backgrounds they opted to use photographs of real places instead of hand drawn or C.G. art which I did not enjoy. Nonetheless, the story was enjoyable and quite nostalgic for anyone who has already completed high school. Whether those memories were good or bad, reading this novel will definitely take you back to a similiar time and place that Yuka is experiencing.
The Last Days Of Spring was a nice read, and I repeat, although very short which was a little disappointing. However, there are Steam Acheivements and Steam Trading cards to collect and multiple endings so there is replayability with this title. This is not one of the most enjoyable visual novels that I've read thus far on Steam but I'm happy to hear that there is a sequel available and I look forward to trying it as soon as possible as I would love to find out what course Yuka's life took after high school. In summary, I would recommend The Last Days Of Spring only if you are a fan of V.N.'s or teen angst.

As a high schooler who is set to graduate in a few months, this visual novel stuck out to me. Yuka Kishimoto is facing questions that can apply to high schoolers anywhere. What's next? Should I go to college? Where should I go to college? What should I major in? What if I don't know what to major in? Is it wrong to not go to college? These are all questions that Yuka faces now that the reality of graduating high school has set in.
Note that I have not played the sequel yet. These are just my thoughts on the first one.

Stranded is a "minimalist adventure game" in which your spaceship has crashed on some planet. You have to explore the area and discover anything that might help you survive. This is the description on the game page on Steam. Now I'm not to judge, there have been many a short minimalist game that have been well done. Music, characters, atmosphere that can illicit emotional response, these are the ideas that come to mind whenever I think of "minimalist".
At first glance Stranded looks promising. You eagerly leave your ship and enter the desolate outer space area searching for either other signs of live or at least something that might pique your fancy. At this point you're in the category of a hopeful explorer. As you search your unfamiliar surroundings you follow admire and wonder about the animated automatons if they might be the only inhabitants of your new home away from home. Sure they don't seem to be able to communicate but you're hopeful that there are intelligent beings of some kind if there's a bunch of stone machines walking around. Surely someone had to have made them. Even more so you soon find temples, which is great! Nothing screams LIFE more than finding places of worship. After you've exhausted your search the music fades and you head back to your ship because well there's nothing left to do.
You're then given the option to come back out at night. And why not, many places come alive when the sun goes down and this planet was no different. Not only does the terrain develop this luminous glow you've got an upbeat soundtrack to go with your renewed search effort. After you light up a bunch of temples you go back to your ship and wait for morning.... then do the same thing again.
Okay, now I feel a bit suckered. Here I was thinking this game might have turned out to be a cross between Don't Starve and Waking Mars. Both decent games in their own right. But I spent about 30 minutes on this game only to come to quite a depressing end but all I felt was a twinge of resentment for getting my hopes up. Even more so when the game asks if I wanted to start over at the end only for me to waste another 20 minutes hoping there might have been a different ending the second time around.
Unfortunately the music was the only thing I liked about this game. The atmosphere was a bit of a let down as there wasn't much to interact with or explore. Heck you couldn't even choose how you decided to end it. If I paid full price for this game I would have felt cheated.

It looks like a classic fighting RPG - attacking monsters and the cruel end boss. It's anything but.
is a mystery game which tells the story of young Aya. A terrible curse has fallen on her father's mansion, creatures crawl through the halls, and ghosts hunt the weak. Knowing she needs to find a way past the atrocities, Aya goes on a difficult journey -- to save her father.
Eager to try this classic gem, I bought the game on Halloween 2016. The look of the graphics made me feel nostalgic, the game play looked like a challenge and the story appealed to me due to its gruesome theme. When do you get to play Frankenstein's daughter? Rarely. And for sure not in Anime-style.
As player, you control Aya with the classical arrow keys (keyboard). Your aim is finding and saving your father. While you solve the riddles in the mansion, you uncover more of the terrible details, and also about your own past. When you get caught by a monster, you'll end up smashing your buttons in order to escape its grasp, left, right, left, up, down, and I'm telling you, you need to be fast.
The game has become a collocation of quick time events and sneak scenes, while you need to figure out where to find and use your items. This leads to a refreshing gameplay and a rich story. For once, you're not the almost invincible main character, but a weak girl who will be left alone if you fail. Adding the multiple endings and the loveable characters, this game is a must have for every mystery/horror fan who is also into Anime. The screenshots don't lie!

Just what I'd been looking for to close my Halloween vacation!  This gore-drenched doujin gave me the same creepy vibe as the PS2's best horror games!
+Great story -- Important for a horror game!  It eases you in with simplicity, but gradually adds many layers, and this well-paced story hits that prime spot between too little and too much explanation.  If you like a blood-spattered tale with an undertone of bittersweet melancholy, I guarantee you'll come away satisfied.
+Great, natural translation -- I can't tell you how much it bugs me when I watch otherwise well-made indie games from
wallow in bad grammar and awkwardness.  Good job, translators!
+Great visuals -- The 16-bit chibi graphics have considerable detail and variety throughout.  Manga portraits and stills look fantastic as well, with a wide variety of emotive/situational variants for each character.  Very professional!
+Awesome sound design -- Agonized screams, the squish of corpseflesh underfoot, the sudden gush of blood from a savagely rent body --  the exaggerated sounds of horror seem like comic book onomatopoeia brought into the aural world, perfectly fitting the manga visuals.  The noises may be cartoony, but they'll still creep you the heck out!
-Bugs --  Some people can't load their saved games.  I had this at first on my Windows 7 system, but I changed the theme from Aero to Windows Basic and everything ran fine after that.
All in all,
is an awesome little doujin that proves the versatility of 16-bit chibi!  Make sure that you get all 21 gems so you can unlock the IF ending; it sets up a potential sequel!
