First thing I want to say before I start the actual review. THIS GAME IS BEAUTIFULLY TWISTED!
In this game you play as a girl named Aya who has a normalish family, from what it seems like at the start of the game. Until one specific night a curse is dropped on your home and everything starts to become hellish. From here you must try to save your father well demons and angry spirits roam about.
This game will give you a lot of mixed emotions during it until the very end when three specific ones hit you. First one is a bit of terror. The second one is sadness. Then the third one is. . . WAIT WHAT?!?
This game is filled with puzzles and obstacles which will sometimes get you stuck on certain parts of the game for a while until you manage to figure them out. This game also has a unique thing where you will sometimes get caught by a monster or whatever and you'll have to mash certain buttons together to get free. You might get stuck a few times at the start thanks to this but once you get a hang of it than it is fairly easy.
In terms of scares this game delivers them. There is a nice little mix of jumpscares and chases which I like. Also well on the topic of jumpscares. This games jumpscares aren't cheap ones. They made me jump a few times. . . okay a lot!
This games story is one that you will remember since it is twisted, dark, and even lovely at some parts aswell.
Overall I will give this game a 5/5 and highly recommend this to anyone who likes horror games or just really likes suspenseful stories and a good scare.

The sequal to Act of War Direct Action, I bought the DVD version back in 2006. so even Steam registered me only played less than an hour, I believe I can still write a fair review.
first of all, you do not need to have AoW: DA installed to play. however

Act of War: High Treason follows the TFT commander Jason Richter to discover and prevent a political scheme. Fight against the old enemy of Consortium and on few instances, the US military.
This sequal carries on the innovative system from AoW DA, where wounded infantry and downed pilot become part of the economy syetm in the game. It comes with new units and new campaign. the new units adds several tactical options for each factions. making it more interesting to play. However the missions are not as well designed as those in Direct Action: some comes with odd restriction and conditions, making it just too difficult to beat. New units includes Naval units, but only available in certian mission and some multiplayer maps.
AoW: HT adds Mercenary system, where carefully deployed Mercenaries can turn the tide of the battle. Be warned, it cost a lot to deploy mercenaries so use it wisely.
Gone are the good Live action cutscene, replaced with CG. I do not believe this was voiced by original actor either. the charactor in this is more playful and the charactors in Direct Action are more collected, focused and let's say, "no nonsense".
One improvement over Direct Action is: HT supports widescreen, 16:9 resolution. Keep in mind, this is after all a 2005/2006 game so don't expect to have top notch graphics from modern game engine. However it is still a fun game to play.
When it first launched on Steam, like Direct action, it suffered from memory addressing issue, but I believe it is now fixed. as I am able to play it with windows 8.1, i7 processor and 12GB of ram without any modification.

Once you deal with the whole exceeds 2gbs of ram ordeal, its one of the best rts' i've played. It runs very smoothly and each faction is very unique yet very simple to use. There's cool mechanics like hiding in trees and proning to become hidden. It's like a prettier, more detailed version of command and conquer generals....but better. That's saying alot.

+ Good graphics.
+ Challenging AI.
+ No redundant units.
+ Does not require the original Direct Action to play.
- Campaign not as good as Direct Action.
- Online multiplayer requires 3rd-party software (Hamachi or GameRanger)
- AI does not support all game modes.
We'll start with the graphics: very good considering this game came out in 2006. The stock maps just as detailed as Direct Action, but with far more variety - Aside from the usual desert and urban maps, you can now play on more forest and jungle theatres.
Infantry play a prominent role right up until the late game. Act of War focuses less on tank rushing and requires the player to think a bit more. Well placed infantry, for example, can ambush a tank convoy from trees/tall grass and gain a x2 damage bonus. Likewise, artillery could be used to clear out forests and potential ambush zones. It's nice to play an RTS where infantry are more than just cannon fodder.
There are some very interesting game mechanics here too. While oil is your main source of income, it is still a finite resource and will run dry eventually. You can take and hold banks to acquire funds, or you can even take wounded enemies as hostages for ransom.
The expansion also adds naval warfare, which actually works rather well once you get the knack for it. Each faction has it's own unique variety of ships with different play styles.
Another interesting mechanic introduced to High Treason is the addition of mercenary units. These are expensive, but very effective specialist units that excel in what they do. For example, you can hire a specialist team of medics to provide a heal radius around wounded infantry - or call in the Rawhide artillery team and level an enemy base with rockets from afar.
The AI does not work in naval warfare, which means you're up against humans whether you like it or not. Only a minor complaint, but sometimes it's nice to practice against the AI and hone your skills.
The campaign is brutally hard compared to Direct Action. Some veteran players might be okay with the tougher AI, but I personally struggled. Also the lack of live-action cut-scenes was also a disappointment.
Compatibility issues lie with Windows Vista, Win7 and Win8. There is a Win7 compatibility patch on ModDB which works perfectly - you can get it
Despite the initial compatibility issues, this game has proven to be a very underrated RTS. It's what C&C Generals should have been.
Highly recommended.

Here's the thing about Stranded- it's not really a game. You can walk, and you can check a very vague map. It takes about 35 minutes to play through the game, and it is very slow. It's much more of an arthouse feature- and a good one at that, mind you. The music and visuals are wonderful, and the story is certainly mysterious in a way I might think on for a bit- but that's about it.
It isn't worth 8$.
If you want it, buy it during a sale for 2$. And you will only really want this game under a specific set of cirucmstances: if you REALLY love the whole "games are art" bend of gaming, or if you yourself are looking to get into the indie gaming scene yourself- this little sequence is a wonderful bit of inspiration in regards to presentation. It's interesting to try out a very polished, bare-bones example of what a small time game can be. I happened to fall into the latter, so I went and bought it for the 2$ anyway despite pouring over reviews.
I personally don't regret it. Stranded has some value, but only to a specific few- take the time to consider that before you buy it.

But it also manages to build a beautiful atmosphere of mystery and quiet wonder that's really quite rare. People complain that it's short, but I think the length works in the games favour - it's a short, lovely look at an beautiful alien world, and anything longer would have lost those element of mystery and wonder that the game captures so well. The walking animation is a little too slow, or else the distances you walk across are a little too large, and since you'll be walking back and forth a lot it does get a little frustrating at times (especially with the slight wonkiness of how the game moves your character in response to a mouse-click). This is a short, interesting little "horror" game (if it can even be called that).  It can easily be completed in under 15 minutes, but the gist of it is a brief introduction into the life of a very disturbed man.  It's chilling in the sense that you can see into the home of such a troubled individual, but only for a few minutes.  You don't see much of an explanation, you just see evidence.  There's no storyline to this, you have to make of it what you will based off of the surroundings.
I would not recommend this to those that are easily triggered by heavy subjects, nor is it a game for young children.  However, from a psychological perspective, this little game is nothing short of fascinating, and it holds an air of mystery that still lingers long after you've completed the game.  For a free game with poor graphics that can be completed in 15 minutes or less, it holds heavy meaning and is rather thought-provoking.
TL;DR it's a good game if you like psychological stuff.

Angels with Scaly Wings is a game where your choices affect just about everything around you (to some degree that is). I wouldn't recommend it to everyone, but I thought it was good. The music is pretty good, I think it fits nicely with the game. The art style is very nice as well, and I liked the character designs. Speaking of the characters, I thought the main five dragons were interesting enough. Bryce is my favorite with Remy being second. However, I was disappointed by how short the game was. Sure there are multipile endings to see, but (spoilers) there are only five chapters in the game. I wish it went on longer than that. It feels like there could have been more drama, action and character devolpment. But maybe I'm being too harsh. What I can say that I didn't like was how your choices really don't feel all that impactful other than it affecting how others treat you. I mean yes it does also affect the story, but some choices in the game really don't matter at all. Like during the investigation scenes, it really doesn't matter how much you screw up. I wish there were more consequences for your actions. And honestly, there feels like some lost potential with a few characters as well. There's one character named Emera who is quite mean towards Remy (one of the main dragons) and she never apolgizes for her behaviour. It would have been nice if she felt bad and said she was sorry to Remy. And then there's Kevin. Now even though he has the best design in the game, he's kind of boring to an extent. There's not much going for him other than the typical college guy attitude he has. All you do is talk about college and it's pretty much the same in the dragon world as it is in the human world. And yes I do kind of understand why that might be, but I still think that there should have been some differences. Being in a world full of dragons means that there should at least be some differences in how they go about things. Remy for instance asks about your hair which he presumes to be fur, while Bryce asks about your tail and clothes. This shows that dragons don't know much about human attire or fashion. It just feels a bit of a shame that the dragons don't feel all that unique when compared to humans. Sometimes they just feel like they could be humans dressed as dragons. Maybe make it so they are more feral and they do things differently than humans do. That's just me though. Anyways I hope that helps. Again, I wouldn't recommend this game to everybody, but it is worth a try at least. Despite what I said, it's not a bad game. It feels like it had effort put into it. I just think they could have made it somewhat better.

It’s been at least a year since I played Angels With Scaly Wings, but it took me so long to make a review because I’m still not sure how I feel about it.
After I learned about AWSW, I gathered the money for it by selling many of my TF2 items - my hype was that strong. When I began playing, I was half worried the game would be a disappointment and half very, very excited. By the end, it was a combination of both these things and several others all messed up together into 1 crazy dragon salad.
To start, this game is a visual novel and has almost no ‘gameplay’ besides choosing different text options to progress in the story. I was ready for this, but some people really don’t like these kinds of games (And given the quality of most of them I can see why). AWSW takes place in a world of dragons, where you are a human who travels from your human world using a portal to try and learn the dragon’s technology to help your own people. The only other human present in this world is a student you once knew: Reza.
Things quickly go wrong with the dragons and Reza, and you have to figure out why and return to your world safely with the technology you need by working with the main dragon characters. I don’t want to spoil much of the story, so I’ll just start with saying that it’s broken down into 5 chapters, and in each chapter you can make a phone call to one of the 5 main dragons to meet with for “””dates”””. I say it like this because AWSW really didn’t feel like a dating sim at all, it is MUCH more of a sci-fi/fantasy story with dragon dating on the sidelines. There is plenty of light humor and antics throughout with your dragon friends, but the overall mood outside of dates could be surprisingly somber and even unsettling.
Before I get to the best parts I’ll cover the absolute worst: the pathways and endings. Here’s the problem – they are extremely repetitive. Each time you do a playthrough to date a different dragon and get a different ending, most of what you see outside of the 1-on-1 date scenes is the same or very similar to your previous playthroughs.

But the biggest disappointment is that the endings are also too similar. Every dragon has a good and bad end, and each good end is almost the same as the counterpart bad end. I’m gonna need an example here so SPOILER:
This is a huge problem I had, even though I didn’t mind going through the same parts of the game again because they were enjoyable to read. Even the True Ending was disappointing, although now that I’ve had a lot of time to think about it I like it more than I did originally.
Okay now for the good parts. The 5 main dragons are pretty well done. They are: Remy, Bryce, Lorem, Anna, and Adine.
Adine is my favorite. She’s everyone’s favorite!
And for good reason, her story is so cute and memorable and that
scene is so damn adorable I want to play it over again. I liked Lorem’s story second most because of the adventure you go on with him and talking with Ipsum back in the apartment. Bryce’s scenes were fun but my least favorite of the 5. Remy’s story is pretty sad but he wasn't my favorite character either.
And then there’s Anna. Even with her unpredictable bouts of anger and that creepy look in her eyes, she shouldn't seem eerie, but in several scenes she really is.
Bryce has one of the funniest and most suggestive scenes
, and Anna has a very suggestive scene too, so,
. Adine has one scene that would normally be very sexual in any show/movie/game
but in here somehow it wasn’t. This scene is much more cute and amusing than anything else (but that’s just how I saw it, not sure about other people).
The side dragons can have very fun and colorful scenes - I loved Sebastian and Zhong especially. I do wish some of the other characters had had more screen time
.
As I mentioned, AWSW’s sci-fi elements, while messy (especially the endings) are more of the game’s main focus than the dating. There’s an underlying mystery going on that is explained well enough by the end, and it’s a cool concept about dragons and humankind I’ll never forget. Your interactions with each dragon lets you learn more about their past and current problems, and this scaly world is really brought to life when you exchange descriptions of customs, places, behaviors, etc. with them. The dragons he selves are most unique in their behaviors and beliefs, though they can have generic traits (Bryce is tough guy cop etc.)
The dialogue in this game is pretty well done, and there are only a few spelling and grammar mistakes throughout. Banter can be awkard at times, but I've never played a visual novel where this wasn't the case.
It is easy enough to connect with the dragons and choose the options that’ll make them laugh (except Anna), and the text usually has well detailed descriptions of your actions and surroundings.
The graphics are pretty good, can be inconsistent. I like all 5 main dragon designs (especially Adine <3) and the backgrounds, while mostly generic, fit each mood and environment. Most of the game is colorful and bright and it adds a lot of life to the dragon’s world.
The music is good too, and
memorable.
For the most surprising and possibly best part of the game - I had gotten every achievement and every ending and thought: Well that’s the end right?
SPOILER:
This thing came completely out of left field and it was perfect - eerie, mysterious, worrying, cryptic. The only other time a game has engrossed me with such 4th wall breaks is, dare I say it, Undertale. Some of it remains cryptic and interesting still
Well, right now I’m listening to the game’s OST, and all I can sum this review up with is that AWSW is unforgettable, despite its flaws. The
2 visual novels I would personally recommend are 999 and this one – Angels With Scaly Wings.
This type of game would probably be best if you really like dragons and/or are a furry, since that seems to be the target audience, but others might like it too, I dunno.
I may have been disappointed at the endings, but I forgot how enjoyable AWSW was. That sounds real stupid for a game described as a ‘dragon dating sim’, but that label doesn’t do it justice. What a long mess of a review! This game is still hard to describe right - it remains strange and wonderful to this day.
PS: Apparently there’s a word limit for reviews, and I just hit it. Damnit

If I had to describe this game in one sentence, I'd put it like this : a better version of Hearthstone.
Everything in this game is inspired from, or is a complete rip off of Hearstone. However what Hearthstone does, TESL does it better, as it's more f2p, more strategic and without the pathetic childish aesthetic of HS.
The biggest problem I noticed is that the gameplay / game style does not vary enough from colour to colour (oh, I forgot, cards are grouped into 5 colours, just like in mtg), which makes TESL a bit dull and repetitive. Also, albeit deeper than HS, don't expect anything special, it's nothing like other games of the genre, like MTG, Gwent etc.
The alternative game mode to 1v1 (ranked or non ranked) is Arena, which is a Hearstone arena rip off, which is basically a draft mode for idiots. As far as I remember, the rewards are pretty poor and before each match there is a commentetor announcing the "gladiators" in a very stupid american manner, which is so unsuitable for a fantasy game. I would understand it, though, if it was a WWE card game. The Arena was my most unpleasant experience with this game.
In my opinion, this game was designed for casual, fun play. If you enjoyed Hearthstone but would like a game a bit more strategic and wihtout kindergarten visuals, you will enjoy The Elder Scrolls Legends. If you want a serious and very strategic card game for a more hardcore gaming, look somewhere else.

An interesting game where you play a detective in a late Victorian steampunk world investigating a series of brutal murders. The story is original, and the game mechanics fresh. The game has RPG elements with a shop that allows you to upgrade your equipment. Every scene allows you to search for fingerprints and clues, and there is a camera mini-game that allows you to take photos for your evidence wall. The HO scenes also contain mini-games where you dust for prints and use an ultra-violet light to search for blood stains. You can find pieces of evidence that you can then research in the laboratory via another mini-game .....
..... and the game is unplayable.
In 30 minutes, the game crashed to desktop 4 times. Although I could restart and continue from the last position after crashing, it just got too frustrating to keep playing and having to restart every 5 minutes.
It's a shame because this is a fresh breath of air for the HO genre, the story and setting are original, the game mechanics interesting, and I really wanted to continue ... but in it's current state, it's impossible to recommend.

This game feels like it was made by someone who really, really loved it. Along with some other people who did not.
Glitchy, multiple crashes to desktop, poor translations--especially important in a hidden object scene (raspberries are not strawberries, ropes are not twine, etc.). The artwork and the mechanisms of gameplay are fantastic, but they're held back by very rough and rushed coding. One planetary puzzle I "solved" multiple times (it played a happy noise and kicked me out of the puzzle), but I still couldn't progress, so I had to wait for the skip button to light up in order to continue in the game. Finally finishing the game was a relief, and when I saw there was a bonus chapter, I noped right on out, and I've never done that before.
It's a pity, because it's got a lot of heart, a lot of good ideas, and some really wonderful settings. But ultimately it's so faulty, I can't recommend it.

after years upon years of having to pirate this gem, its finally available for steam release. This has been a favorite of mine for about a third of my life now, and the awsome, slick looseness of melty blood is something you really dont find in any other fighting game. its one of a kind
the core gameplay here is as good as always. the game is slick and insanely fast-paced, and combos are really fluid (emphasis on "fluid" as opposed to them having a lot of weight). the game is really beginner friendly, too; theres no tutorial, but there isnt an insane plethora of systems here to overwhelm you, attacks are easy to use and combo with, and specials all use relatively universal motions that are easy to execute
its worth noting that this is a game based a lot on combos, which might be weird for some people. a common match involves a lot of moving around really fast, trying your darndest to catch the opponent off guard, and once you can get them, wiping out about a quarter to half of their HP bar. obv a fight is more complicated than that, because peeps arent going to let you get them into good combos, so you gotta have experience to back up your execution
, i think it may be too early to come to a good conclusion, but immediately after launch, connection quality varied wildly. you could get some matches that were good, or sometimes you could get a full second or more of delay. more often than not, a fight would start fine but the latency would gradually creep in during. as it settled down, i suppose, connections started to get much better. maybe its late and so not a lot of people are on; for whatever reason the server was running smoothely, and a majority of the fights i had felt like they may as well be local
i cant really judge the quality of multiplayer lobbies, but its quite functional here. you can quick ranked matches or costumized ones (where you can prefer to fight peeps from your region or whatever), and you can do normal player matches. unranked matches can only be done in rooms (of up to 6 people), and thats pretty weird, but i dont really mind it
i think this game is really worth everyones time, obv i recommend it. $25 is a pretty steep price for this old of a game with so little production value, though

When I first loaded this game up, it became apparent it was no more than a quick port of a mobile game, and I expected to immediately hate it. I was quite suprised then, to find a simple but competent puzzle game beneath the trite mobile trappings. The game ramps up in difficulty, but never reaches a point of frustration. The mechanic is tried and simple, not dissimilar from Pipe Dream, but utilized in creative ways that'll make you think differently from puzzle to puzzle. You earn one to three stars, based on your speed, which is another holdover from mobile games but is a decent measure of your ability to conquer a level. The mouse works as well as any touch controller could have, and I would have been willing to forgive the mobile styled menus and buttons, however I eventually reached level 9. Level 9 isn't a bad level, but level 9 doesn't keep track of your stars, weather you earn them or not. The game doesn't keep track of them from there on, and this cuts the challenge right out of the game. It's also a big tell, that the game hasn't been tested well, if at all. This is just a bridge to far, and I can't recommend this game.

I played this years ago, and returned to it as I enjoyed it; also that I have no game time on this account.
Farcry 2 excels at making the game fun just through the gun play and traversing the land scape;  I would describe it as a gleaming example of what a game should be - as oppose as some superfluous plot with rewards dispensed through progression, Farcry 2 is fun to play at the core.
Its true Farcry is not perfect, there are so many obvious bugs; but it does almost add to the game rather than mock it.  The bugs are often hilarious, i.e. there is pretty much a constant bug where you enter an area and an AI militia will levitate up into the air and suddenly drop.. As lame as it sounds, it is very funny to watch whilst scouting the place out is always amusing.
I think the best thing about Farcry is the stealth and standard FPS mix.  There are many stealth games today, but not necessarily in the past, I don't think it was as frequent.  And despite the stealth component still being very primitive, I can still creep around and kill an entire group of militia with a knife without being detected (even though knife kills are often or not going to get you detected.).  It almost feels at times that the stealth element wasn't meant to be a major aspect of the game, but I think it works reasonably well.
There are quite a few characters , though playing as a different character does nothing any different.  So the character system is quite superfluous which is a shame.  Though its interesting how it all pans into the story.  Story was good enough. Although it seems rather pointless and of course in line with the farcry games - overkill.
The extra stuff such as the chit- chat between the militia is good too, the game certainly has character.  It makes it worth sitting back and observing your environment. However, the Jackal tapes are a questionable introduction.  There are quite a lot to pick up, but once you pick up 5 of them, the following collected say the same thing.  Its almost like the designers were trying to make you remember those words, the hopelessness of war which I can kind of appreciate but it still sucks , they could have added more variation to it.
The gun play is very good I felt. Each gun is different and for example, the sniper rifles; the more expensive one, though it is semi automatic does not make it worth forgetting the others.  The guns are nice to use and generally I felt most were worth returning to.  However, the mortar is an interesting weapon, but I have tried to master it and found it doesn't do anything... I may be wrong though, and it would be a shame a weapon like that was put in only to be bugged out -  First person shooters could do with more deviation when it comes to weapons.
The game design is interesting too.  Its a case of travelling through areas, so instead of walking through a linear level and you are presented with enemies, instead, you need to get from one point on the map and need to get through check points and other obstacles which respawn.  It makes the map very re-usable and again, as the combat and the ai is as-it-is, it can make it work...
I have played farcry 3 and found everything about it was an extension to this game, so logically to say it would be an improvement would be expected, however, it does not play as well as this - it is definitely more boring.
This game is probably the best in the series , or that is my opinion.

- atmosphere: African country egnulfed in civil war feels unique and map is quite diverse
- graphics: OK especially for a 9 year old game
- game mechanics: fire spreading, gun jamming and exploding, malaria, manual map (no Esc menu map). Gunplay is fine OK
- you're doomed to spend long times getting anywhere. Game loves to send you to opposite side of map (barely any fast travel options)
- mission design: no diversity here, get to the blue marker - kill everyone, get to the red marker - kill everyone
- characters: are plain and lack any development(including protagonist). Main villain at least is somewhat better
- voices and music (sounds are OK): everyone mumbles; few music tracks get repetitive fast (not helps considering long travels)
- AI: dudes respawn often swarming you
Have few tips too:
- picked it up on sale for ~3$; would not recommend buying it at full price (8$)
- play this in short sessions (1-1.5h)
- if you're hesitant on this one, consider getting Far Cry 3 instead - it certainly is better

The conversations in the story feel very forced, robotic and too casual (like how one would converse on social media), which is a big turn-off for me. Lines such as 'Is this the train you normally take home?', 'I have to get off at the next stop but that was a seriously cool conversation we had' and 'How west in Tokyo do you live?' fly by. All in all, if you're looking for a nice enjoyable visual novel, look elsewhere.

“A piece of philosophical, intellectual and introspective writing rarely seen in video games particularly in a VN. Get it now.
P.S. The soundtrack is absolutely gorgeous.“

is a very short, mostly kinetic visual novel about a bunch of teenagers finishing high school, and wondering what to do with their lives. Put together, it is not the most successful or interesting visual novel, but it's heartwarming and carries some basic wisdom for anyone just starting their lives.
Our protagonist is Yuka Kishimoto. She is a high school student in Japan, who attends a school where her father works as a history teacher. She is an ordinary, well mannered, bright young woman who is at a total loss about her future. It is the last week of high school. These are the days that you won't be having ever again, right? The traditional Sunset Festival - which marks the end of high school for senior students - approaches, and it's up to you to figure out the ending of this chapter in life for Yuka.
As I mentioned before,
isn't a great visual novel. It has some lazily snapped photograph backgrounds, no animation or voice acting; plus, the narrative has casual grammar errors. Sadly, there is no option for you to play this full screen either. The art style might be considered charming, but nope, nothing captivating. Gameplaywise, I wouldn't count any winnings either, considering it is a mostly kinetic visual novel. There are some choice opportunities, but I doubt that they'd change anything, since you can try each and every ending if you save properly at the last scene. Oh, and the save system gets whacky and fails to save from time to time.
So why am I giving this one an up vote? Well, I personally think the main message of the game is well-put and it's brief and sound advice for anyone to hear. This game is about choosing your own future, and the pressures of expectations. I find the approach of the game towards life, growing up and taking a place in society surprisingly realistic. I was surprised to see that there is more than one nonromantic - and quite logical - endings for you to choose at the end, and also a female option, which is quite rare in any of these games by itself. The game isn't long enough for you to observe any character depth, but some exchanged quotations hide pearls of wisdom that I wish someone shared with me at some point.
All in all,
is a sweet effort in hopes of presenting the player with encouragement, telling you that it's okay to take your time and experiment in your life. No one should walk a pre-decided path and call it a life, just to appease the generation before himself/herself. It's your life. It's yours to seize and make anything out of, and this amateur VN is bold enough to tell this out load.

Well, this is a weird little game. And little it is indeed. It’s only 30 minutes long and even those 30 minutes are only 30 minutes because of the slow walking.
A lot of people accuse Stranded of not being a game at all and I can totally see where they’re coming from but I don’t share that view. It reminds me a lot of the old science fiction stories from the 50s and 60s. The ones with barely any action, characters or narrative, you know. The stories that were a lot about painting a strange, alien world and showing it to the reader and not so much about people caught in some distress that they have to fight out of. It’s a game in which you have to pay attention to details and interpret what you see.
As such, I enjoyed it. And as such it suffers from being too vague, too minimalistic, too bare, too small and too short. Well, maybe it suffers from that. To me it did not, to a lot of other people it does, going by the forums.
Is it worth the 30-40 minutes? Yes, IF you’re a fan of classic, open-to-interpretation science fiction or if you are ok with odd gaming experiences.
Is it worth the seven Euros they want? Nope. Really, really nope.
I bought it in a sale for 75% off and that was fine, though.

The main thing about this game is that it is... short. Extremely so. The one hour of playtime I've clocked in? That's two playthroughs. My first one, with plenty of roaming about and exploration, took 45 minutes. The remaining 15 minutes was poking around trying to see if there were other endings.
I'd like to recommend this game, I really would. The atmosphere and the visuals are wonderful, and remind me of the old LucasArts adventure game, The Dig. I would have loved to explore the world more, see if it had more to offer, but there's so little of it here.
That said, I do not regret the time spent on the game. If you enjoy the sort of visuals that Dig might have to offer and find this one at a steep discount, it's worth at least a quick look, provided you don't come without much in the way of expectations. Otherwise, skip this one.

text:
Chronicles of Mystara is a port of two Capcom arcade beat-'em-ups from the mid-nineties. The main gimmick is that this is not only a solid beat 'em up, but one that's set in the Dungeons and Dragons universe, which means neat little features like access to a limited number of powerful spells that get recharged after a "rest", enemies that have mechanics like their tabletop counterparts (Undead, for instance, can't be hurt by any type of gas attack because they don't have lungs), and explorable environments with a few secret areas tucked here and there with bonus loot, and branching paths that, while not affecting the plot in any way, increase replayability in a MASSIVE way. With four to six playable classes, depending on whether you're playing Tower of Doom or Shadow over Mystara (the later of which has alternate variants of the Cleric and Magic User classes with different spells, bringing the effective total closer to 8), plenty of levels, and a rather ridiculous amount of loot to find, this is one beat 'em up with a LOT of meat on its bones. This port even comes with achievement milestones, adding even more to the pile. It's a fair amount of content for the asking price, especially on sale.
Unfortunately, the playerbase is a bit small these days, so random matchmaking is a bit empty. This is definitely the type of game where buying a 4-pack to split with your friends is a solid investment.

How many of us are old enough to remember the glory days of the arcade? Before all this here internet gaming got itself going, well, we actually had to get out of the house if we wanted to go and play with other people. Oftentimes they would be found out at the mall, as part of a bowling alley, or maybe you were lucky enough to live near something like a Showbiz Pizza (nowadays known as Chuck E. Cheese) or an Enchanted Castle. They used to have all kinds of games that never used to see a home release- shooters, driving games... but my favorite were the multiplayer beat-em-ups. The Simpsons and Ninja Turtle four-player cabinets were really fun, and who could forget that X-Men double-screen six-player game? If you could get six players going on that, it was the stuff of legends.
Out of all of them, well... my favorite really wasn't any of those. This was about the time in my life where I was starting to spread my little nerd wings, and well... I spied a certain franchise on a few arcade cabinets- Dungeons and Dragons. Guess where multiple bucks worth of my tokens could be counted on to reliably end up when I went out to game? It was always a chore to choose which of the two to play- unless I just dropped twenty bucks on tokens and played through both games, one after the other with a meal break in between. Those were the days... until I moved away and couldn't play them for the longest time.
Most of the arcades have closed down- but thanks to some wonderful people, well... these two games have been preserved and re-released on Steam, and to be honest, I couldn't be happier. So go grab your character sheets, dice bags and cheez doodles, today we're looking at Dungeons and Dragons: Chronicles of Mystara.
Consisting of two games- Tower of Doom and Shadow Over Mystara, both of these games take place in the Mystara campaign setting. The premise, well, is very simple- you're one of an adventuring party in each game, choosing between four different classes in ToD- warrior, dwarf, cleric, and elf, with Shadows adding in a thief and a magic-user. You're tasked with finding out just what the heck is going onto cause a rise in monster attacks on villages, and from there, well... no, I'm not going to spoil it! Just play them in order- finish Tower before you play Shadows and you'll get the whole story!
The action of this game brings to mind someone dropping a D&D adventure and a Final Fight arcade board into a blender and hitting frappe- you'll work through a number of levels, knocking the heads of classic D&D monsters like goblins, kobolds, gnolls, owlbears and others as you battle through to find yourselves the culprits as just just what the blazes is going on- picking up massive piles of shiny treasure, powerful weapons and magical artifacts along the way, gaining experience as you bash in heads. You'll hit levels at certain points of XP, granting better health, power and special abilities. The money you collect even has a purpose- sometimes you'll hit a between-level shop and be able to refill disposable things like burning oil, hammers, daggers, arrows...
Oh, did I forget to mention that? Every character gets a number of ring menus full of stuff to use instead of their regular weapon- this is most important for your caster classes, because it's how you access your spells. Just tap the ring button, tap until you have the spell you desire (Spells go by level- you get a certain number of spells per level per life, and once you burn through them all, you better hope more scrolls drop out of chests or you're going to be out of luck and down to whacking stuff. For example, Fireball and Lightning Bolt are both third-level spells), and then select it and hit the action button to let that sucker fly. Just beware that certain spells just won't work on everything- Cloudkill doesn't affect skeletons, for example.
A number of stages contain various routes or selections- you will sometimes be given a choice of routes to take, or you might be up against a time limit to kill something. You could also find secret treasures. All in all, they're both really solid beat-em-ups and worth plying over and over and over...
The best part of these games, however, was actually included- the multiplayer. Feel like risking your sanity with some random Steam gamers? Make a public game and wait for slots to be filled... or you could just get a bunch of your friends together and make a private game- and then invite friends directly from your Steam friends list. Easy, simple multiplayer- you can easily kill a late night with this game, and it's a blast to play because you can keep going as long as you want and then people can drop in and out. That fluid, that seamless. All the other players have to do is wait a few minutes.
Downsides to these games... well... hmmm... They end? There haven't been sequels? The fantasy theme might turn some people off? Each fighter is limited to one of two looks and can't change gender?
The price point is fifteen bucks retail, but it might catch sales that could knock it to half or better. Even at fifteen, though, it's a good purchase, and completely worth it.
You can't go wrong with this one- just buy it, install it, and enjoy.
TL;DR - This will let you slay your boredom for 14d6+10 fun damage. 9/10.

One of the user-defined tags is "Psychological horror".
Yeah, that seems about right.
This game was emotional pain from start to finish - I wound up playing it all in one sitting. Every ending up to the True Ending, 15 hours and all. It was true pain to watch everyone suffer so much, and so many times, before finally getting to the true, happy ending that they all deserve.
It was a hell of a depressing (but fulfilling) experience, each character has their own stories and motivations, and the game looks much more tragic if you begin to think about choices you DON'T make - characters making lethal mistakes because of you not being there to stop or help them.
Now, onto the actual review I suppose.
As one of the other reviews said: this isn't EXACTLY a mystery game; more of a puzzle game meets dating sim, if anything else. As you do more and more playthroughs and aim for more and more endings, the pieces start to come together. Some characters have secrets that pertain to other characters, meaning to save everyone, you'll have to get to know everyone. You may even get a few bad endings in the process - I was lucky and only got one, but I was rather emotionally invested at that point. One was one too many. Even some of the 'good' endings just felt...too bittersweet, too painful. Some were better outcome-wise than others, but the True ending is where it's at. To see that, however, you have to live with your consequences up until then, and do what you think is right. You CAN save everyone, just....not at first. That's something I wasn't used to, as I'd gotten the true pacifist ending in Undertale my very first time playing. Here, you have no choice but to press on past your mistakes.
Many choices and the knowledge you obtain from them persist between playthroughs, letting you (and them) make better choices and avoid unpleasant fates for yourself and others - if you save them one, you save them every time, with a very few unavoidable situations. Plus, there's a few skip functions allowing you to bypass minor dialogue you've already seen before - hence why it only took me 15 hours to reach the true ending, opposed to a few more.
This game was jsut utter magic to me - getting the soundtrack from the digital deluxe version was well worth it. 94 different songs in the game - some of them credits themes, yes, but many of them more ambient and setting the mood. The dialogue is rather well-written, the story gets slightly convoluted but is relatively easy to follow overall.
Now, in case you're still not convinced: the first playthrough can take less than 2 hours, which is within the refund period. The game is 10 dollars - you cna afford it. If you don't like it, you can refund it shortly before or after your first playthrough, which is more than enough to gauge your interest, I'd wager.
Now, if you'll excuse me, I'm probably going to go write fanfiction and maybe continue crying a bit, because I now have a empty void in my heart. I'm dead inside. Buy this game. 10/10.

Melty Blood: Actress Again Current Code has finally made its release years after being unobtainable other than through a $200 bundle with an anime series. It is an impressive game with very fluid character movement and an intuitive combo system, allowing for both new players to quickly dish out pressure and combos after just starting while rewarding long time players for truly optimizing their characters. Surprisingly, the older, PS2 version of the game had made enough of a name for itself in the US to be voted into EVO 2010 over many other popular fighters at the time. To this day, many fighting game players know of it and have tried it.
The translation work done on the game is excellent, as it now allows for some players to appreciate aspects of characters they were unable to read before. Seeing as this is also one the official release of the latest Melty Blood, I am also sure a lot of Japanese players who did not already own it are thankful for a digital copy.
Unfortunately, the game suffers some drawbacks on release. For one, there have been players who have been playing this game, in particular this version, for several years, so some player matches and ranked will turn out to be a daunting experience. However, it is a very easy game to learn, and there have been so many tutorial videos on each of the characters (93 characters if we include moon forms), the game could be played with purely fighting game fundamentals.
The netplay is fairly attrocious; delay is compounded during matches, so the longer a match draws out, the more input delay both parties will have to suffer. The bundled MBAACC that could be purchased years ago contained a solid netplay matching system and recognizable delay. Considering the other types of netplay ArcSys and FrenchBread have developed for their most recent games, this is really a sour experience.
Overall, I do recommend this game for the fun factor. However, I feel that some aspects still need some work to finalize into a great fighter.

Melty Blood is a momentum and pressure-centric fighting game.
I'll try to cover what makes melty unique compared to other fightans:
-Simple and low res, but very fluid and stylish spritework. This makes it easier to see and recognize startup animations.
-Easy motions for special moves; nothing more complex than a half-circle motion. Combined with the relatively large buffer window for specials, melty is an easy game to pick up and mash for anybody familiar with fighting games.
-Very loose cancel window after normals. In C and H moon, you can pretty much press any button after any other button. Gattlings are only present in F moon. This creates a technique called 'reverse beat', in which a move with a long recovery can be wiff canceled into a button with faster recovery. These properties mean that pressure if focused around normals; you want to leave a 1~2 frame gap between normals to catch people trying to do something other than blocking.
-Throw properties. The character waking up has a few frames of throw invincibility and can OS with 1ad. They are relatively weak and hard to hit given the speed and reach of 2a. Once you earn respect, you can't just spam throw to win the round, instead you must continue pressurring with normals in order to get an opening.
-Teching when hitting the ground is done by holding a direction. There is a short hop with invlun followed by a brief vulnerable recovery. During oki there is no vairable timing, which means that the person waking up may get caught in a meaty attack if they choose to tech incorrectly. This heavily favors the attacking player as they can do a combo and follow it up with another one if done correctly. Blocking and teching properly becomes important skills in order to stay alive.
-Everybody gets a double jump AND an air dash. Air counterhits pop the enemy in the air and is untechable until they hit the ground. This is an easy, damaging, and important way to convert into a combo+knockdown. Most characters also lack an anti-air move. Given all this air mobility, the importance of air counterhits, and lack of grounded anti-airs means most of the footsies occur in the air.
-Crossup protection. Seeing how easy it is to hop on your opponent's head, the game has crossup protection, which allows you to block a crossup by still holding back. No gay ambiguous Ryu j.MK setups.
-2abc5c jbc jbc air throw. You now know the basic bnb for almost the entire cast. Less emphasis on combos, more  on spacing, pressure, and oki.
-Huge cast of viable characters. If you can get momentum, you can come back and win the round.
Melty Blood is easy to pick up and play, and if given a little bit of dedication and effort, can become an enjoyable fighting game experience.

Terse and understated, Stranded offers a minimalist interface and a subtle yet poignant plot that you must deduce yourself by wandering through the small world and observing what happens around you. The artwork offers a compelling snapshot of an alien planet, set to a beautiful, ambient soundtrack that makes the silent and lonely setting all the more striking. The overall effect is pensive and haunting, more than compensating for the game's small size and short duration: Stranded can be completed within 30 minutes. Likewise, the player uses a short list of controls--"S" for screenshot, "F" for fullscreen, and left-clicking for movement and environment interaction. Resembling a scifi short story, Stranded is a simple and thoughtful game that I would recommend to any serious gamer who enjoys an artful experience.

The art! The sound! The atmosphere! Oh, how I will reminisce in the good old days of point & click adventures. I thought before I played this game.
The art and soundtrack are unique and amazing. But it's not enough. There is no real feedback in the game, no way to know how or with what to interact. Which is intended, granted. But intentionally being frustrating is still not a good thing, it's bad design. The contols and walking animation just suck after a few minutes. Just let me watch the character cross the screen, why do I have to click twice to enter a path? It feels unpolished.
There is also no logic in what you do. Your instinct tells you to find something to survive, food, fire, shelter and so on. The premise says exploring. But all you do is is go through all screens (six unique ones!) several times and sleep in between. This feels pretentious and artsy, kind of like "The Emperor's New Clothes" of video games.
This is not worth money. This is almost not even worth the 15 Minutes it takes to play through.

Is this a game? Depends on how loosely you would define a game. I don't think Stranded is a game, however, it is interactive art.  In that sense it does have value. If you approach Stranded with the mindset that it is a game and you will be in for a soporose 15-30 minutes of pointless clicking and pretty blinking pixels. If you think of it as interactive art, you may find Stranded to be thought provoking and beautiful [ individual results may vary ]. I will reccomend this game but, you may need to have a deep fondness of art or have achieved some altered state of consciousness [ or both ].

Game uses a point-and-click interface to explore the enviroment but don't expect any active interaction.   You're just here to watch.   Unfortunately, there's not much in the way of story either.   It's also very short.

I really wanted to like this game.  Honestly.  It has some good atmosphere to it and a decent enough setting.  It kind of felt a little like The Dig in the first couple of minutes.  Then my awe and wonderment quickly gave way to annoyance at discovering the only thing you can do is slowly walk back and forth along a very small game world.  There's no inventory system of any kind as you don't interact with anything at all aside from walking into an area and sometimes seeing colored lights flash or a stone golem guy stand around.  The map system seems completely pointless since the game world is small enough that you have no chance of getting lost.  The ending seemed very artsy-fartsy too.  Considering it took roughly 30 minutes to 100% complete the game, $7.99 seems horrendously pricey.  I got it on sale and I still feel a bit ripped off.  Watching a Youtube video of this game would be the same as playing it yourself, minus the disappointment of having spent money on it.  If you REALLY want to play the game bad enough, I'd wait for it to be on sale for no less than 75% off.

Combine all that with a price of

I've been playing this for 7 years, just added it to Steam because I can't stand the Nexon launcher.
You can max level a char on Vinductus in just a few weeks (I'm pretty sure I've seen people do it in 2 weeks on a 'new char' event).
Playing casually (v casually lol!) I spent 5 years taking my Vella to max level, just logging in, playing wild frienzied combat, then logging out again whenever I fancied - in other words playing for the joy of playing, no grind, no 'trying to get x or y or z' no plan or anythign like that, just pure gameplaying hack 'n' slash enjoyment out there in the zones.
This game is fantastic. I find it beautiful and compelilng. It's wild frantic combat, the widespread death and destruction at the tip of your swords (or chains, or whatever) is unreal, you really are locked into split second timing, ultra-focused, the thrill is amazing, either against hordes or against bosses.
There are several different characters to choose from, which are gender locked, some of these types of char I haven't seen in anything else - one uses a mana stone, able to throw it through enemies, and recall it back thru them, or explode it where it stopped! I don't tend to replay games, but I have a few different chars on Vinductus - there is real reaplay value.... My fave is Vella, the twin sword (or chains) user, partly because her 'cross cut' counter move, if you get the timing right, is unnnnbelievably devestating, the highest power effect even puts slash marks on the screen, as if the swords even scraped the 'camera'. I also have a hammer weilder, and the combat with that is brutally satisfying!
I don't think of Vinductus as particularly deep, it's a thrashing! Like most gamers, I didn't read the story in Chapter 1 (the main part of the game) But in Chapter 2, I did take the extra time to find out why I was killing everything - and a pretty amazing love story played out, it was all timelessly haunting and had an amazing ending. And then there's Chapter 3!
The game's regular events I've always found to be generous and awesome, adn there's a huge variance in type of event: some, you have to travel to a new island to take part in, others spring a whole new horde on you while you're going about your ususal dungeon smashing.
At high level, like most games, all you can really do is grind - while you can hit max level pretty quickly, it can take a lot longer to max out your skills, using Action Points (or, I think it's changed to Training Points now) which you get, say, 50 of for doing a certain dungeon type, and need hundreds of thousands of for building your skills -
There are a lot of skills! From char based like stamina,strength etc. to action based like the proficiency of certain type of move, to transformation....
Transformation!!! What an addition! If you get in trouble out there in the dungeons (later stages, you pick up transformation) you can transform! You can be an absolute beast, all your stats raised, your char looks amazing, dripping in some kind of shadow magic, faster and harder than you've ever been. The transformed state is short, it's a kind of 'death or victory' thing, because when the duration minutes are up, you transofrm back, and all your armor is broken... it's amazing! lol!
kk, that's me raving about it, but to be fair to newcomers, Vinductus has a few oddities about it:
1) Pet system. There is a pet system, but it basically sucks. It was never a big part of the game, you don't need one, and you basically don't see people out there accompanied by one. I have a free pet from a very early event in the game, but I think you have to cash purchase them now. They never level very far, they're not much help or good, they get squashed quickly by bosses. They're cute (choice of about 4 different types I think, which start out small and cute.... and stay that way.... ) The pet lasts 1 hour in 24 I think, and it levells better if you feed it. Unfortunately, the feed is astronomically expensive, partly because of the broken in game economy.
2) Broken in-game economy. Games and servers mature, and the markets within them alter over time. With Vindictus, the market kind of sucks. Most combat things (armor and weapons and stuff) are reasonably priced for the level you're at, but materials for crafting are thru the roof expensive - basically, if you want to level your crafting skills, you do it for the pleasuer of being able to do it, because anything you craft is more expensive to make from components than to buy outright.
I konw you're gonna say 'go farm the ingredients!' - the cost of repairs to your armor after each dungeon, while slight and easily affordable, when it comes to rare/ish items, these costs start to build to a scale that outweighs the cost of the 1% drop rate item that you're looking for.
Farming costs more than buying the ingredients, and buying the ingredients costs more than buying the thing ready made brand new on the market. Obv, tha'ts stuuuuuuuuuuupid!
3) Crafting - What? why? it's pointless. Plus, you can only learn two different crafts. On one of my chars, I opted for 'jewellery' thinking that I could one day craft the much coveted earrings for all my other characters.... no way! lol! no way!  crafting jewellery is a HUUUUUUUUUUUGE money sink! It's another - 'it'll never be worth it, even if I get to make the earrings, I should have just bought six pairs off the market by the end of this'.
4) Teaming up - all dungeons can be teamed up against. For the purposes of the game and logging in to hack and slash, you can do it all solo easily enough, and later on you can solo 'easy' or 'normal' versions of the 4-person dungeons as well. But there are 6-person dungeons, more advanced 4-person dungeons, and 8-person dungeons, which are there for the late game grinding.... Most of them are too quiet to form a party for, and the only real teaming up that goes on now is either guilds doing specific runs, or late-game runs on normal dungeons - cuz these give thousands of times more exp than any other dungeons in the game, and players in that 'gotta have it!' zone of being 10 levels from the max are piling into those teams all the time.
5) Fishing - Vinductus has a quirky sense of humor about it, and I think the fishing was added as part of that. It's a fun little minigame in a way, i've spent hours doing it. But it's absolutely pointless lol!
I can imgine pepole not liking Vinductus, but for me it's a rare gem, a game which is juuust amazing to play. Easily worth a hundred hours of blazing away with your favourite weapon :)

Vindictus is a game which executes what it does very well. A solid, responsive game with some split-second reactions needed from the player to be able to fully experience the thrill of completing a battle without taking a single scratch.
This is a long one, so grab a cup of tea and settle down.
This is a game I picked up late 2013/early 2014, as well as that version being the EU client. So don't let my Steam account's tracking fool you of my experience with the game.
We'll start off with the obligatory cash shop (as it is a F2P game, and Nexon at that) as an addition to the game for QoL items in exchange for cash, as well as the cosmetics part.
Not something you would feel obligated to spend money on unless you were in it for the long run, get some good looks if you were lazy or simply get a quick burst of gold if some less fortunate soul were in need of a cash-shop item.
Needless to say, it's not the primary focus of the game; just a mere addition to either make your life easier in exchange for funds, or just simply to make your characters look gorgeous.
The visuals are really well made and sets the mood, as well as the theme of general areas very well.
The effects on combat are really stunning and really put an emphasis on how lethal your blows really are when using that one ability of yours that is capable of pinning giant monstrosities.
The soundtrack is one of the best I've heard for its kind. (
)
It manages to set the theme where the atmosphere, geometry and visuals cannot. Where impending doom is emphasised with the dramatic beats of a drum.
The heroic stand-off with evil as the music is egging you on, making you all the more dedicated to put an end to what lies ahead of you, be it a giant dragon that towers over you; a massive avatar capable of destroying entire continents locked in a tomb for centuries; filled with fury and out for your blood.
The gameplay is unique, fluent, responsive and instant. With mere 0.x seconds to act on certain abilities on characters makes for one of the fastest and intense combat I've had to experience, where learning the bosses and their patterns is essential for your survival.
It's punishing, harsh and ruthless if you're not able to keep up with what it throws your way. Bend it to your will and learn it, that's when it will be a most rewarding experience.
A need to mention the armours, clothing and gear in the game is something I feel worth it, as it is one of the more well-made looks to stem from the scene of F2P.
Physics-based, durability-reactive looks. Where if you move, some parts of your armour will jingle, your clothing will flutter in the wind and even earrings have models that are physics-based.
Your armour, weapons, etc: they all have durability, where repairs are needed once your gear starts to go down the numbers. This will make them look tattered, rusty, bloody; you name it. Repair them and they look just like when you bought or crafted them.
The story is one that sits close to my heart, with it being a rollercoaster; lots of shouting, crying and cheering was involved as the story unfolded, until the first season was complete. The second season followed suit and unveiled more of the grand scheme of the game and its story. Third season I fell short on, except for about half of it; but it certainly kept the spirit of the previous seasons going, tugging at my emotions when it felt I didn't want it.
A very well made story and one of the greatest I've experienced.
So, if I praise it so high, why a negative review?
Well, here's where the foul part of company handling comes into play.
Back in September, 2016; there was the promise of a merge of the EU and NA client, where the EU client would be replaced with NA functions and mechanics. This did not come to pass as the date was postponed to somewhere in Febuary, 2017.
All was well and good except for the massive incompetence that is Nexon NA.
A change of mechanics, where a sprint mechanism was introduced; which slowed down gameplay a lot because it ate away at your stamina bar. This is something I could work around and was fine with.
Removing boss HP bars was a factor, again; one I could work with.
Why is it so bad, you ask?
A little story of Vindictus EU: A lot of countries are blocked, whilst they still are within the EU zone, like Estonia, Latvia, etc.
This did not stop Nexon EU from handling the situation professionally and granted whoever played the game when these countries were not blocked full access to the game, their account and whatnot - the full gaming experience, despite the consequences.
Nexon EU then promised that Nexon NA would take care of the deal the same way - one I have blurry memories of, but something along those lines; given that these players (my boyfriend amongst them) has sunk countless hours and money into the game, because they love(d) it.
So, when the merge happened, all was well and fine up until the point of blocked countries came up. Where empty promises were made. (
)
Where both the supports' and the moderators' responses coincide with eachother, making it all the more unbelievable.
Let alone the fact that Israel was not part of the list of blocked countries, yet it's included amongst them.
As it stands right now, there has been no change to the situation and players are filled with "promises" from the 'handlers', I guess would be fitting.
I'd rather pick the trainwreck EU servers over this, honestly.

Let me start off this review by stating that the only other far cry game I have played, is Far Cry 3. Which is one I have obtained and played for the first time recently along with this installment in the Far Cry series. Now onto the review.
Far Cry 2 is a open world FPS set in an undisclosed country in Africa in between two factions vying for power after the government has collapsed. You choose from a selection of characters in the start menu when starting a new game and then dive into the world of Far Cry 2.
You may see other reviews giving this game a not recommended for having buggy AI, or annoying grievances such as respawn times for guard outposts. But I can assure you that if you look past those, and actually prefer a game be too hard than too easy, then you will more than likely enjoy this game. Many people also claim that the functions of having malaria strikes, (your vision basically turning green and a ringing in your ears as you desperatly mash the heal button hoping you have a medicine left.) difficult tough to kill enemies, and weapon degradation are what brings this game down. But to that, I can say that if you like a game that doesn't hold your hand and makes you think on your feet while not being ridiculous in its punishments, then you will probably enjoy those elements. More than once I found myself panicking and running for any piece of cover you can while enemies take pot shots at you from a meter or more away. Enemies do not take it easy on you. Unlike Far Cry 3, where enemies can lose sight of you and give up relatively quickly, in this game, the enemies will pursue with an intent to hang you above their fireplace. They are brutal, and don't take very long to notice you.
There are reviews I have seen where people say the stealth is non existant, and the enemies sight distance is "unrealistic" but I say that they are wrong, and have simply not managed to find the right way to stealth in this game. The enemies and stealth system work on a sort of "If I can't see them, they can't see me." Meaning that if your definition of stealth is hiding in a single bush and peeking halfway out behind cover, aiming your gun right at the guy, then yes, the stealth is non existant. Same goes for sound. If an enemy is down the road, and you open fire with a .50 Cal mounted machine gun, they WILL come for you.
This game is also very immersive. Turn off the crosshair, and you are left with an FPS experience like no other. There is no mini map like in the other Far Cry's save for the first. You have your own map that you have to physically pull out to see where your objective is. And no, it doesn't half♥♥♥♥♥it and show a big red dot in game when you get "close" to the objective. You have to use all of your senses to navigate, and you will die. A lot. This game also does not have the same sort of regenerative health that Far cry 3 has. And doesn't have the same healing system either. I found in Far Cry 3 that the syringes were useless halfway through the game because the animations for healing were enough to bring me back to full health. In this game, you HAVE to find medkits. You only stabilize your health when you are at one bar of health. And it can either be, (depending on the injury), a  lenghty, cringe inducing animation as you finger your bullet hole, or a quick one, where you rip out a glass shard from your hand. And depending on who you are, you may find this absolutely ridiculous and infuriating, or immersive, and an amazing addition to a game that already challenges you to your limits in terms of FPS.
All in all, I believe that Far Cry 2 is a great game for people wanting an extreme challenge when it comes to FPS games. And tired of feeling like a super hardcore robot killing machine that people fear. Because in this game, you feel outmanned, outgunned, and outlived many times.
So with all that said, Far Cry 2 gets the Blue Thumb of Approval. Highly, highly recommend if you can forget everything you know about other Far Crys', and look past some occasional bugs.

First things first: Angels with Scaly Wings is not a mystery.  If you read its Steam description carefully, you will see that it has not been explicitly advertised as one, but you could be forgiven for having that impression from some of the screenshots and Steam tags.
With the most important caveat out of the way, we can get to the actual plot.  Well, plots, really.
The main plot of the story is essentially a police procedural (but with dragons).  As with many visual novels, the plot is not gameified; there isn't much in the way of winning or losing here, unless you're playing for achievements.  As a result, this part of the game has almost no replay value.  You're not trying to win anything, so once you have seen the ending, the only part left is to explore the options you missed last time.  You do learn a few new things, and in one or two cases you can get better outcomes.  But there aren't any major reveals because they don't know which options you'll take the first time, and can't risk spoiling the ending.  The good news is that the developers knew this kind of material could be really annoying to click through when replaying, so you don't have to do that.  The game makes it easy to skip through anything you've already seen, without accidentally skipping things you haven't.  As a result, the lack of replay value in this section is unfortunate but does not drag down the rest of the game.
As the tag "Dating Sim" suggests, the rest of the story is focused on meeting and getting to know a few of the main characters in each playthrough.  Some of these characters have optional romance scenes, but not all of them.  The emphasis is on companionship rather than sex.  Unlike some dating sims, AWSW mostly fades to black rather than showing anything explicit, although there are a couple of suggestive images here and there.
The term "dating sim" is problematic in its own right.  If you click on the Dating Sim tag, you'll notice that it spans everything from shooters to visual novels, and everything from horror to comedy.  Outside of Steam tags, I have also seen it used to describe "normal" games like Mass Effect (actually, I'm pretty sure everything Bioware ever made has been called a "dating sim" at some point).  In the case of AWSW, it does have a grain of truth to it, since there are failure states for all of the characters (i.e. you can make them hate you).  In some cases, you can trigger these failures quite easily, with relatively little hinting that you're doing something wrong.  But it doesn't matter, because the game specifically encourages multiple playthroughs.  With the benefit of hindsight (and enough replays), you can befriend anyone.
A game like this will largely stand or fall on its characters, especially given that it specifically wants you to make friends with all of them.  Personally, I found them a heartwarming and likable bunch.  You probably won't love every single one of them, of course.  They're a diverse group, and don't always get along with each other.  But they have all been well written, so the average player will take a strong liking to at least one or two of them.
Unlike the main plot, the side plots have a great deal of replay value, and not just because you get to meet more characters.  The gameplay has a bit of a Majora's Mask feel to it, in that you're repeating through the same events, never able to help everyone in the same playthrough.  It's a bit depressing at first, but the game finds ways to improve on this formula.
The true ending is reasonably satisfying.  Most of the bad endings are quite painful to watch, as are some of the "good" endings.  This is deliberate, of course, and well executed.  The only major problem here is that most of the endings are nearly identical for large portions.  The game's skip functionality works as intended here (except for one brief scene which is ever-so-slightly different in each playthrough but still similar enough to annoy), but it further robs the game of replay value it could have had.
Overall, I enjoyed the time I had with this game, but I feel like it squandered some of its potential.  While AWSW certainly has more of a plot than a typical dating sim, it still feels less like a story and more like a vehicle for character development.  If a sequel is made, I hope it goes further, with a less linear plot and greater emphasis on player agency and story-relevant choices.

I don't usually write reviews for games. I've done a couple previously, but after everything I went through in my time with Angels with Scaly Wings, I knew I had to write something. I wasn't sure what I had to say though, so instead I decided to tell about my experience with this game. No spoilers, of course.
... So I tried to tell about my experience with this game. Unfortunately, I had so much to say that I actually ran out of typing space in this review. Let me sum it up easily, then.
I was drawn in by the idea of dragons as characters. What I was given was a handful of amazing, wonderful and very relatable characters. Characters that I genuinely cared for. I was also given characters that I genuinely hated. Ones that made me swear and curse at my monitor, something I haven't done since Handsome Jack in Borderlands 2. Not even to the extent that I did in this game.
I was also given a gut wrenching story. A narrative that tugs at your heart strings at any moment it can. A game that's not afraid to give you hope and happiness, and then suddenly rip that all away from you in one fell swoop. It's a story that will sometimes bring twice as many questions than it does answers. Sometimes you need to come up with the answers for yourself, because this game doesn't always tell you everything you need to know.
Angels with Scaly Wings was an emotional rollercoaster from beginning to end. You have to prepare yourself for that, and you have to push through to discover every secret you can. Do this, and you'll be granted an incredible ending that was absolutely worth the time. I hope that the developers add some DLC to this game, because I'd love to return and say hi again to all the amazing characters I met.
If there was a Dr. Modalot seal of approval, I would certainly give this game one.

First off I wanna say that I'm currently obsessed. I've gotten two endings now out of I can only assume a dozen. Don't go in with the preconcieved notion that this is a dating sim. It's really not. While yes, you can form very close relationships with most of the characters, this game is a very in-depth visual novel with a multitude of endings, and a very thought-provoking story. My first ending, everyone died. Everyone. No one was spared, and I am still recuperating from that fact.
The game has an AMAZING soundtrack, with some pretty good heart-wrenching visuals here and there. While I will honestly say going through the story multiple times was a bit repetitive, the game has a very intuitive mechanic of fast-forwarding, without skipping any NEW dialogue and choices, and when you've done an entire scene before, the game asks if you'd like to skip it entirely.
And lastly, I largely appreciate that in playing it a second time through, there were a few hints here and there that some things carried over from the previous ending. Such as, the main character remembering a very odd detail here and there, and I'm curious to see if this will be prominent as I get more and more endings. Overall, I'm hugely emotionally invested, and there's no turning back.

You won't be killing anything in this game -- enemy encounters are infrequent and invovle you running frantically from these somehow absolutely terrifying fast-moving sprites.
The endings I uncovered were each a nice twist as well.  I'm quite satisfied with the story from opening to close.
Puzzles are clever and the 8-bit scares have you running for your life.  It's a short but satisfying game that I couldn't put down until I finished it -- I *had* to see what was in the next room all the way through to the end.  It took me about a day to play to the end, which I played in a window on the side while I was working on other things throughout the day.
Impressive, extremely unique, clever game.  I highly recommend -- very much worth the $5!

In brief Insane is a Logical remake that's not quite there.
Before I get into why I don't recommend Insane I need to talk about Logical.  I first played it on the C64 way back in the day.  I really liked three things about: it's puzzle nature, the frenetic action and the musc.  Time passed and I moved on from my C64 to a PC and played the DOS port of logical.  It lost something in translation, the music most notably but also the mouse controls never really felt as good as the C64's weird joystick scheme.
Insane, unfortunately, lost something even further in translation.  It's by far the prettiest Logical I've seen and the music is servicable (not as memorable as the strange sad upbeat music of the original).  But...
The problem lies with the controls and the gameplay speed.  The locks turn very, very slowly.  The Commodore version had exactly one frame of animation on the diagonal.  Those locks could be spun fast, literally about 10 to 15 quarter revolutions a second.  And it was necessary it keep the balls in play as they also rolled around quite quickly.
In insane the balls roll slowly but relatively faster than the locks spin leading to many unintentional bounces and missed catches.
This is further exacebated by the mouse controls.  Both the DOS and Amiga versions used a two button scheme.  One button to throw the ball and the other to twist the lock.  Insane uses one button to do both, miss clicking is a constant and annoying problem as there are no cues as to whether the mouse is over the lock or a ball.
Add a little pause to the end of the rotation cycle during which the lock can't be clicked and you have only a slow puzzle game that rarely executes the expected actions.  I hate to write this because I loved Logical and have played many remakes of it over the years; and collected quite a lot of remixes of it's music.
Insane lacks the speed, the varied backgrounds, the tight controls and even the number of levels of the original.  I didn't enjoy it and it's not a game I can recommend.  Sadness.
