Neo Aquarium is a rather strange game. I actually really do enjoy it though. It plays more like a mech game or a naval/space combat game, but with laser firing crustaceans instead of machines. Someone made the joke “Armored Crab” and I think it fits quite well. It also has local multiplayer, up to 4 players, and I think it’d make for a hilarious party game.
The story obviously isn’t meant to be taken too seriously, and while it does have some cringy jokes, it also genuinely made me laugh a few times. I’ve played through the story mode a few times, in order to unlock the extra characters, at the time of writing this, there are two more I need to unlock.
The most daunting part of the game is trying to figure out what’s happening in the battles. I read through the manual that someone posted in the guide section, and it helped me get a handle on what was actually going on, and there’s actually a surprising amount of depth to the combat.
Each character has different abilities and different movement, they all feel quite different to play, and it’s pretty fun giving them all a go and trying to master some of their more technical skills.
The combat arenas are separated into two halves, yours and your opponent's. By playing the story mode, you can unlock parts for the aquarium, and there’s an edit mode where you place down the terrain, plants, and animals you’ve unlocked. The animals will help you during battle in various ways, and it is rather cool to see them all coming to your aid in a chaotic laser fight between crustaceans. The aquarium editor itself is actually kind of clunky to use, but it gets the job done.
I picked this game up during the summer sale for a few bucks, and don’t regret it. It also has an amazing soundtrack to boot, really gets you hyped up for some laser crustacean action.
TLDR: pick this game up on a sale, read through the manual someone posted in the guide section, and have yourself a blast playing this strange game for a few hours alone or with friends in the multiplayer.

I'm having some seriously mixed feelings about this one.
Let's start with the positives:
Art style, 2D graphics, sci-fi setting and eerie robots on a dusty planet make for a wonderful atmosphere and this alone would make it easy to immerse yourself within 'Stranded'.
The ending has an interesting twist, and dashed my sense of hope that I was perhaps being teleported off the planet, even going with the "Lost" ending that perhaps I had been asleep or even dead through the whole experience.
Now I must regrettably move onto the negatives:
This game is far too short. The length of the game is mostly taken up by your character's clunky movement.
It took a lot of aimless wandering and pointless clicking to get to the 4 inconveniently distanced temples, 3 different times.
The ending, rushed as it was, felt cliche and a little insulting to my intelligence. I actually let out a laugh as I'd realised what had happened, and spent at least 10 minutes contemplating my character's fate.
I would recommend this game, were it not for the insulting price of $7.99 (AUD).
A more reasonable amount would be towards the $0.99 range, but even then I would feel a tad let down.
All in all, the game had a lot of potential, but the length and clunky gameplay left me very, very disappointed.

If you're OK with paying $8 for what's pretty much a point-and-click that would be found on a site like Newgrounds, then this might be the game for you. According to steam it took me 33 minutes to complete literally all of the content in the game. The art's cool, though.

Even at a discount, Stranded is a rip-off.
Humanity has given birth to a few very talented modern artists, whose works express deep ideas that arise from high originality rather than craftmanship. It has also given birth to a multitude of talentless hacks, who possess neither craftmanship nor originality, but who claim that people who do not appreciate their works just don't understand them.
I am sorry, but I have to share Stranded amongst the products of talentless hacks.
It is not that it is worthless. But it is definitely not worth the asking price. There is nothing in the game that makes its value rise above a couple of dimes.
I do appreciate that people try to progress the art of games, by steering away from the standard fare and trying to insert something original. An original story, original visuals, original use of sound, original gameplay, original ideas. And I am not the only one who appreciates that: it looks like gamers are generally willing to support such attempts at originality, and buy experimental games in droves.
Experimental games are often commercial successes. I am not surprised that therefore we now get people trying to create games with little work and try to sell them off as "idea games" that "the masses cannot understand" but that you really should buy because they are "high art".
Stranded is minimalistic. It is based on pixel art. It has only about a dozen screens, a great many of which are rehashes of other screens in the same game. It has minimalistic music which gets boring after half a minute. It has virtually no gameplay - the only thing you can do is move a tiny astronaut around, and that is at such a slow pace that it becomes a chore really quickly. And even with that slowly moving astronaut, you play this "game" to the ending in less than 45 minutes. Because there is nothing to do, only moving, and once you have moved to the right places in the right order, the ending automatically plays. You can hardly call this a "game". It could easily have been just a short movie, or a series of paintings, as the player really doesn't do anything.
The only reason to make this a game is to let the player identify with the character that he or she controls, but that doesn't happen here. The player has no reason to empathize with the tiny astronaut or get immersed in the game.
"But," the game's supporters will say, "this is not about the gameplay! It is about the atmosphere! It is about a feeling of wonder and loneliness!" Yeah, right. I hardly felt wonder, apart from wondering what the hooplah was all about. And I definitely did not feel lonely. I felt ripped off.
Stranded has been compared to The Dig. And indeed, The Dig provides a feeling of wonder when the protagonists enter an alien world, filled with weird contraptions they cannot understand, but which seem to have an inherent logic to them. It also provides a feeling of loneliness as the protagonists seem to have no means of escape and have to rely only on themselves. The Dig is not perfect as a game, but it brought original elements to the table which rarely had been seen before.
Stranded gives me the impression that the author has tried to create the same kind of atmosphere as The Dig provided, but was unwilling to put in the required work. He could have created a series of paintings, but pixel art is easier, and games sell better than paintings.
I believe that the creation of originality in games should be encouraged. But the creation of games that try to get sold on the notion that they are "original" while they are actually a cheaply-produced attempt at a quick commercial success should be discouraged.
Rather than buy Stranded, see that you get a copy of The Dig. It provides what Stranded unsuccessfully tried to do, and much, much more.

The story, graphics and combat system are the redeeming qualities of this game, and I mean the
redeeming qualities. This game was at its best (in my opinion) before they changed the crafting system to its current system. It feels to me that the producers caved in to pier pressure. When you have people who play the game, but complain about so many things, the producers have one of two choices; either listen to them and ruin the game or ignore them and keep the game great. They simplified the game
much, it just became massively boring. Until players get to level 90, they are basically forced to solo a massive amount of missions and until a player reaches the second season, everything goes down without breaking a sweat as though they were all Gnoll Chieftains with a few extra health bars. There are bosses like Glas with special ways to defeat them, but completely obsolete because just hitting them with regular attacks is enough to do the job and at a faster pace. Then you got this poor excuse of a crafting system. A system that uses only a half a dozen different types of items, just at a few different qualities, in which are generally useless to begin with thanks to the new Composite system you learn at level 80 to make level 90+ equipment. Even still, is generally pointless since you get a high grade set of armor and weapons when you reach level 90 which will basically be better than anything you make unless you get the final armor set and rank it to 10+. The producers took a great game and only looked at the end result, bypassing
before it. The only qualities I find good about Mabinogi Heroes/Vindictus now are the qualities they haven't changed (or barely did) and that's the story, the graphics and the combat system. In which, unfortunately, is not enough to get me to want to continue playing. I've seen a lot of great games shut down because the producers make bad choices and I fear this game will not last much longer as well. I am not putting the blame on the producers, but on the players as well. In making a game great, players are required just as much as the producers themselves. The players have the role of leading producers to problems so they can be fixed, but because there are players out there that don't like one or two aspects of a game, they have to make a mountain out of a mole hill and twist the arms of the producers just so they can get what they want, leading to the game's eventual shut down. People want to make equipment easier, people want to reach the max level faster, people just want to play someone else's game and expect to be their ideal game and if it isn't, they complain and complain until it is changed to their wants.
When is a game at its greatest? On the day of its release.
If you are looking for a fun afternoon, this is definitly the right pick for you. The replayability isn't great but it a ride worth the price of admission.

I am someone who played Kingdom of Loathing a lot back in the day, and enjoyed it a lot. The first time I heard about West of Loathing was the day it released on Steam. At that point, I hadn't thought about KoL in YEARS, and had actually forgotten it existed. But my good memories (once I excavated them from under years of dust and rubble) were enough to convince me to buy this game on the spot for full price, which is something I virtually never do (though, really, it has a pretty low price tag, which is nice).
It was one of the best buys I've made in a long time.
This game is an RPG, and plays as such. But at its core, this game is about reading. Because, though the RPG elements are perfectly fine, and quite in-depth when it comes to this type of game, when it comes right down to it, we all love this game for the jokes.
The writing is leaps and bounds beyond any game I have ever come across (which doesn't surprise me, because KoL was the same way, and it's made by the same people). Part of the reason for the stellar writing is the, shall we say, unique art style, which some may find a turn-off. But because of the minimalist nature of the animations, a lot of actions and scenes are written out rather than animated, and it just WORKS. It works so well that I've bought this game several times over and gifted it to my friends because I just love it that much.
TL;DR
If you enjoy witty humor, reading, and RPGs, get this game for sure, whether on sale or not. Just get it.
If you prefer serious games, don't like doing a lot of reading in your gaming, or dislike turn-based RPGs, this is not the game for you.
(Also if you don't like stick figures probably don't get it, but eh, it's likely you could still enjoy it. It's great.)

This game is tremendously terrible.  I tried really hard to get into it, but the struggle finally overcame me.  Because it's a free game, it's actually hard for me to write a review about it and tell you that I don't recommend that you even try it.  But here I am: doing what I hadn't thought possible before.
Besides the clunky and awkward user interface, the battles and the decks are ultra-lame.  I got very frustrated just trying to select the card that I wanted to play each round - it's just super-annoying and makes you wonder "Why would a game programmer do something so stupid like this?"
The battles are just glorified suicide missions.  The question again will be begged, "Why would some idiot program my army to kill itself in combat as a part of the strategy?"  It just doesn't make sense that you are expected to burn through your cards with suicide attacks, all the while you are able to hit your opponent's leader nearly always uninhibited.  It just doesn't make sense, and it is the core aspect of this game!
The card decks are not what I expected: something like leading the faction that I chose at the onset.  Rather, I am using a hodgepodge of cards that basically just play to the mandatory suicide strategy.
Again, this game is just so effin' lame.  It angered me to play it!  I couldn't imagine how such a stupid thing was introduced to the world.  Here we have a legendary game franchise (The Elder Scrolls) being drug through the mud like so many classic franchises have been with their idiotic "card" games.  Most of these types of games have been at least somewhat entertaining, as they at least made sense.  But Elder Scrolls: Legends is just plain stupid.
To close, I will say a something nice about the game.  The music, graphics, and voice-acting on the cut scenes are not terrible.  In fact, they are the only reason why I even tried the darn game.  But truly, if you have a brain that likes to be challenged in a fun way, this game is just too stupid and lame to bother with.  But then again, it is free to get into, so maybe just prove that to yourself.  But I was driven to a point where I just had to uninstall the thing.  I definitely do not recommend this game to anyone who likes strategy games, card games, the Elder Scrolls franchise, or video games in general.  The developer should be embarrassed of this monstrosity.

As someone who has never played or even heard about the game, I gotta say this game is pretty good and totally worth the asking price.
I originally saw a post from a local site about this game being newly released on steam. I don't even read the article, I only saw the post's thumbnail and then checked it straight away on steam. As i begin scrolling the thumbnail on the steam page, I see a busty anime woman and a cute loli girl - something that a weeb like me totally dig. Oh and also, it's cheap so I bought it without any second thoughts.
So the first one hour of the game I got bored 'cause I hit a dead end and don't know where else to go. So I googled a bit about the game and to my surprise there is actually a free version of the game. To be honest, even though I already said it's cheap, I actually considered to refund the game and get the free version instead. But eventually I decided to give it another chance until I finally passed the 2 hours mark. At some point I finally got hooked up and I finished the game in one sitting.
Moving on to the game itself, I think Mad Father is a pretty well made exploration horror game. While I don't play horror games much, I think most of the game mechanics are quite similar to the more popular survival horror games, e.g. the puzzle solving, jumpscares, and monster hide and seek. And it manages to do it well in 2D. Coupled with a decent level design and music, you have a pretty sweet $5 package for the gameplay alone. As for the story, it also manages to surprise me and exceed my expectations. The characters are pretty okay, there are some plot hole and obvious plot convinience but overall it's good. There are quite a bit of disturbing mysteries to discover, and it concludes to a mildly surprising climax. What I like the most are the endings, not only the ending themselves but how to get all of them. I was forced to replay the game from the beginning because I missed some of the prerequisites for a certain ending but I don't get mad at all, in fact I realized how much I liked this game after doing my second playthrough straight after finishing the first one. I also like how each ending played out
.
So to sum it up, Mad Father is a great game overall, it has a nice gameplay and a good story. Totally would recommend.

This is a tough one to review. On the one hand I am a massive horror fan and so I am a little biased to always review horror games like this positively. On the other hand however I have spent quite a bit of time playing this game now and at times I have found the game infuriating. Whilst I am no stranger to horror games where avoidance/escape are your only means of defence, if a monster spots you in this game it is very difficult to get away from it... In fact you're probably more likely to run into another and before you know it you have 3 monsters chasing you. This in itself isn't a massive issue, but the save system of this game sometimes means that you can find yourself being unavoidably killed and having to replay 10-20 mins of the game. In all fairness this is very much the way games used to be and in old school horror the threat of dying before reaching a save point added to the thrill and horror... In this game however, it's just been frustrating.
The gameplay is a little clunky in places but on the whole, not too bad. Graphics are decent but by no means great. Voice acting is all in portuguese (unless I've missed an option to change this to English somewhere) so I can't really comment on how good or bad this is but it sounds okay. The ambience of the game is pretty good. Enemy design is one of the biggest weakpoints of the game. The enemies are pretty much all the same and don't look that intimidating to be honest... just typical human style monsters. Storyline from what I've played so far is fairly generic and nothing to write home about.
All in all this isn't a BAD game... But it's not GOOD game either. As a horror fan I may have been inclined to give this game a positive review, but certain factors have left a bad taste in my mouth and I just can't bring myself to do it. I got this game on sale and for me, it was worth it for the price I paid. But at full price, even for a massive horror fan like myself, I think this game is overpriced by quite a bit. If you see it on sale at under £1 and you're a fan of horror then I would recommend getting it just to fill a couple of hours but otherwise I can't recommend this title.

1. You do get to upgrade your gear by buying it from a blacksmith or looting some in chests you can loot,

By the vendor who actually makes the barrels of course!

Don't listen to the people out there crying it's pay to win. As someone who actually put more time into the game than getting salty over the first match I lost, this game is anything but pay to win. Do you have to put some time in to grind out decks and get cards? Sure, but the game is fun and enjoyable and offers so much in the way of tactics and choices to build your deck around. There's also a very enjoyable storyline they are continually working on advancing.
The base game is free. All of the DLC and cards can be purchased simply through just playing the game. Pay to win implies you're able to achieve something through spending money you are not otherwise able to achieve and a few people are attempting to apply this term inappropriately to the game. They cry because "It takes hundreds of hours to grind out every last card". To me that tells me there is a lot of card choices and I'm not going to be limited in my selection and also you don't need every single card to make it to the top of the ranking ladder. There's plenty of very powerful decks that can be assembled from not all that much time invested.
I've been a long time fan of MTG, played it for over 20 years, and am very critical of card games I choose to play. The only downside I have found to this game (I had around 100 hours played through the Bethseda launcher before I added it to Steam) is that when you beat a higher ranked person in ranked mode you don't get any bonus for beating them and similarly, when losing to a higher ranked person, you lose the same amount of rank as if you were playing someone your same level.  If you're playing against higher ranked people, how much you win or lose should also fluxuate as well.
In short, if you expect everything handed to you and to be coddled as you play, you probably won't enjoy this game. I don't mind playing the matches and grinding out the rewards. There are plenty of options on ways to play. You can do story mode, you can do casual matches, there's draft type matches (where the cards you own don't even matter), you can play against friends (and yes, if you are on PC you can play with someone on mobile). And if you don't want to do that, you can always invest money into the game. After all, you didn't pay a penny to download it and start playing it in the first place.

The match finished but if you happen to try to want to click elsewhere you might just click to get into another match. Cancel that and try again? Too bad the pop up to play again window is back.
One might wonder if there's Add Blocker for this game?
Honestly save yourselves the headache, and just stick with Hearthstone. This game is an early attempt at mimicking Blizzard's monetary income.

I play a lot of fighting games. But if there's one game I will take to a deserted island, it would be Melty Blood. Me and my siblings have been playing this for ~13 years.
Originally released in December 2002, this is a visual novel that happened to have a fighting game minigame. This was long before BlazBlue introduced the idea to the mainstream. The game's story is a continuation of Tsukihime and (surprisingly), is canon and explains how dead characters returned to life to fight with the small roster.
The original game was broken. A lot of moves have shield frames (meaning, if this move hits another move, no damage is done but you can cancel to a different move) which lead to anime-esque fights with freeze frames everywhere as players switch moves to try to break through. Also, the post-victory screen will not end until the defeated character is on the ground. Meaning, if you killed your opponent while they're on the air, you can juggle them almost infinitely before the round will officially end (like other airdashers, the longer a combo is, the heavier the opponent becomes).
Regardless, this game has a lot of innovations. Some of them are:
- This game has 3 buttons and a dedicated shield button (think of it like Street Fighter V Ryu's parry but you can cancel to other moves) - which makes each character easy to play.
- Melty Blood has no chip death making to exciting matches.
- Characters can use their meter to gain a new gauge (called HEAT) that slowly goes down. During this time, the character regenerates life AND stops the clock. This makes the timer an important resource to manage. It is common for a player to stop the clock when its almost over and run away (or rushdown) to maintain the lead.
- Super moves on a successful parry during HEAT.
Later expansions in the series include Re-ACT (PC), ReACT Final Tuned (PC), Act Cadenza (Arcade), Act Cadenza Ver.B (PS2), Act Cadenza Ver.B (PC), Actress Again (PC), Actress Again Current Code (PC). ...if you think Street Fighter's naming convention is crazy, French Bread has taken it to the extreme.
The game released on Steam will have the following features:
- More characters! There are now 31 characters.
- Each character have 3 different fighting style which each plays completely different. Effectively, this game has 31 multiply by 3 characters
- Balance
- Updated story (very important for those who wanted more Tsukihime)
This game is so popular that it was referenced in the Type-Moon fan-service OVA, Carnival Phantasm.
The Melty Blood fighting community love this game so much, that we have no problem playing the grand finals at a parking lot or airport lounge. This is how dedicated we are to this game.
If you haven't played this gem and you love fighting games, give Melty Blood a shot. Who knows? Maybe you'll be airdashing with the rest of us for the next 13 years.

A: There are several improvements. Firstly, Mirror Moon was not able to finish the translations of some of the character's story arcade modes. This includes Nanaya Shiki, Roa, and a few others. In addition, this version offers controller configuration and keyboard configuration within the game's option menu. In the original release of the game, keyboard configuration was done in a separate, non-translated .exe. Also, pressing the escape key won't immediately cause the game to exit, like it does in the orignal. This version also lists the combos on the side panels.
Q: The store page says that this is the final episode of a series. Do I need to play the previous episodes?
A: That depends. If you only interested in the fighting part of this fighting game, you only need this game, as it is superior to all previous versions in term of fighting mechanics. However, playing at least the first game in the series (Melty Blood) is essential to understanding the storyline of this game, and anyone who hasn't played Tsukihime will be COMPLETELY lost. However, the fighting mechanics in the original Melty Blood are a bit....crap in comparison to this game. In addition, the original Melty Blood featured a story-to-combat ratio of at least 10:1, maybe as high as 30:1.
Q: How's the translation?
A: I haven't played the arcade mode for very long, but what I've seen appears to be good enough. I'll update this later after I've seen more. I might even upload some screenshot comparisons if i can be bothered.
Q: I don't know anything about Tsukihime. However, I like Guitly Gear and BlazBlue. Will I like this?
A: Yes. MBAACC uses the three-button attack sytem of Guilty Gear and BlazBlue, so any player of these games should feel right at home in this one. Heck, I'd argue that this games is BETTER than Guilty Gear XX and BlazBlue Calamity Trigger. However, as I mentioned previously, I may be a bit biased.
Overall, I recommend this game to fighting game fans and fans of Type-Moon. I also recommend this to people who already "own" a copy of the Japanese version.

- Femme Fatale: a sexy sniper who sneaks her way around missions and has high charisma.

The Bard's Tale is a hack 'n' slash, dungeon crawl style RPG that doesn't take itself seriously. Straight from the off you'll find extremely blunt sarcasm and tongue-in-cheek puns, the humour of which not always finding the mark and at times will leave you cringing, other times providing you with a good chuckle.
Ignore Diablo II comparisons, this is more along the lines of Baldur's Gate: Dark Alliance, there isn't a loot system to speak of, all findings add to your gold tally and you make purchases from shop keepers as you go along. The summon system is functional, if a touch on the conservative side, with choices becoming quite obvious as you get deeper in the game which rules out the need to experiment with your companions.
Whilst The Bard's Tale doesn't provide anything original to the genre by any stretch of the imagination, it is worth a punt when on offer and will keep you engaged for a short stretch of time.

Majesty Gold HD is an unusual game with an unusual history.
While it's billed as a Fantasy Kingdom Sim, Majesty has most of the trappings of a conventional RTS. However, it does stray from RTS convention in one major aspect and that was enough for its developer, Cyberlore Studios, to have considerable difficulty finding a publisher even during the great RTS glut of the 90s.
To fully appreciate Majesty, you need to talk about RTSes in general. Now, the term Real-Time Strategy itself is a little generic -- Crusader Kings II, for instance, is real-time and it is a strategy game but no one would confuse it for an RTS. When gamers use the term, they're referring to very specific types of games -- games like Blizzard's Warcraft II and Westwood's Command & Conquer, the two titles released in 1995 that inspired the RTS glut.
These games required both speed (measured in actions per minute) and efficiency (through optimised build orders) and you needed tight control over proceedings for both. Control was important to such an extent in those 90s RTSes that your army would sit idly while the enemy was marching close by simply because you hadn't given your troops the attack order.
Majesty's major deviation from RTS convention was to give its Dungeons & Dragons-inspired units autonomy and personality. Your units weren't manufactured goods and you didn't have total control over them. You barely had any. Instead of commanding and conquering in this game, you cajoled and hoped for the best. To entice your "heroes" to do what was required of them, you provided them with financial incentives attached to flags. You'd plant a Explore Flag with 200 gold to encourage exploration of that distant area of the map or plant an Attack Flag with 400 gold on the head of the Troll assailing the marketplace. This indirect approach could both be delightful (when the "heroes" performed unexpectedly heroic actions) and exasperating (when the "heroes" demonstrated precisely why sneer quotes were necessary).
Majesty charmed enough gamers with its unusual approach in 2000 to warrant an expansion pack the following year and Majesty Gold bundled both together in 2002. By 2007, the game had sold an impressive 500,000 copies. While there was enough demand for more Majesty, Cyberlore once again had trouble finding a publisher. The developers sold the rights to Paradox which then tasked Russian developer Ino-Co to work on the sequel.
Released in 2009, Majesty 2 was an honest attempt to improve the design but the designers erred in giving the player greater control over the heroes. In doing so, the designers brought the game closer to conventional RTSes rather than taking the design further down the sim path.
It's perhaps telling that Paradox felt compelled to release an updated version of the original three years after the sequel was released. More remarkably, Majesty Gold HD was patched five years later by a Cyberlore developer who's apparently working on the game in his free time. Something about Majesty does seem to inspire loyalty and affection from everyone who's encountered it.
The key question, however, is whether anyone who's unfamiliar with the game could be tempted to play it today. The visuals are dated, the interface primitive and the core concept -- the "D&D ant farm" -- has been expanded upon by the likes of the brilliant Dwarf Fortress and its derivatives. All things considered, Majesty Gold HD's appeal today would mainly be to players of the original looking to revisit an old favourite.
Yet there could still be a place for a Majesty 3 or a spiritual successor to the series. A Sim D&D with Majesty's eccentric charm might strike gold even in today's cluttered market and if there's one lesson Majesty has imparted, it's this: when there's a sufficiently large financial incentive involved, someone will come along to claim that flag eventually.

Basically, placement of buildings, micromanaging the research, production, and upgrading of different things, and planning on a high level are what wins the game.
Pros:
- Funny dialogue from characters.
- Different missions that require you to approach the game's mechanics in different ways.
- An interesting set of buildings with unique mechanics.
- The game is challenging but always fair. I have been attacked by dragons in the first 30 seconds of a mission and pulled through just fine.
Cons:
- Dialogue repeats too much sometimes.

If there is not enough reward, the task is far away and the hero is caught in the middle of something, or the task is too dangerous to get to alive then there is no way that it will get done. This game is all about setting up things in just the right way so your heroes can succeed.

DnD: Chronicles of Mystara is a great package of two all time beat-em-up classics: Tower of Doom and Shadow over Mystara which have been regarded as one of the best Beat-em-ups ever, now with online multiplayer!
Now for people who have never played the originals, i will explain the basics of these two games
Both Tower of Doom and Shadow over Mystara are really good beat-em-ups, but what makes them differ from other games of the genre like Streets of Rage or Knights of the Round is the different paths, secrets, Leveling and items like Throwing daggers or Magic rings
During some levels, you are given a choice. For example: In the first stage you are asked to either help a town or chase the monsters to their lair in the mountains. This gives the game a lot of replayability and makes the 1 hour completion time feel not as bad.
I also mentioned secrets, which include all kinds of bonus equipment like the Ring of Damage Resistance +2 and getting all of them will not be easy as some of them are well hidden.
The first game, Tower of Doom has 4 classes to play as: Fighter, Cleric, Elf and Dwarf. Each of the characters levels up as you progress through the game, granting more HP and more spells to the classes who have magic.
The second game, Shadows over Mystara adds a lot of content over ToD like, two more classes: Thief and Magic-user
Better inventory, Additional combat moves, smoother controls, faster and better looking spell effects, etc.
Both games boast incredibly good music, like most Capcom games back then and also the graphics look really good and detailed considering their age.
If i had one complaint about these games, it would be the arcade difficulty designed to get as many quarters as possible, but thanks to the infinite quarters, anyone can play through these games.
*edit also doesn't support any other controller besides Xbox 360 and PS4, but can be avoided by using x360ce
This game gets my recommendation, so get in there with friends and smack the living daylights out of everything that moves!

Mad Father is an RPG Maker indie horror game created by Sen using WOLF RPG Editor, released in 2012 and translated to English by vgerson in 2013. The game was originally freeware, and an unpaid version can still be downloaded from vgperson's website, albiet without the fantastic rework and extra content included in this Steam version.
$5 is a criminally low price for this game. With a chilling story following the perspective of a young child surrounded by dark secrets, combined with the various graphical and minor gameplay reworkings exclusive to the Steam version, and a new extra chapter only accessible by achieving 100% completion in a playthrough, Mad Father's surprise Steam release continues to scare, shock, and entertain players new and old alike.
Mad Father stands as one of the classics of RPG Maker horror, and this updated version contains enough content to easily warrant a replay from veterans of the freeware version.

I picked up the game because the developer posts a lot on Reddit and, if you're just going by .gifs, the game looks fun. I saw it on sale and figured I'd just go ahead and pick it up.
The game just doesn't really work out for me. The physics are supposed to be a huge selling point for the game, and the first time you blow up a building with a fire spell you'll probably say "well that was cool" but after doing it a few more times you start to notice how weightless everything feels. I would compare the destruction in this game pretty unfavorably to XCOM 1/2. In those games, especially the second game, you can also accindentally end up wiping out a map throughout a battle. The difference is that at the end of a mission in XCOM, there are more reminders that you've been through.
There may be a raging fire still engulfing a building, craters from grenades, just a big mess overall.
Here? It just feels like somebody just kicking around lego blocks. The destruction is just very lackluster, and without that, the game begins to fall apart. Enemies are mostly trash to fight against because it mostly boils down to "shoot them before they rush you". The only fun battles, at least in chapter one, are ones involving other mages, especially in the middle of a town.
Maps are pretty soulless, go figure. Interiors are very detailed and when you walk inside houses and inns, you feel like these are places people do stay and live in. Once you leave though, every map I've come across so far save for a few few like small Skyrim villages with, like, three or four buildings.
Going beyond the maps is the campaign/quest/whatever. If  you've played FTL, you know what you're in for. You move from left to right, completing quests or not and trying not to get caught in the advancing orange wall from the left. The problem is that the game aggressively doubles down on the FTL formula and feels like a strictly inferior versions of FTL.
***
"Rather than starting out as a hapless farm boy who stumbles into his powers and avoids enemies or entire areas until leveling up, players take on the role of an established wizarding badass, hell-bent on his mission for revenge."
I never really feel badass in this game because your only sense of progression is loot-based. Leveling up your spells amounts to just purchasing new runes, which doesn't have the same feel as purchasing a new weapon for your ship in FTL. The game is so loot-based that you have to loot houses to really get things, which is about as dumb and DND as you can get. Why does some villager have a pair of boots that greatly increases your mana reserves? No idea.
The gameplay loop doesn't make sense. In FTL, you go from encounter to encounter and gain fuel and cash that you need to move your ship and buy things respectively. Most of the time, you're getting your weapons from a shop.
Here, you, an allegedly powerful mage, has to loot the homes of some poor villagers to actually become a powerful mage because you need that equipment. Whatever you don't use you'll just sell to a vendor, from whom you can buy things from.
***
Drilling down harder on the FTL comparison is, again, destruction. I feel nothing blowing a hole into a roof or the side of a building in this game. You might kill an enemy, but there is seldom a tactical advantage to this destruction wherea in XCOM, blowing a hole into a wall means you can get to the objective faster or flank an enemy.
In FTL, the way damage affects you over the course of the battle matters. Somebody can blow a hole in your ship that causes oxygen to slowly leak, but also puts out fires. Attacks can start fires, which damages your ship and can spread. Destruction in FTL and damage affects you in many ways, whereas in this game health is just a secondary mana bar that needs to be recharged by looting houses or buying health.
TL;DR
Enemies are mostly boring and just "rush you and cut you". Destruction is a gimmick that serves as the core identity of the game, but isn't really flshed out or interesting as it could be. On-the-fly spell modification is interesting, but spell modifications as a whole have been done far better in games like Tyranny. The game is too expensive because I can pick up FTL or just about nothing.

At first glance, Wrongworld can be perceived as a barebones survival game with charm and predictability, but develops into a small (the map does seem small) mystery of uncovering inquisition. What's the giant satellite do? What do the phone booths do? Meteor showers? You become astounded at what a minimal looking game can show you. The main character comes from what could be a dream (seriously had dreams about similar bear-like creatures with large eyes from space as a kid), but the game can turn into something that of a faint nightmare.
Wrongworld does not hold your hand for what to do and simply allows you to explore at your own accord. I like that about it. If you've played any survival games before, this one is not much different in its mechanics: you harvest, build, tier-based progression, repeat, etc. Some survival games have no endgame, this one appears to have one (leaving the planet?), though what seemed incredibly easy to survive turned into a capricious world of malice and unforgiving. Sure it is easy to dodge enemies, but when you run away and more chase you or pop up from the ground and start a gaggle, it becomes detriment to fight or run away farther.
I laughed many times with the sounds and actions the game takes for humor. My favorite character is the Snoodle (what i call the snake thing) because of its absurd laughs and attempt at attacking by hurdling itself or slamming its own head toward your position. The artwork in general is also very interesting. I love the painted styled sky and celestial entities (however I feel like the wisping shapes of the night sky feels patterned or copy and pasted). I love how it changes from day to night by abruptly spinning, it tripped me out the first few times. The terrains and biomes themselves seem bare and devoid of any character other than the few elements that make the biomes, themselves, identifiable.
Now for the obligatory verbiage of what I didn't like:
What is wrong with Wrongworld is the amount of daytime you lack. I dug up a potato, it rolled down the hill and by the time I caight it, it was night time. Similarly, I dug up all the crops in my greenhouse which is roughly space for 9-12 crops and before i Finished--it was night time. I was upset by this. The reason I was upset by this, is even though it can be easy to defeat monsters, they can become overwhelming when you are just trying to do basic maintenence or cook. The fact you have to have a timed bar for crafting and cooking is annoying because it can easily be interrupted by a creature at the fast encroaching nighttime. Combat is tedious at best, but necessary for survival. I would hope it becomes more interesting. I didn't think there was enough content, but events started happening
and that made me play the game without it feeling like a chore by driven curiosity.
Resources seem expensive and achieved in tedium. It takes forever to get stuff going with how fast daytime goes by. I don't mind the nights being "longer" for it being an alien planet, but they just go by so quickly and trigger events and violent pigs! Seriously, those pigs were the most dangerous... I hope to see more of a base with interior rooms as opposed to just a gated area you claim as your own. And of course, multiplayer would be fun as well!
Also I had mentioned the map seeming to be small... so I didn't understand the point of teleporting across since traveling was not a big deal to me other than getting lost... but large flag poles solved that problem as well as getting used to the map.
In summary, it feels like the game has been made to cater toward young gamers, casual gamers and up to more hardcore survival gamers. The game looks childish, but it is a sleek and abstract art I have come to enjoy. It plays simple, runs smooth, challenges the unwary, and has lots of personality reminiscent to those worlds of N64 games like Banjo/Conker/Mario. I can't wait to see what else is added!
I was also pleased to find that when my inevitable death had grasped me, I was rewarded with some starter items for next game. Pretty cool! I hope more of those come if it remains as difficult as it is. (I refuse to play easy mode).
This concludes my review, and I am going to continue to play it as I have been enjoying it and trying to satiate my curiosities with the elements that may be hidden in the game!

PROS:
1. Very unique and abstract artstyle, which I actually quite liked.
2. Has a bit of personality in it's text, items etc.
3. Great devs!
CONS:
(For every con (or most, at least) I will suggest a solution to it underneath.)
1. EXTREMELY overpriced for the content it is providing.
SOLUTION:  I urge the developers to PLEASE, PLEASE lower the price of this game as it will bring many new reviews and feedback from people while also keeping points like this from arising in reviews. There is just not enough content to justify spending 22$CAD on.
2. Gets insanely boring quickly due to the above issue.
3. Combat is quite easy. Enemies die in a few hits and I have yet to see any real challenges outside of the more exotic enemies in different biomes surrounding the starter area.
4. Combat is bland. Fighting usually consists of strafing whilst attacking enemies from behind, or locking them in a stun lock and killing them before they can attempt to land another blow on you. Out of all the enemies I only saw a few that could've stood a remotely good chance against me, and that was mostly just because of the fact that they have a higher health pool from the others. I didn't see much variations of attack coming from my enemies other than them just launching themselves forwards towards me, which was easily countered by, once again, strafing.
SOLUTION: Make enemies smarter rather than more tankier/more damaging. Make them change their attack patterns often, to confuse the player. Fighting assassins is much more fun than fighting tanks. (In video games, I mean.)
5. All simple tasks such as collecting wood, mining and fishing are extremely tedious to do. Harvesting wood, stone and ore usually consists of just holding right click with your desired tool out and waiting for a progress bar and animation to eventually end and then collecting the resources dropped afterwards. It's just unacceptable, and downright boring, especially for the amount of these materials required in essential crafting recipes.
SOLUTION: Make harvesting resources more engaging to the player by adding different ways of letting players harvest resources.
6. Balancing in crafting needs to be readjusted. It took me 10 wood peices (5 mins of farming) to craft a wooden axe, which barely did anything for me, and then when I eventually obtained a workbench I unlocked a recipe for a stone axe that was only 5 wood and 5 stone, which was much easier and more fun to gather than the previous and much less powerful axe.
SOLUTION: Make items cheaper or make getting the materials for them more engaging. Making it so you need to obtain multiple different types of resources or unique items for a specific thing would definitely solve this.
CONCLUSION:
Decent game, great dev, great community, cool artstyle, but there is just no meat to the game yet and many game mechanics feel quite clunky and unpolished, as well as poorly designed in nature. I firmly support the dev in the development of this game, but right now it is just much too rough of a game to truly be worth 22$CAD. Lower the price of the game, and then it would DEFINITELY be a positive from me.

I wanted to believe in this game, really I did. But I was let down so very bad by what the game offers out of the gate. "Partial Controller Support"? Nowhere to be found. Push a button on my wired 360 controller, character jumps. Push any other button, nothing happens. So there is clearly no controller support here (false advertising?). I don't see any button mappings for controllers, and no way to edit the key bindings. So either I play with mouse and keyboard, or I make do with one button.
Screen resolution is at a severe loss - game does not take into account that not everyone has a huge screen size. If I want to play at a resolution at anything close to my maximum resolution, I have to settle for black bars on the screen, which utterly kills the immersion one would expect from a game like this. Seems widescreens like mine don't get factored in. My top resolution is 1366x768, yet the only usable one is 1280x720 or 1024x768 - and those black bars. Oh, those black bars. The lack of widescreen support also kills the game for me.
The fact that I cannot launch the game before experiencing these problems leaves me wondering what else may be wrong with it - but I'm not willing to stick around and find out. I love horror games, even indie horror games, but this was a letdown out of the gate. Let's Play videos made this game look good, but unfortunately my first experiences (which have the biggest impact) were a huge letdown.
I'm sorry, but I just cannot recommend this game. Save your money for better horror games out there.

Pesadelo is not Perfect-elo, it’s an ambitious indie horror that is desperately trying to avoid the common walking simulator horror tropes. It succeeds in a few areas, while comically stumbling in others. For a first time, low budget, indie offering that could use a fair bit of refinement --it's not devoid of thrilling moments. I was surprised how it turned into a stealth based cat and mouse maze through dark crypts and mausoleums. Good lighting and visuals construct a thrilling atmosphere to dodge monsters in the night. It's flaws will be ignored by fans of creative indie horrors, and this one fits that bill.
- Good lighting, texture, and level design ... pretty good use of Unreal 4's visual prowess.
- Tense cat and mouse gameplay, with some occassional jump scares.
- Pedro (see review)
- Confusing moments, with little or no direction given.
- Really bad animations
- Campy scenes and awkward moments, monsters thwarted by a door.
If you like dark enviroment, original story and being scary, this is the indie game for you !
Don't be put off by the art style there's more creativity and fun here than you might think at first glance.

The Bard's Tale is a great casual RPG that takes  you back to gaming as it was nearly ten years ago. So be prepared for a top down third person view most of the time.  What makes it most enjoyable are the bawdy humor in the dialog and the lyrics to the songs.
Our hero in the game, The Bard, is not really a hero; but a scounderal given to snarky comments and possessed of an ability to get himself into trouble.  His comments are not limited to dialog with NPC's.  He is equally capable of taking issue with the narrator and both seem to have a mutual hate relationship which adds to the fun.  You'll also encounter Scottish, English and French accents with a healthy dose of Scottish words for things, which is fitting for story based on legends from the Orkney Islands of Scotland.
The Bard needs to recruit a team to help rescue a damsel in distress and true to his character, he's not willing to help without a reward, which the damsel offers.  That offer ought to make you chuckle.  Along the way you'll summon many creatures and finally figure out which ones are most useful to you.  After that you'll have an opportunity to really wreak mayhem and get yourself into some interesting situations.  The game is full of cliche's on purpose and they spice it up instead of detract from game-play.  And of course there are always complications along the way to add dimension to the game.
The screen resolution choices are based on what was available at release time.  Don't fuss over them too much.  Pick the largest resolution with the same ratio as your screen and it ought to look fine anyway.  Works fine on a 1900x1200 monitor.
It can be played with a controller, but you may find the onscreen prompts to be confusing and awkward.  If you do use a controller, you can find a useful list of controls at
- seriously though, the game is best player with a mouse and keyboard.  It just works better for a game this old.
The original game was released in 1985 and twenty years later this version was released with much improved graphical content and music.  If you want the full retro experience, the menu system will let you load up the original game and have a go at it.

Not much of a review guy, so this will probably be the only game i'll ever review on steam. This is also going to be a little biased and you'll see why in a second.
Okay first off, the world itself is amazing. For a game made in 2008, the level of detail in the world and atmosphere is phenomonal. The music that comes along with it is great, changing whether or not the game detects you being in a fire fight or not. The character models are also good, no two seem to look the same although they do have similarities. Only gripe would be the voice acting; characters mouths dont always seem to move in sync with the dialogue. The map is massive, and you'll spend a good amount of time driving to locations or maybe just walking like I usually do. If you're not a patient person, and need to have some kind of action 24/7, this won't be for you. The action is there, and explosions and gun fights happen frequently, but if you're expecting the rushed delivery from something like CoD or Battlefield, stray away.
Theres a good selection of weapons to choose from once you've done a bunch of the convoy missions. Some include different snipers (Dragunov, AS50), submachine guns (MAC-10, UZI), Assault Rifles (AK, AR-15) and theres rocket launchers, a dart rifle to sneak around with, a mortar and a 6 round grenade launcher. Theres more aswell I just dont remember everything. All will deteriorate and jam once used too much, so you've got to keep an eye on your loadout or you'll run into an outpost empty handed and get slaughtered. You can only carry 4 weapons at a time, and choose wisely or you'll be stuck in long range engagement with a shotgun, pistol and a flamethrower. You can choose how aggressive or passive you want to play depending on your loadout which gives the game some replay value if you went through the campaign once and only played a certain way.
The game is a ton of fun once you get past the tutorial (which only lasts about 10-20 mins).
If i have to mention some cons, here are some. The respawning enemies at outposts can be annoying sometimes I suppose, but if they didnt respawn youd clear out all of them and then just be driving around an empty map that sure is well designed and beautiful, but wouldnt have any of the action youd expect from an FPS. Sound design from gun sounds to weather to just everything in general is really good, but if you're bothered by a characters mouth not being in sync with their dialogue then...yeah. AI can be a little finnicky sometimes, you can be on a rock in some cliff sniping down on an enemy outpost, put a bullet in a guys head, and his friend right beside wont even notice or react. Other times they'll find your location right away and immediately start firing at you.
Enemies seem to take a little too much damage sometimes. When I played this game before I always carried a sniper so i could kill most people from a good distance with a headshot and its a one shot one kill, but if youre going in with an AR and thats all, you can put around 15 rounds into someone and they wont die. Other times they will. Its weird sometimes, but it doesnt really take away from the game in my opinion. It's just something you get used to.
One thing I was disappointed by when I bought this was there not being any multiplayer. I try to create a
ID and it just says theres a problem with the Far Cry 2 servers. Not a big deal, for only 3.50 its a good pickup especially for a great campaign.
Theres some things i've probably missed, but for just 3 dollars, please just try this game. Its an absolute masterpiece. I played this game for YEARS literally when I bought it on PS3. Had thousands of hours invested online and beat the campaign dozens of times. Havent played in a while so I figured I'd pick it up on PC and give it another go. That's why this review is biased though, I have so many memories with this game and it's what got me into FPS games which lead me into COD4 and then into the cods after that. It sounds nerd as ♥♥♥♥ but Far Cry 2 had a special place in my heart and I wont forget this game. Not too many others I can say that about. 10/10.

Arcade beat-em-up at its best.
I can't stress how much fun this game is, even single-player.  The game itself is challenging and engrossing, just like it was back in the arcade years.
ratings are from 1-5
Gameplay: 5 - No complex formulas.  No intriquet combo systems.  Just pure basic hack-n-slash gameplay of the arcade straight to your steam account and onto your PC.  It's a great romp from start to finish and includes not just other characters, but difficulty settings to keep you coming back for more and pit you against more challenigng enemies.  Discover each character's abilities and level them up by yourself or with local and online co-op (finding people to play this online is a challenge, as not many people set up lobbies for this).
Sound: 5 - Nostalgia-city for most arcade-goers in the 90s.  The music and sounds are spot-on and have aged fairly well.  All the yelling, grunting, and character voices are all here.
Graphics: 4.5 - The grapihcs get the job done with vibrant colors and great special effects.  Still, you may get bored looking at some of the same browns and greys, but each environment differs from the other in some way, making it not so bland.
Control: 4.5 - The controls are flawless, but it does require learing which keys/buttons do what commands.  Still, with a 360 controller, it's nearly a walk in the park.  Using magic, items and having to select them can be a pain, especially in the heat of battle, but it still works and remember: this is an arcade port.
Overall: 4.75 - Even solo, I find myself coming back and visiting Mysteria over and over again.  Though I only have 2 hours put into this game, I've been playing it since I got it a bit at a time.  I first finished the game with the cleric, and am currently working on the elf as of this writing.
For those wishing to take a trip down memory lane, it's well worth the price.  Those looking for an interesting 4-player beat-em-up and have a few local friends to play with, it's definitely worth it.  Fans of hack-n-slash games will also find some enjoyment and there are unlockable items only attainable by purchasing with in-game currency earned while playing.

The random "Aya...I gonna get you", which sounds absolutely nothing like any of the other voice clips used for Alfred Drevis, is just...well, it's dumb. Stick with the original Japanese audio, please. That line seriously made me cringe, and not in a good way.
There also seems to be some missing audio - Dr. Drevis' scream at the beginning is completely silent, for example.
Achievements are also broken, but hopefully those will be fixed soon.
Lastly, Aya seems to have issues with stairs in the version, which got me killed by the first zombies a few times.
So:
Is it perfect? No. Not at all. It's got flaws. Hopefully those will be patched (if the developers are reading this: hi! Also please remove that English voiceover for Dr. Drevis. It's...just bad.)
But is it worth $5? Absolutely. That's not even a question for me. The game has issues, but nothing that makes it not worth the price. Even if you've already played the free version, I still recommend purchasing this.

As I'm scrolling through the reviews for this game, the fact that nobody gets the ending was just as depressing and disturbing as the game itself was, and here is why. When I hanged the character and was then introduced with four different static bubbles, as I was looking at each one of them and then walked into one, the game just cuts me off with the credit. I was as enraged as most of you were, thinking how could someone ship an unfinished game out, but then it gets me almost immediately, at that moment I felt as if the developer was just pointing his finger and laughing at me. This is a finished game by all means, because the ending is suppose to make you feel like: ok... so I just handed someone to death... now what.. let's see... oh man I would love to play a 16 years old girl burn herself to death... wait wtf just happened...
But when I decide to take a second and just contemplating about the ending and the game, I start to realize that: Dude, I just controlled someone to kill himself, how should I feel about that? And my subconscious just almost immediately ignored that thought, and went on try to get some more game play out of being another suicidal at their last day. Now what am I suppose to feel about that... sure it's only a game and I'll never do such a thing in real life, but what if the only thing that's preventing me from doing those things was just real life consequences but not because I'm naturally good, what if those subconscious feelings, and inhuman thoughts I had while playing this game is truly, truly who I am.
As we are all so used to do the things we do in our games (and in real life as well), we never take a step back and think about our actions. At that moment I realized that as I was complaining about this lame developer who didn't even bothered to finish the game, the developer was actually just sitting right there and contemplating about the evil within me, within all of us. And Holy S**t was that an unsettling feeling to have, I've never felt that naked in any games before, heck it might just be the most naked feeling I've ever had in all media, including movies, books etc.
This game worked so well to deliver this feeling to me because, 1. Games are inherently an interactive media, it made me felt directly attached to it and responsible for my action, then was it able to bring out the evil within me like no other media could. 2. I thought it was a genius move to show you all those absurd objectives in game, so it gives you the delusion as if you are not the one who made all those choices and actions, when you should realize that you always have the radical freedom to quit the game at anytime because it was too disturbing.

If you've never played a pen & paper RPG in your life, and would like to know what it feels like to be a game master, then Majesty: The fantasy Kingdom sim will give you a taste of how it can feel.
Majesty: The Fantasy Kingdom Sim is an old RTS (originally released in 2001) where you don't have direct control over your units. Instead you need to treat your units like you were the quest giver from an RPG, in other words, you need to bribe them into doing whatever you want them to do.
The graphics in Majesty: The Fantasy Kingdom Sim was considered to be sub-par back in 2001. The HD edition does not do much for the graphics, other than zoom out a bit further, and it's still not exactly a looker. That said, unlike many 3D games from 2001, the graphics in Majesty has not aged much. The detailed 2D art looks relatively appealing, far more so than the crude 3D graphics in many of its contemporaries.

In terms of sound, Majesty won't set your world on fire. A single song loops in the background, and after a while you won't even notice it. The sound of units attack each other or peasants building things is not anything wrong write home about either. It works, but it's not great.
On the plus side, the voice acting is entertaining. A Sean Connery impersonator reads the mission briefings with enough conviction for it to work, and he also acts as the announcer during the missions. The game would not be the same without this voice actor, and it helps giving it a lot of personality. All units have their own voice lines as well, and they do a good job at conveying the personality of the units.
Majesty does not have much of a story. You're the king of Ardania, and it's your job to make it prosper. Each individual mission does have its own backstory though, and while they are not "good" in the traditional sense, the mission briefings can often be quite entertaining to listen to.
In Majesty it's your job to build a typical fantasy village/town. You start with a castle, and then you build the kind of buildings you often see in fantasy RPGs, like market places, warrior's guilds, rogue's guilds, temples to different gods, dwarven workshops and so on. Most buildings are used to recruit heroes, while some offer services that the heroes can use, and at the same time generate some much needed money that you then can use to build more buildings, or recruit more heroes.
The heroes have wills of their own, which often aligns with their classes. A rogue is a greedy coward, so he's easily attracted to bounties, but if the going gets tough, the rogue will run away. A paladin on the other hand is brave and selfless, and while try to protect the weak, so she will go out and slay monsters on her own. A wizard is bookish, and prefer to read books in the library rather than fighting, and thus might need a really big bounty for him to take notice. There are plenty of different heroes, all with their own strengths & weaknesses, and some are mutually exclusive (sun worshipers won't work with moon worshipers, and paladins won't work with necromancers), so deciding what heroes to use is a strategic choice you need to make for each level.
The heroes also gain experience and level up. Fighting enemies will always give them experience, but certain heroes also have their own activities that will make them level up. A ranger that is exploring the map will for an example gain experience that way. This makes keeping your heroes alive really important.
Sadly the game is not perfectly balanced. Some heroes are better than others, and it's really easy to fall back on the same strategy for most levels due to this. Paladins for an example, while expensive, tends to be really powerful and thus are a better investment than necromancers.
Most of the game comes down to managing your economy. As long as money keeps rolling in, you can recruit more heroes, build more buildings, and cast certain spells. These spells are the only thing you can use to directly influence a fight, and they tend to cost a lot of money. But money spent on keeping your high level heroes alive tend to be worth it.
There's no linear level progression, instead you get to chose from almost any level right from the get-go, with only some levels requiring you to have beaten some other levels first. All the levels are randomly generated, based on certain parameters for each level, so there's plenty of replay value, even if the level layout can often feel a bit generic, due to its randomly generated nature. Majesty is also not a very hard game. Between the core game and the expansion, there are really only 2 levels that can be considered "hard". Many levels give the illusion of difficulty, but as long as you don't panic or give up when things look bad, victory won't be far off.
I love Majesty. Yes, it's a game with its share of flaws, but it's really fun to watch the heroes try to accomplish things. As someone who used to play pen & paper RPGs, I recognize the behavior of my old gaming group, they used to be just as bad at noticing the obvious as the heroes in Majesty are. ;) Fun is actually how I would describe the entire game, because while it might not be the deepest strategy game on Steam, it's one of the most entertaining ones.

So if you like strategy games or RPGs (be it CRPGs or pen & paper RPGs), make sure to give Majesty: The Fantasy Kingdom Sim a try, you won't regret it (and don't forget that you can increase the game speed).

Mad Father is a Wolf Editor Horror Game (think of it similar to an RPG Maker Horror Game) which originally released in 2012 (and was translated into English in 2013). This Steam release marks a rework of the game with an overall nicer layer of polish & some new content. I've only dabbled in the Steam release a bit at the time of writing to compare some early game differences, but I had played the game & gotten every ending back with the freeware version.
I'll start off this review with a general review of the game itself, followed then a mention of some of the new content & early game differences.
-----
GENERAL REVIEW:
-----
The game follows the story of Aya Drevis, a young 11-year old girl who lives in an expansive mansion with her father, Alfred, & their maid, Maria. Aya is aware that her father does somewhat cruel experiments with a chainsaw to people in their mansion basement, but she still loves her father all the same. She has seen his good traits and love he gives to her as his daughter. However, one night she awakens to some odd sounds, & finds shambling corpses and other strange beings wandering the mansion with murderous intent. A curse has been put upon the mansion from the countless people Aya's father has slaughtered, & now the dead walk among them seeking revenge on the Drevis family. The only way to escape now & save your dad is to lay these spirits to rest, either through forgiveness or force.
Mad Father gained a strong cult following for good reason, it has a number of creative & interesting varied scenarios despite its simple nature, ranging from puzzles, to light stealth, story, exploration, minigames, & backed with good gothic atmosphere with just a hint of the fantastical. While the main setting of the game is a Mansion, you quickly begin to descend in it, finding surreal labyrinths with intricate detail & interesting elements to each room. Some play a role in gameplay, others are simply interesting to look at. As you explore you'll come to face a number of challenges & entities who want you and your dad dead. You must find a way to put the spirits at rest, & make your way to your father deep in his underground labs. Along the way there is a colorful cast of odd characters you learn more about, & a number of side-quests off the beaten path you can partake in (they're optional to complete the game, but needed to get the true ending, though of note is the whole mansion is explorable even at the end of the game, you can go all the way back to the starting room of the game from the final room of the game).
While the story isn't surprising, it is well-told and full of charisma. Aya is a likable protagonist and her relationship with her twisted father is interesting, & the members of the core cast and their interconnecting relationships are just as interesting (if not more so). The journey is engaging all the way through if you're into these 2D RPG-Horrors, & will easily give you a good 3-6 hours of playtime (depending on how much you explore, how many endings you go for, do 'optional' stuff or not, etc). It has a charm to it simply due to its tone, a mixture of a Victorian-styled setting & characters combined with a more modern twisted sci-fi mad scientist doctor via our father and the gruesome undead experiments of his, forging a sort of scientifically twisted vs supernaturally malicious scenario. It's an interesting contrast that creeps its way into various aspects of the game I just find wholly fascinating.
I will mention while the game has some good atmosphere, it isn't all that scary, nor is it trying to be. There is the occasional moment or scene, but the game aims more to unsettle you as a mood-piece with a central interconnected narrative and attract you with elements of intrigue, abstractness, & feeling to set a tone than to startle or even shock you. This said, some of the scenes are rather tense and creepy.
If you're into the scene of 2D Horror games that came from the like of Wolf Editor and RPG Maker, this one is definitely worth checking out if you haven't before.
-----
FOR THOSE WHO'VE PLAYED BEFORE:
-----
But then for those who have played it before, you may ask yourselves, "What's new here? What makes this worth $5 compared to the previously free version?"
The first thing you'll probably notice as you play is the graphics have been updated in almost every room of the game. Some rooms have been changed drastically with completely new layouts & details; they hardly resemble the rooms from the original. Others just have nice new touches that help bring them more alive & add character. In the mansion at the beginning there wasn't a room I encountered that hadn't seen some sort of overhaul, and the touches look very nice! Along with the new spritework, there is also a few new pictures that pop up during cutscenes to give more life to them & the previous pictures have been revamped to look much nicer. Also has new enemy sprites, better sprite animation & details, more detailed death scenes, & other touch-ups.
For an example of the graphical difference, here's a comparison of Aya's Room:
Aya's Room (Original Game):
Aya's Room (Steam Release):
And so far, most rooms have been drastically redone like this.
The game had to get rid of things it couldn't use for commercially, with the element that stands out the most being the music. Most of the original OST is present, but there are a few new original music tracks in this version of Mad Father in-place of the few unusable songs they had. I've only heard a couple new songs thus far, but I like them! They fit the game nicely & don't feel out of place. I may even like them more than the originals.
The game also has some new ease of use elements. Aya now will have exclamations pop over her head when near things she can interact with or investigate. Items glitter now to stand-out, so you don't have to observe everything just to find key items hidden in shelves or the like, & the hit-detection feels much better & smoother than before. The UI/Menu is completely reworked, & the QTEs the game previously had have a new gameplay style where instead of rapidly pressing a button, you now must press a series of buttons before time runs out (with an improved UI element as well).
While I can't speak in full length as I haven't quite beaten the new version of the game, there are some new dialogue & scenes in the game. There is some changes to the layout of the locations as I said before, some new areas as a result. The dev has also said there's some new optional side-stories to uncover, new scenes, & some of the gems have been relocated.
There's also a new "IF" option on the title screen, which is unlocked once you get the True Ending (not sure what it is, tho).
Game also comes with the Steam features of Trading Cards & achievements (which there's a 27 of).
Some may not find the new all that new, but it's made revisiting this game a joy for me so far, and as I loved the original I don't mind putting down some money for a revamped version with some new paint & some additional content to support future endeavors.
-----
OVERALL:
-----
While some may want to stick to the free version for its 'freeness', I think this version of Mad Father is an overall improvement which will be the best way to experience the game for either new players or fans of the original. Maybe not the huge expansion some may have hoped for, but the much more detailed & realized world along with the various additions, changes, & fixes all feel in-line with the vision of the original game while in my opinion steadily improving on it. Mad Father had a cult audience & will find new fans. If these type of games interest you, I do think is wholly worth checking out.

I just want to pick up on something that gets criticized by some people.
-> Loot mostly spawns in houses, but if you destroy houses, you also destroy the loot.
Here's why this is a good thing: You can choose to collect the loot or destroy houses right away (which is by the way NOT the goal at all - but fun as ♥♥♥♥). If you destroy a house with items in it, you instead get shards, which is also what you get from selling items. What this means is, you go through houses the first few levels to get some decent gear, but afterwards you can just destroy everything and don't even have to bother collecting, and still make profit. Shards can be used to buy gear at vendors, or even upgrade your existing gear further.
But what if there are epic/legendary items in the houses? Simple: you can press ALT to get some X-ray vision, which shows you the rarity of items inside. White or green? Destroy house. Purple or Golden? Probably wanna pick that up. (And then destroy the house because IT ♥♥♥♥ING DESERVES IT)
This is by far the most ingenious and smooth looting system I've ever seen in a roguelike!
The spells are getting awesome really quick, especially once you have decent mana/mana reg. You can customize them to your needs with up to 3 runes, for example more blast radius, more velocity and seeking. But this highly depends on the base spell you're modifying. Also, runes increase the mana cost a lot, so maybe hold back a bit in the beginning. The itemization is also neat, some items also give negative stats, like decreased movespeed/castspeed or whatever. The interesting part is, if you upgrade an item, the positive stats get better, but the negative ones get worse. There is also gear "of ♥♥♥♥♥iness" which has almost exclusively negative stats that tear you down. I bet no long until someone attempts a hardcore playthrough with fully maximised gear of ♥♥♥♥♥iness.
Ok I'm digressing here a little bit. There are a few cons, which are:
