The game is super fun.  It is not some RPG story masterpiece, and it doesn't claim to be.  The point of the game is that there are a million different ways to kill that enemy, or take out that obstacle blocking your path, and it accomplishes this very well.  The spell shaping system is vaguely reminiscent of the support gem system from PoE.  You get runes with which you can change how your spell works quickly and on the fly.  If you want to shoot someone with a plain fireball, you can.  But a plain fireball is boring!  How it about we make the explosion much larger?  You can do that.  Or make it faster and easier to hit stuff with.  Also an option.  But hey, maybe you'd just like to cast it and watch enemies die.  There's a homing rune for that too.  Come to think of it, you'd like to watch multiple enemies die in multiple explosions.  You can do multishot+homing so you can shoot multiple projectiles and have all of them home towards an enemy.
There are multiple variations of every rune, many of them are element specific, with the advantage of having higher damage.  You can find rare runes which have better stats than their more common versions.  The advantage, and the pull of this game is not in the story, it's in all the different ways you can kill everything.

First off, I'd like to say that the game is a lot of fun, and offers various large explosions that make you feel badass as hell. Blowing up buildings is loads of fun, and once modding gets up and running, the game's potential is going to skyrocket. To be clear however, the game isn't perfect, while using the environment to kill an enemy is unbeliebably fun, it rarely happens and it's difficult to set up.
For another thing, the buildings in the game are rarely inhabited, and are usually left empty, which makes perhaps the best looking part of the game, destruction not worth it, especially since the buildings contain loot, so in terms of gameplay, it's way better to leave the buildings untouched, at least until after searching through them, which can break the flow of play, and it's often better to do after killing the enemies, which defeats the main purpose. Despite the fact the blowing them up is fun, there's not enough motivation to do so in normal play. Then again, I still do it because explosion.
Fighting troops that rush you can be interesting, but it's often easier to just spam 1 spell, rather than use tactics or cooler spells. I would suggest making troops sometimes group up and stay ground in formation, or maybe try and hold a building, unaware that this would be the end of them.
To be clear, the game has a vast assortment of great features, which are highlighted in other reviews, but this is more focused on what I believe could make the game more enjoyable if changed.

Just started playing, but it has an interesting premise. It delivers exactly as the trailers have shown, which is wonderful. The combat is interesting with the spell warping and you'll find that it feels way more natural to do than expected. The AI feels clunky, with a sort of Mount and Blade style "I will run up and kill you now, hya!" type feel to it, so it would be nice to have some better AI. Your spellslinging feels wonderful though, and that's the bulk of the game.
Oh, forgot to mention the destruction. It's nicely put together, the debris has physics and can crush you, enemies, and civilians. Different spells will have different power and distribution, and therefore will do more or less damage to enemies and/or terrain. It's well thought out and again, not perfect but I definitely enjoy it.
The main screen is basically FTL: Wizard Edition. You are hopping from section to section trying to reach the end before the Inquisition catches you. If they catch up, you must fight them and most likely die. When you take damage, it is there until you find a health potion, rest (health regains slowly when you rest), or going to a merchant to heal you.
Overall, not a perfect game as expected from a brand new release, but definitely worth checking out, especially for just 20 bucks.

A surprisingly fun third-person action game with a bit of FTL sprinkled in for good measure. The combat in Fictorium is all about firing off powerful spells at somewhat weak enemies. All the spells are satisfying to use, and there are a fair number of unlockable starting loadouts -- called Titles -- that you can use to customize each run through the randomized campaign. There is also an optional hardcore mode with permadeath -- you can unlock a powerful item that allows you to fly by beating the game on medium or higher on hardcore mode. Go into the game with an open mind and don't expect something as detailed as Skyrim from a small indie studio at a $20 price tag, and the game can be a ton of fun.

This game really feels like it was not ready for release. As lots of people have said, the AI is very dumb and clunky but at the sametime unmoderated in their perceptions of the player. They will charge directly at you or sit and take pot shots with arrows/magic with no strategy at all. But they know where you are even if they can't see you which means the only way to fight them is direct and head on. Not very 'RPG' when it forces you down one route of attack.
The main selling point of this game is pure unadulterated destruction. This it provides. However, destroyed buildings so not behave in a very realistic manner which is utterly immersion breaking. A house is obliterated totally, yet all the furniture and belongings inside are prefectly fine (?!) and untouched. The building fracturing and seperation effects are also extremely last gen. You just get geometric chunks of building rolling or even bouncing around which looks extremely unrealistic, and the physics leaves a lot to be desired. Like in Django where the woman is shot from one angle yet flies off at the normal to it. This happens here and is even visible in the promo shots on the store page. A kinetic blast to the side of a structure will cause parts to fly at 90 degree up into the air.
Now the RPG side of the game which it touts. Very limited customer characterisation. The story arc is very limited and not well fleshed out. The narrative is limited and the quests themselves are repeated "Attack this, go destroy it" or "Protect this, destroy the enemy". Also some mission prompt would be great, like a notification to inform you that the mission is complete or even a way to find enemies that have scuttled off (lack of these things seriously drags the missions out in a bad way).
Ontop of this the console controller input is not good,
TLDR; A magic based poorly adapted FTL game with poor graphics, poor controls, poor AI, limited RPG elements, repetitive missions and not worth the price tag it currently is. Hopefully future updates and modding will improve this game.

Far Cry 2 is set in a large, beautifully crafted rendition of the African wilderness.  It includes very satisfying gunplay and it allows the tactical use of fire in skirmishes - set the savannah ablaze or lob a molotov cocktail to flush your enemy out of cover with realistically modelled fire propagation!  The fire and explosion mechanics are great and the weapons have a good feel to them.  Enemy AI is generally pretty good - they will search for you and respond to stimuli in a realistic manner.  Annoyingly (because it is so obviously incongruous that it breaks immersion), the distinctive black and white character voices often seem to be assigned to minor NPCs of the opposite race.  The wheeled vehicles don't handle anywhere nearly as well as the weapons, but thanks to the beautiful world design, exploring the wilds by track or river is still enjoyable, at least at first.  As the game goes on, the driving becomes a bit of a chore (realism sucks sometimes).  I found travelling by boat to be more immersive and enjoyable - they certainly seemed to handle more realistically than the wheeled vehicles.
You play as a mercenary tasked with killing an unscrupulous arms dealer that is supplying both sides of a civil conflict with cheap weapons.  Given your role and mission, you take a fairly detached approach to the civil conflict.  For most of the game, the story was of some interest, but I did not find it particularly gripping.  At times, it felt like little more than an excuse for various assassination and destruction missions, although they were thrilling enough to keep me motivated to do all the requisite driving.  Approaching the end of the game, however, the story became substantially more interesting to me, as a new perspective on the conflict was revealed.
There is quite a wide variety of weapons available, although I found myself using only a couple of favourites most of the time.  The world is massive and lovingly detailed.  With multiple African biomes, dynamic weather and wind that affects both vegetation and fire behaviour, it really is a wonderful place to explore.  The excellent gunplay is icing on the cake.
By far the most realistic of the Far Cry series, with destructible environment and weapon degradation (including jamming), I found Far Cry 2 to be a challenging and enjoyable game.  The spawning of enemies at checkpoints was annoying at times and I would have liked an option for even more realistic damage levels (people don't often patch themselves up and fight on after being shot with an AK-47).  Although playing this way would have been a very difficult proposition, I think that it would have driven the use of different, more realistic tactics.  With such solid fundamentals, Far Cry 2 had potential to eclipse S.T.A.L.K.E.R. - Shadow of Chernobyl as my favourite First-Person Shooter game ever made, had it been more mod-friendly.  Sadly, Ubisoft had other ideas.  Nevertheless, even as it approaches a decade after release, Far Cry 2 remains a great open world FPS.  I strongly recommend trying it f you like open world games and planning your gunplay engagements from stealth.  The world is gorgeous, the gunplay satisfying, and I think it's worth playing just for the realistic fire and destruction effects.

Evil Defenders is one fun and addicting game. The gameplay is challenging and varied, and there are plenty of towers to pick in planning your defense (not too much, but enough for diverse and unique strategies). There are also many different kinds of enemies, each with their own characteristics. Couple this with unique levels with their own landmarks that affect gameplay, and you have yourself an enjoyable tower defense game. For each level, there are four difficulty modes and one challenge mode, which you must complete in order to gain all 15 stars in a level. Accomplishing levels also give you 'souls', the currency you need in order to upgrade your towers, power-ups, hero, and game bonuses. The graphics are excellent, as well as the music, sound, and voices. There are plenty of references, my favorite of which is the 'arrow to the knee' joke said by one of the tower goblins.
Overall, this game offers a lot of enjoyment for a fairly low price.
Would recommend it 8/10

What you expect from a TD, with a little bit more.
Fast shooting arrow towers? Check.
Slower AoE Splash towers? Check.
PBAoE Slowing towers? Check.

The mechanics of the game are pretty much what you'd come to expect from a Tower Defense game.  But Evil Defenders does stand out on one or two points that make it better than some of the other ones I've played.  The first and foremost is the art style.  The graphics in this game are all very well done and feel like they were really crafted as a labor of love.  From the noseless ... somethings ... that attack you endlessly to the detail on your towers, the graphics are really top notch.  I wouldn't have thought this would have made a difference in a TD, but it really does.  It's that little extra oomph that makes it stand out against others in the genre.
But the graphics aren't the only selling point.  Multiple difficulty mode helps increase replayability.  Sound queues and effects that made me not want to insta-mute my game.  Plus the cut scenes are kind of adorable.
If you like TD games, this is one of the better ones I've played on steam.

It scratches the "CCG itch" (when you want to play a CCG (collectible (or customizable) card game) but don't have anyone to play it with. It is F2P to a certain point but after the first storyline, do expect to pay a good chunk of money ($20 US for 3 more story lines). You can play in various events and what not to get certain "cards of the month" and such. Is it a fun game? Yes. Does it have staying power? No.
UPDATE: A couple more insights in to this game after playing for a few weeks:
1. It has a Facebook-like encouragement to constantly logon as well as watch other people play on Twitch.
2. The CCG is very limited. For example, each turn, you get a "magicka" (basically, money to spend towards playing cards), but there is no way to compensate when you have played all your cards but have extra "magicka" left. Other CCGs (Star Wars, Star Trek, Babylon 5, etc.) have mechanisms for dealing with left over Magicka/influence/Force/etc. so you can draw extra cards. There is none of that here. Some creatures/cards let you draw extra cards as an effect, but there is no inherent coping concept of dealing with an empty hand like other CCGs do.
3. Certain sets are only available if you pay to get the Story lines that go with them. They don't come in boosters (ex. Clockwork City, Dark Brotherhood). So, if you don't pay the money to get those cards, you could easily be playing against people that do. If you do pay the money, they do give you a complete playset (3 of each card), but that just paints a bigger target on those that don't buy the story lines.
4. If you play in the monthly ranked events to get yet even more exclusive cards, there comes a point where you start only playing with folks who have EVERY card. Unless you have ground out the crystals (or bought boosters, etc.) to get all the cards, do not expect to go any further.

Majesty is a classic game that I remember well from years past, and the recently-released Gold HD edition works flawlessly through Steam on Windows 7!
This game is unusual in that it is really a sim and not an RTS. While it is up to you to build guilds and hire heroes, once recruited those heroes go off and do their own thing - exploring, finding loot, and killing monsters. It is up to you to use the money you collect in taxes to build structures that support your heroes and make them stronger, allowing you to expand your town and your economy. Rather than issuing orders, you offer incentives, in the form of cash bounties, to entice your heroes to explore a specific spot, take down a certain troublesome monster, or band together to besiege a dark lair.
The game doesn't have a campaign per se - rather, it is a series of independent missions of varying difficulty. However, each of these scenarios is unique and tasks you with achieving a singular objective, sometimes under a time limit, other times without access to certain kinds of structures and heroes. You can also generate your own freestyle quests for endless custom action!

Shu is a fairly traditional 2.5D platformer with beautiful and colorful art style.
The visuals are certainly the best part of Shu. The art direction is great and the backgrounds look gorgeous. Characters look nice too, even if some of the animations are fairly basic.
Unfortunately the game only supports a pretty limited set of resolutions and there's no support for 16:10 or ultrawide monitors.
The soundtrack is decent but not particularly memorable. The sound effects are quite basic, but get their job done.
Shu is a pretty standard platformer. You jump and glide through the levels, collect various items and avoid spikes and other dangers. The level design is decent enough but not particularly inspired.
Shu's default move set is pretty basic, but in most of the levels some of Shu's friends will tag along and grant you additional powers and abilities. These range from double jumping to a bell to activate moving platforms.
A single hit will kill you and the checkpoint system is rather punishing. You are given five lives per checkpoint and if you lose them all, you need to restart the whole level. Most of the time this is not a huge issue as Shu is not particularly difficult game. However, if you are not very good with platformers the checkpoint system can be extremely frustrating.
Controls are decent enough on a gamepad. However, there were times when the controls felt somewhat unresponsive. Shu can also get stuck to scenery at times and this can be deadly when you are running away from the Storm.
The game only has a very basic framing story told in a few simple cutscenes.
Apart from the gorgeous art style Shu is a rather mediocre platformer. The game has a number of minor issues and doesn't really bring anything new to table. There are a lot of better platformers on Steam and I would only recommended Shu for big fans of the genre.
This review is based on playing through the game (main campaign + 3 currently available bonus levels) once.

Colourful and creative. Those are probably two of the words you can use to describe this little platformer called
.  And Shu is also the name of our birdtagonist jumping and gliding through a current total of six worlds. The story is told without words and mainly consists of one cutscene at the beginning of the game and at the end of the game. In short you are running away from the all-destroying evil storm trying to save your village.
Well, let's start with the gameplay. Like mentioned before Shu can jump and glide. And those are all of his abilities. At least until he finds inhabitants from his village. Each one gives Shu another unique ability ranging from double jumping, walking over water or time slowing. To keep the gameplay different you will never have more than two companions and they will change in each world.
To support the uniquness of the worlds the design changes as well.  You have the Coast, the Forest, the Windy Heights, the Ruins and the Ancient Civilizations and since yesterday the Caverns. And all of them are looking good.
In regard to the difficulty I would say that Shu is pretty tame. You have several checkpoints and have five tries per checkpoint before you have to restart the level. You have the (sadly) typical one hit killers but they are not placed as unfair any annoying as in most platformers (although I really think that the hitbox of the thorns is larger than they appear -_-). The only potential problem for those not accustomed to this type of game might be the chase sequences. There are several parts in the game where you have to run away from something (mostly the evil storm). Although even between those sequences there are still checkpoints so it is still very doable. BUT here it is also where the games most critical flaw may hinder the joy. Shu has some kind of weird computer dependance influencing the fps and also how fast you are running and how far you jump. So depending on the current workload of your computer it may be possible that you die in those sequences without being at fault. Add to this a sometimes hard collision detection which stops you from full run and you have some cursing potential. Keep this in mind while playing the game. This is especially troublesome if we regard the fact that the game seems to be catered to speedrunners.
For the achievement hunters there is enough to do as well. Collecting 90 % of the butterflies per level (really fair), collecting all babbies per level, finding the mural pieces (also needed to enter the endgame tower) or completing the levels without dying. In total most of the achievements are really fair and less painful and rage inducing as other competitors in the genre.
All in all
is a colourful and also fun platformer with a minor critical flaw (mostly troublesome for speedrunners if at all). The music didn't leave a deep impression which means it is neither outstanding nor annoying so it gets its job done.
Now to my PERSONAL motivation for this review. While Shu is a good game I don't think I would have recommanded it normally as I mostly review just the stuff which left a deep impression to me for different reasons. So WHAT is the reason I recommanded this time? There is one area where
is outstanding and it is an area not so obvious. It is the developer team of the game. Since the release they are constantly present in the forum and on Twitter. They are always nice, helpful and professional. They made a speedrunning contest and despite rather poor participant number they pulled through with it and delivered the prices like promised (Thank you so much for the Shu Box and the Steam Link again!!). And if this wasn't enough already they decided to create and release another world (#6) as additional content months after the initial release as DLC ...... for free. Coatsink has either to much money on their hand or to much love to spend. Either way they give the impression that they really care for their product and they always acted in the interest of their customers. With this in mind I can only recommand
and praise Coatsink for exceptional behaviour. Buy and play the game and support them. They definitely deserve it.

Where do I even start? First of all I want to point out that the hours I have on PC do not represent all of my playtime, most of it has been on console. I'm going to put this review into several parts, first listing the pros and going into detail on them, and then listing the cons and going into detail with them as well. I will avoid spoilers, and I won't include mods since that's unfair to the base game.
-- Pros --
- Story, quests, and choice -
This is the absolute best part of the game. The amount of choice that you have in this game is unprecedented compared to Fallout 3 and especially 4. You aren't relegated to Yes, Yes, Sarcastic Yes, No (but actually yes). There is no voiced protagonist, allowing for more dialogue options and your own personal voice for your character. Your character's backstory is not preset. Want to be a wandering desperado that doesn't take♥♥♥♥♥♥ but has a heart of gold? You can do that. Want to be a mass murdering psychopath? You can do that (no NPCs are immortal like in other titles, something that I absolutely love).
The game doesn't break if you do something out of the ordinary. Want to kill that faction leader as soon as you meet him because you just don't like him? You can do that, and the game will more than likely account for it with dialogue and another branch in the story. That's another thing I want to talk about, branching storylines. Nearly every quest in this game has several possible outcomes and they often branch into different quests and events. It isn't a series of reskinned fetch quests that only have some surface shine. The quests have depth, the characters actually have personality, and overall it's very memorable.
- It's an actual roleplaying game -
I shouldn't have to say this, and I think I made the point clear in the first pro, but it's actually a roleplaying game. You can make anyone you want, do anything you want, build your character how you want (and your build does matter), etc. That leads to my next pro.
- Stats and Progression -
In New Vegas there are skills, SPECIAL attributes, perks, and traits. Skills are things like Guns, Science, Sneak, Speech, and more, and they help with various related tasks throughout the game. The SPECIAL attributes are Strength, Perception, Endurance, Charisma, Intelligence, Agility, and Luck. They are more or less what they sound like, the only one that isn't very useful is charisma and I'll get into that later. You get a perk every two levels, and they add some sort of weird bonus or ability to your character. Perks include being healed by sunlight, damage increases with certain weapons, critical hit bonuses, and more. Traits are optional things you choose at the very beginning. Traits have an upside and a downside. There's a trait that adds +1 agility but makes your limbs easier to cripple, there's another one that makes it so glasses give +1 perception but having no glasses gives -1 perception. Combined, these allow you to make a fairly unique character.
- Open World -
You can go anywhere in this game, and there's plenty of quests and places to explore. One thing I'll say is that the Mojave Wasteland is packed with interesting people, it doesn't take long to find an interesting quest of some sort. If you follow the main quest, you'll naturally find loads of things to do. With the DLC this increases even more.
-- Cons --
- Combat -
The combat is quite clunky and awkward. Don't get me wrong, you can have fun with it, but I don't want to put too much shine on a turd here. Compared to Fallout 4, the combat isn't all that great. One thing I will say is that the combat seems more difficult in this game, at least if you aren't an armed to the teeth hardened adventurer of some sort. There's a casino in the game that has employees that only use canes to whack you with if you act up. It's very easy to die to them if you didn't bring some serious firepower or really good stats, and yes, they do search you for weapons before you come in. Combat is mainly a result of the old engine that's been in use since The Elder Scrolls: Morrowind, unfortunately. Keep in mind, this is the *improved* version of the combat after fallout 3.
- Graphics -
The characters look ugly. This has been true since Oblivion I'd say, so it's nothing new. The colors are pretty bland, though I suppose that's just the theme of the post apocalypse. Not much I can say about the graphics other than they're a bit dated, even for when Fallout: New Vegas came out.
- Glitches -
This game has a pretty large amount of glitches. A lot of the game breaking ones have been patched out, but there are still some. Save a lot, don't enter The Thorn, maybe install the unofficial patch (yes I'm breaking my rule at the start but I'd be a criminal to not tell you), and you should be fine. I want to point out that this amazing game was made in 18 months, and this IS Bethesda and its engine we're talking about here, so it's unfortunate but not surprising that it's in this state.
- Charisma -
I'm just putting this here for completeness. Charisma is basically worthless in this, the only useful thing it does is increase the health of your companions. On the other hand, Speech and Barter are both useful skills, so don't think charisma being useless means the associated skills are too.
--- Conclusion ---
Overall I have to say that this game is incredible if you're looking for a proper RPG and a classic experience in the modern era of games. I'm a bit saddened by saying this, but I think this is one of the last classic mainstream RPGs we'll see for a very long time, though it will stand the test. Obsidian was given 18 months to make a masterpiece, and that's exactly what they did. If you want me to give a number, I give this game 9/10. It would be 9.5/10 or higher if it was given more development time to really flesh out the loose ends. I entirely recommend this game to anyone, especially those of you who are coming from Fallout 4.
Edit:
I want to add that I've played Fallout 1, 2, Tactics, 3, New Vegas, and 4. I've actually beaten Fallout 1, 3, New Vegas, and 4 and have spent a good amount of time on nearly all of them.

(I don't usually do reviews, so I'm sorry if I come off as sort of cheesy as I write this, but I thought I might as well give my opinion on my favourite fallout game.)
OVERVIEW
If you've ever played any of the Fallout games, you'll constantly see praise for Fallout: New Vegas, with many championing it as the greatest Fallout game, and, in my opinion, for good reason. This is mainly due to just great storytelling. Fallout NV feels more developed than the more 'mainstream' Fallout games (3 and 4) in the story department. Every faction, no matter how small, feels human, with both shortcomings and advantages.
The prime example of this is the differences in the portrayal of the Brotherhood of Steel in Fallout 3 and 4. In F3, the Brotherhood are the 'holy good' faction. Their intentions are noble, they do no wrong, to the extent where their only goal is the restoration of clean drinking water to the wasteland, whereas in F:NV, the Brotherhood are xenophobic technophiles, reeling from their loss to the New California Republic, and constantly pursuing isolation as a last ditch method of defense. As I stated before, no faction in New Vegas is entirely good or evil. Even if you manage to (minor spoilers) assist the brotherhood and allow them to leave their bunker, they still refuse to adopt new methods that would allow them to develop themselves further, and assert their position better (spoilters end).
However, despite the improvements in storytelling, New Vegas, in a gameplay sense, retains the shortcomings of Fallout 3. The gunplay still ♥♥♥♥ing sucks, stealth is still stupid broken (but I suppose that's more of a bethseda problem), but some improvements have been made, such as decreasing the amount of skill points you earn per level, forcing you to specialise your character, instead of it just being able to specialise in everything.
OVERALL
POSITIVES
- Possibly greatest storytelling in the Fallout franchise.
- All the factions in NV feel human, both flawed and developed.
- Slight improvements on gameplay from Fallout 3. (In terms of player progression being more balanced.)
- Great soundtrack.
NEGATIVES
- Same gun play weaknesses from Fallout 3.
- Same limitations from Fallout 3's engine.
- Game crashes a ♥♥♥♥♥on on Windows 10. If you want to play it for more than 10 minutes at a time, you're going to need to put in work modding the game.
- Due to age, modding the game can take more effort than games such as Skyrim or Fallout 4.
FINAL VERDICT: 9/10.

Dungeons & Dragons: Chronicles of Mystara is actually two games in one. Both are excellent remakes of the old arcade games D&D: Tower of Doom (1993) and D&D: Shadow over Mystara (1996). The story of the games overlap - Shadow over Mystara begins shortly after the end of Tower of Doom's campaign - but they can be played in any order. The game has you (and up to three of your friends) play as a noble team of adventurers on a grand adventure through the land of Mystara, a classic fantasy realm populated by elves, goblins, kobolds and fearsome dragons.
PROS:
- One of the best options out there for anyone that enjoys oldschool brawlers/beat 'em ups.
- Very faithful port, and runs well. Spectacular visuals that hold up even today.
- Several different display options; scanlines, different views, etc. Including a view of the entire "cabinet."
- Online and couch co-op for up to four players, drop in and out at any time.
- Visual design is great, and soundtrack does a good job of immersing you in the game.
- Stays true to the original D&D feeling; the game features spell slots as well as loot in the form of new armour and equipment for your character.
- Limited character customisation and progression: Choose from classic D&D staples like Elf, Thief, Fighter, Cleric, and Magic User. Gain levels and grow stronger as you journey on.
- The second game (Shadow over Mystara) features a more complex spell and equipment system. There are many types of weapons and equipment to find that change the way you play and deal with enemies (e.g. shields that enable you to block attacks that would otherwise be unblockable).
- Branching storylines (Do you rush to the defence of the castle yourself, or do you seek help from the soldiers in the city? etc), and many optional areas. Lots of secrets to find.
- An unexpectedly deep combat system for an oldschool brawler. Each character feels very different, and you'll have no trouble finding one that suits you. There are double jumps, dodge rolls, dashes, shield blocks, aerial maneuvers, attack combos and more to find and experiment with.
- Very clear and accessible menus. No troubles getting things up and running.
- Lots of challenges to clear, such as defeating enemies or using certain spells and attacks.
- Tons of extras to unlock, including houserules (e.g. higher gold gain, or no respawning).
CONS:
- These games were originally coin-op style arcade titles, where you insert more coins to get back into the game when you die. This means the game is designed to be lethal in order to hook the player. Until you get a good grasp of the mechanics, you will die. A lot. Capcom has opted to go with a more lenient approach in the remake, giving you infinite credits (there is a House Rule that lets you play on a single credit). Although this is a good thing for those that want to have a casual experience with friends, it also means that you can blaze through the entire game without stopping as you have infinite continues. This also means that there is no real reward for doing "well" (although there are difficulty levels that determine the HP and possibly amount of enemies).
- Game is based on arcade stick controls and is best played with a controller. It's definitely possible to use the keyboard, but you might find it tedious.
- Although online co-op usually runs very smooth, you might run into some issues if you are playing with three or more players and some of you are from different time zones. I experienced occasional slowdowns when running through Tower of Doom with American friends.
- Certain enemies can be frustrating if you are playing alone, since groups of foes that can disable you (e.g. setting you on fire) can end up chain-stunning you for a long time if you are unlucky.
- Aerial controls can sometimes be a bit clunky due to the way depth works in this game (It can be hard to determine if you can hit an enemy, or if they are too far away from you vertically).
- Although this experience may be unique to me, I had one major issue: achivements bugging out. I played through the entire Tower of Doom game without unlocking a single achievement. Eventually I managed to fix it by verifying the game's cache, but the challenges were already unlocked in-game, which means I can no longer get these achievements. UPDATE: After contacting Capcom Support the problem was handily solved. I applaud their support staff for the swift reply.
The bottom line: should you buy this game?
YES - Especially if you are a fan of oldschool brawlers, and/or you're looking for a fun co-op game to play with friends.

PRICE isn't a horror game as much as it's a Grimm fairy tale or perhaps more along the lines of Gothic literature.  There are certainly disturbing moments and I guess a few "scares," but as a self-proclaimed scaredy-cat, I didn't get much of a horror feel from the game.  I would describe the story as more macabre.  Regardless, PRICE is an excellent game.  I found the story very compelling and the characters, especially the hero Ivry, even more so.  The visuals were phenomenal and the music was pretty much perfect.
The only "problem" I had with the game was the puzzles.  They were a little hard... or maybe I'm just not smart enough to be able to solve them?  Generally, I knew what to do and was able to follow the clues in the game to the next piece of the puzzle no problem, but I did end up having to consult a guide.  I messed up on the order of things a few times, which caused me to become stuck, and there was one part of a puzzle in particular that I would have never thought to do until seeing it in the guide.  But despite the challenge I had with the puzzles (which arguably could kind of be said makes up the whole game) I didn't find that the difficulty subtracted anything from the story or made me enjoy the game any less.
All in all, PRICE was a wonderful game.  I really can't get over the story.  I absolutely loved it!
I recommend this game to everyone really, teen and up.  It's tame enough in the scare factor that even people who aren't a fan of horror can enjoy it.  And really, the story is just so beautiful that I want everyone to play this, although perhaps the theme is a little niche?  Anyway, the game is relatively short, free, and has achievements, which I know is a big draw to a lot of people.  I see no downside to playing through PRICE.

Is this game the best game I've ever played? No, there's definitely some things I would change. But it's free, so I recommend it.
First off, it's not a "horror" game like most think of them. It's more like a traditional horror story. I've been reading an anthology of the the history of American horror, and this games atmosphere definitely reflects that type of horror. There are no zombies, you don't have to kill anything to survive, just a little bit of blood & creepy illustrations and a serious feeling of dread. It's very absorbing. It's short though, so you don't have to worry about losing hours of your life to it. The art is very good. I liked the characters and the setting. The ending is fairly open ended, letting you draw the conclusion you liked best.
The things I didn't like were mostly in the transition between the two parts of the game. There were some characters that showed up whose purpose wasn't clear and you mostly had to guess what was intended by those cut-scenes, but this is not in the good way that the ending did it. Also, I recommend opening up a walkthrough in another window or on your phone, because not all of the mechanics are explained too clearly. And sometimes you have to do things in a certain sequence so you see things that weren't there before. There's a good walkthrough on the community page here, so you don't have to hunt far. Once you sort of figure some things out, you shouldn't need it too much.
If you are expecting a modern horror game with lots of gore and jumpscares, this is not that. But if you'd like a short but interesting game with literally no risk to your wallet, definitely check this out.

The Guardian of Light is among the many spin-off games to the Tomb Raider franchise. Due to the difference in gameplay and continuity from the console games it is classified as a "spin-off". When labeling it as "spin-off", meaning this game is not a sequel to the "Avalon/Atlantis" trilogy that precedes it. While Keely Hawes repraises her role as Lara Croft, there is no mentionings of Amanda, Natla, or the Excaliber for this game. It is therefore a standalone "no need to play the other games" type of game. With that lecture put aside I will discuss the plot. Lara travels to an unspecific country in Central America to obtain an artifact called the "Mirror of Smoke". After making through a dangerous and perilous journey through the jungle, Lara finds the mirror of interest. Unknown to her, a band of merceneries lead by an arrogant warlord were tailing her. Upon the mishandling of the mirror, it sharders and unleashes the merciless Xolotl the god of lightning and death. At the same time the statue of Totec comes to life, who immediately gives Lara aid in her new mission to stop the newly resurrected Xolotl before the light of dawn or witness the rise of Xolotl's army that will plunder the planet. The Guardian of Light offers an over head camera view gameplay that differs from the traditional Tomb Raider games. While in the other games the camera is controllable, in this game the camera is always in over head view. Despite this small change, the game is fun with the abundences of puzzles and power ups. It offers a straight up action game that isn't as deeply written as the traditional Tomb Raider games. But it offers something different and just telling you "Hey, we're making a fun puzzle adventure spin-off, nothing more". It's worth checking out, if you like to take a detour from the bigger and more noteworthy Tomb Raider games you are use to playing.

This game is clearly a mobile port and it shows in the game design.  I bet that in that version you could "pay" to get quick upgrades.  Not in this version; it demands that you grind and grind you must.  You quickly realize that all of the towers are prettty much worthless without some significant upgrades. In almost and any decent tower defense game, the player should be able to cruise through the the lowest difficulty without too much issue.  This usually prepares you to tackle the tougher difficulties.  By the fourth or fifth map, I was already seeing difficulty spikes (on the lowest difficulty) that made any strategy I used worthless (that's with some grinding too).  I believe this was also a relic of the mobile version as this game appears to have been designed such that you would hit a "wall" and pay to advance.  Except that in this version you don't have that option.  You either pay by grinding or you don't advance, simple as that.  No strategy necessary.
All in all, this games screams free to play with microtransactions (typically the kind that gates progression), only it's not and you've already paid.  If you are looking for a good tower defense game, try out Kingdom Rush or Defense Grid 1 & 2.  I realize that Kingdom Rush is also a mobile port but it's game design is so much better than this and way more balanced.

Far Cry 2 is my favourite title in the series. It will probably be yours if you like your games challenging and frustrating, but at the same time fulfilling to complete. The plot differs from other FC games; rather than embodying some variety of quirky evil, your nemesis - The Jackal - is shrouded in ambiguity. He sells guns to all sides, and so he must die...however, is it as simple as that?
The AI isn't anything special, yet battles are made fun or even thrilling as you are handicapped by several abiding traits:
- Malaria - this impairs your vision, ability to sprint or even walk, and total health.
- Weapons jamming; this is painfully common in the heat of battle.
- Vehicles are easily made immobile, making hit and run style attacks tough to pull off.
- The environment of heavy foilage, dull browns and greens means enemies are easily camouflaged.
- Health recovery is slow, to the point where fleeing is more viable than taking cover, which also tends to be difficult.
Even patched, the game suffers from a few glitches, including one where a side mission failed to start, requiring me to load an earlier file. Navigating, with your handheld map, can be cumbersome. But these shortfalls are forgivable, for Far Cry 2 is punishingly hard, has atmosphere, benefits from a decent story, and makes diamond hunting near-compulsory in service of you getting reasonably equipped; for even more of a challenge, don't hunt or spend them.
The visuals, while dated, remain passable several years after its release in Autumn 2008. The tropical forests and plains of sub-Saharan Africa have since been used by popular series such as Metal Gear Solid, but remain generally unfamiliar to gamers. Shu is an amazingly vivid and gratifying 2.5D platformer title that offers much to both the casual player as well as a more seasoned gamer seeking to push themselves with timer based levels.
The game itself takes place after a dark storm attacks Shu’s small Cliffside village. The player then finds themselves traversing five different zones—each complete with its own unique set of progressively more challenging levels and varying encounters and mechanics.  Right away, this game meets all expectations. It’s easy to get into and get the hang of but also challenging enough at times to keep even a experienced player interested. Shu also features an action component as well, making it more thrilling than an atypical platformer. Periodically throughout the different levels the “storm-monster” will begin chasing Shu until you reach a safe zone at the end of the level. If caught by this storm, you are forced to restart at the closest checkpoint achieved. When the storm is combined with the challenge of navigating the level it can make for exciting and overall enjoyable gameplay.

This is a forgotten classic, one that I don't think ever got enough recognition.  Majesty is a real-time strategy/simulation set in your typical fantasy world.  Wizards, knights and elves battling vampires and goblins.  Like an RTS, you place buildings and train heroes, while researching and gathering money.  Then the game throws you the first twist...you don't command the heroes.  You are the king, you don't run the battlefield.  What you do is use your money and influence to persuade the citizens and heroes of your lands to act on your behalf, going on quests and fighting battles.  It's almost like Dungeons and Dragons where you are the quest giver...but you can watch the heroes battle, earn experience, and buy things to improve their questing.  It's a hard concept to sell, but the game itself is a lot of fun, even if it does get challenging sometimes.

Majesty 2 was pretty good, but the original Majesty is a classic that never gets old! Paradox was very cool by releasing a HD update to the original game. Plays fine on new systems, at last! If you had Majesty in your library already you got the update for free but if you don't own it it's totally worth buying.

Majesty is a wonderful, unique hybrid between strategy and city building games. The gameplay primarily consists of constructing buildings, hiring units, and researching while the rest of the world behaves on its own accord. Players who get bored just observing the game can adjust the game speed, and there are a number of methods to interact with the world (beyond posting the occasional bounty) by researching into a variety of spells to cast directly onto the field. The graphics are dated, especially with the intro cinematic and menu, but I still find the game asthetically pleasing. The game itself is broken down into a number of different missions, and has a random map generator to draw out the longevity of the game even further. The game's difficultly curve can be a little steep, as it starts off almost boringly easy and ends up being fiendishly hard, and the steam port of this game crashes for me periodically, but if you see it on sale, it's definitely worth buying.

This game feels nothing like the devs showed it would be. The AI is clunky and will only follow you around not diverting from the course you are on. The enemies are all the same just with different skins, you have the zombie like enemies which chase you around, some look slightly different and explode when you hit them. But over all each enemy is the same just slightly faster or slower.
The spell casting system is really interesting and can make for something special but there is no reason to only select just 2 runes when making a more powerful spell, the rune system requires no strategy, just select all 3 runes and you have the spell but just better, but select only 2 and the spell will not differ, only being less powerful. The spells seem to be the same just one goes further and one explodes better. The lighting spell is in almost every way the same as the fireball only that it can go further and is therefore better, it can do the same damage to a building but bounce off it and take out multiply enemies at once.
The destruction system is under developed. A hit on a wall with the lighting bolt will cause the entire roof to come down, but no damage to said wall. The towers you must destroy to keep going require only the slightest bit of it missing near the top to fail. Enemies rarely enter the buildings giving you very little reason to destroy them apart for a bit of mana.
Visually this game looks outdated, even on highest the game looks only slightly better when compared to lowest. This game from the trailers seems to look very good, but in game it fails to achieve these graphics. This game is also horrible optimized. (For context i have an i7-6700k, 16 GB ram and an 1070) At the start of the game I got 60 fps, but as the enemies increased only by around 5 the fps would take a huge hit dropping to 35 fps and varying after that. For a game built around destruction, it can't handle to much destruction and is forced to remove the wreckage to get anywhere near 60 fps again.
Each level this game has is overall the same. A mountain map, with around 10 - 15 houses which pretty much all look and feel the same, each having the same type of loot no matter if it is the mansion or the small little houses. Then there are a few enemies scattered around in groups with you either have to, run around destroying the towers, or killing all the enemies while destroying the towers. This game is clearly trying to do what ftl does, with its top down map, where you pick the location you go as the army chases you. But ftl has varying encounters. Each enemy having different sets of systems, weapons and races. But Fictorum has none of these and makes the game feel rushed and all in all the same.
Overall this game is enjoyable for the first 20 minutes before you notice that it is all the same. It looks outdated and plays horrible. You can see where this game is trying to go, but it falls flat each time it tries. I would not recommend this game. Most early access games are better than this but alas this game is not in it.

So, I have been looking forward to this game for quite a while. Seeing all the gifs and youtube clips have been piquing my fantasy intrests in all the right ways. My overall experience with this game has defintiely been positive overall and I can't wait to see what more will come.
Game feels solid, basic, but solid. You really do feel like an INCREDIBLY powerful spell caster taking on enemy after enemy. Being able to cast MASSIVE fireballs from the sky, arcing lightning bolts, and deadly ice spears is an absolute treat. I feel more powerful at the START of this game than I do by most other games end-game time, yet I still find my style evolving with the different runes and new abilites to change thigs up consistantly. The maps themselves also feel, again basic, but different enough to make most every area feel unique and have its own mini town in each. The story is also very enveloping. With an old school "choose your own adventure" feel with a multitude of options and choices that can make or break a run with a brand new legendary item or an ambush of enemies that will make you to fight for your life.
Now for the bad. For starters, the AI is... dumb... putting it nicely. Enemy fighters run STRAIGHT at you, with little reguard to what's in front of them. Archers stand in place and NEVER move. The most intelligent enemies are the ~invisible~ creatures, and spellcasters which will try to move around you in a circle until they can attack you. This game also has 2 terrifyingly painful enemies. One is melee enemies with FIRE AOE and HASTE and the other is, of all things...
. Bushes will conceal spellcasters and archers, with them having perfect line of sight on you, forcing you to have to throw AOE spells in the vain hope of hitting something. A lesser problem that I had was with the maps and story lines. While nice, can get repetitive reeeeaaaaallllll quick seeing litterally the same story choices within chapters, and sometimes even the same maps multiple times in a row. And overall the "RPG" statistics in the game feel like a tiny numbers game with minor incremental increases without really being able to "feel" the changes, barring a major power spike.
Now I do have quite a few more hypercritical analyses, buy my overall appreciation for this game far outweighs any nitpicky gripes that I could say to ruin it. This game is clearly low budget, with a small studio of some 4~5 people. The game is filled with TONS and TONS of potential with very unique elements that... frankly DON'T SUCK, and I find it crazy that I've never seen like this. I can only imagine if this game had even 1/2 the budget of most any other MAJOR game that this would become an
classic. I can't wait to see what more this company has to bring to the table, and definitely recommend giving this game a shot.

One of my fondest memories is dumping quarter after quarter in the Tower of Doom arcade machine at a small ice cream shop in Ocean City, Maryland.  Such a complex beat em up and the fact I'm a fan of Dungeons and Dragons never hurt my chances of throwing down $20 in cheap thrills.  Well after years of not getting ports in America, it came to Steam and I could share this experience with my friends and, one day, my son (Or any future kids as well).  Adding online functionality means I can even share it with my pals all over the world.  It's a lot of fun.  And with the unlockable game modes means theres some new experiences even for old dogs like me.

An excellent little bundle with two really fun games and some nice unlockables to keep the game interesting.  The price might be a deal-breaker for some, but if you ever see it on sale I wholly recommend it.  Every class has a unique feel and the branching paths and general pace of both games keeps things interesting for numerous playthroughs.  The Tower of Doom is the first of the two and feels somewhat limited in its controls, however the game does get easier once you get a feel for the momentum of your character.  While I do prefer Shadow of Mystara for its faster gameplay and smoother controls, I still suggest that you give the Tower of Doom a try.  Shadow of Mystara is the second game in the bundle and feels much smoother in controls.  Characters move more naturally and the inventory system is more complex without being cumbersome.
One thing of note is that the game seems to have trouble accepting any controller that isn't an official Xbox 360 controller.  That seems to be my luck, anyway.   If you can manage to get a game going with other people the game gets even better, but I suggest you check a guide to ensure that you can manage a proper setup for multiple players if you plan on using the local co-op function.

Viridi is exactly what its described to be. A "sort-of" game that you open once a day to both water your plants and relax for just a moment. The app is really for anyone who doesn't have the means or patience to care for a real plant but wants the satisfaction of virtually maintaining one. You've got pleasant graphics and soothing music to place in the background of your screen and, over time, you get to see your babies grow into big, beautiful succulents.
As a player/gardener there's a limited range of what you can do (pick your plants and particular pot, pull weeds, water plants) which makes sense because Viridi is a casual simulation of gardening so that's not anything you can hold against the game, however, what really annoys me is the viewing mechanism. There's an element of realness the devs seem to be going for by having the pot spin with inertia despite my finger having already lifted from the left key, which might appeal to some but only makes it more difficult for me to seamlessly view my plants. A small con, for sure.

I love this game. Just a nice place to watch some little succulents grow! Also really enjoy the calming and delicate music it plays in the background. The little cute snail (who I named Monkey) is now my best friend. Viridi really is a safe haven! :D

Cast your minds back to the holiday season of 2008, the original Dead Space released as a suprise hit, as well as the highly anticipated Fallout 3 from Bethesda, and of course Gaben graced us with the superb Left 4 Dead, and Far Cry 2, a sequel to a game that, by all accounts, had all but been forgotten to many, released on October 21st in North America.
Showcasing a modified version of the CryEngine, dubbed the Dunia Engine, Far Cry 2 was certainly an impressive technical feat for its time, featuring dynamic weather, volumetric lighting, a realistic physics engine and perhaps most impressive of all, dynamic fire propagation, with fire acting in a realistic and driving manner.
Ubisoft Montreal had taken over the reigns from Crytek who had moved onto pasture news with their Crysis franchise, and it was clear that the Dunia Engine was to be an important tool for the series, with future games in the series continuing to use the engine, as well as being used in conjunction with the Anvil engine in Assassins Creed 2 and Assassin's Creed Brotherhood. When looking back, 8 years later, its still hard to deny just how Far Cry 2 continues to look, holding up well with many more recent games in the series.
Far Cry 2 takes place in a small, failed Central African state, currently embroiled in civil war. The government has recently collapsed, leaving two factions vying for control. At war are the United Front for Liberation and Labour, or the UFLL and the Alliance for Popular Resistance, abbrieviated to the APR. Your main goal is to find and assassinate the Jackal, an arms dealer who has been selling weapons to both sides of the conflict. It's worth noting also that Far Cry 2 is a sequel in name only, featuring none of the supernatural elements from the first game at all, though these elements were re-introduced in later games.
Throughout the course of the games story, you are forced to work with both the UFLL and the APR, each using the player as a deniable agent in order to avoid a full-scale war. In addition to the hunt for the Jackal, you can provide the Underground with stamped travel documents for refugees in exchange for anti-malarial drugs, ambush convoys of weapon shipments in order to gain access to a greater variety of weapons and equipment from arms dealers, and assassinate targets acquired by intercepting signals from various cell-phone towers in the area. There really is no shortage of things to occupy you in this game, and while many people lament the all too common 'malaria attacks' for being more intrusive than compelling, it does help to break up the pace of the main plot, without feeling too much like padding out the games length.
Realism was something that Ubisoft really wanted to push with this game, with features such as weapon degradation, the previously mentioned  dynamic weather system, a day and night cycle, as well as the aformentioned fire propagation mechanism. Weapons will become dirty over time and prone to jamming, eventually becoming completely unusable, you have to hold a physical map and use a handheld navigation system to get around, when vehicles are damaged you must perform a short repair animation and on top of this, you have to deal with a worsening affliction of malaria, having to take a pill in order to combat the blinding and potentially fatal effects of the illness.
Many saw these 'realistic' features as little more than annoyances that distracted from the overall experience, and I disagree, these quirks were what made the game unique, and set the Far Cry 2 apart from its generic FPS roots. Far Cry 3 and 4 dumbed down the realistic features, and I felt the games regressed as a result, feeling more like an average open world shooter that are all too commonplace in the current market.
The dynamic weather system allowed for different weather conditions such as storms and strong winds. And the time of day also affected the behavior of enemy AI, heightening their awareness at night, but hindering their ability to see the player in hiding, while during the hot part of the day the enemies might sheltering in the shade in groups, but be able to easily spot the player from a distance. Several species of animals can be encountered in the game, and while none of the wildlife found in the game pose any direct threat to the player they are able to distract the enemy, as well as make them aware of the player's presence.
The previously mentioned dynamic fire propogation also played a key factor during enemy encounters, allowing a small fire to spread and eventually cause large brush fires, which could be used to the your advantage during combat if handled carefully. The behavior of fire is dependent on many factors such as wind speed and direction, rain, as well as the type ofvegetation. With fire spreading much more freely in the dry, grassy plains and savannahs compared to the humid jungle environments.
These elements forced you to make tactical decisions when attempting missions, and is something that I really enjoyed during my original playthrough, it also added a great deal of replay value, with each encounter playing out differently depening on the conditions and time of day.
Without going too much into it, as I sadly never got the chance to really play it back in 2008, there was also a multiplayer component to the game, which attempted to include many of the dynamic elements of the single-player game such as the use the of fire. As well as including a quite comprehensive map editor, something that was seen in the Far Cry also.

This map editor was incredible, almost everything can be tweaked and tuned to your liking, and I actually had a lot of fun playing around with the various features of it, even without getting to actually use said maps in multiplayer, though I have since some pretty creative and impressive maps made online. Thankfully, the map editor managed to keep its place in future games in the series, with the exception of both Blood Dragon and Primal which were sadly solo experiences.
Far Cry 2 will always be a bit of a difficult game to judge, it tried to do so much that I can't help but appreciate and commend Ubisoft Montreal for their ambition, even if some features could be considered annoying to many.
None of the later games in the series have ever managed to capture the sheer scope,  and sense of freedom that this game had and for that reason it has to be considered the best in the series, and one that you should definitely pick up and play, either for the first time or for 100th time.

Far Cry 2 is one of those games that any reviewer on youtube loves to♥♥♥♥♥♥all over, hell alot of Steam reviews will♥♥♥♥♥♥all over it and rightfully so. Despite being an amazing game, Far Cry 2 has a lot of design issues. Outposts can respawn within an hour, there are long periods of tedious traveling and driving to destinations followed by sporadic moments of shooting two dudes in a car, all of the missions are basically the same "kill this" or "blow this up", the buddy system is underdeveloped, picking a character has literally no effect on the game and the soldiers of both factions are out to kill you, even when your doing a mission for one of the factions! With the lazily given reason for this being that your mission is supah secret and no one knows about it. The Malaria gimmick is more annoying than an interesting part of gameplay and the world feels very static, with no sight of civilians around the country-side (which the intro cut-scene shows). Instead  they're hiding inside huts waiting for you to give them passports in exchange for your malaria medication. The actual world is populated by respawning soliders and mercenaries and the wild life is just there so you can watch the hilarious ragdoll physics go into effect when you hit them with your car. Finding Diamond briefcases can be frustrating (and also makes no sense), increasing your "reputation" does nothing except make the enemies say different dialogue and have better weapons over time. And finally the way you heal damage by viscerally resetting broken fingers and pushing bullets out of your gaping wounds is brutal and awesome to watch at first, but reaches Monty Python levels of comedy when it is done multiple times in a single gunfight.
And yet, This game is ♥♥♥♥ing fantastic because what it does it does better than almost any other game. Its firefights are fantastic with smart A.I. that leaves you with a exhilarating sense of an adrenaline rush combined with a real sense of fear due to the fact that the enemies will do everything in its power to ♥♥♥♥ you. Along with a fire mechanic that frankly is nothing more than a gorguous piece of artwork as you watch it spread throughout the dried grass and trees of the country-side and into the enemy base with the backdrop of an orange setting sun.
The African environment feels so real, like you can really feel just how hot and unpleasant it must be just by looking at that beating sun in the sky and the shriveled up grass in the plains. Enemies constantly complain about the heat and there are empty plastic water bottles scattered everywhere. Furthermore, when you enter the bases of the Factions, you can almost feel the humidity and the laziness it would create as papers and garbage are thrown on the floor as its occupants are to drenched in sweat to really care. It reminds me of my apartment in the Summer.
NPC dialogue is interesting to hear, especially in gunfights as they try to take you out and their hectic screams and grunts make them seem less like the super badass soldiers from every other shooters but simple mercenaries who are desperate to survive and leave this♥♥♥♥♥♥hole country. A combination of their smart tactics and scared dialogue makes them seem like a threat that would play out similarly in a real life scenario and at times you even feel bad for them as it's clear despite their advantage in numbers, they're just as scared ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ as you are and do their hardest to look out for their fellow comrades.
In fact the sound design is fantastic all around, all the voice acting is great and the standout performance of the "villain" The Jackal, provides a small amount of social commentary as he justifies his lifestyle as an arms dealer. All of the guns sound really good and the cracklings of that fire are pure eargasm. The music of conga drums being violently beaten as combat starts really provides a minimal but effective approach that makes the firefights even more savage. Though an issue with the latter is that the congas start anytime you fire a gun and only stops when it's clear you were just ♥♥♥♥ing around with a goat or chicken. lulz.
Alot of the issues I mentioned in the first paragraph were fixed with Far Cry 3, which is also an amazing game. The world is lush and colorful and there is a lot to do other than shooting, there are soldiers that are on your side and also patrol the country side and will fight with you. There is Flora and Fauna that is actually dangerous to the player along with a hunting aspect. The Story is more developed with popular characters like Vaas, and of course, the ♥♥♥♥ing bases don't respawn.
But Far Cry 2 still manages to remain relevant despite all of the improvements the third entry made. Simply because Far Cry 3 can't beat the 2nd game at what it does best: Gunfights and its fire mechanic. Far Cry 3 is an amazing game, but it feels very "video gamey". Far Cry 2 is less like a traditional Game and more like a simulation. Short Version:
A simple TD with more grinding than what is welcome, skip unless you have time/money to kill.
Long Version:
Gameplay: I don't love TD's where you can't build your own maze (like this one), but that doesnt't mean they can't be well done, unfortunately, that's not the case here: tower places have little to no effect on the greater scheme and there aren't many chances to sinergize towers. That being said, the game introduces map specific activatables and wave events that can spice things up, a nice add. You get your typical array of towers with a nice new addition (the summon tower) but what really breaks the game for me is the tower progress tree: want to make your tower better? Spend skulls, want more skulls? Clear more maps. Rinse and repeat. If you remove this you'll find the game to be very shallow.
Story: You get the bare minimum to context why humans are trying to pillage Evil's land (pure statement, it's just a quick TD game, can't really fault it for not having story, though I could sing its praises if it had a goon one).
Sound: No breaking ground stuff here, just a cute jingle to acompany the passage of time. Tower upgrades get some irky lines, not a fan.
Graphics: This game looks very much like a smartphone one, maybe it originaly was? As so graphics go for the cartoony style and do a decent job at dilvering what you'd expect from a TD for the mentioned platform.

Evil Defenders is a basic tower defense game. You have a handful of towers at your disposal, and each can be upgraded, but also specialized for AOE, single target, dot damage, etc. You have several abilities at your disposal as well, such as summoning a large demon to assist, teleport the enemy, lightning strikes. The game is rather short, as far as the number of levels, but in order to get through those levels, you will need to do some grinding. The grinding most likely takes place of IAP, since this is a mobile game conversion (it no longer has IAP, but you won't be strong enough to advance unless you grind out each level probably 4-5 times each, going through the different difficulty levels). Normally, that fact turns off a lot of people, myself including, but despite the fact the game is based on a mobile port, and you need to grind a bit, the game is fun enough that if you can pick it up for a low price (low price is the key here), I think it's still worth it. It's more of a diversionary game you can play for a few minutes mindlessly rather than an in-depth head-scratching tower defense where you figure out tons of strategies or replay maps endlessly trying to figure out the best path to take. The story is cutesy, but almost nonexistent, the graphics and music are pretty good for a basic TD game. I'd probably give it a 6 out of 10, meaning while I do recommend it, it's not with gushing enthusiasm, but it's a decent distraction for a few hours, and I found it addicting. There's not a ton of strategy here, and you are playing more in order to level up your towers than anything else.

Chronicles of Mystara is a collection of two of the best beat-em-ups to come out fo the golden age of arcade gaming, Tower of Doom and Shadow Over Mystara.  Selecting from a diverse group of classes with unique strengths, weaknesses, and abilities, you have an unparalelled level of control over your character and the path you take through the game.  There are a number of normal and unique items throughout the game that you can pick up that will influence the way you play the game, like frost swords that allow melee characters to keep the front line endlessly stunned, and items like the egg of the owlbear that will summon one to fight for you.  The different paths you take will result in different levels and bosses, leading to an ultimate battle that will test your skill.  This game had endless replayability for me when it was in arcades, and it still keeps me drawn in nearly twenty years later.

It's a great game.  It's a Roguelike.  Think "Hand of Fate" but with a powerfull mage protagonist.   If you're obsessed with power mages that send pieces of buildings flying and laying waste to armies of men that charge at you for a fight..you've got to try it.  And the best part of any Roguelike is also here....LOOOT!!!!!  Scouring around and finding loot that improves your character.
That being said it's not without it's issues.  The game needs something akin to a AAA developers love and polish.  The Unreal Engin has proven to be highly robust but it's not properly implemented here...leading to various stutters and lag and sometimes collision bugs that will outright have you restarting missions.   Even the mouse tracking has a small delay that can  test your patience when trying to aim precise spells like Ice Spear at far away moving targets.
On top of that you'll also find yourself doing different missions on maps that are a direct repeat of previous encounters.   Things like that attest to a certainly amount of laziness  in the development of the game, which once exposed can be expected throughout the rest of the title.  You won't find an RPG worth 100 hours of play here.  The NPC's in an ecounter do not speak or hand out missions but questing is still present.
So to wrap it up..Roguelike, LOOOOOT, powerfull Mage Character, custom "Hand of Fate" type story telling... It's a good game.  It just needs some love (patches) and polish.
It's more of a casual experience (making $20 is a little steep in price) so put it on Hard difficulty, set it to "Hardcore mode" and enjoy a couple of rounds seeing how far you can get one evening here and there.

I played this game back 3 years ago and i'm here to tell you a bit about the differences and of course the pro / cons.
Some quick things said:
The game itself seems to be still the same but over the years they of course changed certain things.
The game had back then 5 unique classes :
Lann a double sword / double spear melee warrior.
Fiona a sword/shield or hammer/shield melee warrior
Evie a staff or scythe weilding magician melee - medium range.
Karok a pillar or cestus weilding melee warrior.
Kai a customazible bow who can be used as a short or longbow.
Now they added 6 more and a seventh is incoming to see their stats and weapons go to the wiki site.
Now I started played for about 1-2 weeks and I already made a lvl 90 character with full gear within those 2 weeks playing. What I liked and disliked the same time is I had to many gifts and to many events going on the same time.
I got VIP for 7 days and double exp double AP which made the game a bit odd satisfaying.
I heared it had a good story but I skipped it to see how fast I can get into lvl 90.
The pro:
Nr. 1 skill based game (which I really love)
11 classes with unique features and gameplay. Some require more skill some less but all are fun to play.
Active combat system ! The best thing about this game and what I loved the most was the combat.
You can grind most dungeons really fast and without a problem but once you reach lvl 50+ the boss fights getting intense. From there on the game becomes more skill based than other mmo's out there.
RAIDs are in this game pretty epic and good made. The bosses are from the lvl 30 raid until the 90 all equal the lvl hard.
Gear / equipment / armor is really easy to get + a lot of gifts from the game itself.
Cool looking skins and outfits.
Friendly players
AP shop allows you to buy 7 day hair and inner clothets (no benefit just to look good)
Easy crafting system
A "decent" pvp system
The contra:
The Nr. 1 the bugs (after so many years not fixed) marketplace while trading you get 9 of 10 times stuck on some dungeons you can get stuck somewhere (/escape) you have to write chat command to get ported out. I mean wtf after more than 5 years and they can't fix it??
Still lag spikes and specially on certain dungeons with multiple players the game lags happens not so often but still sometimes and it's annoying.
The lag on the normal maps once you start the game you get instant lag spikes until all characters on the map are shown.
FPS drops (due to the lag spikes)
Every skin / outfit you have to buy with real money (20 euro for 1 single outfit)
No open world
Gear binding system which sucks cuz you have to pay with real money to unbind gear.
Not pay2win but pay to look good
Low player base / you find people on the common played times.
Bad activities
To much grinding to gain gold
Dungeons are almost the same over and over again
I guess that's a short pro and contra list from me.
All in one I can say this:
For people who want to just have a game to waste some time but want to be challanged I can recommend this game.
It requires high skill gameplay on the end game and even on the lower lvls there are a few hard dungeons bosses.
It's fun to play alone and with a team.
The active combat is pretty fun and a lot different than the other mmo's have.
It's not really meant to be played for long time players cuz it just offers not so much to spent to much time on it. Once you get a full gear of orange (rare gear / highes tand best) there is nothing else to achiev.
The game has/had big potential but the creaters / devs are not doing enough for it. As mentioned the bugs and lag spikes who are there even from over 3 years ago still exist which ruins it a bit.
It's sad cuz the gameplay and characters are unique and fun to play :-/
Thx for reading hope you got a quick view over the game with this review.

I played Legends via the Bethesda Launcher, when it was first released (before it was on Steam). I'm not sure why I stopped, but I later decided to get it on Steam. I recently thought about playing it again, so I spent some time with it last night. I really enjoyed it, even more than Hearthstone, because it has a deeper single player mode to it. In fact, there's single player story mode and the solo arena.
I was surprised, when I opened it up with Steam, that I was continuing from the progress I made from first playing it via the Bethesda Launcher. So, I didn't have to restart at the beginning. I learned a bit more about the game. In most battles there are two lanes for cards, sometimes there is only one. Sometimes they contain bonuses, for instance the right may give cards cover, so they can’t be attacked until they’re exposed. Sometimes the left lane may give cards a bonus, too. It’s interesting.
I usually won (in single player mode), but when I lost, I'd switch decks (from what I obtained) and win. I've now finished the first story and I believe I've unlocked all the modes. Now I need to earn more gold or spend real money to unlock more.
To complete some dailies, I had to fight real players. I lost each time, but some of the games were close. I didn't feel bad about losing, because my daily goal was just to play in versus mode. So, that was an easy one to achieve. In contrast, Hearthstone often has dailies that include victories, certainly not a daily I enjoy.
