Here's my review, not that it's needed. #TLDR... Just play it.
Game beats Hearthstone hands down. I enjoyed that game for a while, but the constant push to be something else over there eventually drove me to leave. I've enjoyed this game immensely and have been able to grind almost all the cards, including Madhouse and Skyrim additions. Grinding is actually worth doing here as I only occasionally feel like fodder for the high dollar/high tier elitists, and that's mostly because of my own choices about which cards to grind/decks to build.
With Hearthstone, the decision to purchase was a temptation that I felt myself manipulated toward constantly. With Elder Scrolls, the decision to purchase has been more of a feeling of "I really should support these guys for what they've done here." Disclaimer: I've never spent a single penny on either game, and no I don't feel guilty. I don't feel guilty because I'm not going to be able to compete, more than likely, with top tier decks from what I've seen, without dropping some cash here or copying what works. DISCLAIMER: I don't netdick/I mean deck. I make my decks my own way. I pay for that here with wins/losses.
Almost 800 hrs in, I do have almost all of the cards for this game. I don't think I could grind for another year or two on HS and ever come close to being able to say that. I always felt with HS it was about money. ESL feels more like its about a truly excellent game. In your eye, Blizz (Finally about to forgive them for the money I felt they took from me for that crappy WoW. Yeah, I'm one of those. No, not everyone simply adores that mediocre crapfest.). Anyway, you don't have to take my word for it, jump in and start grinding. If all you care about is winning, and you're good with other peoples' decks, you'll do fine. Get yourself Universal Deck Tracker if you haven't already, however, as that is something I wish I knew about from the very beginning. Gives me good insights into what's currently working.
As a result of experimentation and an unwillingness to netdeck, my ratio is about 65% overall wins, and that's as a player who's seriously contributed to the ever-evolving deck styles. I'm not going to claim my contributions, but if you've played in casual for any length of time, you've encountered maybe one of them. As a result, I'm sure that if I'd just copied what others do, burned all my extra unused cards to get started, stayed exclusively to fifty card builds, and avoided too much experimentation, I would have done much better w-t-l-wise. I don't like that and refuse, however, because I hate playing the same decks over and over and insist on being my own player. I like a little RNG and randomness, even though I know that's not a great thing for competitive play usually.
That's the biggest downside to playing a lot of this, if you do. You'll see the current flavor of the month a lot, the current flavor of the week a lot, and the tried and true a lot, but isn't that the curse with these games? What works rises to the top and everything else drops. If that bothers/bores you, like me, ESL has enough variety in it that you don't have to play the same things everyone with zero creativity/originality seems to play, but you will feel that pressure to conform if you want to climb or achieve overall wins consistantly above 75% on every deck.
One more thing that most people don't seem to notice, probably because they haven't played the number of hours in a short period that I have or just don't pay attention--there's something in the RNG on this game that bugs me badly. I can usually tell on first draw how the game will go. I cannot tell you the number of times, but it's quite high, that I'll mulligan a card or two and get back at least one of them on first turn. I tend to play 60+ card deck builds. 70 more than I care to admit. Tell me, how odd does it seem to you that with only 3 or fewer copies of a card in that deck, you will draw that same card two draws in a row out of 70 total possible cards? Also, if I draw all high cost cards in mulligan or all items, for whatever reason, the next several rounds will be more of the same, more often than I think is reasonable. I don't want to hear about confirmation bias and that's why you only put a few high cost cards in a 50 card deck, blah-blah-blah-blah. I know about all that, but still something feels off. I use universal deck tracker, and over time you see that if you don't stick to the exact builds that others use, but create your own things, this such-and-such deck will tend to be matched against 1-3 specific deck types more often than others. I think many miss this because they're too busy playing tried-and-true deck builds. I have a crusader build that UDT says has been matched against monk 10 times, while the closest after that is Spellsword at 6 times. After that the numbers fall off pretty quickly. Seems not so random to me.
Now, it's definitely a good thing to have good matches. But if my better creations keep getting pitted against certain decks, I can't get a clear picture of how those decks would actually fair in totally random matchings against totally random skill sets of players. So, I find most matches challenging, and they've done that well overall. But I think it would be nice to get a fully random sample of the player community sometimes. To do that, I might have to make a ghost account and dive in again to see how the experience compares. If it's exactly the same, then I'll know I'm off. Is it worth it? Still debating at this point. Games worth some time invested tho'. So give it a go already.

Orbox C is a Sci-Fi puzzle game, and not Sci-Fi in that it has many science fiction elements but that it takes place in space, with a square little probe guy trying to solve puzzles, IN SPACE! Who doesn't love a bit of space? I know I do. Regardless, there are a total of 7 packs of 30 levels each, each with varying levels of difficulty based on the name of the pack, it should be obvious on what is what. The hard difficulty pack definitely took me the longest to complete.
Now this game was given to me for free by the developer, and I have made the entire game into an LP on my channel, a link at the bottom of the review is available.
Within the LP I addressed some replayability concerns, that this game definitely doesnt offer, such as a star system - there is no way to really indicate how well you completed a level compared to everyone else, or what the min-max values would be. The lack of a star system defeats knowing there is a better solution available and the strive to get to it, and without it, you honestly dont know, and not many people wish to spend a few hours a level to see if they could potentially beat their previous score on it.
With that said, there are other options for replayability that I addressed in my LP such as a storyboard that changes between playthroughs similar to NIER or other games of the sort. This may be unheard of in puzzle games but it is a possibility to add repeat playthroughs each time, perhaps expanding the ability to add additional blocks types, etc.
There are no unlockables in this game outside of unlocking the next pack once the previous has been finished, no custom backgrounds, no alternate backgrounds, blocks, etc, forcing only one look for this game. It would have been interesting to see some of the other levels in alternate styles.
Settings are a bit lacking, I get a full screen/windowed, SFX and BGM on/off buttons. That is it. No options to set resolution (needed for recording to YouTube), nothing for skins, etc as I mentioned before, no in-depth video settings, or any of that sort. The settings are very straight forward and minimal.
Now, do I recommend this game? I do, for the price point it is offered at is perfectly fine for the amount of levels (>200) it offers and is a good time killer, however for those who want to replayability in this game, it may not be quite at that level for you unless you enjoy min-maxing on your own without knowing if there is a better solution available. Though keep in mind the lack of settings can drastically hinder ones desire to play this game if you're looking for customization via options.

At about 12:30am I received an email from Arseniy Shkljaev wanting me to shoot a gameplay video for Orbox C. I’d been working at the time and was due for a break. I hit the game’s Steam store page and immediately knew that I’d enjoy playing the game.
You see, Orbox C is a puzzle game. Further, it looks like the type of game that has some action gameplay components to it. It requires critical thinking and quick thought. As one may suspect, this is entirely up my alley. I’ve played very similar games before – it’s not a new concept per se – but it’s a very interesting take on the genre.
One of the things that I love about this game is that gameplay mechanics are introduced at a relatively rapid pace. You’ll get a few levels of the same mechanic and then a new mechanic is introduced. This mechanic is generally not just a small change but something that adds significant depth. This prevents the game becoming tedious and increases the challenge.
Speaking of increasing the challenge, the game isn’t as easy as it appears. Most levels had me repeating them to find the solution. However, at no time did I ever feel that any of my failures were unfair. The game kicked my♥♥♥♥♥until I logically moved through each level.
What makes the game magical, however, is that it is simplistic in its nature. But it gets it so right. It doesn’t strive to be more than what it is. Consequently, it delivers an all-around puzzle experience.
I’m used to writing these protracted reviews lately. My reviews generally are around the 1200+ word mark. Consequently, I carefully consider what I believe my readers will read and what they won’t read. There’s not much here to honestly criticize. My biggest criticism of the game is an external issue that I want to address on my business blog. I urge anyone who cares about marketing to read the blog. Hopefully, you’ll learn something.
Having said that, the game is lacking in overall polish and pizzazz for it to appeal to the mass audience. But it’s a $2.99 indie game made by two guys for crying out loud. It’s supposed to be a little rough around the edges. The point is it does exactly what it is intended to do. It has more than sufficient amount of content to satisfy fans and that’s what it’s done.
If the developers can clean up the game’s marketing image they’ll be doing extremely well for themselves. I hope that people keep an eye out for it during the upcoming Steam sale or indie bundles if they’re not willing to hand over the equivalent of a cup of coffee.
Coffee or the game? The game’s going to last you longer than a cuppa. However, if you’re addicted that probably won’t matter. If you’re a serious puzzle gamer then get your hands on this hidden gem and have some fun.
Rating: 8/10

KNOWN BUGS:
- If you decide to make a custom title screen it breaks the "Return to Title" option in-game so you can't return to the title screen you made.
- The demo area where it shows you how your game looks breaks CONSTANTLY.
- All font is forced to be italic if you use a custom font.
- 1080p Graphic Glitches during transitions
- Can't loop audio files, can only loop music
11-26-2017 UPDATE: There are graphical glitches on most Intel Embedded Graphics cards such as Intel Iris and the Intel HD Graphics chips.
I still would not recommend this software at the current price point, but the developers are doing their best to address the bugs and will work with you to help you out. I have managed to build about 1/4 of my Visual Novel I already created in Ren'Py and TyranoBuilder and on the upside I would like to point out that the visual effects are far more powerful than TyranoBuilder, and everything looks very good.
PRO: There is no doubt that this is the most powerful and comprehensive Visual Novel Making software on the market
CON: The numerous bugs will make you overcome tremendous hurdles to have a professional release, and you could save money and build a project faster with slightly less control over advanced features with TyranoBuilder or Ren'Py.
This software is going to be your only choice if you want to develop a highly advanced Visual Novel with lots of custom scripting (or Ren'Py if you are adept at coding, would be the best choice) but for people who want to just tell a story and keep it simple, TyranoBuilder is a better choice.

Excellent scripting support. Not only is the engine open for changes and extensions, but scripts can interact with the editor itself as well, so we can create custom windows, forms, buttons and such for developers to use.
The documentation for scripting seems really well-written and complete, including a full API Reference and some guuides and examples.
Includes a built-in ACE IDE, but it's also easy to setup the game folder as a project on any external IDE.
This is Degica / Enterbrain most robust Maker for programmers so far, I believe.

Visual Novel Maker is promising, but feels like a product still in beta.
A couple of concrete examples. There's a library of common event calls, one of which is "Enter Text", a basic functionality of any game UI, asking the player to enter some text. The description of the common event says it takes two parameters: one for length, one for what variable to return the entered text. It doesn't. It takes one parameter, the length, and returns its value in magic variable which you can find by looking at the sample game, but won't find in the documentation.
This does not engender confidence diving in; it's literally the second common event call in the example game and it doesn't work like the documentation says it does. Figuring that out requires some basic comfort with coding.
Second example. It's great that there's a lively plugin community already producing plug-ins, two days after release. For example, from their twitter account,  "@SumRndmDde just made a cool extension to VNM that gives you a “wysiwyg” style text editor for creating Show Message commands".
That's cool, but surely that functionality ought to be in the product already? Visual Novels have a LOT of messages, so a product designed to make it easy for non-coders to develop them should offer such a visual editor for messages out of the box.
Similarly, "Moe is adding Quick Save and Quick Load functions to the engine". Great, but they're standard features of VN's, so why aren't they already in the core product?
I'd prefer the developer to have worked with the community developers to add this sort of functionality in the beta phase, without having to download and manage a whole bunch of potentially-competing plugins from different authours.
They're working on uploading a whole bunch of tutorial stuff including more extensive games, which is great, and I'm sure the active community will produce tutorial videos in due course as well. But again this is something sorely needed which should really have been sorted out in the beta phase.
Clearly the community are excited by the engine, its extensibility and flexibility. In a year's time hopefully they will have developed this into a fully-featured product with lots of community support and great things. If you're itching to get your hands on extensible scripting and write some code, it's a brave new world.
But for now if you just want to pick something and get started, I'd say Ren'Py already is where VNMaker will hopefully be in the future. (You'll need to understand a fair bit of coding either way).
VNMaker may ultimately prove a more powerful solution, but if you just want to get stuck in and you're not especially techie, in my opinion it is not ready for you just yet.
(My background- not a games developer, but I've done software development professionally in the past, and now work as an artist. I like checking out tool-kits for stuff I'm playing with, which is currently choice-led computer games & VNs. )

Everything about this game gives the appearance of shallowness, from the stick figures and black and white line drawings, to the silly humor, to the simple mechanics. However, there is a surprising amount of depth here for anyone who cares to dig.
It's genuinely funny, beyond the silly. A lot of the humor is pretty damned sharp, and it's clear that the creators know about serious comedy. Some of their gags are actually references to much older acts, not to mention a lot of inside jokes from the comedian community.
The silly, though, is done to perfection. There is a constant delivery of lines or actions that catch you off guard, and make you laugh unexpectedly.
The gameplay has depth, too. There is marrow beneath the bone white surface. With the fights, it's not apparent until some of the the later levels that strategy is important (it is quite possible to grind to over-level most battles, though).
Also, there is so much stuff to do and get and discover, you can't possibly experience everything without multiple play-throughs. Optimizing your skills and equipment to your play-style is easy and has a noticeable effect. Random things will pop-up too, and also things that seem random but aren't, and that helps to keep things fresh. There are a lot of adventure game puzzle elements, too, in that whole mess. They don't ever bog the game down or get you stuck, it's just more game-gravy if you want it.
It's not perfect, by any means. The music is fantastic, but incredibly repetitive. A lot of the smaller battles could be put on auto, you seriously don't need to be there for them. Grinding is a thing: it's too tempting not to do it, but incredibly boring once you get on the treadmill. As cute as the graphics are, they will strain your eyes after a while. The menu is amusing as hell, but could use some functional tweaking.
Play it for the lols, just don't be surprised if you keep playing it because it's actually quite good.

When I first played the game through, I thought I must have missed something, given all of the positive reviews it has received, but upon a second playthrough, I only found a couple more lines of flavor text.
I had a strong emotional response to eating the shrimp, particularly after finding the picture the protagonist had commissioned of his "babies," but in the end I think that speaks more to my own attachment to animals than any feelings that the game imbued in me.
I'm sure this is going to turn out to be a metaphor and I'm going to look like a fool for asking, but a question: if all of the power in the apartment has been diverted to "the guest," why are there piles of TVs lying in the hallway playing static? My best guess is that it ties into the title of the game, and it's "not literal" or whatever, but it doesn't add anything to the experience of the game.
Anyway, I'm not a fan of stories that are built on ambiguity and provide very little substance to spark that feeling. If this was intended to be a depression/suicide simulator, it, uh, didn't do a great job. I KNOW it's "not literal," but I still feel a bit indignant if this is a portrayal of my illness. Also, obsessions are part of another disorder, so good on y'all for missing that.

Even though time has been slightly unforgiving for Tower of Doom (much less so for its sequel), both games included in this mini collection prove to be among the best and deepest side scrolling beat'em ups ever created, up to this day.
From classes to monsters, the world of D&D and its rules (with obvious "artistic" licenses) came perfectly to life in a way that can satisfy both arcade fanatics and avid players of the famous tabletop game.
Multiple paths, a remarkable amount of variety and a multiplayer co-op mode (online and local) that is a blast to play make Chronicles of Mystara a must have even though you didn't have a chance to try the original in an arcade, given that you can appreciate the dated graphics.
There are also a bunch of challenges that earn you some kind of diamond currency, which can be spent to unlock artworks, sketches (taken mostly from 2E and 3E manuals, a little disappointing if you were expecting original material) and house rules, special settings to make the game easier or harder.
If you like brawlers and/or fun multiplayer games, Chronicles of Mystara is certainly worth a closer look.

$3.39 is a steal! Buy it now...or read my short review and then buy it.
Note: My experience was altered using the Far Cry GES(Graphical Enhancement Suite) and Dylan's Realism Mod, I INSIST that you download these as they turn the game into what it was meant to be. If you decide to play with the Dylan's mod, play on Infamous diffuculty...trust me.
Graphics:
Stunning when using the GES, as it allows you to alter the saturation, contrast, and brightness (the game can be quite dark in the jungle). The jungles are vibrant, the deserts are scathing, and my goodness are the sunsets gorgeous. The weapon models are fantastic and the animations that go with them are even better, particularly the jamming ones. My only problem would be the environmental textures aren't great.
Gameplay:
This is a hardcore mercenary sim, whether it's CQC with shotguns and assault rifles,  wiping out a base from a safe distance with a sniper, or torching the whole base with a flame thrower, the heat of battle is intense and visceral. The guns handle great and the recoil is really nice, especially on the silenced makarov. Another great system is how fire works, when it's windy you could chuck a single molotov and the fire would spread to engulf the base in flame. One mixed bag in the game is stealth. Sometimes it works amazingly, other times not so much. For example: on a mission where I had to sneak into an old greenhouse and destroy an old pump, I took out a sniper on the outskirts of the base and then proceeded without taking any other enemies out. I snuck in and placed an IED on the pump and snuck out. It was glorious. On the other hand there are times where you are sneaking up and a sniper who is not even looking at you will all the sudden turn around, tell the other enemies where you are, and open fire. So stealth is definitely hit or miss. The AI can be weird at times too. Another system that is FANTASTIC is the buddy system, Quaribani, you will always be remembered as my first buddy. You really build a reputation with theses guys, and then all the sudden they can ripped away from you, you try desperately to save them as they are wounded, but you know it won't work and you have to do it, pull the trigger. You have various types of missions to choose from, the main story ones, buddy missions (different from the buddy objective in the main missions), assassination missions, and weapons dealer missions which unlock new guns.The main missions and the buddy missions take a little while, while the other two tend to be quicker. So overall the gameplay is really good, some of my favorite FPS gameplay for sure.
Story:
The story sets up like this: You're a mercenary who is hired to take out an arms dealer named the Jackal. He has supplied arms to two different factions in a civil war. You do work for these factions and in turn they give you information on the Jackal. The games faction missions can be very interesting if you do some of the Buddy objectives which make the missions longer, but they can also be VERY repetitive. If you're used to open world games this won't be a problem. Besides that problem, when the story picks up, it REALLY picks up. And depending on which ending you choose (yes, this is one of those games) it has a great ending(one word: briefcase).
Sound:
In short: weapons and sound good, voice acting is on fast forward, and everything else is hit or miss.
Replayability:
This is my one major problem in the game. There is no post story mode playability, you could load up an old save but I have so many it takes awhile to load. Your only other option is to start a new game. I don't understand why there isn't a feature like in the new Tomb Raider where at the end it tells you are now free to explore the island and do side objectives.
Final Score:
8.5/10. Buy it when it's on sale if you're unsure, but if it sounds like your type of game, go for it regardless of price.

This game isn't for the faint of heart. It's a brutal slog through a nameless war-torn country in Africa where everything is against you. Both warring factions will attack you on sight, vehicles break down, and guns will degrade and jam on you when you need them the most.
Whereas Far Cry 3 & 4 give the player a sense of empowerment over their surroundings, this game makes you feel oppressed by the terrible environment you're in. Few game franchises could actually take this setup and make it fun but Ubisoft pulls it off.
Game has aged well, still looks and sounds great. Gun-play is top-notch and just what you'd expect from a Far Cry game. AI is hit and miss. Story didn't make much sense to me but doesn't really matter. The African environment can be monochromatic at times but overall looks good and even gives a surreal element to the game (where are all the citizens??).
After playing FC3 & 4 it was nice coming back and playing through this game for the contrast. I give major props to Ubisoft for taking a huge chance to make a game like this and mostly succeeding.

Although there is a good deal of strategy to be used in tower placement, this game relies way too heavily of grinding in order to level up the towers enough to barely squeak by to the next level. It is a shame, the visuals are bright and pleasant with smooth animation and unique characters. Aside from the mind numbing grinding the game play has potential. This COULD HAVE BEEN a wonderful casual game, but if I sit down to play a game it should not feel like work, work is what I am taking a break from.

I really wanted to like Visual Novel Maker. I met with the company at Anime Expo 2017 and it sounded exciting. Unfortunately, I got software that was buggy, inefficient, and in no way an upgrade from the alternatives out there (that I have tried).
The first thing I did was fire up the test game. There I found my first complaint. Even compiled, the game only progresses when you click the text box rather than anywhere on the screen, which is fairly odd. There is very likely a work around to this, however.
Some things are easier on this than RenPy--such as adding animation to sprites and filters to backgrounds and images, but even that only saves you an extra thirty seconds--maybe up to four minutes if you aren't familiar with RenPy's script. The only thing this has that RenPy doesn't already have and do better is the Live 2D support, which you can work around easily enough.
Immediately afterward, I began to work on piecing together a few test scenes to test out every feature I could. I cannot help but compare to RenPy, my current engine of choice.
Compared to RenPy, if you spend a day or two figuring it out, or just use their extremely well-documented forums, this is only going to save you a marginal amount of time in the set-up (defining resources and characters). The real time-deficit would be during the actual writing. It takes significantly longer to add in and construct messages, which is ultimately where you will spend the majority of your time.
Furthermore, the Live Preview did not consistently display what it should. Sometimes it would, sometimes after no changes and some clicking around, it would not. Probably the worst was that the Live Preview crashed completely for me several times.
*I would like to see perhaps a keyboard shortcut to adding text more quickly
*An option to import all their underwhelming artwork into your current project for placeholders
*More reliable Live Preview
*Easier sprite movement / scaling (I may have just missed this, but I'd think it would be best to move in the Live Preview window, if it worked)
*Clicking on non-UI buttons advancing the text
*Seemed to lack a UI builder and other features I would have expected
There may be more, but at that point I decided it was not going to do what I had wanted of it and would be a sharp downgrade from the Free RenPy.
Much of this may change with time, but as it is now, at release, I am sorely disappointed.

Frankly, the program doesn't seem to be for me, and I'd recommend new developers at least try the free/cheaper alternatives before assuming Visual Novel Maker will be good for them.
For anyone who's curious about a detailed breakdown of the built-in assets at launch, right off the bat:
-
, most of which have roughly six to eight expressions and two outfits. A tinier group have two arm poses, while an even smaller handful only has one outfit. You can get a look at a lot of these in the videos above, and while I don't love them, I expect a lot of people to use them a lot!
-
, one of whom has a secondary outfit. I don't know much about Live2d, so I'll defer to any developers who use it regularly here.
-
, with a hefty number on each background variations ranging from two (typically time of day adjustments) to ten (zoom-ins, new objects in the background, or shadows to populate settings like the theater and the festival). These are great. I love them and would buy them independently in a heartbeat. Unfortunately for Visual Novel Maker, I ended up looking at them and thinking "I wish I could use these in another engine".
-
, ranging from sky shots to some extremely pretty patterns. I also like these, so my similar thoughts on the setting backgrounds add onto this.
-
. The sound effects especially seem to be useful, if only because they're essentially decent quality "freeware" effects consolidated in one place, but none of the music stood out to me. Even if I were to make something with this engine that used the pre-provided sprites, I don't think I'd ever use the music.
Edit: As Trey pointed out in the comments below, make sure you check the licensing on these assets. Visual Novel Maker's assets are made to be used in Visual Novel Maker, so if you're a new developer, always check the licenses on pre-provided assets like this!
(I'd recommend any aspiring developers interested in looking at the assets in their copy of Visual Novel Maker to open up the program's local files through steam; for me, they were located in the subfolder labeled "dlc". Looking at them through the Visual Novel Maker interface can get a little bit tedious.)
I think a big selling point of this engine is its ease of access, but if you're like me and get overwhelmed easily by trying to keep track of too many visual aspects, this engine's built-in "ease" (and some of its dense body of tutorials) can be a bit too much. One of my key thoughts looking at Visual Novel Maker was that it didn't feel easier, it felt more like a repackaged way to look at the same information you'd be able to access in programs like Ren'Py.
And you can't escape the comparison to Ren'Py, if only because of the field this program exists in. When it comes down to it, this engine is absolutely more powerful than Ren'Py in some aspects, namely the Live2d support. That's something I'm interested in seeing more of from developers who know what they're doing. But as I was navigating through a drop-down menu to add another drop-down menu to choose "my character's expression changes from happy to sad", I kept returning to the question of whether that was actually simpler than typing "show charactername sad" in Ren'Py and achieving the same result.
The question of a steady progression of growth is one of my big questions about Visual Novel Maker, too; does it enable new developers with bigger ideas than they're actually able to achieve by making it look easier at first, when it's ultimately a powerful and dense engine under the hood, so much so that I could see a lot of players getting bogged down in making their earlier projects a thousand times more complex than they need to be?
That's one of my bigger concerns about it as an engine, because I don't think any engine that wants to make things look easier will escape accidentally laying that trap for some new developers. (And it's one I mention so new developers who are delighted by the ideas they're having a chance to execute for the first time and read this review are at least conscious of what they're doing!)
A note to the developers of Visual Novel Maker themselves: I've seen some of your replies to a lot of people on social media who mention Visual Novel Maker, so I know you're aware that people have difficulty with earlier stages/outright not being aware there's documentation so far.
The "templates" included were a good demonstration of what the engine could do, but if you're going to bank your engine on ease of accessibility, having a comprehensive tutorial built in to the software itself will do wonders.
For now, it's not worth my money to me outside of a few of the asset categories, which is why I mention them in such detail. If you're a Live2d developer, someone who wants to access a bunch of assets at a great price (edit: see my note above), or someone who prefers choosing off a drop-down menu to typing text, definitely check this out. You'll get what you want out of it, I think.
But if you're a new developer who's never used any text-based programs like Twine or Ren'Py before in your life, and you're just jumping into a sixty dollar purchase on the grounds of it being visually-based alone, I'd recommend taking your time and trying other things out. Sixty dollars is sixty dollars, and the expenses of game dev are the expenses of game dev, so it never hurts to explore the field before making a financial commitment!

At about 12:30am I received an email from Arseniy Shkljaev wanting me to shoot a gameplay video for Orbox C. I’d been working at the time and was due for a break. I hit the game’s Steam store page and immediately knew that I’d enjoy playing the game.
You see, Orbox C is a puzzle game. Further, it looks like the type of game that has some action gameplay components to it. It requires critical thinking and quick thought. As one may suspect, this is entirely up my alley. I’ve played very similar games before – it’s not a new concept per se – but it’s a very interesting take on the genre.
One of the things that I love about this game is that gameplay mechanics are introduced at a relatively rapid pace. You’ll get a few levels of the same mechanic and then a new mechanic is introduced. This mechanic is generally not just a small change but something that adds significant depth. This prevents the game becoming tedious and increases the challenge.
Speaking of increasing the challenge, the game isn’t as easy as it appears. Most levels had me repeating them to find the solution. However, at no time did I ever feel that any of my failures were unfair. The game kicked my♥♥♥♥♥until I logically moved through each level.
What makes the game magical, however, is that it is simplistic in its nature. But it gets it so right. It doesn’t strive to be more than what it is. Consequently, it delivers an all-around puzzle experience.
I’m used to writing these protracted reviews lately. My reviews generally are around the 1200+ word mark. Consequently, I carefully consider what I believe my readers will read and what they won’t read. There’s not much here to honestly criticize. My biggest criticism of the game is an external issue that I want to address on my business blog. I urge anyone who cares about marketing to read the blog. Hopefully, you’ll learn something.
Having said that, the game is lacking in overall polish and pizzazz for it to appeal to the mass audience. But it’s a $2.99 indie game made by two guys for crying out loud. It’s supposed to be a little rough around the edges. The point is it does exactly what it is intended to do. It has more than sufficient amount of content to satisfy fans and that’s what it’s done.
If the developers can clean up the game’s marketing image they’ll be doing extremely well for themselves. I hope that people keep an eye out for it during the upcoming Steam sale or indie bundles if they’re not willing to hand over the equivalent of a cup of coffee.
Coffee or the game? The game’s going to last you longer than a cuppa. However, if you’re addicted that probably won’t matter. If you’re a serious puzzle gamer then get your hands on this hidden gem and have some fun.
Rating: 8/10

My review:

For video Review:

Presentation
While the graphics of this game are nothing special to look at, they are at least pretty nice. The particle effects are decent, the textures are fine, just overall what you would expect. The music is pretty good, but it is a little too loud. I could just turn down the volume of my computer, but that would be annoying if you were talking on discord or trying to record your own voice, etc. You can only turn the music off or on. I feel like it would be way better suited with a slider. The buttons on this game are huge, leading me to believe that this is most certainly just a mobile phone port, which is fine, at least it runs well and looks nice. Truly any computer made past 1998 should be able to run this game pretty well. 
Gameplay
For a puzzle game to work, it needs to meet two criteria for me. 1. The mechanics of the game are unique/ maps are well designed and 2. It should be easy enough to get into, but hard to beat. I think this game nails that personally. While the mechanics are nothing too special, the stages are very well done. Basically all you do is move a cube left, right, up, and down. The cube doesn't stop until it hits another surface, basically meaning you can shoot your cube into space and you'll have to start over.  There are a good amount of different objectives to complete to finish a level. Sometimes you just need to get to the end, sometimes you have to destroy blocks, collect orbs, or touch every side of a block. Some levels are a combination of 2 or 3 of those objectives. There's a good amount of variation, and the levels can be very challenging at times. 
Content
First things first, this game is only 3 bucks. Even keeping that in mind there is plenty of content in this game. There are 210 levels to complete across the various difficulties. Each level takes about a minute to complete, give or take depending on how good you are at completing the puzzles. Basically you get at least a few hours or gameplay from this game, about what you would expect. My goal for any game is to get an hour of gameplay of every dollar I spend. This is a game where you should be able to do that easily. Again, this is a puzzle game, so there really isn't anything other than puzzles included in this game.
Overall
This is a very solid game in every category. Doesn't do any one thing great, but it does everything very well. Plus, it's very cheap and will run on anything. If you are into puzzle games, or just want to kill some time, this isn't a bad buy at all.

Does a good job of keeping a constant amount of challenge, while also not being so difficult that you get excessively frustrated.
I would certainly recommend this game. Simple concept of a momentum sliding puzzle game, with loads of different Sci Fi Mechanics to keep you busy.

Like others, I have very mixed feelings about the game. I have really enjoyed it, and getting my first character to max level at least seemed somewhat rewarding. But, once you get to end game, you realize that the whole things is just a massive grind fest/ pay2win. You will spend countless, and I mean countless hours grinding for gold or materials for armor and weapons etc. and soon realize that it is futile. Your weapons permantly break when trying to enhance or enchant them unless you pay a ridiculous amount of money for protection. It costs 20$ simply to protect your weapon when enchanting! Mind you, that is only good for one enchant, if it fails, you still have your weapon, but you have to pay another 20$ just to attempt an enchant again. This is only one example, but it gives you an idea of the system that Nexon utilizes (Not to mention success rates top out at around 35%). All in all, no matter the amount of time you spend, you will realize that your stats are absolutley nothing compared to the people who drop literally thousands of dollars on the game and walk around as titans. To me, I simply feel cheated. I have put in over 1000 hours into this game just to have an average end game character because I haven't spent that much money (Still 100s). And then there are definite issues with the servers. Overall, the game saddens me because the combat is simply amazing and can be very rewarding when mastered. However, this is largely overshadowed by the obvious money hungry company that is Nexon. The game is slowly dying, and its heartbreaking to see the demise of a game that had serious potential to be one of the best mmorpgs of all time. Fictorum is an interesting game/concept that makes my inner dnd nerdgasm. The game has a promising premise, power system/use and punishes the player for mindless play. The game as a whole package is worth $20 but it leaves much be desired for npc interactions/behavior, movement fluidity/animation and overall level design.
Levels are just islands that feel almost sculpted abruptly with little to no time put into development for them and loot feels awkwardly placed throughout the landscape.
The player has no option of approach trying to sneak up on citizens/npcs when suddenly they all become alert to my presence to which seems based on distance even if solid objects are directly between us. The npc system feels extremely lackluster and rather mediocre.
Not to mention the glorious fun of zapping buildings to blow them up only to have a tiny piece of rubble take a chunk of your hp out of nowhere. Building pieces/parts/furniture have no connection between one another when you zap an entire wall into oblivion only to see a table with some flowers unharmed behind the now shambles wall. It takes the appealing almost sexual joy of blowing buildings to smithereens and dampens it to casual "meh"
The movement feels somewhat wonky as the character seems to almost glide over the landscape and animations for falling and moving feel static and unadaptable to the already lackluster levels/surroundings. Also, my character doesn't make a sound doing much of anything besides taking damage, add some grunts and HAHA'S and make 200 of em, already better than no reaction at all until he takes damage.
Final Judgement: The game is very lackluster on many aspects but excels at a few, the game in its current state does not feel like a complete product, even for an indie company. (perhaps my standards are too high) Regardless, you'll notice I recommend this game because I think you should try it for yourself, keep your play time under 2 hours, see the promise in this title, and refund and follow/wait for future developments or perhaps you're a risk taker and want to buy it and wait, whatever floats your boat. This game has potential. Potential that has yet to be utilized but potential nonetheless. I will be watching this game perhaps weekly excited for news and updates and possible fixes to my personal issues with the game.  For $20 and a hopeful future it's worth it but Scraping Bottom Games hopefully pulls through and continues to develop this game further. That in itself will be the surest sign of my continued support. Buy at your own risk.

Note: I backed the game on Kickstarter, thus having played since the game's alpha.
Fictorum is, in a word, wonderful. For me, it was the first experience I ever had with magic that actually feels really powerful. Magic that I can throw at a nearby house and watch it get blown to bits. But let's start from the beginning.
In this game, you are a mage. The last mage of your order, the Fictorum. And you're pretty mad at the ones responsible for the death of your order, and also pretty powerful. Logical conclusion, annihilate them all. And anyone that might be foolish enough to stand in your way. Or... just annihilate absolutely everything. You can, believe me.
You start off on the world map, which is fully randomized. On this map, you move between mountaintops, with a variety of things that can happen whenever you visit one. Maybe soldiers will try to stop you. Maybe you find bandits. Or maybe, a despaired citizen of a nearby town pleads you for help. There's a lot of possibilities. In some cases, you can just move on. In other cases, the action begins.
'Action' means that you control your mage, walking through the area and flinging magic around. The best part of which is the Shaping. Each spell can have up to three runes applied to it. Increase the area that a spell affects, make the projectile fly faster or even have it home in on enemies... There's a lot of effects. Once you begin casting your spell, you can bring up an interface where you can freely change how great the effect of each rune is supposed to be. Go all-out on the explosion? Make it faster to catch that enemy sprinting at you? Or just have maximum effect from all runes? Your choice. Just beware, as even though time is slowed while you are shaping, your mana continues to drain.
I'll let you find out more on your own, but I do need to point out one last thing. Despite how powerful you are, the game is not necessarily easy, depending on your difficulty setting. Your health does not magically restore after an encounter. If you take damage, the damage stays until you either rest (giving your enemies more time to chase after you), find health potions during encounters or heal yourself by spending essence, the game's currency, at magical vendors. For the ones that truly enjoy a challenge, there's also a hardcore mode with permadeath.
That much is sufficient for a general description of how the game works. But to go back again to my first point... I love magic games. And I've played a lot of them. But Fictorum was truly the first time where I could actually use my magical powers to go on a rampage. I can kill those that I'm supposed to kill. I can also kill all the innocent villagers that run away trembling in fear. And destroy their houses. I can fling fireballs, shoot lightning and icicles, even call down meteors from the heavens. And it is way, way too much fun.
Conclusion:
If you like magic, you're very likely to enjoy this game. If you like the thought of using magic to go wild and level an entire village, you're even more likely to enjoy this game.

Everything great about HL2 is carried over to this installment with much more open and beautiful environments, a thrilling end fight, deeper character development and an ending that is still just as heart-wrenching as it was when I first played it. The pacing is also great, something that Half Life 2 definitely needed improvement on. It's much more action-oriented than the preceding games, but somehow it still finds time to flesh out this interesting and believable world.
My only negative is that replaying it reminded me how incredible these games are and how much I want a Half Life 3. It's a shame the only real closure we got was the would-be story from Mark Laidlaw.

the first few quests are a bit dull. but once you get past your first run-in with the powder gangers, this game reveals itself as one of the most layered and rich experiences you could ask for in a game. yes, even with a bunch of mods and fixes it's still buggy as hell. you'll absolutely get way too angry when you get killed by a cazador for the umpteenth time. but when almost every named NPC has a quest for you, when you still find cavernous new areas 30 hours into the game, and you haven't even TOUCHED the dlc, you know you've stumbled on something really great.
there's magic in this game. i've never been particularly good at the mechanics of games, but this one rewards returning and replaying more than anything i've experienced. (and if you're not playing with mods, you're not really playing -- the community is amazing and you can easily add another 50+ hours with everything there is to offer.)

Although I've long outgrown anime, I did my best to take my time with the story. The translator has done a great job making this accessible to English speakers, but I felt like aspects of the story are being 'lost in translation'. Without any exposure to or an understanding of Asian media (specifically their take on the horror genre and anime), players may have trouble following the plot. The game seems to blend elements of Asian and Western suspense, thrillers, and horrors; it would have benefitted from being focused and dedicated to a single genre and style.
Overall, the game still needs a bit more polish before it can be taken seriously or compared against other anime games. Having said that, I have to commend the development team for taking on such an ambitious project. I was surprised to see a well-animated intro and some high-quality illustration; it gave a good first impression, but it just wasn't consistent all the way through.

The drag-and-drop system is excellent, and it's easy to modify events by clicking all the variables. Putting text into message boxes (what VN makers will be doing the most, probably) is extremely easy. The only detractor is that it's not immediately apparent where to put in custom assets, and there are a few random buttons that do things that are a complete mystery to me.

The documentation and tutorials are in-depth and as idiot-proof as possible. I didn't have the chance to get deep into it yet, but I found what I've seen to be quite useful. The only issue is that with there being so much documentation, it's a little hard to narrow down exactly what you're looking for.

The interface is simple and concise. It is intuitive and pleasing to work with, with clean navigation buttons. I'd like a dark version instead of white and blue, but that's just personal preference.

The built-in BGs really shine. There are lots, and they come with tons of well-done variations for time of day and such. The music, on the other hand, is a big disappointment. There is very little of it, and it sounds sadly MIDI-ish. The system sound effects have that same MIDI sound, but they do their jobs. The other sound effects range from awesome to barely serviceable. The premade character sprites, while absolutely stunning and with multiple outfits each, are a bit limited in quantity.

There are tons of powerful built-in tools like movement pathing for sprites and image tinting. Live2D is worth mentioning as an important feature that is supported fluidly. Another excellent I especially like the Live Preview feature. It can play in-editor, or "Detach" and play like the game would from whatever point you choose.

At $59.99, this is the most expensive VN-specific engine on the market today. Compared to Ren'Py, this engine is much simpler to use (and supports Live2D, which Ren'Py does not), and the premade assets contribute value too. It's up to you to decide whether the convenience and coding-free experience is worth the price to you.

VNMaker appears to be a very flexible and powerful engine. It makes the "boring" part of creating a VN much less boring and painful, and it takes very little time to learn the basics. I know it has a lot more potential beyond the simple things I tried. I'd recommend it to anyone who wants simplicity or a coding-free experience. The only large detractor is the price; however, $59.99 is still a small price for software. I believe it's definitely worth the cost if you can budget it.

I really like the software so far. Hard coding has never been a strong part of my knowledge, so to be able to piece together a story with the click of a button is very nice. I've used Ren'py for a long time, but I'm most likely moving everything over to VNM.
Haven't run into many bugs so far, maybe a few crashes but that's to be expected with so many things running at once. Looking forward to see what the community makes.

This is a great piece of software if you are new getting into the world of visual novels. Visual Novel Maker is a powerful piece of software that makes putting together a visual novel not only fun but easy. With the 60+ hours I have spent on the program so far I can say that it runs very smooth. Putting something together is as easy as dragging and dropping, but you also have the options of writing in your own code or adding extensions in to customize the game you are making. For myself, someone who knows NOTHING of coding, I only needed an hour or so to get used to the program and start creating. The program also comes with an extremely helpful help guide pointing out a lot of functions to learn and look up. I would definitely recommend taking some time before starting a project to look over the guide so things are not too confusing when you start.
The program comes with many premade assets you can use, or you can be creative and import your own assets like music, characters and other graphics. Doing all this is super easy and once you get the hang of it you can make your own cast of characters! The program also comes with built in test scenarios you can load up and learn from to get the idea of how the program works. If you are interested in giving this program a shot it is a fantastic tool for beginners to experts.

When I first saw the Steam store page for
I was intrigued. I love a good casual game and the game promised puzzles and adventure. It also mentioned being about exploring and offering players a challenge, so I decided to take that challenge. However, I will say this right now that I disliked this game very much, however that does not make this a bad title. But full disclosure, there is a lot of walking and wandering around with long spans of time where you will be doing nothing but exploring, if this doesn’t sound fun than I caution you.
The story starts off with the player controlling a nameless person who is in jail for murder with no chance of escaping. That is until Veilia shows up, a floating spirit who needs your help to regain her body. She helps you out of the jail and then you go on a journey to find shards that have been scattered around different realms. Find out the secrets behind these mystical realms and prepare to battle the sorcerer who cursed Veilia in the first place.
Gameplay is where I had the biggest issue. The game thrusts you into action without much of a tutorial or any help whatsoever. You have no map, no hint system, nothing at all. Your only solution is wander around and try to discover what’s around you. If you enjoy doing this then you’ve found a good game but it’s not for everyone, myself included. I will say, there are things I wish were included to make the lack of direction bearable. The game works with a keyboard and mouse setup, you use the WASD keys to move forward, space to jump and the perspective is first-person. My main issue was since you spend so much time just walking that there was no way to run, I found myself just sitting here holding down the W key and staring off into space. I will admit, there might be a way to run but the game doesn’t have a tutorial on what keys did what except for the WASD, jump and flashlight.
The graphics in the game are good -if you force players to explore the world for hours, then it better look good for them. However, I started in the desert level and I was met with a world of sand, nothing but sand. Anything that wasn’t sand felt miles away from each other and the game cycles between night and day, during the night everything is just too dark and even harder to explore. The game’s soundtrack isn’t bad, it’s simple and does not distract from what you’re doing. The characters don’t speak, they have a sort of tone-ish sound instead. Veilia’s sound his high pitched reminding me almost of a certain blue fairy from the
series while her personality reminded me of a certain sardonic imp from another entry in the series.
Just because
wasn’t the game for me doesn’t mean it won’t be for you. I do feel controller support would help a bit, as well as some options for players who need help. I don’t mind exploring but from what I’ve seen there is more empty walking space than mystical wonders to find. Journey through different lands, solve challenging puzzles and have fun getting lost. This title also offers Steam trading cards and achievements to collect as well. I found this game to be promising but because of the aim to avoid a “hand-holding approach” with gamers it threatens to alienate part of its audience.

Chronicles of Mystara is a classic arcade brawler from the 90s.  It contains two games, Tower of Doom and Shadow Over Mystara.  They are remarkable in that they both stand up remarkably well for being nearly 20 years old.  Branching paths, level ups, weapon upgrades, shopping...  Basically these games, for their time, and even now, do a fantastic job of capturing much of the Dungeons and Dragons formula.
That being said, these games run on the Advanced Dungeons and Dragons (AD&D) rules, so if you play a character who casts spells, don't expect to be able to blast away willy-nilly.  Spells a ultra-powerful abilities that are extremely limited in their use until the party makes camp for the night, and this only happens at set story moments in the game.  You don't get to choose.
All in all, it's a fantastic game.

I can certainly appreciate the marriage of RPG and beat-em-up elements that Capcom's Dungeons & Dragons arcade games offered, especially given that it was innovative at the time (and still sort of is). I can also readily understand loving the games' aesthetics, because the graphics and art direction still hold up well. However, like every beat-em-up of its era, these games had nothing to do with skill and everything to do with how many quarters you were willing to part with. Clunky movement and horrendously imbalanced damage ensured that you would lose repeatedly, and the fact that this rerelease allows you infinite credits is telling of just how much of a massive scam these games were. What's more, if you're buying this version, you're paying for some "features" that make some pretty bad games even worse. Playing on an emulator that supports Netplay is not only cheaper, but it will also rid you of the terrible bezel that takes up damn near the entire screen, in addition to allowing you the opportunity to find far more people to play with.
The apex of 2d beat 'em up. An eternal arcade classics, now and then.

Definitely an Arcade game, it has a crapton of features for a Beat-Em-Up. In total there's 100 items across 2 seperate games! Mix that with new "House Rules" and local/online drop-in/drop-out multiplayer for up to 4 players and you've got a game that's worth the $15 in my eyes.
The combat system is pretty basic, but each of the 6 characters are indeed in-depth enough to make things interesting. Unless you're the Magic-User, combo potential is pretty good for beating down your opponents. The Magic-User can also combo, but not to the same degree of depth. Spells make up for this though, and BOY does he have a lot of them.
Unsurprisingly, this game has a Level-Up system. The Score you gain from grabbing items and killing enemies are the Experience Points you gain for leveling-up, which increases your Health and makes you more powerful to some degree. I mean, it's Dungeons & Dragons, so it's kind of expected, even if it doesn't make too much sense for a Beat-Em-Up.
The game is kind of unforgiving in terms of difficulty, so expect to die a lot. I got game over 30+ times during my 1st and 2nd playthrough of Shadow over Mystara. I haven't tried online play yet, but I hope to if my friends pick the game up. Maybe more players will make it easier, although I doubt it. This still won't deter me from playing it!
All I can say is, if you're a fan of old-school Arcade Beat-Em-Ups, you'd be missing out on a gem if you've never played this.

People think LA Noire is great because of the facial animations. I'll tell you what, Episode Two did it first and it did it better. They look at you and say something with their face when someone turns their back. It's unbelievable. All in all, Episode Two is the proof that Half Life is a masterpiece, even 10 years after its release.

This is a port of two classic Capcom brawlers with a Dungeons and Dragons theme.  You get both the Tower of Doom and Shadow over Mystara. Brawlers easily became quarter eaters in the past and with enough coins you could always trudge them them.
Still there is enough content left to warrant owning this game.  However, the asking price of $15 is somewhat steep.  This is a prime canditate to add to your wishlist and pick it up on Steam sale.  50% off or more is just the right price.  It is worth playing eventually, but not necessarily immediately.  It will also provide poor satisfaction for someone who only plays single player games.  Brawlers are at their best when played with a buddy.

Kingdom Rush series is one of my favorite Tower Defense games around, it's a shame none of its other chapters have come out on PC. In comes Evil Defense, another mobile TD come PC game. How does it fare? It has charm, and the same strategic elements that makes KR such a fun series.
However Evil Defense lacks heart and soul, it does little to really differentiate itself from other TD games. You still lay out ground troops, and you still back them up with mages, archers, and mortars. This PC version keeps endless amounts of grinding which can be a complete bore to push through. That may fly well on mobile devices but on PC, its easy to get bored. Yes, you will have to grind the same levels 5+ times to gather enough souls to upgrade further and play the next hard level 4-5 more times. Not at all what I look for in an engaging TD game.

The best of old school arcade beat-em-ups! Great graphics, great visual and character design, good music, responsive controls, incredible variety and depth in characters and tactical options, branching paths that add some variety to repeated playthroughs, tons of secrets to discover... what more could you ask for?
Well, yes, some of the "secrets" are key to surviving, let alone winning. And yes, some (alright, MANY) of the bosses are downright cheap ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.
But really, those are just common design features of coin-operated arcade games, deliberately built in to keep you feeding the machine and squeeze every last coin out of your pockets - and then make you come back for more! With this port we have unlimited free credits and a bunch of optional "house rules" to smooth the way, as well as the Internet to spoil us on every little secret, strategy and easter egg there is to know.
What's not to love?

Evil Defender is a tower defense game in the purest sense, and a rather blatant Kingdom Rush worshipper (seriously, the towers are EXACT copies 80% of the time). But if you're like me and you're upset with the guys over at KR for going over to mobile devices only, then what better way to stick it to 'em than buy a game here on steam so similiar to theirs?
It is a SOLID game with plenty of hours-played in the bang for your buck area. Completionists beware, if you want to get all of the game's rather staggering 98 achievements, be prepared to dump in about 40 hours into this relatively simple game.
About six levels in you'll notice that your towers just aren't cutting it anymore. You need to power them up using souls. That is, the currency you get for killing, having leftover gold, earning star ratings and choosing higher difficulties. So yes, there is some grind-factor to be had here, if you want to reach the upper levels. Have fun playing "The Wastelands" level over and over for hours (It has the highest soul output for your time in the game, about 2500 per playthrough).
That aside, once you've powered up your towers, abilities, and summoned demon you'll be an unstoppable fighting force that the game simply can't keep up with. I guess instead of balancing their towers to be suited for all levels, the devs just thought it would be better to make you stronger for time spent, like a traditional RPG. I don't like the idea, but I understand it.
TDLR:
-Play Kingdom Rush (also here on Steam) FIRST, and then if you want more play this game too.
-This game steals a LOT of concepts, even towers, from Kingdom Rush.
-It is a SOLID game and a good example of the genre.
-There is going to be some SERIOUS grinding levels if you want everything (5 hours+)
-Despite any complaints it's still a strong, functional, well-built game. No complaints.

How good is it? Well, I waited for this game to go on sale. When it did, I purchased one for me and gifted 3 other copies, so we could test the co-op play. The game became an istant hit! I've put in almost 65 hours of gameplay in just 5 days! (Thankful for the extended holiday weekend because I need some sleep badly!) I love the 50's era sci-fi theme. The comic book, pulp fiction, cut-scenes & music are done so well and translated into a 3-dimensional world so nicely! We found the game to be very enjoyable, but also MORE challenging in co-op rather than in solo play. When you have co-op, the beginning funds available for purchasing your support units (a.k.a. "structures") is automatically divided among the number of players at the begin of each campaign session. Most of the times I felt I was preparing for the invasions bare-boned, but the flip-side is that it made me chose my startup structure(s) more wisely. Thus far, I've managed to play all four of the architypes. My favorite is the Spaceman, but I also like the Rocket Scientist! If the game issued just a little more money to start in co-op per each player, I would not complain at all! lol  In addition to the Campaign mode, there is also an Invasion mode which I guess is there for those who like waves upon waves of increasingly difficult hordes of robots coming at them. I've tried it a few times but never made it past wave 4. You are EXTREMELY limited on space for placing your structures... like, just 20 feet from the rocket you are trying to protect and the robots clearly have an advantage as their mothership makes airstrikes from above at the same time you are dodging deathrays from the advancing alien army! I spent more time waiting to respawn than actually doing any good. Total fail for me! lol So, I stick to campaigning and solo play (which I was surprised to find was much easier to play... up to a certain level). There comes a point where teamplay is essential because of the multiple invasion landing zones there are on a map vs. how many zones you must protect... it gets a bit insane. All-in-all it's a great tower defense game with a decent theme & music and any repetitiveness is forgiveable (at least, for me) due to the captivating constant action. With every defeat comes a new determination to strategize smarter. I'm not a big fan of strategy games... they make me think too much when all I want to do sometimes is just blow things up! lol But I really like this game! Ok... I'm rambling now... If you have any doubts on whether to get it, then wait for it to go on sale again and start playing solo to get a feel for the game and then join a co-op game in session or get your friends to buy a copy and play a private (invite only) game with them. I think Fortified is definitely worth adding to your game inventory because good co-op games that are family-friendly, are hard to come by these days.  =)

Sebastien Loeb Rally EVO is a decent game. Unfortunately, being decent isn't good enough these days. Ultimately, in a world where DiRT RALLY exists it will always be overshadowed and compared relentlessly. It doesn't stand up underneath the pressure of such comparison, and so will undoubtedly be consigned to the dusts of time wence it came.
PROs:
SLRE is visually pleasing. It has sharp graphics outside the cockpit and a straightforward menu system that doesn't have any of the annoying DIRT RALLY 3 teeny bopper voices. The noise from the engine is clean and pleasing to wind up so no complaints there. Even the HUD is customizable which makes driving so much more of a pleasure.
CONs:
Unfortunately, the cons have eclipsed the long-term viability of the title. The driving feel from overhead feels plastic and the driving inside the cockpit feels like a high-speed boat cruise. It's so hilarious that the moment you steer you have op-lock immediately to keep it going straight - kind of like a bumper car. But, after some time with the title I doubt many would complain.
CONCLUSION:
I don't recommend buying this title at full price, but if you can manage to snag it on sale I would do so.

A deeply flawed game that's still worth checking out. Play it because of the brilliant gameplay mechanics the sequels dropped, such as degrading weapons and the buddy system. Get sick of it because of the awful gameplay mechanics the sequels dropped, such as Instantly respawning roadblocks and the malaria mechanic.

Your mission is rather simple: Get to an unnamed African City in an unnamed African Country. Whack the bad guy, an arms dealer  responsible for fuelling the ongoing civil war with a steady influx of foreign weapons. Easy peasy, right? Game over! Roll the credits already! We got this!
As expected, things go horribly wrong. Not long after your landing, while riding a taxi to your hotel, you begin to feel kinda sick. Faintly you hear the cabby: "Are you alright sir? You don't look so good...", just as you loose consciousness. Shortly after you awake amidst a fierce gun fight. All you have now is a fancy new Malaria infection, a rusty Makarov, an  even rustier machete, a crude map of the world and no fluffing idea what the hell is going on. Welcome to the world of Far Cry 2!
Now its up to you to make it out of this hellhole. This world is not just gritty, murderous and unforgiving --- it just doesn't care about you in any way.  Autosave, minimap, hitmarkers, healthbar, handholding? Nope, none of that in here. Instead, five minutes after you clear a location, new enemies will spawn there -  more than willing to carry on the murder show. Are you up to this?
The game has believable physics and good shooting mechanics. The driving is a little silly, but its manageable. While being a little short of story, it is the alternative draft to the recent "icon-em-up" Far Cry titles. If you haven't experienced this shooter until now -  well go right ahead and make up for this. It aged quite well and still is one of my favourite games. Totally recommended.

text:
TL DR: do you want to have fun with friends/brother/sister/boy/girlfriend etc? This is the game for you. Even if you aren't familiar with the TR series you will have quite some fun with it. (Two controllers recommended)
Are you looking for the typical Tomb Raider game with the pretty graphics, intense storyline amazing quality effects and that sexy Lara's A$$?
This is not the game for you.
This is not the typical Tomb Raider game and is not even the typical gameplay you could find into a TR game.
Yeah indeed, there are several artifacts to find (some are even really well hidden), yes there are different puzzles, yes there are even some difficult challenges.
But the gameplay itself is not the usual.
First of all the view is not a third person one but an isometric one (if you like RPGs or Diablo you will love this).
Second there is a lot of action; yes there will be a lot of enemies to kill and you will find yourself surrounded more than one time.
Third you can play this co-op and some puzzles will even change during multiplayer to "force you" to cooperate to go on.
I really recommend the use of a controller even because it's a simple and plain game with simple commands (keyboard + mouse in this particular case is not that comfy like on Diablo 3 for example).
The gameplay itself is pretty much linear even if, in some levels, you will need to go back and forth through the map to go on.
If you take your time to do everything you will find several relics and weapons (and you will be amazed...there are quite plenty of them). The relics will give you different advantages (or disadvantages) on speed, ammo, health and so on. (Like the objects on a RPG game but in a very and more simple way). If you get the most rare ones (both relics and weapons...yes there are some quite unusual weapons) you will technically become immortal.

This is without a doubt the best game I have ever played. When people say that games have the potential to be art, this is what they're referring to.
You are allowed an unprecedented level of control over what happens. You can kill literally any person in this game and it will not break the story, with the exception of children and literally (and I do mean literally) 2 NPCs who you are technically unable to meet until the end of the game anyway, when they then become killable. There is also one immortal robot who can resurrect himself despite your best efforts. You can play this game without harming a fly (again with the exception of a small number of very specific NPC encounters where you are attacked outright, and even then running away is an option) or you can leave a trail of blood behind you and eradicate all life in the Mojave.
Though the combat may not feel quite as smooth as a more traditional shooter, the variety both in weapon design and type is admirable. Take an already massive pool of conventional firearms, add in flamethrowers, plasma weaponry, lasers, as well as some explosive weapons, and you've got a recipe for success. The weapon pool from Fallout 3 is back with a vengeance, adding not only a massive number of additional weapons within these categories, but adding in multiple ammunition types and plenty of unique weapons, too. The uniques often have their own models and tweaks to make them feel distinct from the standard pool of weapons, giving them their own niches and allowing them to feel really worthwile to collect.
When building your character, there are plenty of skills that govern everything from how fast you draw your weapon to how many points you get when you level up. In addition these skills are often used in dialogue "checks" that may determine whether you are able to do certain things. These checks are also present in the environment, often allowing for you to interact with the the world around you and giving you an even greater sense of being and accomplishment, thereby increasing immersion even further. The great variety of perks that can both be chosen and even earned through specific quests and dialogue options help to this end as well.
The level of detail and quality that was put into every aspect of the story and dialogue amazes me to this day. Obsidian found creative ways to make each character feel unique by having them participate in many quests and questlines, thereby allowing them to have real presence. Their dialogue is full and rich, giving you a sense of the world around you. Each faction is unique both in their goals and their philosophy, feeling distinct and interesting. The quests are creative and often equate to more than merely fetching an item from a dungeon. Instead, quests often involve things such as convincing people to do or not do what you want. You have to pay attention to what the characters are telling you and respond accordingly, failure to do so has consequences beyond a single line of dialogue. Your actions throughout the game affect the world around you and the ending quite nicely, allowing for you to have a real sense of accomplishment by the time you're through and really seeing what change you have effected in the Mojave.
Each location has plenty of its own flavor, allowing for settlements to feel distinguishable from one another. Whether it's the striking neon lights of the vegas strip, or that familiar green dinosaur in the desert, or the snowy mountains of Jacobstown, the landmarks are unmistakable and remind you constantly what part of the Mojave you're in.
All of what I have said here applies to the expansions as well, each having a unique story and of course even more unique locations and intriguing characters and factions to meet and/or murder, if you so desire.

As of this review, I have been playing this game for only 6.1 hours according to Steam. Don't get me wrong. I have been playing this for years now, and I have reasons for that low gameplay hours.
Viridi is not a game where you can play for a couple of hours per session or much longer. It's just a plant simulator. You plant your seeds on your little pot, water the plants, and take out the weed, which will take you two to three minutes at most. And you leave them for, say, a day or a week, and you can come back later and see how your little plants grow. It's like you are planting real little plants. Sometimes I even forgot to check my pot for a couple of months, and all the plants are withered, but not dead. I just watered them, and, lo, they sprang back to life, with all the vivid colours it had just before I left them.
The point of the game is not to shoot anyone, get the high score, or stressing yourself out. Instead, the point is to take some time to relax yourself with these virtual plants, and share free seeds (obtainable weekly for free) with your friends with love. Hell, we have been through a lot out there, so why stress yourself some more? Why don't you spend a couple of minutes escaping the grim of this world and have a look at your lovely little plants on your lovely little pot?
Also, the soundtrack is very soothing. You should try listening to them, or else they wouldn't sell them as DLC. (That sounds like a fallacy to me by the way.)

Evil Defenders:
~~~~~~~~~~~~
Hell is about to break loose, my dear minions! The peasants managed to find our lair! It’s time to setup our defences and crush the insurgence of do gooders and protect the lands of Evil!
Evil Defenders is a well-designed Tower Defence / Strategy game where you are in control of the Devils army.  You will have at your disposition up to 60 different towers across 15 maps. Each of these maps have 6 levels to beat, an awesome 90 levels to play. Upon success, you will earn souls which you use to upgrade your units and abilities.
The enemies are the nasty humans and they have 15 units from peasants to berserkers (by Belzebub, this one is mighty hard to kill!). During gameplay and depending which level you are at, you will have to eliminate waves of the human onslaught. The first level has 10 waves and the last levels 30.
I really like the content available in the game, great library to read about all units (yours and the nasty humans), upgrades and abilities. As you progress, the game gets quite challenging - make sure you accumulate as many souls as possible by beating all level per map before jumping to the next one. Otherwise, you will be stuck (just like I was) trying to beat it over and over with no success at all. What the Hell!
I really like the graphics in the game including the artwork, the audio is catchy for a while (that is until you get stuck and you blame it on the boogie). The game runs really well and it is well priced.
One small downside is you are not able to access the leader board (I certainly can’t)!
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Addictive, challenging and fun
-	Good content
-	Great selection of towers with plenty of upgrades
-	Good graphics
-	Stacks of achievements & trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Leader board is not accessible
