My opinion on Evil Defenders attempts to answer the question. Is this game worth your money?
On first glance Evil Defenders seems to be just another mobile port of a tower defense game. However after taking a closer look there is a surprising amount of content here.
In my 5 hours of gameplay I've seen 5 base line towers each with 3 upgrades which then convert into 3 specialized towers with 3 additional upgrades. 2 special abilities and 1 big mean deamon buddy.
On top of the towers you have a list of specilizations that you spend "Souls" on in between rounds. These specializations improve your normal towers greatly. Depending on the map your running you may need to change specializations, thankfully there is an easy way to do that with only a 10% decrease in souls per use.
Considering there are over 90 levels in the game atm and 15 different maps this translates into a crap ton of content. Each map has 5 different difficulty settings that increase the rewards for mastering plus a challenge mode that you can run repeatedly to gain souls to buff your towers abilities.
That graphics are very well done, the voice acting is hilarious, and overall a damn good purchase for the price of a movie. If you enjoy tower defense games with some meat to them and a ton of content this is a solid buy.

My all-time favourite twin-stick shooter! Fantastic gameplay in both single player and co-op modes. Maps are slightly differnet in co=op, requiring the abilities of both characters to progress. A couple of levels are a bit wonky in co-op because the game tries to keep both players on the screen and in some areas ends up pulling one to his/her death.
There are a good variety of weapons and special items which grant bonuses, like increased speed or health/ammo regeneration, but I found myself sticking to a couple of favourite weapons and I got a really good special item early on, which regenerated health and ammo, and used that throughout most of the game. Lara's twin handguns and Toltec's spear have infinite ammo. Only the other weapons require ammo pickups. Weapon unlocks are specific to the character so levels have to be replayed in order for both characters to get them.
Puzzles and platforming are simple enough, as the main focus is on the action, but they are a bit more challenging in co-op. Challenges for extra unlocks and 100% completion were not overly difficult, and thus were mostly enjoyable. I've only played local co-op so I cannot comment on the online functionality, but I'm guessing there isn't much online activity due to the age of the game. I doubt I would have played with random people anyway,. Local co-op with friends or family is the way to go, imo.
My play time doesn't accurately reflect the time I put into this game. I've played though to 100% completion in both single and co-op modes several times on another computer. Despite a couple of minor faults, this game is a 10/10 for me!

Cons:

Money hungry company (NEXON)

Almost all cosmetic items cost real money
Very small player base (because of mentioned cons above)/ you end up soloing most missions
Dungeon heavy game/ lack of exploration - There's only 3 different towns that you revisit over and over again (boring)
TL;DR:
The game is fun in the beginning because of its different combat system and gameplay style, but once you keep playing, you'll realize that this game has a lot of pay walls and the grind ends up being pointless. The game has bad optimization so it's only ideal for really powerful PC's when ideally, a decent PC should be able to run this (made on Source engine).
Just play Black Desert Online if you want similar combat but in an open world with nicer graphics and a much nicer and better optimized game without pointless pay walls (other than the $10 one time purchase).

Once upon a time there was a game called Kingdom Rush, it was popular, it was popular because as Tower Defences go it was polished, easy to get into and well balanced, whilst at the same time maintaining a solid, and interesting set of upgrades as well as a good set of unique twists that made the game genuinely great in it's own right. There's been other genuinely excellent Tower Defences as well (Defence Grid : The Awakening being the prime example), however, these are few and far between. Most of the time, you get "decent" attempts, or ones that are just forgettable...
... until now.
Take a bow Evil Defenders. Please, come forward onto the stage, and be showered with roses and cheers, for you are most definitely one of the greats, and deserve to be welcomed and feted. Now that's not going to be unreserved praise. There's a few things I will take up with you, but considering you get so much right, I think we can get along
Evil Defenders doesn't do anything particularly new or novel, it doesn't break ground in any significant one (save for a minor twist, which is actually rather neat in it's own right), but what it does is take what exists, and it applies polish. It applies polish over and over, until there's this worn in lacquer that's almost, almost Blizzard worthy. At a price point that makes this a real bargain.
Now to be fair, the first impressions are going to have you sit back in the seat and make you wonder if the game really is all that. The intro video screams "Mobile game, Clash of Clans, Free To Play", it's got -those- kinds of vibes about it. The options menu is utterly bereft of anything bar a couple of sound sliders and a toggle for health bars over the tops of things (Really? That needs to be an option? If it was a choice between bars and numbers, that'd make sense at least...), still, you fire up the first map and then things begin to look up, there's a set of difficulties (some locked off) and a challenge mode.
Normal mode to begin with is merely the appetiser, it's generally pretty easy as long as you don't fall asleep at the wheel or make entirely dumb choices, as the tower positions are fixed all you need do is make the "correct" choices as to what goes where. However, there's another -four- difficulties after that, going all the way to inferno at the top which throws a marathon number of waves, comprised of advanced mobs from later maps and forcing you to adapt and improvise, taking lessons from much, much further in, and applying them to your earlier levels. Things begin to look up...
... and then you open up the upgrade tree.
Ohhhh lordie lordie. The upgrade tree is -massive-, not only does it branch like a massive set of snaking vines, along multiple paths, with individual paths for each tower and power type, as well as a utility tree for things like "Bonus bounties" from killed mobs. But you can level the upgrades iteratively, so buying the same upgrade multiple times improves the bonus it gives. This means setting up specialised builds is a thing (at least before the eventual maxing out of -everything- if you're OCD about minmaxing your towers).
The game goes from being this rather generic looking tower defence to being this amazingly polished and genuinely deep tower defence that offers real replayability and a serious flexibility in how you design your defences and how you guide your playstyle. The level of customisation as a result is absolutely incredible, not counting the sheer level of upgradability in game (each tower has three tiers of base upgrade, followed by their specialist three tiers depending on the path you pick). On top of this, each level has a landscape feature that may help or hinder you to some extent, learning how to use this to your advantage can be critical in helping stem the tide (the prime example is the oil river on the desert map that can be lit up to cause DOT fire damage).
There ARE complaints though. First, no endless mode. For me this is a minor issue, but one that should be noted nonetheless. Some people might care about it more than others. Secondly, the game can feel grindy at times, you will need an awful lot of souls to max out your upgrade trees, but again, that's only an issue you intend to minmax the whole lot. Finally, the game, whilst amazingly polished, doesn't do -much- to move things forward, but then this is one of those "reviewers" things, for most people this isn't even going to be a consideration. If you're looking to try something really -new-, this is something to bear in mind.
These are however, in case you've not already noticed, nits. Minor complaints, these are small hitches in an otherwise stellar presentation of Tower Defence, and easily one of the strongest TD's since the likes of Defence Grid and Kingdom Rush. At the price point it's pitched at, it's a very, very easy sell.
Verdict :

The more i play this game, the less i like it which is really sad as it stands out through its clever level design, being very well polished and a decent number of different enemies and towers.
These are the things it does well which make the game stand out from the others. The problem however comes with the things it doesn´t do well.
If you set aside that you are basically playing the same missions over and over again, which didn´t really bother me that much, the fact that the first time you play a mission (standart difficulty) is by far the hardest and most recognizable one doesn´t go well with it.
The ONLY challenging waves are the early waves which doesn´t change with increased difficulty. There are some exceptions on this, more to that later, but this makes the later waves (and thus the higher difficulties) feel even more like a grind as you´re just sitting there on speed x4 waiting for it to be finally over. Once you figure out which towers are good and which aren´t (which is the sad truth this game faces) you will find yourself rarely slowing down the speed to actually use your abilities.
When the game completely fails however, is when you make it to the final wave and get completly destroyed by it´s wave. It is not always the same which strong enemies you get which sadly reeeeally matters here. Getting a juggernaut, a summoner or a paladin makes up everything in the earlier difficulties as you can´t build defenses against all 3 types in such a short time making them once again way more difficult than higher difficulties.
There are some exceptions to this however and overall what i took from this game was not the grinding of later difficulties but the overall design it has. That´s what makes this game special and that is the only reason why you should buy it. If you don´t own a lot of the TDs here on steam i´d still suggest getting another, as there are better ones out there, some even with nearly the exact same tower scheme.

text:
Fortified is a game that I really wanted to like, and don't take the dislike as strictly not enjoying it, because there IS some fun to be had in the title, but ultimately it falls short in too many areas for me to recommend when there's so many other options currently.
Let's start with the good.
The best part of the game is the general presentation. Everything has a very unique and good art style, portrayed like an old comic book would be both visually and aesthetically. There was one point in one of the earlier levels where the lighting was set up in an ingenious way, casting the shadow of incoming martians onto the wall before they rounded the corner just like so many old movie trailers used to do, it was something I was not expecting to see in a game like this and it blew me away. Whoever managed the art style of this game is great, and I do want to see them handle more projects.
The game works fine. I didn't encounter any bugs personally while me or my friends were playing.
The idea of commanding troops around the map is new and worked pretty well.
Despite my review, I did have some decent fun with the game.
The Aethetics are all done really well and really help serve the game. The issues that keep me from recommending this game are all to be found in the gameplay itself, unfortunately.
The player count balance seems off. Enemies scaling to the number of players is nothing new, but it's pretty insane in Fortified. The difference caused by adding a single player to my game was astonishing. We later added a third person, thinking that two players was a really rough spot. While it was slightly better, it still was too bogged down to really be enjoyable to anybody. The game feels balanced around two scenarios: A full party of players, or one player.
The heroes all have overlapping gear, but have a unique weapon, tower, and ultimate. I didn't level all the classes up to see their unique weapon and tower, but the ultimates are definitely not balanced well. As an example, the Space Man becomes immortal and freezes everything around him solid for several seconds while still being free to attack as normal. This is pretty good. It stalls a wave and buys time for your towers to attack. The Rocketeer, to contrast, gets infinite ammo. This may sound impressive, but it really isn't for one major reason:
The weapons don't feel effective. The first of two things your tower defense/shooter hybrid NEEDS to get right to rise above the others. Weapons don't have any OMPH to them to make them feel satisfying, and most of the weapons don't deal enough damage or have a good enough gimmick to be usable. Some of them, like the grenade launcher, can actually hurt your team by hurling aliens past your defenses. All while dealing minimal dps.
The towers are unreliable and poorly balanced: The second of the two necessities for this type of game. You don't get very much in the way of money (ESPECIALLY in two player, which had both of us starved for resources nonstop. We couldn't even try and pool our resources together, there's no way to share.) This wouldn't be a problem save for the poor tower balance. Here's an example. There's an anti-air tower in the game. It's really expensive, targets only air. Seems good, right? No. Its fire rate is so slow and its range is so small that it is entirely ineffective at handling air units unless you only have one in a wave, and thats assuming one of the turret disabling aliens doesn't off it first. It's far more effective to take the tesla trap and put it one slot higher than normal on the wall, where it proceeds to be much cheaper and more efficient as it nukes both air and ground. The air tower is a dump option in almost every way, and that isn't something you want to see in towers when your game has so few of them. This is definitely not the only case of dump towers in this game, unfortunately.
Placing traps/towers is also completely linear and uninspired: Most tower defense games get around this by making you maze, or by making the terrain pose advantages or disadvantages based off where you place it (figuring out where to place your tower so that it will have the largest fire arc, placing your tower at a certain elevation. Figuring out where to put a trap so that it hurls people into that conveniently placed bottomless pit, etc.). This isn't the case here, the maps are mostly designed of longish straightaways with sharp right angles and perfectly flat ground. There is no environmental interaction. You never really have to think about where to put your towers, and when you do it's an absolutely minimal ammount of thought.
So in the end, would I say this game is worth your time and money? Well, It depends. If you're really into the artistic direction as well as shooter/tower defense hybrids, This might be enough to pull this game through for you. If this is one of your first forays into the genre, however, I would have to recommend some of the other options before this one. Try the Orcs Must Die series or Sanctum 2 first. Perhaps even try Iron Brigade if you want to try something in the same price range. If you enjoy those games enough to still want to try this game, then go ahead and give it a shot. You'll find some enjoyment here, it's just not quite as tasty of a course as the others.

A surprisingly deep F2P point 'n' click mystery game with some rather dark undertones.
The art style is exceptional, with a gothic narrative that meshes well with what you see. The plot is a bit obscure at first, but after solving a few of the game's (somewhat head-scratching) riddles, things become more clear. The theme is rather strange,  but moving, and progression never feels like a chore.

Video Transcript :
Before we can talk about Orbox C I think it only appropriate that we discuss Orbox and Orbox B. As you might have puzzled out from the names this is actually the third addition to the orbox catalog. The previous two titles are free browser flash games that can be found on a plethora of different websites. It appears the developers wanted to go down a different path this time and create a more substantial marketable game. Which brings us to today.
So being that this is the first game in their series they’re asking money for – what is it you get exactly. Well –  for starters you get 210 levels of varying difficulty packaged into a surprisingly good puzzle game.I should mention that I had never played nor heard of an orbox game before being approached for this review. So I had no idea what to expect.
I do try to keep a neutral attitude going into every game I review as I want to give a fair chance. That said, I was a little hesitant as I thought this was just going to be another generic puzzle game. It is – and - it isn’t. Let me explain
I didn’t find anything that I felt I hadn’t seen before, however, it takes solid timeless mechanics that are continuously
successful and implements them together. There’s nothing wrong with taking old ideas and recycling them. As long as it’s done well. Games have been doing this for billions of years why change now?
Alright, let me explain the basics to you. It’s quite simple- you’re a box and you can only move up, down, left, or right. You slide along a fixed path until you hit a block or encounter the endless pits of spcae. And that’s really all there is to it. Beyond that there’s five objectives that you may encounter within each level. Each one differs slightly and gives a good change of pace so that you’re not mindlessly repeating the same thing like a zombie.
Getting more specific - the five objectives you’ll face are the default get to the exit, destroy the bombs, collect the blue orbs, activating the sensors, and breaking ice blocks. Mind you, not all levels rely solely on just one of these. I’ve had several times that require multiple hurdles before I could complete the overall challenge.
Moving into the music – we’re greeted with a cool spacey set of tracks. It doesn’t feel out of place or get too repetitive – which if you’ve watched any of my other reviews you’d know is one of my biggest gripes.
Difficulty is always key to a successfully puzzle game. And this game nails it right on the head. The challenge ranges drastically from quick and easy to mind-numbingly hard. I got halfway through normal for this review and really started to feel the heat ramping up. There was more than one puzzle that had me swearing and throwing empty bottles around my room.
There’s several game modes or “packs” as this game likes to call them. They do group the game difficulties in with them, however, looking beyond the standard game - there’s a speed challenge if you’re feeling up to setting some records.
I care little for achievements and cards, but, I know there’s those out there who live for this kind of stuff. There’s currently 31 achievements that can be gained… They’re not particularly hard to get though seeing as I’m sitting at 55% with just a little over 2 hours of gameplay.
My final thoughts on this game are more positive than I would have thought. Honestly, I’m not that fond of puzzle games to begin with, but, I found that I didn’t have to push myself to complete this review. I’ll likely put a couple more hours into it which is impressive considering I don’t normally enjoy these types of games. It is a super casual game – I don’t even think that need be said, but, you’re getting about 5 or 6 hours of content for almost nothing.
This game is currently up on steam for $3. I will say that there is a flash version out there – though – it only offers a fraction of the levels that you’re getting here. The developer has also setup a demo with a generous 30 levels for you to try out. So if you’re a puzzle fanatic then I’d recommend you at least check that out.
Orbox C is a scifi themed indie puzzle game with good music and engaging, variable puzzle mechanics which keep the gameplay fresh through a large catalog of levels.

WARNING: THIS REVIEW IS SUBJECTIVE. ALSO THERE WILL BE MANY COMPARISONS TO HEARTHSTONE, CAUSE I PLAYED THAT BEFORE FINDING ES:LEGENDS
I am enjoying this game SO much more than Hearthstone (its also funny because i am enjoying Elder Scrolls Online more than Warcraft, but thats for a different review). In Hearthstone, i would normally complete my quests, attempt a few ranked matches, and then stop playing. This game has so many things you can do, all of which are rewarding, and gives you many oppurunities to build your collection. The only real money I spent on this game was to buy the Dark Brotherhood campaign, which I would have bought with in-game gold, but if i bought it I would get a Doom Wolf mount for ESO. Besides that, I have not found a need to spend real money...yet. Ok let me get to pros and cons
Tl;dr
Pros
+Mobile app for on the go (I play on my phone more than on steam)
+Story mode to ease you into the game and give you early unlocks and rewards
+Many things to do besides normal versus matches: PVE arenas, PVP arenas, Events, Achievements.
+Cards are divided into one of 5 classes and neutral class, similar to Magic the Gathering's 5 color system for the cards. I like this better than Hearthstones 9 classes and neutral card system. Allows for more customization and deck variety
+Generous rewards for playing. 3 versus wins will give you 20-40+ gold and a card. Much better than Hearthstone's 10 gold reward for 3 wins.
+Cool personalziation options. You get to pick a character portrait and a title. There are 40 character portraits total, 4 for each of the 10 playable Elder Scrolls races. There are also titles you can apply to your character, which can be unlocked by doing achievements.
+Card crafting system
+WEREWOLFIES!!!!! (and vampires but i dont give a crap about them)
+Can exceed the 50 card deck limit (i dont recommend it though)
+Comebacks are more likely because of the rune system. When your life drops down to each multiple of 5 (25, 20,15, etc). you lose a rune and draw a card. Also there are some cards that have an ability that when drawn from losing a rune, you can play immediately for free, disregarding whose turn it is.
Cons
-It would be nice to see card sleeves, and other personalization options.
-I prefered Hearthstone's table top tavern setting to ESL's playing over a parchment in an undisclosed area. Having custom playmats or something would be cool.
-The dual lane mechanic isn't utilized enough imo. I love seeing the lanes have different bonuses or effects in the story mode and solo arenas. But in versus matches i feel like it shouldn't just be a normal lane and a shadow lane all the time. It would be cool to be able to pick a specific dual lane effect set before a battle or something like that.
This is a pretty great f2p game. While there is of course pay to win options in the game, the grind to increase your collection and get in-game currency is pretty fast and not painful or annoying. Definetly give it a try, but play through the story first before doing versus matches.

After completing the game I am very disapointed by a lack of depth in every aspect of the game. Combat was straightforward, the leveling system was shockingly basic, and the rebellion management felt more like an extended fetch quest than an actual part of the game.
The leveling system is pretty screwy, for example you do not increase in maximum health as you level up. This might have been fine, except there are skills which grant 1% recovery of your maximum Vitality, Morale, and Technique points which do not appear to work because they seem to round down to 0 because your related stat will always be very low. Also, the skills in the Training section offer either a 10% or 25% increase to one of you stats for 3 skill points (one level's worth). The Passive section lets you upgrade the same stat by a total of 9% for 6 sp so thay's pretty messed up.
There aren't really characters or a storyline; the game follows the open world format of giving you a vague objective (specifically conquering the next city) and then just lets you wander around until you randomly find the missions which let you do the two-part fight (regular fiights, not boss battles) to get the next city. There are quest givers and companions, however, the only one that you talk to more than once is the guy who tells you the name of the next city you have to take over and not much else.
While there are a decent number of weapons in the game most of them are worthless because katanas are pretty easy to acquire and outperform lighter weapons by a large margin. Weapons which require training are better than the katana, however, the katana is good enough to beat the game with so there's no real need to do so. Armor works in a simailair fashion; the most expensive medium armor you can buy in the first city is more than enough to beat the game with. You can find one merchant that sells better armor, however, there is no real need to do so.
As for leading a rebellion, I never saw the Shogun do anything and the only upgrade/purchase that did something was the Leadership upgrade letting me use more characters. Everything else was either a prerequisite to taking the next city or completely pointless, like unlocking a merchant in my "upgradeable" town with an inventory that matched the shops the first city next to it.

This game is worth your time and hard-earned cash. Essentially, the game is a jrpg about Japan in the late sengoku jidai. You get to pick your starting class and skills and sex which can really make the game interesting.
The best part about this game, is that it really does all it can to make you feel like you are taking on the role of someone's life. A lot of role-playing games these days sort of play like a power fantasy as the player does his or her best to reach a point of apotheosis, or Ultimate Warrior. However, this game's goal isn't to make a God out of the main player or the character, as the main character is more or less known as a great warrior for being one of the first in the region to rebell against the unjust nature of the current Empire. The biggest rewards come from taking part in the story and completing side quests, rather than grinding repetitively.
You mostly gain skills and power levels from just taking part in the main story, and all of your companions can be found pretty much from the start. As the game progresses you will have a core four or five Fighters that are the best among your group, but in battle you can trade them out without any cost so the more characters that you have in your party the more hands you really have to carry equipment and help beat up your enemies. Also, in the middle of fights, the easy start of game enemies can be beaten with a quick "all attack" command... but later foes will start to block and perry attacks if you don't start putting effort into it. Unlockable skills and buffs go a long way as well.
There are very few Random Encounters, so it's not really about grind. There is a pit of fighters in the hardest region of the game, but it really doesn't add much Beyond a place to get money and level up a bit. It's almost like the game is saying " here we go You insecure Maverick Renegades. You go ahead and level up so that you have absolutely no challenge when it comes to the final boss whatsoever. Make these characters we've taken so long to get to know into game prolonging chess pieces, that have just as much power and half the personality as the hero from fable 1." Meanwhile the perfectly capable adults will sort the empire out.

What was a 25-minute playthrough soon became a 3-hour addiction. If you haven't already discovered it, Evil Defenders is a tower defence title where the player dons the responsibility of making sure creepy, noseless peasants don't invade your domain. Equipped with a large arsenal at your disposal, ranging from foot skeleton soldiers to Orc-operated cannons, the player must choose the most efficient way to dominate the playing field. Keep in mind that each tower requires payment by gathering money after defeating each opponent, and additional bonus cash for quickly accomplishing each wave. This game requires you to utilize every tactic to gun down your enemy before they get the opportunity to inflict some serious damage on you.
Visuals are beautifully illustrated along with a well thought out menu layout. The in-game combat is sleek and simplistic, with each map or location having a set of 6 areas which require stronger defences over time. However, with each successful victory, the player is rewarded with a currency in the form of souls; this soul cash is then used for your tree ability list, enabling you to seriously lay the hurt on intruders after upgrading.
It's easy to understand the combat system and all of its functionality, it also gets more challenging as you progressively unlock levels. The only thing this game would ever need to have is more levels to play through! :) If you're having trouble deciding on whether to try this game out or not, check out my preview video to see for yourself!

One of the better tower defense games I've played in recent times. Yes it's a mobile port but a good one, with zero micro-transactions. Purchase grants 100% of the game. Huzzah.
Includes a fair bit of content for the price. 100 odd levels are spread across 5 different regions. 60+ towers providing alternate upgrade paths along with global leaderboards for each and every single quest. I'm still in the early stages playing through on normal, though it's already become quite challenging to 3 star levels. Story is presented with a tongue in cheek nature that actually provided a few laugh out loud moments. No in-game options were available, a slider for sound volume would be welcomed but otherwise nothing was really required. Graphics stayed crisp scaling up to 4k resolution via the unity launcher.
Evil Defenders has great presentation and screenshots don't do the detailed animation justice. Something that particularly surprised me was the cut-scenes which were comprised of some lovely cg work. With a ton of achievements, decent soundtrack, responsive controls  and your typical TD *one more round* hook, the game gets my thumbs up. Recommended to any TD enthusiast and I feel the price is spot on. Cheers folks.

I've been putting off writing a review for this game for a while. I felt, as a TCG, in order to get an accurate grasp on the game I needed to play a lot. I've gotten to level 40 of 50, own all DLC, and have collected a good portion of the cards in the game at the moment. Here are some notes:
Value. You do not need to pay a dime if you do not want to and you could (hypothetically) get as much out of this game as someone who pays to win. There is in-game currency in the form of both Gold and Soulgems; the former is used to buy packs, decks, DLC, enter drafts, ext. It can buy MOST things (aside from some promo content). You rack up gold just by playing the game, or even watching streamers play it on Twitch. The Soulgems are used to craft specific cards, allowing you to avoid buying hoardes of packs just to get a couple singles you are chasing. Along side all of this, you now get daily rewards just from logging on, along with daily quests you can complete for gold. All in all, very satisfied with the ingame currency and microtransaction system used for this game; balanced, fair, and well worth.
Content. Even though the game only has 2 sets out (excluding Dark Brotherhood and other Promo/DLC content), the variety of gameplay along with modes of play is vast. It is a brewers paradise for constructed, and the draft system in great and very easy to get the Gold to play. There are even quest story lines which implement various gameplay changes to make the experience feel unique and fresh. My only complaint with the current meta is it vastly favours the late-game. Aggro is very hard to make work, usually relying on the other decks inconsistencies and luck. Prophecies, while a good idea on paper, do not help with this, resulting in one of the only succesful Aggro decks in competeitve right now to ALSO bank on Prophecies. Hopefully in the future, as with many other TCG's, more cards will eventually lead to more viable early game and thus better Aggro in the meta. For now, expect board wipes, ramp, and boardclogs.
Flavor. God I love the elder scrolls series and the universe it encompases. Every card is beleivable in regards to TES lore and feel. If you like the idea of getting into a strategy card game and love TES, this is your opening.
All in all, I like the game. I still think my TCG of choice is Magic, but this still takes a good cut of my dedication and resources due to the uniqueness of it. Very standout game, worth a few hours of your time to give it a try.

First Impression Gameplay:
Disclaimer:  Game key was given to me by developer.  Impressions of this game are genuine and not paid for.
Orbox C is a fun little puzzle game where your objective is to manipulate a box through space in order to accomplish certain objectives; such as arriving at a destination, collecting all "coins", etc.  The game starts off simple, where the only objective is to get your box to a target location by using other stationary blocks.  Every few levels a new mechanic is introduced to keep game play fresh (such as bombs, teleporters, 45 degree angles, collections, etc.).
-Fun concept
-New mechanics keep gameplay fresh
-Background music is good and doesn't distract from gameplay
-Art style is simplistic, but does not detract from gameplay
-Large amount of levels to keep you busy
-Difficulty progresses at a decent curve
-No bugs or graphical issues
-Would have been nice to have a course "par" for moves on any certain level.  I wasn't sure if I was doing good or not.

Good relaxing puzzle game with plenty of content.  The puzzles get progressively harder but do have logical solutions. I've completed the easy puzzles and about half of the normal puzzles. The speed puzzles are quite challenging too although not so much to my taste.
Recommended and very reasonably priced.

A deceptively complex puzzle game with good music and a great price. You must move your box from the start to the goal, but the difficulty is that you go in a direction until you hit an obstacle. You have to plan your moves carefully to avoid flying off into the void or getting stuck, but a simple hit of 'r' restarts the stage. Each new element is added in with a tutorial on the stage they're introduced in, so you don't have to ask yourself 'what the heck is that' when a new thing appears on the puzzles.
If you like puzzle games and don't have a lot of money OrboxC is an excellent intersection of that.

If you want to watch some gameplay and listen to my thoughts on this game, a link is below. If you’d rather just read my thoughts, those will be typed up beneath the video. If you do choose to watch my video, please be warned that there are vulgarities in the video.
It’s very rare that I find a puzzle game that makes me break down my moves step by step in order to find the solution. Usually I can simply click buttons until I pass the level. This puzzle game is not so… simple. This puzzle game requires thought, planning, and understanding of the mechanics in order to beat a level. I found myself struggling with the levels around level thirty. Don’t get me wrong though, it was a good level of frustration. There was always that feeling of reward at the end of the level. That all too familiar feeling of “How did I miss that? That was so obvious” If you’ve played puzzle games before, you know that feeling.
If you’re looking for a puzzle game that you can kind of do halfheartedly and blow through with relative ease, I’d say this game is not for you. There is thought required to be good at this game. And that is a good thing, a very, very good thing when it comes to a puzzle game. I will not lie, I am not good at this game. I am happy to admit that I struggle to beat some of the levels in this game. But these are amazing qualities for a puzzle game to have.
I definitely recommend this game to anybody looking for a good mental challenge.
I spoke with one of the developers during the period of time of me recording this video, he is a very generous guy who showed that he really cares about his game. And really, there’s nothing more you can ask for from a developer than for them to care more about the game than the money. This developer proved that to me and because of that, I will be a repeat customer of the games these developers produce.

First got into this game after watching another person’s video clip on this game where he went through the first few levels.  Took a look at the description on Steam, and given it’s only $2.99, decided to give this a try, as I’m into puzzle games.  No regrets on this decision, as this is a very nice puzzle game with many interesting elements in it.
Graphics:  When you open the game, it starts in full screen, but you can modify it to a smaller screen size, which I usually do.  Nice Sci-fi space graphics that change from level to level, so you’re not looking at the exact same background each time.  Sprites are simple and easily labeled so that you know what you’re looking at.
Sound:  Space-like music atmosphere is nice to listen to, but you can mute the music and sound effects at any time if you want to.  However, it may not hurt to have a few more soundtracks to choose from to listen to as you play to increase variety.
Controls:  Not too many options to have to worry about, as the controls are pretty self-explanatory.  In reality, all you’re using is the directions on the keyboard (WASD or up/left/down/right) and R to restart if you get stuck and can’t go out of bounds.  Controls are responsive with no lag, and if you push 5 directions ahead of time as you’re going through a long part, the Orbox will move in those directions with no loss or delay.  Orbox moves quickly, which is nice for the longer stages, as they flow better with no real delays.
Gameplay:  I'll break this down into pieces.
= It’s easy to get the hang of this game, but you’ll quickly see how the later puzzles make you think a bit.  Luckily, there are no enemies, and you can scout the board out before moving to see what you’re dealing with.  There are no lives, or game over, or anything like that to pressure the player, so feel free to try various things out.  If you go out of bounds, you’ll just go back to the start point (you’ll want to go out of bounds a lot anyway to get a few of the achievements).
= There are no time limits on the levels, so feel free to take as much time as needed to think through possible routes.  You’ll need to look ahead a bit in later levels to see any tricks that may be present.
= You can play a level as many times as you want, mainly to go for your best score, time, and moves (though the moves record is a bit glitched, as it doesn’t keep your best move score, but rather your score on the last time you beat the level).
= I like how in Easy, the levels start very simple with just getting to the goal.  A few levels in, new elements get introduced, one at a time.  This allows the player to learn how to best deal with these types of elements.  And as the levels progress, the player sees how these elements get combined together in having multiple tasks to do in a level.  The player will deal with anything from collecting stars to dealing with gates, grow blocks, sensors, ice, and bombs.  Nice job with the symmetry designs in most levels, giving a little more substance than just the basics to many of the levels.
= There are a whopping 210 levels, split into seven packs of 30 levels.  You start with the Easy pack and unlock more packs as you complete the packs you’re working on, which include Average, Normal, Hard, Easy 2, Speed, and Bonus.  There’s a spot for an eighth pack depending on feedback.  Difficulty progresses steadily on Easy -> Average -> Normal -> Hard.  I would guess Easy 2, Speed, and Bonus are somewhere in between in difficulty.
If you’re into puzzles, I would give this game a try.  $2.99 is a good price for the amount of content you get.  With the multiple puzzle elements and levels present, Orbox C makes for a solid puzzle game.

Oh well, Vindictus....
It has been such a long way down between me and this game.
I first started playing it way back in january 2012, when Arisha was just released a few months earlier and instantly fell in love with this game. (Back then it wasn´t the steam version)
Let's start with the gameplay, which is, by far, the best I have seen in an MMO in my entire 21 years of existence.
I have never seen anything even close to this perfection. While some quests require to do the same dungeon over and over and OVER again, it doesn´t get too boring, even though very repetitive.
I admit, you CAN just keep buttonmashing all the time, but combos are way more awesome to performe.
Also buttonmashing won´t work on a boss, since most of them can´t be stunned and getting a few blows might incapacitate you, depening on which class you play.
A huge issue in this game is the performance. I´m not gonna lie: It's really crap. I have a Nvidia GTX 1070 and 16GB of RAM in my computer and sometimes still drop down to 6 FPS. This can be a death sentence during a Boss battle or a raid.
While the lag during the raids has gotten slightly better over time, it´s still horrible from time to time.
Now to the storyline.
Now here it gets a little confusing. Vindictus' storyline is written in different seasons or episodes, which all somehow have nothing to do with each other, while at the same time crossover at some points. Every part of the story is like a piece, which all together form a big puzzle. The story itself is rather well written, even though it lacks the chance to bond with the characters in there. So, for most, you don´t really care if they die or not.
Last but also not unimportant: The soundtrack.
I´ve rareley seen any game with such great soundtracks. The music in the towns, during dungeons or boss battles are just great and always on-point. The theme to the City "Malina" is, to me, by far the best of all the soundtracks in Vindictus.
The music makes a great atmosphere in the world of Vindictus and is, as well of the gameplay, one of its biggest advantages.
Free to try it so if it looks like your kind of game then by all means try it out, might be surprised at how good it reaally is. I enjoyed iit and still do to this day.

Brilliant, classic, ancient, arcade beat em up game remade for PC. I absolutely love the fact that they've reworked the original game quite a bit and even added Online Coop feature. You can host or look for games, join others drop-in style or from the beginning if you like. Lag can be a bit of a problem but they've also added a ping limiter apparently so you can filter out the people outside your area and whatnot.
Controls can be a bit messy until you get used to it, it takes a while to get used to even for a beat em up game. Another thing that bugged me was how they left the magic as it was, it looks fantastic when you're playing alone or in an arcade game place but not online when it pauses the game for everyone for about 3-4 seconds to watch the special effects, they'll have to sort it out asap.
The game itself seemed a bit sandbox-ish, at least for a 2D sidescrolling game, there's quite a bit of exploration and looting, and you can do certain combo moves as you attack, not to mention you do all these with 3 other actual players. The inventory is stacked and divided to 2-3 parts, you can choose to use magic or throwing weapons or simply potions and various items instead. When you die, you can just respawn right away at the cost of your "score".
It's definitely worth a look if you've got friends to play with and definitely worth the price if you ask me.

I was just skimming through my Steam library trying to find something new to play when I stumbled upon this interesting-looking game.
You play as a girl with multiple personality disorder who is trying to piece together her broken memories.
I expected this game to be an adventure game where you fight enemies and solve riddles, but this is a pure puzzle game. The screen is usually divided into two (or more) sections with one personality (character) in each section. Both personalities will (usually) move in the same direction. You press up, they both go up. You press right, they both go right.
The goal of the game is to move each personality to a certain point on the map at the exact same time, however the layout of the two sides of the map are not identical, so you need to plan out your moves in order to avoid traps and enemies on both sides.
The four chapters, each consisting of more than twelve stages, provide you with some varying abilities specific to that chapter, such as the use of keys, throwable crosses (that can break/create blocks), teleportation tiles, and so on.
The art and music is in my opinion very good, however if you don't like the gothic look this might not be for you. Each personality is dealing with their own worries and traumas, some of which can get pretty dark, which is reflected in the illustrations.
I honestly can not remember where I got this game. I was just looking through my library when I found this game, and as I liked the art style I decided to give it a try - and I'm glad I did.
I did encounter a couple of bugs during my playthrough, however the developer replied to my forum posts and fixed the bugs right away.
If you like the style of this game and/or enjoy puzzle games then this should be just the game for you.

A huge range of games are being released regularly in the world. Independent developers, as well as titanic corporations with multimillion budgets produce these games. Reflection of Mine is a game made in fact by one person. And it is amazing!  Against the countless soulless assasins, dull Call of Duty series, monotonous GTAs and lots of MMO games that differ from each other only in decorations, and have cosmic ammounts of money spent on developing and PR, Reflection of Mine looks like a ray of light in the darkness. It is exceedingly atmospheric. It captures and holds you. It is unique (at least for me: I don't know many games of this genre, but among the ones I know there is nothing like Reflection of Mine).
When you start to play, the eye immediately catches the author's attention to details. Levels are well designed and drawn. You can see various game mechanics on different levels of Reflection of Mine, they make the game diverse. The main character of Lilly is deeply developed, you easily beleive in her very existance and in her history from the first moments of the game. Music in the game is a subject of a special attention. It ideally suits the game, it complements game's atmosphere and it organically gets used to the world of the game. It is easily memorable. I haven't met a soundtrack of such a quality from the times of the first Space Rangers game.
Reflection of Mine is a difficult game. It is a puzzle, and it really makes you puzzle over its solution very hard. It is not easy to complete the levels, but if you want to get game achievements, you have to blow up your brain! If you are a person who don't like hard and difficult tasks, this game is not for you. Reflection of Mine is made as good as were made good old fashioned games of the period when developers didn't follow users' whims like "this game is bad because it is too difficult to play".
And when you think like "Oh God! This game was made by only one person! That can't be true!" But you know it is true, and you want to get back to this game over and over again. And I can't say this about huge modern games made by corporations. Thats it. Reflection of Mine is a marvelous, fabulous project, made with soul and author's love to his creation.
Thank you for this game! And good wishes!

Like em’ or hate em’ Sports games (particularly sports sims) are by and large the biggest earner for the games industry.  With a reliable fan base leading to high sales year over year and the implementation of microtransactions in games like FIFA Ultimate Team, earning over $800 Million in revenue alone for that series, it can be tough for non-sim games to stand out.  However, these types of games that skew reality in favor of making a more surreal experience, are often the ones I come back to playing the most.  Whether it’s Super Tecmo Bowl, NFL Blitz, NBA Jam and other Midway sports titles of old; I generally find more enjoyment in these kinds of games over the realism-focus found in iterative EA Sports and 2k Games titles.  Sociable Soccer, from Tower Games and Combo Breaker, aims to re-capture  this same kind of arcade-focused feeling: simple controls and shorter games.  And for the most part it hits those same old feelings that drew me to those games, but stumbles in a few fundamental and crucial aspects.
“You’re a goal scoring superstar herooooo..”
The game’s available modes are quite sparse at the moment.  But the majority of your time in this Early Access builds will probably be spent in the “Boss Mode.”  This mode functions similar to a standard fighting game ladder mode: Pick a team from an available group and beat all of the other clubs to win a trophy and some currency (it’s not quite clear what currency can be used for at this time other than moving to more advanced ladders).  As you can already imagine, you start with the lower skilled leagues before making it up to the Premiere and BBVA equivalents.
Speaking of which, Sociable Soccer, like Pro Evolution Soccer, doesn’t have the licensing for these clubs or the likenesses of the players.  That doesn’t stop the developer from getting as close as humanly possible to replicating the rosters of over 200+ clubs.  You’ll find some clever lampooning of familiar clubs from the familiar MLS (USA’s pro soccer league), teams to the major clubs in European countries, to even the most obscure teams in Saudi Arabia or South Korea.  National teams are available as well, however the amount of effort put into reproducing these club teams and their rosters is downright shocking.  You’ll find Lionel “Macci” on Barcelona or “Idrehimovic” on the Manchester Reds, and 30,000+ other players.  I can’t speak to all of those being faithful recreations of each player but it is still noteworthy amount of depth for a simpler soccer game.
The menu music track is also fantastic as well.  I have even gone so far as to put the lyrics of this jazzy ditty in the headers for this review.  Seriously, it gets super catchy after a few hours of playing.  It sucks that this track isn’t in anything but the main menu however, as it would be really cool for this to play after a goal is scored.  In fact, the game could use way more personality when it comes to its presentation.  There is no commentary during matches, crowd noise is low and only seems to get marginally higher after a goal is scored; the in-game experience as a whole feels sterile and unengaging once it gets out of the main menu.
“And every goal, goal, goal you miss will make you mad”
Perhaps the most maddening choice is the absence of a player switching function. Anyone who plays FIFA or any other soccer game knows that auto switching is the worst way to play those games and it makes the act of playing defense a huge bummer.  The AI seems inconsistent as well.  The CPU will play competent defense against most strategies, but seems incapable of comprehending how to counter the 2-3-1-4 formation or any others that emphasize offense.  When these formations are picked, the Keeper will lazily kick the ball in the general direction of one of your guys; allowing you to take way more shots on goal than other strategies.  Penalties are also given with inconsistency; I’ve slid into the back legs of a striker without gaining a foul while other times I immediately get a red card, perhaps the developer intended to have inconsistent officiating as a touch of realism to the game. I also noticed, after receiving a few yellow cards on players in play, it is impossible to manually substitute bench players in to prevent another foul putting you a man down.
Gameplay also could use a few more implemented features such as a turbo bar and dribble moves to help modernize the game a bit.  It is quite difficult to finesse pass defenders if you don’t have an open passing lane and if you move backwards you tend to lose the ball immediately.  The omission of dribble moves seems diametrically opposed to the game wanting you to keep moving forward, punishing you by losing the ball when you try to move in the opposite direction.  The sense of speed and flow of the game also feels more like a sim like FIFA, holding down sprint for even the highest skilled players doesn’t seem to go much faster than regular running.  Hopefully, these negatives can be fixed as these would go a long way for improving the overall experience. Again this is an Early Access game so some jank is to be expected.
Verdict
Sociable Soccer is a game with interesting ideas, but the execution leaves something to be desired.  I love the idea of a more arcade-like soccer game, but Combo Breaker could definitely learn from some other games in the non-sim genre and lift some of their ideas to refine the gameplay so they can attract a decent online player base.  A Blitz-like soccer game sounds so awesome and has huge potential in a marketplace where EA and Konami currently dominate, hopefully the day will come when a game can satisfy that audience.

When I first launched Sociable Soccer, the first question was immediately - why? Who wants to play something like this in the 2017 when we have FIFA / PES franchise? But few minutes and then suddenly hours later , the strong memory  began to take over. The memory of Sensible Soccer, the predecessor of this game, the game  I  played at my 16's. Suddenly I  remembered the tournament charts drawn in the notebook and taking it with me to friends place, playing different tournaments with different friends. Will Sociable Soccer be capable of creating similar memory for me - today - 21 years later?

This is an arcade football game, where it's pointless to expect reality like FIFA / PES series. The pace of the game is very fast and is not something I've got used to playing different football games.  But if you get some minutes into the game and start getting used to that pace, it will be a completely enjoyable experience. To my surprise, I discovered that it is like cycling, once learned, you know it forever.  Quite quickly, the fingers on the xbox controller I'm using,  were already able to move correctly, as if it had not been 21 years since the last play. And like back at 90's it's still the same now - the key to success is fast and accurate passing together with insane curve balls behind the goalkeeper.
The game is easy to play, since only 4 buttons are available for use - for passing, kicking, and tackling . In addition, one button is still needed for sprinting, and in the future one should add the option of form selection directly in the game (it is still missing). Currently, there are only two choices in the game, where the first one is quite rightly called the Boss Mode and it represents a lot of tasks that can be played against computer - starting up more easily and moving towards heavier levels. The second option is the World menu, which simply includes various tournaments and leagues, plus the opportunity to play with two friends. Unfortunately, in the current version, the game AI is too weak, so 10-0 victories are more common than the exceptions, and after an hour or two  the game gets a bit boring.  Fortunately, the developer is well aware of this and the changes are to include a fix for the AI and make the game more difficult.

In the game there is  a large number of countries and leagues. All who now search for authenticity here, they will be quickly disappointed - there are no licenses, they are in Fifa's hands. Fortunately, the developer has not fallen behind on this point and clubs and players have had name changes. They are so familiar yet far off from the real names. The effect of this is that anyone who knows football is well aware of who are players and clubs mentioned in the game.
I definitely want to mention the artistic side of the game - I like how beautiful the drawn pictures are in the menus and the appearance together with the use of words make the experience whole.  On the technical side, it's not a game that requires a lot of resources. The look and feel of this game for me is the graphics  upgrade from 1992, which in this game is more of an added value than minus. From the sound side, there is nothing special to bring out at this moment. Only maybe the fact that the music that was playing in the menu becomes so frustrating fast that I turned the speakers off pretty soon.

Since it's a game with the early access program, I would rather recommend a couple of updates before buying.In it's current state, getting several hours out from it might be  a bit tricky. Certainly, at this point there is some pressure on developer who now needs to add more content into the game together with the fixes.
Currently there are few of the items under development..
Starting with the multiplayer support and beta should arrive "soon", which, hopefully, is not something that Blizzard has  almost trademarked - "very soon". Next one in line is a separate Manager Mode. It has been said that this is meant for those who want a more tactical approach, so what exactly it represents, we do not know yet, details to follow when it's closer to release I assume.  The most interesting thing in development for me is the game mode called "My Team". Again there's currently almost no information about this, but it should be a part of a multiplayer where you will compete with your club against others. The developer has now said that there will be over 30,000 players to collect, develop and also exchange with others.
The games predecessor has been also mentioned as the best football game ever made, so the game's author Jon Hare has pretty big slippers to fill, 25 years later. Today's success will be based on Sensible Soccer heritage and the involvement of older gamers living through nostalgia, but also those who have never heard of Sensible Soccer. In any case, I wish Jon Hare the strength and the jacket and I'm looking forward to seeing where the game is going.

Lara Croft and the Guardian of Light is a great game overall. You get a great Third Person Action-Adventure Shooter game mixed with Puzzles you need to solve and a wealth of collectibles to find! I prefer Single Player as I can get challenges done on my own time and can explore the land freely, but the Multiplayer has some nice advantages and the good part is you can actually play the game with one of your friends!! Anywhere from Spears and Flamethrowers to Pistols and Rocket Launchers, this game will keep you busy trying to choose what weapons you want (as you can only have four equipped, however you can always change them out in one of the Menus.) First, I had great fun for hours with the almost zen-like simplicity and the hypnotic flow here; this is fun already and has massive potential. Thanks, guys! Brings back good memories.
Some feedback from my side (I will omit the AI/difficulty/goalie issues you're already well-aware of; seems to be mainly a matter of tuning):
1. Low shot/pass without recipient
This feels a bit weird right now because it is a relatively weak shot, and it keeps reacting for a long time to bending. This has a somewhat strange effect I'd like to describe, for it seems the only behavior that somewhat doesn't immediately klick or feel right imo:
- I run up
- I pass up, no target in sight, ball starts off
- My nearest player is up+right; I want to make him run left to approach the ball
- But this also makes the ball bend to the left side - /away/ from the now-approaching player
Maybe I am missing some other, more inventive uses of the low pass&bend.. Potential solution might be to make the "bending phase" (ie, the time period where this command is interpreted from the stick) shorter - the ball could even "bend on" afterwards, but the stick would then only controls player movement, no longer ball bending.
2. Sprinting
I did not experience any drawback of sprinting - is there one? If not, this feature would seem tacked on - everybody could just tape down the sprint button.
Is it planned to make this into an actual choice? For example, each player can only sprint 20% of the match time, and then his speed reservoir is done (or he maybe gets even slower than normal afterwards). Sprinting then would have to be managed.
I read some tweet that proposed making the ball less sticky when sprinting; certainly also a way to throw in some trade-off here.
3. Shot philosophy
Right now there's (i) passing with semi-auto-target, (ii) low shot, (iii) proper shot, and (iv) chip. They all seem to live in different worlds.
Now, you've probably spent ages thinking this through already, so just some humble thoughts.
What if we had just two types of shots: passing with semi-auto-target like now, and anything else is a shot (from low to high=chip) controlled by aftertough (ie, chip=aftertouch in opposite direction). That would appear to be more organic and probably also easier to tune within such a unified framework. This could also easily be single button.. don't know what game that reminds me of.
That's it for today - keep up the good work. You bear a heavy duty: this will probably be the last time anyone dares make such a game (=one that is fun to play and no mere footy-on-rails with cut scenes). Break a leg!

This is my review for the West of Loathing. -WARNING- This review contains spoilers. -WARNING-
I haven't played much of the Kingdom of Loathing, but I prefer this game to the kingdom alot more. So first off,
Combat - 9/10 - The combat in this game follows a standard turn based combat system, with multiple statistics for each enemy, and multiple attacks especially for you. However, on standard mode, you can easily farm experience to become exeptionally stronger than your enemies. Luckily, hard mode, which can be enabled via a hat, called the Hard Hat, obtained in the prologue of the game.
Companions - 7/10 - There are five companions in this game, not counting the temporary summoned ones. Your main companion is obtained through the prologue, and there is an additional companion unlocked in the buffalo pile, named Buffalo Buffalo Buffalo Bill. Buffalo Bill cannot be controlled by the player, adding a wild card to combat. He does not appear out of combat and the initial discovery, and is completely optional and easy to miss. The other companions appear in and outside of companions, and will make comments on locations, or mark locations on your map matching their area of expertise.
Susy Cochrane is a former rancher, and will mark ranch themed locations on your match. She utilises a rifle in combat, doing damage to individual enemies. She also can unlock a lasso skill, temporarily stunning enemies, and gains exp from killing cows.
Doc Alice is a doctor obsessed with the undead, and will mark graveyards on the map. She utilises a shotgun in combat, doing little damage to mulitple enemies. She can also unlock an attack that will instantly kill skeletons, yet is useless against other enemies. She gains exp from killing skeletons, but will also leave you if you become the Necromancer at the end of the Necromancer side quest.
Crazy Pete is a former miner, who has gone insane. He will mark mines on your map. He uses an attack that does hot damage to an enemy, which can be exeptionally good, or next to useless depending on the enemy. He likely has another attack, but I honestly haven't played with him that much, and never leveled him up enough to unlock his other attacks. He gains instant levels, via random encounters.
Gary the Goblin is a goblin, and will mark goblin occupied locations on your map. He uses an attack that does little damage, but he preforms the attack multiple times. He can unlock another attack, producing an identical copy of himself with slightly worse stats. He gains instant levels by you purchasing "Shroom-Gro" and giving it to him. This obviously the most expensive companion in the game, as Shroom-Gro multiplies in price every time you buy it, but also the most comical.
Replayability - 4/10 - I have played this with each companion and class, and while there are choices in the game, you really only have to play this game three times to experience everything, which is why it gets a low rating. If the developers would update this game like they frequently did with KoL, it would surely add to the longevity and replayability of this game. There is DLC to this game, however it is simply bought in KoL and unlocks cosmetic horse armour. It really doesn't do anything. In comparison, I've spent 59 hours in this game, and 413 hours in Fallout 4, which is a game everybody should buy.
Exploration - 8/10 - This is an open world game, meaning you can visit anywhere you want, when you want. The map is unlocked in four parts. The proluge, and then the main area, divided into three seperate areas. You unlock the areas by firstly completing the prologue, then progressing through the main questine will unlock the other two areas. There are alot of locations to discover, and is very fun. However, as I said before, updates and/or DLC would definitely make the game better and more expansive.
Storyline and Quests - 8/10 - There are many little side quests and three main storylines. The side quests consist of trapping the infernal Duke Bovicus, leader of the satanic cows, tracking down items to summon a shiny skeleton named Dave, and locating skeletons for the Petting Cemetary. The three main storylines consist of helping the railway reach the town of Frisco, which serves to unlock the map in the WoL. There's also the El Vabrito questline, which is the player attempting to save the world of Loathing by repairing the containment for an evil diety called Roberto, who will destroy loathing if the containment fails in 420 years. Lastly, is the necromancer questline, which consists of the player attempting to find clues to the location of the Necromancer, who is terrorizing the world of Loathing with his undead army. It ultimately ends with the player eaither destroying the Necromancer, stopping the necromancer from raising more of the dead, or becoming the Necromancer and taking the army for yourself, if you have enough skill in Nex-Mex.
Final Rating - 7/10 - A very good game, with lots of intentionally bad jokes. As I've said multiple times before, however, DLC and/or updates would definitely make this game alot better. Still, if are contemplating buying it, I highly recommend it.

TES:L is equally good if you're new to the CCG genre or already familiar with the basic principles. The game offers a well-made tutorial/story mode to introduce you to the general concepts of gameplay and deck building, so you won't struggle to get into it. The overall game design, while clearly inspired by Hearthstone in many ways, also takes care of what I consider to be the Blizzard giant's major problem: the rune system of TES:L ensures that slower control decks get card advantage when facing an aggro onslaught - and thus a chance to make a comeback.
Currently the game is insanely F2P-friendly: you gain a new card after every 3 wins against a human opponent, you get new cards after leveling up, you get daily login rewards (which include packs, Arena tickets and even a Legendary card once a month) and you also get some freebies from Twitch drops. Of course you can't expect to obtain the full collection in a few weeks, but you'll notice your catalogue growing just by logging in every day and finishing your daily quests. Finally, Solo and Versus Arena modes give you a chance to gain even more rewards if you understand the strategy well enough.
I wholeheartedly recommend jumping on this bandwagon while it's still relatively early (2.5 sets released so far): if you enjoy CCGs but consider Hearthstone too expensive/broken/random/unrewarding, TES:L is definitely a game for you.

A Shadow of Mystara review
At first, this game might seem bland and out of balanced, yet if you give it some time you discover how much fun it can be, that is, if you like the genre. For a beat em up you have tons of variety in spells, items, classes and different paths you can take on, adding lots of replayability. It should be noted, that some people have some crashing experiences in the main menu, but I haven't heard anyone dropping from the game yet, so all things considered, it gets a pass in my book.
Multiplayer is for up to 4 players and there is 6 classes to choose from: Fighter, dwarf, elf, cleric, thief and magic user. They have some of the basic things in common, like basic combo and slide, but there is major differences in how they actually play. For example, dwarf has a lots of tankiness but is somewhat slow, while thief is weaker but can backstab, double jump and steal items.
Game rewards people for teamwork, and a right team saves of a lot of continues, since every class is tailored for something: Fighter, dwarf and thief are good for killing standard mobs, while cleric has a heal and stat boosting abilities, lastly Magic user and elf are useful for killing bosses. This doesn't mean you can't solo the game with any class without dying once if you have played it enough and know it's gimmicks.
At the moment of this recommendation, there is a a few players in online, so you still have a chance to play this on multiplayer even if you can't get your friends to play this. This game is made in 1993, however, it has aged well since it was made for the arcade board. Just remember to change filters and resolution from the options first.
For a nitpick, I'd say it is a bit on the easy side, because you get unlimited credits by default. You can later change survival mode on, which causes everyone to have only one life, but it would've been better, if you could set the amount of credits yourself.
With it's good replayability, animation and presentation, this title was a classic of it's time and before Dragon's Crown comes out, it doesn't get better than this.

- The person's thoughts on why and how s/he feels that way
- Longer gameplay
- Story about other people (like what I saw in the ending)
Overall, the only saving grace that I could think of in this game is there is no jump scares.

Disgraced is an RPG Maker game that is very well done. Amazing quality for a game made with this particular engine, really, as we are used to very average games that do not aspire to much.
This is not such a game. It features a very deep storyline, great character development and a complex game system. Graphics assets are original as well!
Gameplay:
Set in feudal Japan, you play as a character that is forced to work for a tyrant until you kick off your own rebellion. There's a deep character creation system, a lot deeper than what we're used to on this engine, and a "skill" system that is not really class-centric.
All these work very well for this title. This is one of the most polished RPG Maker titles that I have seen! The game is very feature rich!
Graphics:
Graphics-wise the game is not much different than other titles made with this particular engine but the assets utilized are original. Not reused sprite packs etc.
Music/Sound Design:
The music is very beatiful and fitting the theme of the game, setting the atmosphere perfectly into the feudal era of Japan's Daimyo!
Pros:
-One of the best RPG Maker titles I have ever encountered.
-Great character creation
-Great skill system
-Great story
-Based on historically accurate data.
Neutral:
-It's an RPG Maker game. I know some players just can't stand them but frankly even those would probably find this a great game!
Cons:
-Frankly I can't see any con with the game. At least not as far as I've reached in so far.
Conclusion:
I can easily recommend this to any RPG fan. If the developer can make such a game on such engine, I really want to see what they would be able to make in better engine and with a bigger budget for assets etc.

This game is total garbage.
Oops, did I spoil the review a little early? Should I have put in all of the negative points first? Well, probably, but people on the internet have short attention spans for long review posts. They probably only look for the yea/nay and call it a day. Anyway, Disgraced is a total disgrace (see what I did there?). Let me explain.
Disgraced is an RPG Maker game, and RPG Maker games are already a plague on the Earth because of their terrible graphics and awful copy/pasta scripts but this game goes way beyond that. First, let's talk about the introduction. To introduce you to the game, Disgraced copies George Lucas. That is, they do the text scroll thing like in Star Wars. Which by itself... can be excused... maybe. Put some ambient music behind it, have scenes playing in the background, sure. I could live with that. I wouldn't like it, I think it's lazy, but I could live with it. This game just runs text up a black screen with way too much blank space between lines. You ever program? Imagine like 40 newlines between every line of code. Obnoxious and terrible execution.
The plot of the game is that you are a deserter that gets conned into leading a rebellion. Your qualification for this seems to be - you are a deserter. You didn't kill the guy you were working for. You ran like a little girl. Your task is to 'liberate' (hostile takeover) three cities and gather enough support to take on Kyoto. You do this by walking all across Japan and going to every town. You need to gather the support of villages (usually via bribery) because you're not allowed to attack the cities unless you have enough support.
Get enough support, fight samurai death squads, and beat the Shogun. Sounds awesome, right? Well, it's not. The combat in this game has to some of the most poorly balanced combat I've ever seen. You will miss almost every single attack. You have two (2!) health bars to manage Vitality and Morale. If you run out of Vitality you die and if you run out of Morale you desert.♥♥♥♥♥♥ it's the same damn thing for the purpose of combat. May as well dump all your points in Vitality because my Morale never dropped below two-thirds.
And you best make all of the offerings to RNGsus because if you take a single crit you may as well reload your save because that person is likely dead. Like, dead dead. No revivals. Normally this wouldn't be the worst thing in the world. After all, Fire Emblem does it too. But Fire Emblem's RNG isn't terrible. But combine that with the fact that your party does NOT level together, losing your level 7 dude with only level 1 goons to replace him means grinding or (in my case) reloading your save. And it wouldn't be so bad but every attack (barring one skill, I think) is single-target. You have 3 people, they will almost always have 5. Which means you get 3 attacks a turn and they get 5. Combine that with the terrible RNG and you get a game in which combat is cancer. The SFX are too loud and the BGM is non-existent. Well, it's there but even at max volume you can hardly hear it. Isn't really any good either.
In fact, if I had to pick two words to describe this game, they would be 'Needlessly Complicated'. There are so many skills (which again, many are functionally useless because who needs morale?) that leveling up certain skills makes you wonder where the newb traps are. The stats you level up (probably) don't matter. I only ever leveled up 'Might' and I swept the game just fine. The resource management is also needlessly complicated, and serves only as means to bribe the villages to assist in your cause. This support manifests itself only by resources you supposedly collect once a day but I'm not sure that collection ever happened. You can collect a ton of allied units but because of the problem I mentioned above, there's no reason to. Just use your first three goons to sweep the game (that's what I did anyway).
The choices you make have zero impact on the game. I could've sworn I saw 'Choices matter' somewhere associated with this game. They don't. Don't waste your time. Press space through every dialogue, there's nothing of value there. One you get some money rolling and can afford decent equipment (highest damage/accuracy) you can win any battle by killing enemies in one or two hits. This drastically improves your 3v5 situation to 3v3 or 3v2.
Let's take a quick look at the map design. The game uses stock sprites from RPG Maker (exclusively, I think). And you can really tell because the wolf sprite doesn't have the same style as some of the box sprites (among other things). And while this is terrible by itself, it becomes much, much worse when you don't make it clear what you can walk through and what you cannot. Combine this with narrow passages and an NPC that stands LITERALLY IN YOUR WAY then navigating towns becomes insufferable.
This game is not worth $10; this game is not worth $1. It's a short game (takes, maybe 4 hours to clear?) and you will not enjoy it. I guarantee it.
