Looking at the game from a sim-racer's point of view:
I tried again the other day to get to grips with this game...
...only to come away saddened, that I did not.
Mostly this has to do with the horrible implementation of input-controls.
This is clearly a title built around consoles and their gamepad-devices. With my wheel-setup (T300 Ferrari Integral edition + TH8A shifter), setting things up is an excercise in frustration to begin with. UI is horrible and does not give any visual feedback for the different input axxis, so figuring out what the associated modulators do is a pain.
It does get worse on track: The built-in steering-damping(!) goes directly against the promised analogue control you should get with your expensive toy-wheel. Really Milestone?
Brake-axxis seems to behave more like a button than an actual braking-system, default weighting prefers sending more stopping-power to the back wheels (which is just short of stupid on a RWD or AWD car). Now who thought that to be a good idea?
There are some promising aspects of the game, for as little content that I actually "suffered through" trying to make this work: Some rally-stages seem to have a half-way decent length to them. And they look pretty nice all-round (in terms of flow and difficulty), resembling real-world backroads and gravel-tracks very closely.
Just a shame that the way this game-engine was implemented, it does not allow me to truly evaluate them nor the handling-model without getting seriously frustrated.
Graphics-wise, this seems a bit "dated" in the shiny-department - although that one coast-line stage in Wales really had some nice and believable lighting to it, looked really proper.
Sound: no contest when comparing to the direct competition. Dirt Rally sounds like a small universe ahead of this.
So all-in-all: for realism-seeking wheel-users I would advice to stay clear for now. This is just too frustrating
Maybe for the intermediate pad-user (without a current-gen gaming console) this might a worthwhile console-port. Otherwise I have been told the PS4-version might enjoy a better implementation than seen on PC/Steam.
Personally, I cannot - and will not - hide my disappointment.

Trying to write a honest review. How does one recommend a game that has great playing huge content hidden behind a wall of showstopping, hardly fixable tech screwups? SLRE is *that* kind of a title.
So the game has a slew of great looking and driving, various rather long super stages (dawn/dusk/noon/night) and some nice hillclimb / rallycross stages. Sound FX is mediocre at best. Graphics is ok for 2017. There are many well modeled customizable cars with nice realistic handling qualities. Career is well thought through and there is a lot of player freedom of what and where you want to play.
Now take all those features and contradict them with lack of wheel support, ghosttown multiplayer, crazy fps dips in some areas, not being able to reassign control keys at all, no force feedback at all and having to tinker with the video settings just to get the game to play smoothly on whichever hardware.
If you can`t be bothered with any of the above issues then don`t even try. There is no troubleshooting help.

I absolutely hated the tinkering. Fixed most of it, loving the game. Now make no mistake, this is IMO the best of Milestone since WRC2. It`s probably my main rally title now.
Buy it *only* if you are able to fix the problems yourself. If not, just forget this game even existed in the first place.

75% off, why the hell not? Because its a bad game, thats why.
I played 2 hours, and have requested a refund. The game has poor audio, even worse physics, and appalling optimization. The way that the game procedurally re-renders the environment as you get closer to something slows down the game and resulted in me having to turn down the graphics from medium to low (on the recommended GPU, the GTX 960) in order to even have 60fps for a majority of my playtime.
The audio is garbage, it uses fmod, but not the way fmod should be used. The cars all sound very similar, and when I take my headphones off and switch to 5.1 surround, it gets worse. The co-driver's voice comes from the subwoofer, and very muffled so I can't even hear him, and the pops from the engine come straight out of the front speakers (and much louder than when you are accelerating too). WHY? You could have at least gotten the audio right!
As far as the physics and gameplay, no way. The car's handling is extremely twitchy (I have been using an Xbox 360 controller, as I don't have a wheel setup) and I can barely keep it under control. The sense of speed is terrible, at best, motion blur is pointless as you never seem to be going fast enough to even notice it. The spedometer in 3rd person mode is of a poor design and I, personally, don't like its appearance. The gearbox when shifting is very unresponsive a lot of the time, getting a good launch or getting into reverse when I screw up is hard since the game has so much input lag. Even the terrain of the rally stages has so much lack of design and input, the surfaces all seem smooth, unlike if you were to drive these stages in real life. Developers like Turn10 (Forza devs) actually go to the locations they add in their games and make sure that almost everything is perfect (how else are the puddles in FM6 and FM6:Apex pretty accurate), and their graphics and audio are actually good. I've heard Dirt Rally is good, I'll probably try that at some point, but this game has a poor representation of rally racing and puts shame to such an awe inspiring sport. If you have any sanity, don't buy this game, do yourself a favor.

Loeb shines in the typical, single-car rally mode.  The visuals are nice and the phyics are acceptable.  In fact, after playing this and Dirt Rally back-to-back, I'd say I even prefer this to Dirt Rally.  The courses are more visually interesting, and the on-track visuals are nice (though some textures in the backgroud could use some work).
Unfortunatley, there are races where multiple cars are on the track.  This is where Loeb fails, massively.  It hinders the experience so badly that I might delete this game and never go back to it.  AI drivers will consistently spin you, push you off the course, and stick to a line as if it's a demolition derby.  I restarted the last race three times and was knocked off the course each time, before finally just quitting.  Additionally, the car physics get really wonky--I witnessed an opponent tap the wall and subsequently flip on its side, cartoonishly, as if a Mack truck had smacked into it.
If you think you can push yourself through the miserable driver AI, there is a good rally experience to be had.  I would have left the rallycross races/elemination races/etc. out of the game altogether and just focused on the one-car rallying.

So I read a lot of the reviews and it seems everyone is having very different experiences.  Personally, I couldn't use my Steam controller or my old wired PS1 controller, but after an hour of getting frustrated with a couple of attempts using the keyboard I tried a wired PS4 controller and everything was right with the world again.  This is so important for a lot of people I'm sure it will be fixed very soon.
So the game itself.  In my opinion it looks beautiful - I love the design, the graphics, the club names and badges.  When it comes to playing the game - which let's be honest, that's what most of us are here for - it plays well, with a few caveats.  'Keepers are static... You can shoot at them with a little bend and they miss catching easy shots like a bespectacled four year old girl who doesn't like sport.  The AI is appalling, but I have laughed at the 20 or so own goals they have thumped in from close range on my behalf.  The computer offers very little competition, and scoring 8 or 9 goals a match isn't uncommon with the easy teams at the start of Boss Mode (which auto saves, just make sure you don't quit out).  The game does get a little more challenging when you play with the better teams.  The ball also feels a bit light and you can't quite score 40 yards curlers into the top corner like you could in SWOS.
I haven't noticed the view changing randomly after a goal unlike some people, and I would urge everyone to give the overhead camera a go, even if you are coming to this game from the likes of PES and FIFA.  The camera itself seems quite juddery, this was something that happened with Sensible Soccer 2006 but the community managed to fix this so I'm sure the real development team could adjust this too.  I would like to be able to zoom in and out but it's not a massive issue.
There are lots of little things that need looking at - players don't collide with the net and can walk through it, there are no walls at free kicks and the AI always shoot in the opposite direction to the goal, the own goals by the AI team, player numbers in the database are odd, goalkeepers wear outfield kits in the squad page, you only see the last three scorers on the game screen, in Boss mode the formation reverts to the default every game, there are no injuries or suspensions (although it's nice to see AI players getting sent off which never happened in SWOS) and I managed to score a couple of goals through the side netting.  And I'm not sure why every button has to make your player slide tackle when you don't have the ball... although I guess that's what happened in SWOS.  But the main thing is getting the gameplay right for now.
HOWEVER, the game feels great, you can tell the people behind it want it to play like SWOS and I fully expect them to make good progress. This review is geared more towards new players as I am new to deck builders myself. There are some TIPS at the BOTTOM that may help new players get though the early grind.
This is a different style game and while I kind of enjoy the game (when i dont lose 90% of my games), some wont. Do NOT play RANKED matches at night. Mostly veteran players are on at night and you will LOSE 90% of your games if you dont own all cards needed for a meta deck.
Positives
-game visuals and audio are amazing
-good explantion of basic mechanics
-great introduction game for non card players
-great long term playability with collection and customization of cards and decks
Biggest complaints
-match making system doesn't seem to account for P2W players
-the grind is real for new players after you complete the main story
-main story is to short with not enough deck expansion for new players
-need better explanation of how to build competitive decks (why some work WAY better than others)

The game starts you in a main story tutorial. Once completed, you can play PvAI arena, PvP arena in which both modes require you to build a new deck on the spot. Also, you can play PvP casual or AI practice matches. Usually on the weekends they have a sort of tournament mode. Both arena modes and the tournament mode require a ticket or 150 gold to enter.
The opening tutorial of the game covers 8 games. And has a great way to explain the machanics to new players. Especially players like me that don't play these type of card games IRL. The main story feels a little short in its 20 stages (including the 8 tutorial games). I feel like the main story should be 30 to 50 stages long to allow better deck building for new players. As when you finish the story you really have to engage in PVP and that can be discouraging as a new player when you dont have a META deck and dont completly understand all the cards and mechanics. The game does a decent job of explaining the game features with the daily quest system and continues to update until most features are explained.
Most of the negative reviews come in the form of Pay to win complaints. Honestly, I kinda agree, BUT... all deck building games are that way. Someone who buys $500 worth of Magic the Gathering (MTG) packs will have a better deck than someone who spends $50. The ideal fix for that problem, in this game, should be a better match making system that takes into account card collection % to help keep new players with base cards away from those that have every card in the game. It can be frustrating and a turn off to lose 10 games in a row due to P2W and long term players trumping your whole deck.
Advice
-look up budget or new player deck builds for PVP and a different one for AI gem farm
-Link your bethesda account to twitch and recieve free items daily when you watch a stream of this game (frequency of drops randomly changes)... that is in addition to login rewards
-Use 3000 gold collected to buy all the Dark Brotherhood DLC, most new decks use these cards for meta play
-save up 500 gold to buy a special pre-built card pack from the shop (builds collection faster than small packs)
-play the game for the fun of it and not as a competition, especially for new players that dont want to spend real money... you will enjoy it more

Fortified! is a third person tower defense game much in the vein of Orcs Must Die! or Sanctum in that you are playing both a third person shooter and a tower defense game and your job is to know when to switch between the two to gain an advantage. Fortified has a very stereotypical sci-fi feel to it since it has that comic book style with typical martian style aliens that look like something to come out of a sixties sci-fi movie. You play as one of four different characters and each one unlocks their weapons and towers in a different order and even have a few different towers based on playstyle. Fortified isn't particularly unique but it takes what other games like Orcs Must Die and Sanctum have done and fine-tunes it and gives it a nice sci-fi 50's spin.
In Fortified you have four characters to choose from and each one of them has a unique ultimate ability based on what that character is like. For example there's a character called the rocketeer and she has a jetpack so her ultimate ability activates her jetpack and gives her infinite ammo for the duration. Every characters ultimate is pretty unique but more importantly it feels tied to that characters defining characteristics. Every level ,in traditional tower defense style, your objective is to defend a rocket launch site for however many turns that level requires. You'll be attacked by different kinds of aliens hitting you both from the air and the ground and every alien feels like it was directly ripped from a 50's comic book which only adds to the feeling the you're playing a comic book. Every alien essentially differs only in health and model but they each feel very distinctive such as the tiny little spider robots that scurry around or the UFO's that capture you in their stasis beams. There's quite a lot of variation between all of the aliens and they all have models that fit the setting too.
Depending on what character you play you will have different towers to choose from and a different order in which you unlock them. You also unlock different weapons as you go and what weapons you start with depends on what character you chose. Every tower has two different upgrades you can purchase for it and each one changes how you use that tower in the future or how it can synergize with other towers. The towers all fit the setting and each one is both unique and incredibly fun to see in action such as the rocket tower which fires a huge missile that obliterates any martians unfortunate enough to get caught in the blast. The towers meld perfectly with the character using them and so you end up working with the towers you choose rather that having them do all the work or having you do all the work.
Fortified! takes the style of Sanctum and adds a teaspoon of martian invasion with just a pinch of retro sci-fi to make it one of the best tower defense games on the market.

Fortified is a tower defense action game, developed and published by Clapfoot, releasing on the PC in February 2016. The game follows the same style as the extremely popular classic tower defense title, Orcs Must Die!
The gameplay is played from a third-person perspective of one of four characters. You have a selection of four different classes to play as, each with their own unique special abilities. Each map has a target which you must protect from oncoming martian invaders. You are able to do this by taking on the enemies yourself as well as building defences along the enemies routes to your base. Those that have played Orcs Must Die will feel very much at home with the style of gameplay on offer here. You are able to build defences for your base on the fly in the midst of battle and at the beginning of every level. This allows you to redeploy different units in the middle of a level depending on what enemies you are facing in oncoming waves. The gameplay does get a little bit repetitive towards the later stages of the game as you get used to the different types of enemies. Enemy types can range from drones, robots, flying space ships and giant bosses.
Visually, Fortified hits all the right notes. The game is graphically based on a 50s movie with some neat character designs and top notch animation along with them. The environments are a little bland, to say the least, but other than that, the game looks really good and that’s mainly down to the interesting art style being used.
Fortified is a tricky game to master; the first few stages do a good job of introducing you to the game, but you soon get thrown in at the deep end as you find the need to min-max your defences almost to perfection once you hit the halfway mark in the campaign. The boss fights are probably the trickiest aspect as they have some really interesting mechanics that prove more of a challenge than the rest of the game combined. Even with a state of the art defense system in the works, you may still fall victim of a boss simply just waltzing through your base and wrecking everything you have worked so hard on.
The levels throughout the game are nicely designed; the beginning stages only have one entry point for enemies to join the fight, but as you get further and further into the game, you soon have to deal with three or four points of entry; this is when things turn very hectic and you’ll be zipping to opposite sides of the map on a reoccurring basis. The game does miss out on having a teleporting system that Orcs Must Die had which does make transporting a bit of a chore, especially when the character’s sprint ability isn’t much faster than their regular run.
A single play through the game using one character took me just under four hours to complete; the game has tons of replayability with three more characters to use which will make for a different experience each time due to their variety in abilities. Fortified also has varying levels of difficulty which will also keep the hardcore tower defense fans amongst us jumping with joy, with the likes of Orcs Must Die! Relying heavily on higher difficulty levels to keep you coming back for more.  This game could quite easily reach twenty hours of content if you try and complete everything.
The game runs very well at higher resolutions with a wide selection of graphical options for you  to change to your liking. I preferred using keyboard and mouse for my playthrough but full controller support is available.
All in all, Fortified is a good tower defense title, it does a lot of things right but it did WOW me at any point. The price point of £10.99 is fair and you’ll easily get your monies worth, but if you haven’t played the more staple tower defense titles out there, you’d be better off trying them first. Veterans of the genre will for sure want to be picking this game up, though.

Although I have just bought the Steam version with all the DLC, I have extensively played this on my old Xbox 360, and I can tell you it is one of the best games I have played.
Unlike other games in the series, this one feels the most like an RPG. I say this is because it was developed by Obsidian Entertainment. Whenever that company picks up a game, they put their heart and soul into it no matter what. Bethesda is not terrible, but I feel they are less interested in making a great Role-Playing Game when making their Fallout games, and more interested in the shooting and exploration elements of the game. While nothing is wrong with that, if you can really focus in on those classic RPG elements, it always makes it an instant classic in my book.
The main story presented in the game is not that interesting at first. You're a Courier. A mailman. You were supposed to deliver a package, but you got shot by a man in a checkered suit. Doesn't seem engaging, but as you keep playing more and more threads keep getting introduced. The multiple factions that are having disputes across South-Eastern Nevada. The tales the many people you meet have to tell. The locations you discover and loot. There is so much more to this game than just a linear story about finding your killer.
The gun combat is a step-up from it's predecessor Fallout 3. While that is not saying much, it's so much more satisifying being able to use the iron-sights the guns have, rather than sort of just zooming in the screen and hoping that increases your accuracy. It also introduces new types of guns and goes into more detail about their damage outputs and such. There is so much more the guns now than just damage and fire rate. There's DPS, shotgun spread, and a lot of other things. By itself, the gun combat is still pretty bad (especially compared to other games at the time), but it is still a considerable improvement from Fallout 3.
The features that are completely brand new are great as well. The faction reputation system is one of the most fantastic ideas to come out of the 3D Fallout games yet. You have multiple levels of reputation you can get. You can be loved in the community and be rewarded for doing so, or you can be vilified and be shot on sight. And it's not just the big factions that have reputations either. Small towns give you a reputation. This means that every action you do, positive or negative, has an impact outside of karma. Now, karma is a good system, don't get me wrong, but the faction reputation system is just another layer that adds so much to the game. I'm surprised it wasn't included in Fallout 4, considering the huge importance of factions is that game.
The only problems this game has have to do with it's many year old engine. The people look like plastic dolls, and while that can be fixed with mods, that means people who play in vanilla won't have the greatest looking experience in the world. However, this is a problem that Bethesda introduced, not Obsidian, so I can't blame them for these problems. Other Bethesda-related problems include constant crashing, bad HUD, etc. If you don't bring these things into mind, then this game is pretty much flawless. If Obsidian had enough time to develop a brand new engine for this Fallout game, then I am sure that it would have been much better. If Obsidian had enough time in general, this could have been a much better game.
Obsidian was only given an 18 month development time. A year and a half. In the game developing world, that is effectively nothing. If you look at the concept art for the game, New Vegas (the city) was supposed to be HUGE! Dense, crazy, bustling with activity. But because of how short of a development time they got, they could only make the puny in comparison New Vegas we see today. I'm sure if Obsidian was able to remake Fallout: New Vegas with Fallout 4's engine, we would be able to see the New Vegas Obsidian would have wanted.

Dungeons & Dragons Chronicles Of Mystara holds up well. Even today.
The graphics aren't high definition, but still sharp enough and are definitely an improvement over the original graphics, thanks to our high resolution monitors.
Like the original games; the gameplay is all about beating creatures up, while collecting money, gear and finding secrets. Basically a beat 'em up with light RPG elements. You can pick one of the many available classes. All of them come with their own armor and moves. A nice and great idea back then, but when you compare it to (action) RPGs of today it's, obviously, disappointing. Especially when you can customize pretty much anything these days, from the looks of your character to your own playstyle by selecting the specific skills *you* want to use. I agree it's an unfair comparison, but I couldn't help but notice it, because the game is linear and short, and the current asking price is steep for what you actually get. There are so many other games out there, for the same price, or even lower, that give you much, much more value for your money.
Anyway, the developers have also added challenges to the games. Kill 10 enemies for example and you'll earn in-game currency that you can spend in the virtual store to buy artwork and magazine pages, as well as things that can help you beat the game like making your items unbreakable. It's a fun idea that I'd love to see appear in other 'modern retro' games. It does give the game some replay value.
As I mentioned the game is short. This is thanks to the unlimited continues. There's no penalty for dying. So beating these games in approximately 2 hours, well, that's pretty fast. And the other available classes aren't all that different to warrant a second playthrough, but I guess you could give the drop-in/drop-out co-op a try though. Or I could see you play it again to complete some more of the challenges.
To make a long story short; buy it if it's cheap (because it is a fun game), but for the current asking price (€15) it's just not worth it.

It's been a bit rough since the first alpha, but Disgraced is starting to pull together. It's not content complete yet, but most of the features are already in game.
What makes Disgraced different from more basic RPG Maker games includes:
Reasonably challenging combat - As you level up and choose skills you will become considerably more powerful, but especially early on you'll find yourself challenged by many enemies. You only gain hit points via taking certain skills and stats, not every level, keeping combat often quick and brutal.
Equipment degradation - Similar to Fallout 3 every piece of equipment you own can degrade with use. You need to bring it to the blacksmith for repairs regularly, but not so often it becomes a chore.
Survival elements - You have a provisions meter that decreases as you move about the world and particularly when you sleep which is also how you save. You'll want to sleep save often as you gauge which battles to avoid, but doing so  too often will strain your provisions.
Limited base building - Not as complex as a sim type game by a long shot, but the element is there. At different points in the game you can spend four basic resources to build different improvements or take other actions that benefit your cause.
It's still a bit rough around the edges. Writing is eh, but the gameplay is better than the writing. As of now (September '16, now in Beta) it looks like there's still content to be added to finish the game, a few bugs to work out and points to be polished, but you can get a fair idea of what the full game should be. Developer is quick to respond to bug reports too. Case in point, he just now replied to a post I made two minutes ago.

I've always been very cautious about this particular game. Sure, it got high reviews but I've never agreed with IGN on a review for a game ever, and I was always comfortable with my familiar Tomb Raider game formula... but damn!
Lara Croft and the Guardian of Light is a very Diablo-esque game, wherein you control a character in a top-down perspective, fight hordes of demons, and loot tombs for special upgrades and treasures you can manage in your inventory. Except Guardian of Light is more interested in progressing through linear levels, which I personally prefer.
The game's story sucks. Random thought, but yeah. It's absolutely trash. It's rushed, the characters aren't interesting, and Xolotl is one of the most yawn-inducing villains I've seen ever. But, to be fari, Guardian of Light isn't interested in story... it's interested in gameplay.
The gameplay is excellent. You move fluidly, puzzles are excellently laid out, and combat with hundreds of enemies on screen feels as hectic as it does therapeutic. And the different artifacts and upgrades are actually useful, so breaking off from the main level to do a five-minute puzzle is both hazard-free and can end up benefiting you later in the level.
And the icing on the cake is the graphics. You can tell that the cutscenes were made on a budget- as the camera always conveniently hides behind Totec and Lara whenever they talk, but the actual in-game graphics for the enemies, levels, and textures on everything look very pretty. If your a graphics-snob, this game does look very nice.
Despite the story sucking so bad, Lara Croft and the Guardian of Light is one of the best Tomb Raider games in the series. It's game play is new, as it is polished to a mirror shine, with the player's intuition in mind. I highly recommend this fun, little game, and I'm giving it a 7/10

In the grand scheme of things,
sticks out like a sore thumb. Although on the surface level,it shares certain elements like open ended missions that involve crawling through jungles and other exotic locales with the other titles in the series, Far Cry 2 was built on an entirely different vision and concept.
many fundamental gameplay elements, the ambition and unique vision that drove the design and mechanics of the game is undeniable. That being said, ambition and intent alone does not make a good game. If anything, Far Cry 2 falls so frustatingly short of a spectacular game because of the half-hearted and disjointed way that the gameplay mechanics mesh with one another.
game mechanic has you suffering from unsettling nausea and headaches at random moments that can only be cured by taking pills that are only gifted to you by resistance members as a reward for completing their side-missions. What seems like an interesting mechanic in the end only serves as an excuse to prod the player into doing the repetitive side missions or risk getting debilitating headaches at the most random and inconvenient moments.
The guard posts that are sprinkled throughout the map at regular intervals have guards that respawn after you leave it for a while. On paper, it was probably designed to make the map seem more hostile. However, it ends up just being a major annoyance to the player because the highly vehicle-centric gameplay forces you to travel on the same roads that have all the same guard posts. Clearing these guard posts serves only to give the player a sense of futility, as the guards will respawn regardless of what you do.

Far Cry 2 is not without its positives. The gunplay is solid and gun condition which can lead to jams and failures is always something to consider going into a fight. The buddy system with other mercenaries is also very cool and a feature that should be in other games more. The map provides highly varied and beautiful landscapes and terrain, but upon closer inspection is totally shallow and unremarkable. Which serves as a summary for the entire game.

The short explanation of this game is that it's kind of the wrong way to do open-world. It's empty, everything is spread out from everything else just to make you wander around more, the constantly respawning enemies and patrols force you to either stop and fight every 250 meters or take long, slow bypasses,the collectables are practically impossible to find except by dumb luck, the RPG elements are almost nil, and there is little actual need to explore or experiment or plan for more than just getting from point A to point B. The story is predictably laughable, it is a Far Cry game after all, but it's not even engaging; there are almost no characters that aren't just 1-dimensional cut-outs, including you. You don't even play a decent guy, you're a mercernary engaging in a civil war that isn't your own to further a pointless job. The only saving grace is that you mostly kill other mercenaries (actually, it's hilarious; I don't know if the intent was to avoid charges or racism or something, but you almost only fight other foreign mercenaries, most of them white or asian, the locals appear to have almost completely fled the entire country). The overall tone of the story is depressing and heartless, all about the horrors of war and the immorality of profiting off of it.
The only good things about the game are thus; the gunplay is good and satisfying, it's very beautiful, it has surprising detail in some areas, and it focuses fairly heavily on realism, with a very clean feel and a minimal amount of "game-y" elements. That's really it. It was frustrating at first, then fun for a bit as you play around with the mechanics and enjoy shooting things, then ultimately boring because there's no variety, there's no depth, and there's not even much concentration of those good elements, as you spend most of them in transit. Only get this game if you like the older, more primitive open-world games and have A TON of patience. I tried to force myself to finish it, just to say I did, but no, I can't, I'm done and I'm bored. Back to Far Cry 3 and 4, monumentally superior games despite their flaws (and I confess, there are a few small elements I wish they had kept from this game).

Ahh... The childhood classic! I was pleasantly surprised that it was picked up and re-released in its remastered form nearly 2 decades later after the original's release. You are Manny Calavera, a grim reaper/travel agent in the Land of the Dead, assigned to sell travel packages to the recently deceased people in order to make the trip to the Ninth Underworld more convenient. If Manny makes enough premium sales, which good life-leading people qualify more for, the travel agent will have worked off his time in the Land of the Dead and follow suit (no pun intended). However, despite his professional experience and promising clients, Manny has been caught in a slump with low-qualified sales. Deciding to do things his own way, he finds a special client who could turn the course and save his job: Mercedes Colomar.
Around that point is where the Grim Fandango story starts off, as you familiarize with the noir-tinged environment and solve different problems using your wits and objects you find. The game's Land of the Dead is a modernized take on the description from the Mexican (Aztec) mythology, which makes the world immersive and diverse with both fantasy creatures and real-world cultures. This setting helps the plot stand out more for its originality and can leave some aspects to gamer's imaginations. Besides the Mexican day of the dead as the main source of graphic and aural inspirations, there are plenty of noir-style elements that add to the tone of the experience including jazz and bop music, as well as graphic designs taking cues from the landmarks of early 20th century.
The game characters are colorful and diverse to the point that each one of them sticks easily out. That's why I have a soft heart for Manny's demon companion Glottis of the entire cast. It also helps that, in contrast to the humorous interactions you're provided throughout the game, the plot's darker undertones augments the immersion with the cast as well as the world itself. Tim Schafer and his dev team has succeeded in making the Land of the Dead a stage that's able to leave a mark on the inhabitants and travelers or vice versa. This game shows what can occur around visionary people, the corruptible,
...

I have a real love-hate relationship with this game. I'll try to be fair in my review however.
ESL is basically a CCG game that's similar to Hearthstone but (in my opinion) improves on the formula greatly. Two lanes, along with some other interesting mechanics (and the Elder Scroll lore) make this game more interesting overall than Magic or Blizzard's brand.
What really makes ESL shine is the ability to get quite a few legendaries and epic cards at no-cost. By simply grinding out a few daily quests and practice sessions you can build your library in just a few months (vs pay  2 win games where it'll cost you a house to be competitive). Modes of play include casual, practice (for gems), ranked and arena. Along with the occasional "Rumble" or special arena event. It's a great game you can just pick up and play and its available on most mobile devices as well.
Now the cons:
The RNG (read random draw) on this game is ridiculous. You can spend hours studying the best strategies, hundreds of dollars buying extra packs and read every online tip and still lose horribly to somone that just has the "perfect draw". The arena mode is also frustrating as you have zero control over what cards you can choose from (so forget about synergies) and you're damn lucky if you even get to select cards that are halfway decent - meanwhile your opponent may get several legendaries to choose from - complete b.s.
Ranked is OK. But again can be very frustrating as you'll often get mowed over by O.P. decks that some 12 year old with their parent's credit card bought.
To put it bluntly - Elder scrolls Legends is 10% skill and 90% dumb luck. So pick it up and have fun but try not to get sucked in too badly - you'll wind up screaming at your monitor and punching a hole in the wall.

This is the game that re-invigorated my interest in Western RPG's. It is one of the most "open" open world games i have ever played. None of that "You can climb that mountain" crap; just options.
Don't want to fight an end game boss? Well, if you leveled speech enough, just use diplomacy and reasoning to diffuse the situation! Or just blow his head off from halfway across the map with a high-calibur sniper rifle. The choice is yours.
Apart from that, this game is perhaps the most morally stimulating pieces of media i have ever consumed; Do you...
Side with a group of cruxifiction-fetishising genocidal legionarres with some valid critisicms of democracy?
The enigmatic Mr.House, who allthough he has humanity's best interest in heart would achieve it through installing himself as dictator of New Vegas?
The NCR, who desire law, order and democracy but can be a bit iron-fisted?
Or do you proclame yourself as head of the New Vegas strip?
It is this and more, that has lead me to (at the time of writing) put 40 hours into this game, with no intent of stopping there. The only things that i think diminish from my enjoyment of the game are the sometime dodgy gunplay, the small amount of progression-breaking glitches and the somewhat rushed endgame. However, these are only minor blemishes on what i otherwise consider to be a damn-near perfect game. If you wnat a truly epic RPG that encompases both stellar story-telling and enjoyable gameplay, then you have no reason to not play this game.

Misled by the reviews, I held out to try this one out. Turns out it's pretty good, at least in present form.
Pros:
Lots of content, many terrain types, time of the day.
Typical race types: Rally, Rally Cross, Pikes peak
Career mode, buying cars and tuning them
Livery, team colors, names and even plate
Nice physics, car bounce and tumbles feel good even in an accident.
Nice dirt in windshield and car
Wheel support works, it didn't take much to get it there.
Wheel feels great, nice road grip feedback
Cons:
Can't choose cars in quick race outside of what you own in Career. This is bad for party gaming.
Damage is very simple graphically (on/off), head on crashes look very unrealistic, as the car just stops with mild damage.
Gamepad racing feels terrible
Several tmes during each stage, there's a hiccup. I believe it's loading the scenery ahead, but whatever it is it's noticeable (with an SSD!) and takes you out of the zone,
Meh:
Can't pick the stage or number of stages for a rally: it's either the first stage or all of it
No VR support
Supports only one controller device at a time: no multi-device racing!
Graphics are passable, but no HDR, looks vastly inferior to Dirt.
Sound is passable. Inmersion is not great, but does the job.
Force feedback on crashes is nonexistant
Conclusion: not as bad as reviews would led you to believe, but not awesome at all. A decent game, with more content than Dirt but of inferior quality.

This is very weak although it does have some plus points.  Unfortunately the serious shortcomings outweigh the rest.
You can't adjust controller properly, no deadzone adjustment is ridiculous, meaning on a lot of pads like my 360 pad, which have stick drift, the car will steer to the side without any input from you.  No linearity or sensitivity settings so you can only turn the wheel at a fixed speed.  These major omissions mean cars handle poorly on a pad.  The DiRT games have these options, so do Project CARS, Forza, NFS Shift etc. etc.  Basic stuff.
Serious performance problems even on powerful systems.  Doesn't matter if you're getting 100+ fps, it looks like 30 and stutters like mad.  A workaround which was partially successful was to use Rivatuner Statistics Server to cap framerate to 60, then it's very smooth but still stutters sometimes.  (60Hz and vsync is NOT the same in this game, like it would be in most games.)
Mediocre presentation which is Milestone's hallmark.  Dull career mode, sluggish menus, the 'career' feels like a grind, totally uninspired and unimaginative like all Milestone's games tragically are.  There's no feeling of progression, achievement or joy in playing this.
On the plus side, there's a lot of cars and locations, some of the tarmac tracks are quite decently designed and the voice acting for the co-driver (in English anyway) is actually very good - streets ahead of WRC 6 for example.  Unfortunately the non-tarmac events are weak, the roads are all perfectly smooth and flat which is completely unrealistic, there's no bumps or camber, it's just like a tarmac road painted brown for mud or white for snow.  The Colin McRae Rally games were doing better than this 15 years ago.

This is not Sensible Soccer. Unfortunately it is not even close. The game is so slow it rivals FIFA in it's lethargy. Whilst on the attack, I went to make a cup of tea and still came back in time to defend the resulting counter. Unfortunately due to the indifferent defence and appaling goalkeeping, 'Sfarling' managed to slide-tackle the ball off the cross-bar and into his own net for a most spectacular oggy.
Passing it out of defence, Guardiola-style, is also not an option. The midfield and defence stand so far away from each other that the Hindenburg could've landed between the two with room to spare. Not like the good old days of 'Sensi', where you could pass it around all day long between defence and midfield before finally sliding a sweet ball up top for Cantona to run on to for a classic corner-goal.
I remeber the days when 'Goggs' could pick the ball up on his own halfway line and pace-abuse the socks off the defence in what was reminiscent of the 1999 FA cup semi-final goal that the real-life 'Goggs' rammed past Seaman to secure victory and his own God-like status. Unfortunately those days are also gone, replaced by infuriating players who can neither sprint nor keep the ball at feet for further than a few yards.
Sitting down in only my grundies after a hard day at work, can of Special Brew in hand, ready to be amazed and astounded, I was utterly astonished to learn that I now have to use more than one button to kick the ball. The pure simplicity of the original and best 'Sensi' is gone, replaced by the most mediocre copy of FIFA controls. No longer do I only have to concentrate on how long to press the kick button, I now have to attempt to coordinate my three good fingers in order to get that ever-elusive top-corner bag. I quickly realised the Special Brew was a bad idea.
The graphics also leave much to be desired, being more akin to 'Italia 90' than the the great 'Sensi'. Added to that the inability to quit goal replays, this game makes for a most infuriating experience.
As a man who does not believe in the almighty, I hope and pray that this game is a rough and uncut gem, that the final release will be something worthy of it's progenitor, and that, as an Early Access release, it will be the harbinger of the greatest footy-game revival of all time.
All one can do when faced with futility is hope.

For example, early-game fights are a bit unbalanced and rather difficult for first-time players (Another review mentionned something about accuracy being unbalanced too, and I must slightly agree on that). Also, saving in the game feels somewhat punishing, taking ressources away from you every time you save and sleep, which can be a big problem after a while. Those are little things that make the experience a little bit less enjoyable for people starting out.
Other than that, I do believe that Disgraced RPG is a great game for fans of the RPG genre and that it is very much worth its price.

Great game even though its 2016. I already owned this game for a couple of years but never completed it for various reasons. I've played Far Cry 1 + Far Cry 3, so I've got some experience with the Far Cry franchise.
I did not play this game vanilla, I installed these compatible mods from the beginning and I can recommend you to do the same:
- Dylan's Far Cry 2 Realism Mod.
- Real Africa - The Ultimate SweetFX Config ( Best graphics mod, trust me).
- Night Vision Mod for Far Cry 2 by Masson.
First of all, what immediately striked me when playing this game was the nature.
From the way the wind was blowing trough the grass and trees, the birds and other animals making their pressence known. It just felt alive and breathing.
The transition from day to night, the different weather types, every little details adds up to something really beautiful. TIA, from Blood Diamonds, one of my favorite movies, comes to mind.
I haven't finished the game yet, but I can already tell the story is realistic but not really fascinating to me.
The villain in this story is intriguing, but Vaas was way more badass. Then again, wich game villain was ever more badass then Vaas?
I like the buddy system, it adds another layer to the game. Especialy because they can die.
Obviously if you quick save allot then you can prevent this, but I like to play hardcore and only safe in safehouses.
If they die on missions, they die. Brutal, but this game ain't about fairy tales, such is life.
I already mentioned the nature and sounds, combined with the mods, the atmosphere in this game is absolutely perfect. When you are shooting african warlords or south african mercenaries, you get a sense of the cold (or should I say warm) hard reality of Africa. There is no higher moral ground whatsoever, you are in it for the money/diamonds, altough at times you are portrayed as the Good Bad Guy doing some of the dirty work that must be done for the good guys.
Something I don't like in this game are the limited amount of vehicles and there is a weird invisible speed limiter at 70/110 (kmh), depending on the vehicle. I know it's africa and they don't drive Lambo's, but I feel this aspect could have been done better.
Then again, this game was published in 2008 so I can definitely forget this flaw.
The four weapon slots one weapon each are a bit anoying. But for gameplay purposes I can understand why they have done this and it fits the grim realistic setting of this game.
The weapon jamming of rusty old weapons you got from killed enemies can be a big liabilty in battle. A grenade-launcher jamming in the middle of the battle with two nearby shirtless wild african UFLL soldiers screaming for your blood, can be a little daunting to put it mildly.
The reloading and unjamming animations are awesome and rewarding. At times it makes you want to play with unreliable rusty weapons, just for the thrill and risk of having to take cover in battle and unjamming your weapon as a badass, maybe opting for your machete when the enemy gets close. Russian roulette at its best.
The navigation map was very frustrating for me in the beginning, but I've gotten used to it. I still prefer a radar in the corner of my screen, but it's playable and again fits the setting of this game.
There are some animals in this game, but they could have added more variety, like hyena's, rhino's, flamengo's et cetera.
All and all, I've already taken way too many screenshots of this game and I'm going to enjoy finishing it.
So far this is my favorite Far Cry and I think it's way too underrated. I wouldn't say this game feels old, to me it feels more like a 2012/2013 game.
I hope there will be another Far Cry in the future with this setting, because it's one of the best. I give this game a 9 out of 10.

It's your typical trading card game, not substantially different than any other card game. I'd give it a mixed rating if I could, it's not bad, just below average. I got my "money's worth" in term of gaming hours, so to speak.

=The game punishes the attacker at set intervals of damage dealt by giving your opponent a chance at playing free cards. It annoys me and I don't care when it's in my favor, but it's by design. Some might... like it? I guess?
-It is de facto "Pay to push beyond a certain rank"/"Pay to be competitive"/"Pay to skip a nightmarish grind"

Bottom line: It's a licensed trading card game based on another video game that's really popular. Try it for free, but don't expect much.

The standout of Loeb Rally is the sheer amount of content, there is much to do in this game and thus it is perfect for single-player gamers ... if there are more of us left than myself that is. Dirt Rally and WRC 5 both have much less content in comparison.
Judging by Steam reviews, 98 % of all gamers only care about multiplayer, the same applies to this game ... which is highly unfortunate because it really misrepresents what this game offers.
The Steam community's obession with multiplayer is bad for the sim-racing industry, because these gamers are so fickle and only play their games for a short time. Whereas us single-player gamers stick with these games for the long-term.
Back to Loeb Rally though. I would liken this game to the first Dirt game, minus the trucks and buggies. You win races to earn credit, which then unlocks more stages. This is also reminiscent of games like Forza and Colin McRae Rally, where you simply won't make progress without effort and grinding.
If you only want multiplayer racing I suggest ProjectCars, Assetto Corsa, F1 or Dirt Rally. Better yet, try iRacing ... since it was actually designed and built for multiplayer only.
The other standout of Loeb Rally is that all the stages are more or less copies of the actual real-life stages. This means that they are quite lengthy for a rally game, and also feel more realistic or authentic.
On the negative side, the stages are not as tough and challenging as in WRC 5. The biggest challenge in Loeb Rally comes from the driving physics rather than the stage designs, which is the exact opposite of WRC 5.
Visually Loeb Rally looks great. Some tweaking is always needed as a PC gamer, regardless of genre. We all have to live with this fact, if we are honest enough admit to it that is ... which most "reviewers" on Steam don't seem to be.
These people don't complain when they have to tweak their Witcher 3 and Fallout 4 games, or their favourite F1 or Dirt game, yet it becomes a sudden disaster when they are forced to tweak certain other games.
Compared to WRC 5 and Dirt Rally, Loeb Rally does not look as good visually speaking, it does not have the same crispy depth of colour. If visual immersion is very important to you I recommend Dirt Rally instead.
Apart from the SBK games, Loeb Rally is the most sim-like of Milestone's games. It is significantly more techncial and demanding than Milestone's WRC rally games, as well as Kylotonn's WRC 5.
Disabling all the assists I would compare the technical difficulty to that of Dirt Rally, they are both very challenging games. The physics itself is quite different between each game though, but 'different' does not mean 'bad' ... it simply means 'different'. All racing games, whether arcade or sim, demand that you as a gamer adapt to their physics.
As a side-note, it is healthy to remind people that even the most hardcore of sim-games are still just 'games'. They are poor representations of actual racing. The Steam community's obession with imagined realism in racing games is silly ... because it is just that, 'imagined'.
What makes Loeb Rally different from WRC 5 and Dirt Rally: the stages are almost perfect copies of the real-life stages, there's a substantial amount of single-player content, you get a chance to walk in the virtual footsteps of a true racing legend (Sebastien Loeb).
What it does better than WRC 5 and Dirt Rally: the sheer amount of single-player content.
Where it is not as good as WRC 5 and Dirt Rally: the graphics (especially Dirt Rally), multiplayer opportunities (vs Dirt Rally).
I would recommend this game to people who want lots of single-player content, or something that reminds them of the first Dirt game, a game I'm a big fan of.

Disgraced is a game currently in Early Access. It was made by the same developer who created
. It follows along the same style of features as Waste Walkers, with the same dark, gritty tone. It's set in feudal Japan, at the start of a new Shogun's rise to power. You play as a character who was newly conscripted into the Shogun's army who deserts it faster than cherry pie. No, wait, that's dessert. My bad, I'm craving sweets.
Anyway, you leave the army and quickly find yourself part of the resistance against this new Shogun. You work with villagers, spies, and rebels to create a fortified town to fight and defend yourself against the Shogun's army and to probably kill the Shogun himself. At least that's what I'm hoping.
For gameplay, the core features that made Waste Walkers enjoyable are all here. You have to survive by eating food and keep an eye on your stamina so you're able to cheese it in case you're low on health and can't fight enemies. The game also focuses more on the building mechanics which had a small highlight in Waste Walkers. You need resources to build up your rebel town, and to get them you'll have to work hard and find them or earn them (or probably kill for them, you are a rebel after all).
New sounds and Japanese themed music keep this game's setting in tact and appear interesting. I can't say much else about sounds in general because that's not my expertise, but all I can say is that it definitely fits.
Currently, as the game is in Early Access, I would recommend to purchase it and wait, as the price will go up as the game continues to near completion. There isn't a whole lot to do currently, but the game is expected to retail for $10USD rather than what it costs right now. So if you liked Waste Walkers, or are interested in supporting RPG game developers, it's a rather solid buy. You can expect a finished game from the developer in under a year.
It's really polished as it is so far and it is unique. Looking forward to more.

Grim Fandango Remastered
by Double Fine Productions
Genre: Graphic adventure
Release: January 26, 2015
-----
Something is rotten on the streets of El Marrow, and that’s definitely saying something, being that it is the City of the Dead…
You are Manuel Calavera, Travel Agent in the Department of Death located in the city on the edge of what passes for civilization in the Land of the Dead. In this Mexican Dia de la Muerte-themed place, Manny and others employed in the DoD help the recently departed souls find the fastest path to the Ninth Underworld, the Land of Eternal Rest. What the people did in life determines how fast they’ll get to the Promised Land; whether they’ll just have to walk on their own two bony feet, or whether they get golden tickets on the Number Nine Express, billed as getting you there in four minutes instead of four years!
Well, shortly after you start, you retrieve (illicitly I should add) the pure soul of one Mercedes (“Meche”) Colomar, who was a saint, a selfless nun in life. This beautiful child of God was assigned to your churlish rival within the company, Domino Hurley, but you snatched her because you were itching for a way out; you had been at the DoD since time immemorial and it was time to leave.
Unfortunately two horrible things happen to Manny, which lead to the revelation of something BIG going on under the city streets (in one case, literally)! First, Meche is discovered as being assigned a bog-standard walking route to the Ninth Underworld. This is a grave (heh) injustice, so Manny does some digging (heh) and discovers that all the golden tickets on the No. 9 are being stolen, and auctioned off to the highest bidders at some remote location! And the DoD is in on it, as Manny discovers when his “soul fraud” is discovered and he is fired from his job!
Fortunately, he also discovers his former secretary’s working as an intelligence officer for a resistance faction, which seeks to expose this vile corruption. You are first tasked with getting a pair of pigeon’s eggs from the DoD’s rooftop…
That’s it, I’ll say no more. This is such a wonderful, deep story from the creators of many fine graphic adventures from the past, that you must experience it for yourself.
Controls are similar to that of a tank, actually: you turn on the spot and move forward or backward, running as you wish. This, being similar to Resident Evil, can be a bit clunky, but you get used to it.
The Remastered version puts the pre-rendered backgrounds and 3D character models through a filter, remasters the music and pops the action out into widescreen, as well as allows you to change the aforementioned tank controls to a scheme which is more relative to the game’s fixed camera views. (Doing this locks you out of an achievement, though, so I’ll not be doing that.)
I most highly recommend this game for anyone who loves great stories!

I played this game initially in the 2000s after finally finding a copy for around $20 at a local store. I was young and adventure games were really hard for me. I resorted to using a walkthrough to play this game, but even then, it was completely worth it. Grim Fandango is a game that does not get replicated much and, as such, its unique aspects will largely remain unique going forward into the future. The characters are full of personality, they have their own agendas, biases and motivations. The day of the dead themed environments of the ninth world of the dead stood out, provided for a lot of imaginative set pieces and stayed consistent throughout the game.
In 2017, the improvements made for the remaster helps the game stand with today's AAA titles. The visuals mostly relied on creative imagery rather than real life representation; thereby, the visuals did not require much of a touch up. What I can notice compared to the original version is obviously the resolution. Characters are less grainy and I can play the game on a bigger screen largely without noticing it is a game from 20 years ago. The music has been redone and now sound fantastic.
The biggest inclusion that helps this game is the inclusion of point and click, in addition to the original tank controls. Though Tim Schafer is still a strong proponent that tank controls is the only way to play the game as intended; I, for one, am truly thankful for these new controls.
A minor hindrance of adventure games is the set path is the only path to take. If you miss an object, or fail to talk to an individual, you are stuck until you've found out what you've missed. There were a few times where I did not notice an active area of one of the screens and I was stuck running around aimlessly. This can be bad in Year 2, as the area is huge and going from place to place to try a new combination of actions can be time consuming. In these places, I did have to resort to using a guide again to help me. But in large part I was able to figure out most of the game on my own.
I'm glad this game was remastered. I'm glad I got to play this game again. Everyone should buy and play this game for themselves. I cannot recommend Grim Fandango more than I am right now.

I know the game has well-known problems like: lack of post-release support, poor optimization, lack of compatibility with simulation hardware. This is Milestone's signature move, nothing new here. But I'm also seeing a lot of people just jumping on the hate train without thinking it through.
If you're lucky to be in the compatibility zone (Logitech wheels, single monitor) it happens to be a great sim. Actually, it's more sim-esque than DiRT Rally. DiRT's a much better game overall, but SLRE is able to give a quick fix of nostalgia from Richard Burns Rally. The driving physics are great, very reminiscent of (and easier than) RBR. Cars may not have as much personality as their Codemasters' doppelgangers, but they're fun to drive too. Both games have an awesome, respectable roster of historic rally cars, and I wonder how Milestone managed to acquire Toyota's licensing rights while Codemasters didn't. FWD handling is better than in DR, and the other traction systems, while not being better, give a good feel and never feel unpolished. Some cars have really bad stock setups and require some tuning to run fine, just like happens in DR. And, differently from DR, the downforce works correctly. After 200 hours of DR I was starting to believe cars really do float in the air like they're on the Moon. SLRE's driving pace is more lifelike, DR may get arcadey-fast sometimes (not a bad thing). Of course I never drove a real Lancia Stratos on tarmac, but I bet a kidney that the SLRE's rendition is much more faithful to reality, and boy, it feels good. Small, powerful FWD cars like the Renault Clio Williams and Suzuki Swift 1600 are really fun to drive.
For me, the biggest surprise was the track design. MUCH better than in their last rally game (WRC 4), with a lot of narrow, tight sections alternating between wider, faster sections, and many variations of surface and height, all on a same stage. They're not lively and dangerous as in DR, but the force feedback works properly and can be a real handful. Also, less repetitive than DR, since it has more stages than its rival. Mexico, Finland and Sanremo really stand out among the available rallyes, with excellent stages. The game's definitely a grower.
Sadly, it lacks a good online component, like the always updated online events of DiRT Rally. Since you get on top of the AI leaderboards, there won't be much to do anymore. Visuals are just OK and sound design is really poor, with a lot of bad/missing sound effects, but the overall package gave birth to a surprisingly good sim, which could be considered the finest rally title today if DiRT Rally never showed up. And this is quite against the odds, since it came from a really sloppy game developer that still can't understand basic, essential things like support, hardware compatibility and community feedback.

NEW Review:
After getting over my frustrations with the developer (see bottom), this turned out to be a really pleasant rally sim. Rally sim is only as good so long as you are able to play the sim without being able to predict the next turn, and rotating between SLR Evo and DIRT is a nice way to delay track memorization from setting in.
Pros
- Maybe oddly timed, but excellent detail with co-driver call-outs. You hear the phrases 'over', 'and', 'into' way more than in DIRT and it makes creating the mental map of the coming road a little easier
- Associated with the above, the are many more compound call-outs than in DIRT (e.g. Crest over Left 3).
- I have a Thrustmaster T500 (wheel) and separate TH8A (shifter), and have no issue assigning the shifter as the hand brake. I get that many people are experiencing hardware issues, but there are some combinations that work (buyer be ware)
Neutral
- As stated many other places, the driving physics are more RBR-esque. The ability to dig the tires in a heavy oversteer (to recover from entering a turn too fast) is more limited and car momentum when swinging through turns is much more pronounced. I'm leaving this is neutral, because people can argue until they are blue in the face if this is good or bad.
- Location variety on par with DIRT, would love to see either group tackle all 15 locations....even at the expense of the eye candy detail (as should any rally purist).
- Really clean pace note delivery. Pace notes in DIRT have a lot of surrounding noise and are much more difficult to parse out between engine and road noise. The latter is more immersive (and realistic), but SLR Evo works as a nice starter (or refresher) environment for mental road mapping.
Bad
- Scripted career mode; there are events that take place on a specific set of tracks. IF you fail the event, then you simply retry until you succeed. This is crappy, because it is a perfect way to memorize a track, and track memorization is the antithesis of rally racing. DIRT shares this same ailment (only WRC 5 gets it right), but it's especially bad with SLR Evo, because you have to progress through the career mode to have any hope at buying new cars.
- The cars are locked, and this is especially frustrating. The locked car career progression is a an RPG gaming perspective that's really out of place in the simulation world.

As KoL helped me slog through a few years at a very unpleasant job, I felt obligated to play WoL, as some sort of absolution. I have since repaid my debt (to my satisfaction), and will now celebrate by mixing myself up a tasty Corpse Island iced tea.
But seriously...
Should you, dear reader, be mulling whether or not to play this game, then let me say this: The writing is strong, the world is  more vast than it seems at first, and your choices affect your experience in ways both subtle and not. And don't let the simplistic art fool you -- this game is highly atmospheric. (The music helps a lot, in that regard.)
This is a game where you can take a fairly direct path from beginning to end, if you wish. Along the way, however, you'll encounter numerous seemingly-loose threads just waiting to be pulled; if you do so, you'll find yourself going down the various rabbit holes that exist in this game. Some are small (for example, a small collection of clues to a puzzle waiting to be solved), while others are quite vast.
The joy of WoL is following each of those threads to completion, and finding all the possible resolutions that are available, be they interesting, silly, confusing, new pieces of equipment, etc.
I mentioned earlier that your choices will affect the game. This isn't taken lightly in WoL...so if you want to experience everything this game has to show, expect to play through it multiple times.
If this sounds good to you, then WoL should make for a fine purchase indeed.

A few disclaimers before I begin:
1. I had never heard of Kingdom of Loathing prior to discovering this game, and as such I have never played it before.
2. I bought this because I watched a let's play of the beginning bits and my curiosity was piqued.  I highly recommend that if this game sounds like something you want to buy, *do not* do this.  You do not want the feeling of "Oh I've heard this joke before," as the comedy is worth experiencing for the first time on your own.
Overview:
After picking a name and gender for your character, you are given the option of magic-wielder, melee fighter, or a rogue/thief class.  (For the record, in my one playthrough I have completed thus far, I picked magic).  Your character has decided to leave your family's farm to go west, where small towns and demon cows are awaiting.  That's basically all of the story in a nutshell.
THE GOOD:
- Laugh-Out-Loud Funny
Seemingly everything has a goofy description, a peculiar story, or is just a strange thing in general that will probably make you crack a smile.  This humor is not high-brow, but it doesn't have to be.  If you allow it, this story will make you laugh.  The game thrives on player exploration, so you are doing yourself and the game a disservice if you do not check out everything you can.
- Surprisingly Open-Ended
Instead of formal levels, the progression in this RPG is mostly through using XP to increase stats.  In a way very reminiscent of Fallout, having certain stats a high enough level will allow you to avoid the game becoming a series of never-ending fights, while also hiding some of the game's best gags.  Of course, no one will blame you if you mercilessly fight everything that looks at you sideways either.  The game shows you this choice early on when you are first given the option to kill a bandit or talk him out of his life of crime.  Not only that, but the short time you spend with side characters while helping them with their varying problems does often lead to actually helping them.  There's a strange amount of impact you leave on the small game world.
- Intuitive, Easy Combat
This is as simple to grasp as it gets. Fighting is standard turn-based fare, with melee weapon, gun, and magic attack options.  Each fight you start with a certain amount of AP which you use to cast spells, but guns and melee weapons are unlimited.  Characters are on a grid, but this really serves no change in combat.  Guns become blocked off by cover (either yours or your enemies) or another enemy standing in front of your target.  Because magic and melee still work in these cases, however, I can't say this made much difference.
- Interesting and Likeable Characters
From the most evil enemies to your choice of "pardner," every npc in this game has an adorable charm.  Part of it is of course the stick figure aesthetic, but characters stand out for their quirkiness and deadpan acceptance of the ridiculous world they live in.  Some moments with characters are even downright sad in spite of the obvious comedic theme.  One character that you choose from a few options follows you throughout the game as your "pardner" and fights in combat with you.  Each of these characters was interesting and I wanted them to go with me for different reasons.  Hearing their dialogue and using their abilities is warranting of multiple playthroughs, as far as I see it.
THE BAD:
- Little Quest Variety
Almost every mission, whether it's part of the main quest or not, is at the heart of it a fetch quest.  Characters have lost this or that, or had it stolen, and it's up to you to find it (and you'll probably have to kick some♥♥♥♥♥to get to it).  The game seems to make fun of itself for this late in the game during one of the main story missions, with your main character actually getting pretty frustrated at a particularly ridiculous endeavor.  For me though, this was just a reminder of how I was beginning to grow tired of the superficiality of the actual tasks I was doing.  I often used the ability to ask my "pardner" where I was supposed to go next for the various side missions just because I started getting bored of quests and would go off exploring instead.
- Combat Growing Tedious
As I said previously, I played the magic-casting "beanslinger" class so my best attacks were spells that I learned from books I found throughout the world.  Once I had found a combo of spells that allowed me to take a good chunk of health from an enemy in turn one, there was no reason to do anything else.  Battles started to become all the same, and I started spacing out while doing them just to get to more of the funny dialogue.  One particular annoyance came in a fight which had three enemies attacking me and 2 others buffing the whole team's attack and defense each turn.  I had to kill the attackers first so that I wouldn't be killed (more an annoyance that anything, as you can come right back), but this left the other two enemies with 100+ hp health bars buffing themselves into oblivion.  By the time I was fighting only them, they had buffed themselves so much that I could only do 1 damage at a time to them, and had to just speed up the combat speed in the options menu and wittle them both down one at a time.  This is of course a worst-case scenario, but as I said just going through the motions once you are super strong quickly becomes the worst part of the game.
THE UGLY:
-The Ending (NO SPOILERS!)
The game just sort of ends once you complete the last mission of the "main" storyline.  You are free to watch the ending cutscene, as well as go right back into the world and complete any remaining sidequests, but there's something so dissatisfying about it.  It's a feeling of reading a very good joke book, and the empty feeling you get when you close the back cover.
TL;DR, West of Loathing is game that is a solid RPG that just barely overstays its welcome.  It's hilarious for people who don't mind some simple humor, but the game design could have used a bit more complexity.
If you don't mind an RPG not being very deep in its mechanics and instead being a charming, ridiculous world, West of Loathing is your game.  You're either going to play it once, enjoy it, but never feel a need to play it again, or want to try every "pardner" and replay for hard mode and show all of your friends.
For the low price, the length and potential replayability, and the enjoyment I personally got from it, I can whole-heartedly recommend this game to anyone looking for a chill time and a good laugh.
