"See that plane? Last one out of the country"
This review contains a good amount of history so the game is less confusing to people who arent fresh on African History, you have been warned.
Farcry 2 is a game that will at first, confuse people from the newer games in the farcry series.
To the untrained eye, this is a brutal, not fun, masochism sim. You will die, you will kill people you care about because they beg you to. You will run in the jungle away from packs of native Africans who are dying to cut your tendons and leave you to starve, but Malaria will get you first.
To kill the confusion, lets have some background
Farcry 1 was essentially a linear half life style shooter, albeit an incredibly difficult one. It has almost nothing in common with farcry 3 and 4, which can be summed up as giant playgrounds of 0 difficulty.
Farcry 2 is a mix. Open world, brutal, Quick tutorials, no holding your hand. This is Africa, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, not some cute little island, not the scenic mountains of India, every ♥♥♥♥ing thing in this country wants to kill and eat you, the people most of all.
The big components of later games, stealth, vehicles, first aid in first person, etc, are present here, but are not given to you nicely. You may not even realize the stealth system, exists until you are in a bush with 10 men with machetes walking by on the road, and they dont see you.. puzzling you as you realize this game is deeper than it looked.
In addition to all the features of later games, this game also has a ton of immersion. Your map is actually pulled out to use it, you get to pick from a selection of (Sadly only male) Characters and your choice affects your viewmodel, etc. Fire is even more realistic than later games and will change entire battles for minutes at a time, and is dynamic, If say for instance the fire spreads over a guys dropped gun or an ammo cache, the bullets might start going off from the heat, and best of all, guns deteroriate, and actually jam, realistically. One last mentionable feature which is quite interesting, is enemies in this game actually behave like people. They arent ludicrous men of no fear, they actually panic, and even flee. You will find yourself sniping a small outpost, and the last man you try to kill will book it into the jungle, the battle music stops, you raise a brow, you run around in the outpost like a tard trying to get him to notice you, assuming he just lost sight of you or ran the wrong way by accident,  but hes gone, he didnt want to die and instead of sitting around like every other NPC in every other game waiting to be shot, he ran away, Fight AND flight are represented here.
To be fair and describe both pros and cons, the game is missing a few features. There are no dangerous animals such as lions or crocodiles (The game devs felt this would make an already unfair and cruel game too frustrating, but I wish they had added them) Theres some very "African" scenarios that were never played on, such as hunting or big dangerous game with a large caliber gun, for instance. And one feature I feel would be super nice to have had is the ability to use a gun in cars, not while driving like Farcry 3 and 4, but just pull up your gun, letting go of the wheel, that kinda thing. You get ambushed by people in cars with massive machineguns in the back ALOT in this game, so having to change seats or get out of the car every time is a -massive- pain.
If you don't know anything about Africa, this game will also fly completely over your head, so let me spell out some stuff.
This game models itself after African countries such as Angola, which were heavily affected by the cold war. Multiple sides, sporting nicknames like UNITA or the MPLA, sprouted up. These sides usually were based on their tribal and ethnic origins, but they pretended to be for whoever was sending them weapons. An MPLA officer may scream joy for the soviets who buy my guns, joy for communism, but what he means is "Joy for my Tribe" the two sides in most of these battles cannot be told apart, and in this game that occurs too, which confuses many a player trying to find which one they want to support.
Once the cold war died down, these factions had lost their free toys, so now we have a bunch of tribes armed with ridiculously lethal weapons and no backers, so they start mining Africa's rich Diamond deposits and selling them off. These "Blood diamonds" fund wars in Africa that essentially still go on today.
So, in this game, you are a merc hired to track down a man who trades weapons for these diamonds. To do so, you work with various factions whose names are all acronyms just like real life African war-factions. You may also get jobs from certain locals, missionaries, "Princes" to take care of dirty work in a country abandoned by the world.  You will fight men with machetes, rockets, flamethrowers, but Africa itself is your worst enemy. Between psycho wildlife, malaria always a mere spell of sickness away, and the humidity and weather rotting your guns into dust in your own hands, this country wants you dead.
Do not buy this game expecting Farcry 3 africa edition. Buy this game expecting a rust-style survival simulator. Buy this expecting to be confused, afraid, lost, and desperate. Read heart of darkness, watch apocalypse now, get in that mood, that is the point. Do not buy this if you are afraid of unfair odds or unwinnable situations.
The last bit ill touch on is the buddy system. This was introduced to make resource management and the overall stress level even more horrifying. You have people, who will try to help you stay alive in various ways. You have a main one and can have side ones, and theyll actually exist and can be found in "Mikes bar" and they interact with eachother and you. They can do a number of things, giving you info, offering alternate ways to take on missions (These ways drastically alter the way a mission is played and are up to you to choose or not) and If you "die" they may save you, drag you to safety, etc. But they can die, in battle, on the way back, heck, you might be saved, 30 minutes later find your bleeding out on the side of a riverbank, some militants in an airboat shot him up? Why? because he was there. You can heal him, with one of your expensive needles, but what if you are out? then you can leave him there I suppose.
But he will beg you to end it... Embrace the pistol you put to his face, and you will pull the trigger.
The last plane out left as you arrived. Death is the only way out now.

Far Cry 2 is an open world FPS where you play as a merc hunting down "The Jackal"; a notorious arms dealer that has armed two warring factions (APR and UFLL) in an Unnamed African Country (UAC).
In terms of gameplay, you will spend most of your time doing the following:
-Driving through the jungle, savannah, desert, and rural town settings of the UAC.
-Shooting, exploding, burning, or sniping your way through hostile outposts, infrastructure buildings taken over by enemies, and the roads of the UAC.
-Looking for diamond cases.
-Completing main missions for both the APR and the UFLL; (kill this guy, destroy this outpost, destroy part of the UAC’s infrastructure) and side missions that include buddy missions (kill this guy, blow up this structure, retrieve this object) , underground missions (give these passports to these refugees to get Malaria pills) gun runner missions(blow up this weapons convoy), and assassinations (kill random guy in suit and his bodyguards). These are all the mission varieties you will ever have.
I listed driving first because you will be doing it A LOT in this game. There are only four fast travel points (bus stations) per section of the map (two sections); and most of your missions will force you to drive even if you take a bus to be closer to your destination. Unfortunately, driving in Far Cry 2 is hampered tremendously by two things: enemy patrols and the overall terrain. You can't go for even 4 minutes of driving without some patrol truck hunting you down. It gets worse at the second act of the game, when they get heavy mounted MGs and even one hit kill grenade launchers. Your vehicle will get stuck all the time in small holes in the ground, rocks, tree roots, small trees, other cars, etc. At least there’s a wide and believable variety of vehicles to choose from, ranging from trucks, ATVs, actual Jeeps, and even a buggy.

The shooting in this game can be immensely satisfying. You can either go in guns blazing with machine guns, snipe from afar, use a mortar to thin out enemy positions, burn them with a flamethrower, or blow them up with RPGs. Stealth is supposedly an option, but the game isn’t really built for it since shooting even with silenced weapons alerts all the enemies in the vicinity.
There are a lot of weapons to choose from, including assault rifles, pistols, machine pistols, LMGs, RPGs, sniper rifles, grenade launchers, etc. Experimenting with these will be your main incentive to obtain more diamonds, which will allow you to buy more of these weapons and their respective accuracy and reliability upgrades. Weapon jams and explosions are a feature of the game. The longer you use a weapon, the more prone it is to jam and eventually explode, and since all enemies use worn out weapons, buying from the arms dealer with your diamonds is a must.
The combat AI in this game is well designed for the most part. Wound an enemy and his ally will come to his aid, allowing you to kill them both. Enemies will shoot towards your last known location, and if you’re no longer there, you can flank and shoot them with ease. The AI feels dynamic and believable, but it is relentless. If you’re spotted by an enemy patrol they will chase you, even on foot, and shoot you until you take them out. It can be quite overwhelming to face more than five of them at a time, because the foliage will prevent you from shooting back properly.

Now, this game has several underdeveloped ideas that all aim towards a more “realistic” experience, but only interrupt gameplay and annoy the player. The worst offender by far is Malaria. You will need Malaria pills to treat your symptoms for every 40 minutes of real time. If your Malaria goes untreated, you will faint and magically reappear at the nearest main city. It breaks the flow of gameplay during exploration and missions. Were it not for Malaria, you wouldn’t even touch the Underground missions.
You can repair any damage to your vehicles, (from explosions to machinegun fire) by tightening a single socket in the engine. Buying the vehicle’s manual (10-20 diamonds per manual), allows you to tighten the socket faster, but there are no changes in the animations or in the way you repair vehicles. Overall, it’s much simpler to find a new vehicle instead of stopping every 5 minutes to repair.

In terms of player progression and overall changes in the game world, this game is quite lacking. When completing main missions,none of the factions will care that you recently murdered their leaders and hundreds of their comrades. Your missions are supposed to be “top secret” which supposedly explains why every outpost and soldier wants you dead even if you’re doing missions for their faction. But really, it’s too obvious that the developers simply didn’t code friendly AI for the soldiers. You will destroy a lot of the country’s infrastructure: the train tracks, the morphine production centers, the Malaria pill shacks, the WATER PIPELINES, the diamond mines, etc. You can visit these places again and see the destruction firsthand, but the amount and types of enemies, the amount of drinking water, diamonds, Malaria pills and the way to obtain them, will pretty much remain the same. Your efforts to support either faction end up feeling pointless.
The same happens with buddy missions. You can have two buddies: One for upgrading the many safehouses throughout the UAC, and one that can come to your rescue if you get fatally wounded. You earn points by doing additional mission objectives for your buddy, or doing buddy missions, which is really pointless considering that a “level 3 buddy” will give you all the same benefits as a “level 15 buddy”.  You never learn anything new from their stories, which are summed up in two or three sentences at most.
Hunting for diamond cases can be a lot of fun, but some of them seem to be impossible to reach. Nowadays it can be regarded as a way to pad out game length, but I found entertaining.
*SPOILERS*
The story in this game won’t pick up until the second act. You will support the equally tyrannical and selfish APR and UFLL because you’re looking for information about the whereabouts of the Jackal.

The developers need to be given credit for how gorgeous the game looks even for 2016 standards, and the style that they chose for the game. The game runs smoothly and beautifully on modern rigs, and asides from a few AI glitches, everything looks, sounds, and feels as if you were in an actual African jungle, savannah, or desert. Structures, vehicles and weapons look used, broken down, barely functional, worn out. It really adds to the immersion in a spectacular way. The way you can create dynamic bushfires in this game is amazing and a viable strategy in the drier regions of the map.
Despite all all of its problems, inconsistencies, glitches, and underdeveloped ideas, this game can be a lot of fun. It took me a while to complecomplete my first playthrough on Infamous difficulty, along with all the side missions, almost all of the diamond cases, and all the weapon and vehicle upgrades. All the while, I was having a blast on the combat segments; even if the driving wasn’t so smooth and game progression was non-existent. I can safely recommend this game to anyone remotely interested in open world or FPS games, just know that this ride can get a bit bumpy.

The puzzles aren't difficult, the bosses aren't difficult and only a few secrets push the boundaries of 'well hidden'. Ever since I was a child I have loved retro 1950’s sci-fi comic book style news announcements. You know the ones. During the introduction we’re advised of the imminent threat on the world. I find that they serve as a perfect hook to immerse you into their media form immediately. You’ve seen them on television, in movies and a number of video games have used them perfectly well. Fortified uses it perfectly to establish the tone and to introduce the characters and the setting. I found myself hooked and immersed into the game before gameplay had ever gotten underway. The campiness of the retro-futurism is something that I certainly appreciated.
It really is just the first sign that the game has been developed with intelligent game design choices throughout the entire creation process. Clapfoot have known exactly what they wanted to create, the elements that were required to be in their game and have clearly worked tirelessly to meld everything together into a fantastic tower defense game. For those who have played the Orcs Must Die games you will be immediately reminded of those games. There are also a lot of similarities between this and Dungeon Defenders as well. The games are essentially sharing the gimmicks that made both games such successes. That’s not a bad thing. There are differences, however, and those differences are enough to differentiate the two. Others have written of the similarities between this and Dungeon Defenders as well.
What differentiates Fortified from those games are the differentiated characters as well as the upgrade and status effect systems. Each of the four playable characters come with power ups that essentially make them invulnerable or overpowered for short periods of time. These can be powered up over time and utilized in one lengthy burst or simultaneously.  These systems are arguably the highlights of the game. Players combine their own abilities and weapons with constructed defenses to combat waves of enemies. When you complete each level you are granted experience points – the better you do the more experience points you get – and ultimately when you reach certain levels you will be granted levels. When you level up you are awarded unlock points that enable you to purchase both upgrades and new and better weapons.
If there is one major area of weakness that limits Fortified from becoming one of the best that the tower defense genre has to offer is a lack of depth. Unfortunately this is because status effects reign supreme and have a strong tendency to overpower every other weapon in your disposal. You’ll soon pick up on what weapons were optimally well for your play style and knowingly avoid the weaker weapons. The weapons that generally are overpowered are those that freeze and cause damage over time. You are also limited in what weapons and constructs you can take into a fight with you and thus your temptation to experiment is diminished.
What I did like about the constructs is that if you ever change your mind about the placement of one of them you can cash it in for a complete refund. That you’re not penalised for a poor choice for the remainder of a round is a nice bonus that will certainly please those who are inexperienced with games of this nature. Other games tend to favor a partial refund (generally half) so the change is nice. This system also enables you to place better systems in between rounds so on your second and consequential playthroughs you’ll learn to know what constructs are needed and where to place them. Each wave sends different numbers of enemies and in different placements than the previous wave. While it doesn’t solve the depth issue it does change the strategy.
There are 12 levels in the game and an estimated 6 hours is required to complete the game. With four different characters you can extend your gameplay but with the lack of depth you may not find enough variety to make it worth your while after the first playthrough. However, you can play with, up to, all four classes online. The game scales in difficulty dependent upon how many players are playing and thankfully the netcode has been well implemented.
If not for its lack of depth I would consider Fortified to be a great game. However, it falls short of that and is still a very good game recommended to those of you who are fans of tower defense games and especially to those who enjoyed Orcs Must Die!

FORTIFIED:
~~~~~~~~~
The Earth has been invaded by Martians! The population is terrified to the see flying saucers, robots and god knows what the hell these little creepy metallic spider thingies are coming down the street! Oh god, what are we going to do? Well, our prayers have been answered! The American Army has assembled a small and unique task force to pulverise these rather nasty aliens! Welcome to the 1950’s!

Fortified is a 3rd person shooter/strategy/tower defence game inspired by the 1950’s comic books genre. You will be able to play 4 different characters (The Captain, The Rocket Scientist, The Agent and The Spaceman) either on a solo or co-op game and try to beat 12 progressively challenging levels.
At the start of each level, you will choose your loadout which is 2 weapons and some structures. Each characters have their specific structures or weapons. Structures will cost money to layout, so choose carefully (important when you get further into the game) and place them in the right spot so you can inflict maximum damage to those “NASTY INVADERS (1950’s commentary voice)”. In a nutshell, you will defend one or several rockets and destroy the upcoming waves of aliens. The waves can attack from the ground or from the air so make sure you have the right combination or your rocket will probably be destroyed. Upon successfully beating the level, your character will increase his level and you will be given points which you can use to unlock new weapons and structures; you can also choose to upgrade your current weapons or structures.
I like the gameplay - it is fast and frantic especially in the latest level. Either you play solo or co-op. Killing Aliens will give you money and even during the gameplay you can purchase and place a new structures and you do not have to wait between the waves to do so.
The graphics are great and the game runs brilliantly and the audio is perfect. This is FUN, FUN, FUN gaming time!
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Great graphics
-	Solo & co-op modes
-	Great Gameplay with good replay ability
-	Straight out of the 1950’s comic book
-	Frantic & Fun
-	Achievements & trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Probably need a matchmaking for multiplayer
This is a brilliant game, good on every aspect and the price is right!
9.5/10

Short Verdict:
Basically just reskinned hearthstone, with a few additional game mechanics, that don't really change it that much.
Long Verdict:
Differences between heartsone and this:
Hearthstone only has a single board, whereas the board in this is split into 2 lanes, one of which has a special effect on it.
In hearthstone, the player who goes second gets the coin, which lets him gain 1 temporary mana whenever he chooses.
In this, you basically get 3 of those if you go second.
In this, you get to draw cards every time your health drops by a certain amount - this feature is absent from hearthstone, and is actually one of the few unique things in this game that give it an advantage.
Also a few other things, like hero powers being absent, and you instead get these... supports? Basically hero power, but a card.
Hearthstone's main advantage is that it's tried and tested, and very extensive. Meaning, it has way more content, and just feels a lot more polished.
All of these new features just feel like feeble attempts to differentiate this game from Hearthstone.
If ya want a card game, go play hearthstone.

The best of the Wizardry games. It lacks the occasional obtuseness of the earlier games(both in terms of puzzle solutions and actual mechanics), not to mention their often poorly-aged interfaces, and it's a game that rewards clever ambushing and positioning.
It's just a shame that it never quite got finished. The end of the scenario has some parts that just don't happen(like your allies, if you have any, showing up at Ascension Peak), and the end of the game also has some gameplay issues. Firstly is the part where it tends to involve much larger battles than any other part, and the game's combat speed, even at max, means that battles against 20+ enemies tend to take forever until you start murdering them. Secondly is the issue where enemy magic resistances in the endgame are rarely lower than 90, meaning that a caster-heavy party is essentially useless at that point if they're not backed up by some physical bruisers.
Nonetheless, for all its flaws, it's definitely a game I'd actually recommend people play.

I'm recommending this game. While the lack of polish, lack of key features and numerous bugs is initially off-putting, this game does the most essential aspect, the driving, really well. SLRE has a great handling model, and offers a nice variety of vehicles and a quality set of tracks. Racing those narrow, twisty courses is challenging and very intense, yet intuitive.
Driving the rally cars is a lot of fun. On loose surfaces the cars are quite sensitive to weight shifts and you can gleefully throw them around corners. But you have to watch out for high speed corners and for jumps. On tarmac the cars feel planted, but can be easily upset if you are careless (it's hard to recover if you lose traction), and there is good feedback from wheel slip. There are a multitude of surfaces: dry and wet gravel, mud, snow, dry, wet and icy tarmac. They feel naturally distinct and it's a total blast to ride the mixed tracks.
The FFB is good. You can feel the SAT, torque steer, weight shifts to the front, etc... It's complemented by an effective and unobtrusive bump/suspension feedback.
The tracks are of great quality. Narrow, meandering, bumpy, with elevation changes and varying surfaces. Each of the 8 locations has 4 tracks (2 long and 2 short) totaling about 31 km, plus the reverse versions. There also are 5 RX tracks + tarmac Pikes's Peak. There is not much weather variety, but the night lighting is well done.
The career mode is quite varied. It's basically a random collection of races restricted to a vehicle or vehicle class. Besides Rally, RX and Hillclimb, there are a few other somewhat gimmicky game modes. Then there are the Loeb related events: you can unlock some cars and learn about the champion's career.
There are a few disappointments. Given the lack of communication from the developers it's possible they will never be addressed.
In some ways the game is a perfect complement to Dirt Rally. SLRE lacks the polish and all the key features that DR has, but offers a better handling model and twice the content.
Now for the sake of bookkeeping here are a few of the most annoying bugs/deficiencies.

Let's be realistic.  For the size of the developer this game is great!  It's best played with three monitors and My Fanatec gear works flawlessly.  I don't like the fact that it can't support my handbrake but I work around it by assigning my sequential shifter as the handbrake and use paddles for shifts.  Adding this feature would drastically help immersion of the game and improve its status to a true sim.  There are three simple reasons to get this game:
1. Amazing tarmac feel and rally stages
2. Best weight feel of the car out of any rally sim
3. Weight transfer feel when braking.  You actually have to slow down when approaching a corner, unlike other rally sims, and not because you are sliding, but because you can feel the weight of the car either causing a slide or shifting the car out of balance.  This is very unique to this game and has helped my driving in other sims as a result.
I used to be all for Richard Burns rally, but I would rate this game second to Dirt Rally, and RBR third.

Far Cry 2 is an action open world game developed by Ubisoft Montreal and published by Ubisoft. It was released in October 2008. You, play as a mercenary sent into Africa in the midst of a war between the APR and UFLL. Both sides are wanting power and control of the nation. This review will discuss the campaign and the open world element and provide a general recommendation in the conclusion.
Far Cry 2 features a very good and tight campaign. The story is simple, you are a merc and you will bid for any of the factions that pay you the most. The caveat is you have to complete missions for both sides, which do eventually learn that you are doing work for the enemy. Story-wise, the game really drives down the power hungry aspect of things in which you have to assassinate leaders, and multiple of them. It’s a strong narrative and I immensely enjoyed the story and the twisting elements of it. Furthermore, I did not experience the 'Ubisoft bug' where it hits about 15 hours in the game and it feels like a chore to complete it, which is a refreshing thing to say about an older Ubisoft game.
The main characters in the game, whether it is enemy characters or allied buddies, have distinct personalities. In particular, your buddies have a very brief journal in the game that allows you to discover and learn of their background. Buddies are important because when you gain a main mission they contact you to provide an alternative approach to the mission, which has many benefits including making the mission easier, increasing your reputation and upgrading your safe house. Further into the game it becomes fairly irrelevant as you get more powerful.
The open world element is very nice, it isn't too large but it isn't small. There are two maps, both have safe zones, and a variety of areas including enemy guard posts, gun shops, and so forth. All of these provide the open world aspect of it. Furthermore, the side missions actually add to the game. For instance, you can get missions from the church to help you cure your malaria illness, which is essential. Or, you can go to the gun shop and do their specific missions to unlock more weapons for you to purchase. In other words, side missions are not filler, rather the majority of them add to the experience of the game.
The gameplay portion is absolutely fun and realistic. If you have shoddy weapons for example, they can jam mid-battle causing you to flee before retackling the objective. The story is realistic in that there is no money, rather the currency is diamonds. I enjoyed the little things in the game per say as they added realism to the game.
I experienced some notable annoyances and glitches. The first was the health system because the enemy somehow have very accurate accuracy as it hurts if they hit you and it takes several bullets to hit them, which actually becomes annoying and unrealistic. Furthermore, I absolutely hated enemies automatically respawning at guard posts. Second, when you answer the phone during missions or at any time during the game, the dialogue does not pop up on the screen and there is no sound, meaning there is a glitch. Lastly, there were multiple crashes when trying to save the game.
Far Cry 2 is a pretty good game. It features a thrilling story that is both compelling and immersive. It provides a very realistic and accurate take on the current state of civil war in Africa in contemporary times. I enjoyed the gameplay, in particular the elements that made it more realistic such as weapon jamming and weapons getting rusty. In contrast, there are major glitches relating to dialogue and crashes that did hurt my play-through. I feel this game would have been excellent provided there was no multiplayer and the focus was the single player as it was nearly great. In saying that, I totally recommend this game, as I enjoyed it considerably.
8/10
- Excellent story with twists and turns.
- Gameplay.
- Realism.
- Side missions as they did not feel like filler content.
- Crashes.
- Bugs within the game.
- Enemy AI, in relation to gameplay but also enemy respawning.

Far Cry 2 is the sequel of the FPS Far Cry, this time set in the heat of Africa. It involves hunting down "The Jackal", the feared arms-dealer that fueled the war between two nations. Meanwhile, you're also constantly fighting against your contracted malaria.
PROS:
+ Pretty long gameplay
+ Good graphics despite its age and can run well on lesser devices
+ Immediate freeroaming (in both areas once you reach the next)
+ A good variation of satisfying-to-use guns
+ Lovable open nature of flora and fauna (as cheesy as that sounds)
+ Raiding outposts and towns is incredibly fun
+ Has a map editor which is pretty funny to fool around with
+ Packed with the Fortune's Pack DLC which includes a few more weapons, alt machete, vehicles and lore
+ Fair price/content ratio
CONS:
- The missions and various subjects (music, sounds, voice lines, etc.) are slightly repetitive
- The health system and certain damage sources are a bit odd/unrealistic
- The voice acting sounds like it is sped up somtimes
- During my probably 200 hours on both the disk as well as the Steam version I've come across numerous small bugs like missing or invisible textures, sound malfunctions, AI glitches, odd mechanical behavior, etc.
It's a little hard to explain why, but this game really feels like a masterpiece; it plays smoothly, it's fun, let's you freeroam rather quickly and feels a little realistic as well. Definitely one of the most enjoyable and memorable games I've ever played.

Welcome to Loathing! If you've been around the Kingdom before, please allow a few moments for your corporeal self to adjust to the transition from text to animation. If you're  a KoLMafia user, you'll be glad to see an abundance of that blue text that tells you what stuff does when you're making decisions. If you're big on referencing the KoLWiki during your travels, a quick google search will show you that there's one out here, and the West doesn't have to be seat-of-your-pants-blind-flying wild unless you want it that way. Also note that Ascension doesn't happen here; you have but one life to live per save game. Like the full Kingdom, this game does benefit from more than one playthrough (how else will you ever own all the horses?!), and is totally worth the admission price of 1.1 Mr. Accessories.
If you haven't been to the Kingdom before, please allow several hours for your spiritual self to adjust to our denser than normal textual and contextual humor and our puzzles that may take a few tries to solve. Keep your eyes peeled, look at everything you pick up, use google or check out a guide if you get stuck (KoL has always had a lovely and active community of smart, sweet people), and don't forget to have a good time.

If there's one thing I like, its pie, if theres another thing I like, its simplistic RPGs with comedy elements. That sort of thing is, unfortunately, quite rare these days, but West of Loathing took on that challenge with pride and a beautiful spitoon on its head. Having a game that is not only fun to play, but genuinely funny, is probably one of the strangest and best combinations in the world. Its been a while since I've had a game make me fall out of my chair, (and I'm not saying that for the cliche, I actually fell out of my chair at one point in the game) and West of Loathing managed that and quite a few other lovely little niches that have made me fall in love with the game. So yes, play West of Loathing, play it again and again until your tower of spitoon hats has reached Pluto.

Nothing was better for my relationship than Guardian of Light, because it taught me to never trust my girlfriend when I cross a pit of spikes.
The experience of playing GoL can easily be compared to Trine, and approaches the same level of co-op/ killing each other excellence. GoL is a mixture of puzzles, combat, arcade elements, and platforming all done from an isometric perspective. Most of the puzzles are clever and juggle between challenging players’ finesse and problem solving skills. There are deadly traps to avoid, and a fun physics system helps transform something as mundane as a boulder into basketball, transportation, or even makeshift artillery. A lot of these shenanigans will lead to player death, but that is also part of the fun.
The combat is a mix of shooting and planting bombs that are detonated remotely. The controls feel tight, and dodge rolling keeps combat fair and exciting. Combat is also the area where the arcade elements are strongest: each level has a set of various challenges that are completed to boost score and unlock new items directly. The unlocks ranges from new weapons to stat boosts and offers players a healthy amount of options when comes to fighting foes. The arcade style of challenges also pushes players to die less, complete levels faster, and complete some neat tasks. None of the challenges ever get in the way of enjoying the game, and are generally a mix of things that can be done easily on the way to completing the campaign, and more difficult tasks that require practice.
The absolute most important aspect of the game is the cooperative experience. Having someone to race with leaping across platforms, blow up with bombs, drop into a pit of spikes, leave behind, lock into cages, lead into traps, and just betray in general is a large part of what makes this game fun. Lara and her partner Totec are designed to rely on each other: he has a spear that he’s too fat to climb on but can help Lara reach new areas or a shield to lift and shield Lara, and she a grappling that can support the elephant that is Totec. Co-op also allows players to revive each other, which comes in handy when killing each other. Throughout the game it is simply a lot of fun to work together to find secrets, complete challenges, win, and mess around in general. With every person I play this game with, we end up making our own little challenges and games: balancing on a boulder as we mow down enemies, tag, horse with explosives and boulders, testing how far we can fall into spikes before being saved, etc. and it is an excellent diversion.
Lara Croft and The Guardian of Light hits all the marks of a great spinoff and a great co-op experience. I had more fun with this than any other Tomb Raider game, so much so that I bought it multiple times on different platforms. The levels are well designed, the mechanics all feel balanced, and the game is well paced. Sure there is a story that can easily be ignored, but that pushes the game towards an arcade experience focused on having fun with your friends. Out of all the local co-op games I have played, including the old console days, GoL easily ranks high up on the list. That being said, solo is pretty fun on its own, but never quite reaches the same level of satisfaction.

What can be said that hasn't already been stated? This game is great in so many ways, and the modding community only makes it better. It's one of those games that you really should try, and some say it's the best of the 3D Fallout games. Others even say it tops the original isometric games. It certainly tops Fallout 4 in terms of roleplaying experience, though not as much with combat. Still, it's a very fun game and definitely worth a purchase if you like RPGs. I encourage you to get the Ultimate Edition though, especially if you have an interest in trying out mods, as some of the better mods require the DLC. Still, the vanilla game is quite good on its own, but modding is one of the game's main selling points, as it can only personalize your experience and make it even better.
For example, while there are a number of bugs, there are mods that both solve bugs and increase the game's stability. And of course there's mods that improve graphics, animations, and gameplay. Some even add hours and hours of quest content and new places to explore. Plus, this game is really freakin' orange because of the desert setting, and it used to bother me and hurt my eyes after a while, but even that can be fixed with mods that give the environment more clarity in color.
If you want a game that's great and perfectly set up right "out of the box" so to speak, then this might not be for you. While it is a good game, I can't imagine going back to vanilla after jumping on the modding bandwagon and making the game look and function much better with mods of my choosing. Once you can mod in sprinting functionality, it's hard to go back.
Modding itself is quite addicting and almost therapeutic when you start to get into it. Setting things up, making everything work together, troubleshooting when it doesn't - it takes time, but is worth it and ultimately the experience is what you make of it.
Regardless, whether you mod or not, I can easily say that I recommend this game. It's one of the best and most memorable RPGs I've ever played.

I originally wrote a negative review about the game, and while it does have its faults and shortcomings, after playing it more and a patch from the developers, I've grown to enjoy it. The game is very enjoyable, it's pretty to look at, runs well and smooth and coop is easy to setup and play. The developers have already released a patch and fixed a few major issues that inclined me to write a negative review initially. They did an AMA on reddit and seem like cool guys so I expect and hope for continuing support for the game.
- The texture and model work is really well done and pleasing to look at
- Pretty and orginized UI
- Game runs smooth in and out of combat and is well optimized
- 4 individually leveled classes add more replayability
- Can manually control unit-based defenses (Go to waypoint, hold position, follow, defend objective)
- 5-7 Hour 12 level campaign
- Occasional bosses
- Pleasantly difficult
- Coop is easy to setup and play
- Good balance between being a TPS and a TD
- Chill and dedicated developers (so far)
-----
The game has a hint of being underdeveloped or not quite finished. It could use some polish here and there and could definitely use more content. The campaign is long, but the defenses and weapons start overlapping when you start playing new characters, leaving you with things you've already had just at different levels. I'd love to see more TD mechanics like defense attack priority, in game statistics (enemy count, defense unit stats, etc), more upgrades and more defenses in general.
- Bland level design and lack of world detail
- Character animations can look really cheesy and don't match up with movement/look floaty
- Most defenses and weapons are accessible with every class
- Very simple game, not a lot of in depth mechanics or content
- No incoming or remaining enemy count
- Can't see attack radius of all allied defenses which makes it harder to plan out defenses
- Combat can feel unresponsive at times with certain weapons
- Enemies and players can get (permenatly) stuck in/on world objects
- No in game text chat
- Cannot mute voice chat for specific players (likely to change with patches)
- Only ~3 lines of dialogue for each character so get ready to have them memorized quickly
- Max out character level/unlocks fairly quickly
-----
I recommend it. It's cheap, it's fun, and it's coop. If you're a hardcore TD fan you'll notice that the TD mechanics are relatively simple and shallow, but in the end it is a blast to play. It's a great game if you're into Action TD's and takes a lot of influence from Orcs Must Die so if you enjoyed that, there's a good chance you'll like this. After spending over 6.5 hours in the game, I have identified a game-killing bug which breaks the entire profitability model of the game.  Essentially there are only two selling points.  One to sell logs (you don't make much money here), and one to sell boards (you make a bit more than just selling logs).  When you sell boards at the board selling point, the game immediately crashes to the desktop every time.  I've tested twice on two separate saves, and confirmed the crash 3 times.  I'm confident it will continue to crash.
On top of that, the game's engine appears to be the same or a newer iteration of the game engine from Professional Farmer 2014.  There does seem to be a lot more detail on the map compared to Pro Farmer 2014 though.  It is a completely different map though, just to be clear.
Certain assett (like some buildings, etc) elements and sound effects are also identical to Professional Farmer 2014.
The overall graphics are good, but not great.  There are indeed some beautiful day and night effects, but then the main vehicles that you'll be using in the game all look like toys that a 5 year old would play with.  Many of the controls are also incredibly simplistic.  For example, cutting down a tree requires a single right click.  To pick up a log, you just take your loader and right click it once, and it pops into the loader.  Take it to the trailer, right click, and bam!  it's in the trailer.  As such, this game is probably going to appeal more to smaller children who haven't developed their motor skills yet, or for people who want a logging experience without the complexity of other games.
As far as other bugs go, there are several places in the game where there are buildings, log piles or other objects floating in mid air.  Cars constantly weave left and right like drunk drivers.  Roads and streets are lazily laid out on the map.  The game's engine is really just horrible.  Either that or the graphics artists responsible for creating the world are just horribly lazy.
I'm running an Intel i7-5960X processor (currently intel's BEST i7 as of March 2015), 16GB of RAM, an NVidia GTX 980, and the game is installed to an SSD.  Average FPS is about 50-60fps at 2560x1440p.  No idea how the game performs on lesser machines, though I may do some testing on my older gaming PC.
Also, the game REQUIRES DirectX 11.  If your video card is a bit older and doesn't fully support DirectX 11, then this game will never run on your PC regardless of what you do until you upgrade your video card.  If you've got a laptop that doesn't support DX11, then you're pretty much entirely screwed.  You'll need to buy a new laptop with a video card that supports DX11.  This may or may not kill the deal for some buyers.  Personally, DirectX 11 is a better engine for games, but only if you can run them.
All said, as it stands now, I cannot recommend this game.  It seems to be more of the fodder that we've been fed from the likes of Playway and UIG (or in this case, UIE.  Same company, same crap).  If they can fix the fatal crash and fix some of the other bugs, then they game might be worth about $10 bucks, but not much more.
For a much better forestry experience, just do yourself a favor and pick up Farming Simulator 15.  It has much better forestry overall than this game.

If you like Farming Simulator 15's tree cutting... don't buy this, run back to it as fast as you can.
The physics are from 2001, tree cutting is automated (you just drive to a spot and press Right Click when it tells you).
Let me save you some money and don't buy it :)

One of my favourte games of all time, everytime I stop playing its lure draws me back into it, a fantastic world while not adding to the gameplay with random events, immerserses the player in a war torn Africa. Gueardpost litter the road which creates an uneasy feeling of isolation as you, a lone mercenary must choose to sneak past or run in guns blazing. Having started a new playthrogh on the Infamous diffiuculy (Dylan's Realism Mod) I must say that the tension is a firefight keeps me engaed for hours, stalking an enemy outpost as you silently kill the snipers is a as satifying as the moment you clear out the gurardpost and not a single shot is fired by the enenmy.
However the game does have its nagetives, the respawning outposts may make you angry, I do appreciate the added challenge having to tackle it agiain, maybe this time I attack from a diffrent angle or try a diffrent weapon. Keeps the game feeling fresh, the only time this really beacame an issue is there a outlost near the fort where you must give the Prince his Father's ring, the outpost tends to respawn too quickly and because of the dense foilage, its very hard to engage in combat. The stealth mechanics aswell appear to be very strange, ranging from "Wow how did he not hear that',"I'm so clsoe to him how does he ot see me" to "How the heck did he know where I was". The enemy AI reacts strangly to stealth as they could be as oblivius as a rock or as aleart as an eagle with x-ray goggles .
Other than a few dumb moments the AI is this games is fantastic! If you fire apon them with a sniper rifle they will run into cover and hide, while other gurads will flank your location. They communicate in comabat and dicuss and carry out tactics in real time. If they lose sight of you they begin searching the immidiate area, confidently shelling put insults, while if you slay too many of his buddies, they begin to get scared. If you wound a soldier, his friend will carry him to safety.
One point that really set this as one of my favourate video games is the games interaction with fire, one small ember can set a whole guard post on fire and these interations with the environment that truely creates an authentic game world, where the AI reacts postivly or naegtivly to the spreading wildfire. You start one simply by shooting a oil lamp with the dart rifle creating a distraction as you move in. While fire does carry over into Far Cry 3, its lush tropical forests does not really empashise the deadly viral spreading of a wildfire like Far Cry 2 can.
If you always thought about playing this game, get it on a sale and the Dylan's Realism Mod, it truly pushes the game into another level as you are as fragile as your enimies. If enjoy a game where you like choosing to fight or stay stealthy, this game for you. At 4K on the GTX 1080, this game looks stunning and runs like butter smooth!!

Most reviews I've read of this game painted a pretty grave picture of how bad of a game this is. Well, coming from Dirt Rally, a great rally game in it's own right, I was certainly skeptical going into this one. The demo didn't really work well with my control setup and I wasn't stoked on the menu system and having to exit the race to adjust your controls.
The narrator has a funny voice. I guess the american language version of the game isn't quite up to the english version, but sometimes you get random voiceovers glitching in so you can hear what you're missing every once in a while.
Setting up the controls is a huge pain, because there is no support for multiple inputs. Meaning, you can't have a separate USB handbrake work at the same time as your wheel. My TH8A shifter works with my Thrustmaster wheel and T3PA pedals, thank goodness, but it really is a setback not being able to use my handbrake and button panel.
Having said that, once you DO get your controls set up as best as you can, the game is a lot of fun. There is lots of fun in unlocking things and earning money in the game to graduate through the world championships or whatever this game calls it. ALSO, going through Seb's carreer is also pretty cool.  Though the framerate can be bad and there are a bunch of funny glitches (random navigator language change mid race, lol) It's really a lot of fun. Especially the RallyCross section, which I think actually does better than dirt, though the lack of a guy in your ear is sort of a letdown.
TL;DR: Not Dirt Rally, but a fun almost-sim in it's own right. This game has the best rallycross of all of the rally games I've played. If you get it on sale, it can be a fun time.

West of Loathing is a lot of things, but what it is most of all is an epic Stickman Western. Part Spaghetti Western, part Eastwood Western, part Monty Python, but all fun and hilarity.
The story in West of Loathing is one of love and loss. You are the witty protagonist, a stick man teen set off from his family’s home to explore the world. Unfortunately, Cows from Hell are rampaging all along the countryside, and so you begin investigating that while simply exploring your world, meeting new stick people and forming friendships (and enmities) along the way.
The comedy in West of Loathing never relents, and is very much in the fusion of Clint Eastwood meets The Holy Grail. Of course, this is a western, but the memes and pop culture references also never relent, and to optimal effect. The writing is just awesome, tongue in cheek, and hilarious.
9 out of 10
West of Loathing is a stickman game, and so you can expect sketch art as the medium of expression here. Mostly black and white, minimalist sketch art. Again, this is done to optimal effect and it really becomes endearing and comfortable. While the artwork is sparse, it is as evocative as it is effective. Also, the style really assists in the healthy serving of sarcastic exposition you will encounter throughout.
9 out of 10
The gameplay in West of Loathing is really a combination of 2-D open world exploration and JRPG style combat.
There is an overlay map, from which you will explore the open terrain finding towns, old mines, ranches, forts, and other random spots. The 2-D map, from which you will handle direct exploration, combat, dialogue, and so on is set up in pretty basic fashion. You have your base areas and then buildings/caves/etc…that you can explore. No one area  is very large, but each makes complete sense as far as its design goes and fits perfectly with the overall theme of the game.
The combat system is handled in traditional JRPG style face offs with some very forgiving RNG’s (random number generators), base attacks, special attacks, and of course item usage. It’s actually a pretty easy game and you really shouldn’t die very often.
To assist in this, you have an infinite number of inventory slots with which to carry the various  weapons, limited use items (such as food and drink for buffs, items which cause specific types of damage, healing objects, lockpicks, and of course crafting materials.
Crafting is an essential part of this game and you will craft a lot of items through the course of your adventure. It happens in a variety of ways as well. For example, you will need a stove to bake bans, a silversmiths table to craft silver bullets and lockpicks, etc...
Additionally, you can and will build relationships, via conversations and/or side quests. The side quests often poke fun at the standard RPG tropes by making you do them almost to the point of exhaustion while also making fun of the situation as you do. In fact, this game in general is about breaking down and making fun of the RPG standards.
There is actually quite a bit more to this surprisingly deep game, but I’ll leave off for now.
9 out of 10
The audio is actually done to perfection. From the ambient sounds you would expect from a western to music that would fit in any Clint Eastwood film, you are in for a treat with regards to the audio in West of Loathing.
10 out of 10
West of Loathing is a game that, simply by appearance, can be easily dismissed. However, that would be a mistake as it actually ended up being an excellent game worthy of at least on and possibly even two or three playthroughs. You will be doing yourself a favor by picking this one up.

I was naturally drawn to Wizardry because I'm a fan of the old Might and Magic games.
No regrets.

I have owned this game for many years, its still ugly and quirky (be sure to enable xp compatibility mode). BUT it is an interesting "first person" like version of a classic wizardry game. Create your party however you like, this will not only allow you to play in the style you choose, but bringing along different races gives you different opportunities as you explore the world. Oldschool, no hand holding, just explore and have fun.

They just don't make games like this anymore. I consider Wizardry 8 to be one of the last tobust party-based dungeon crawler RPGs. It offers a TON of content in a charming fantasy/sci-fi world with a lot of attention to detail. The developers clearly made this game because they loved doing so and wanted to share that with the players. They spared no expense (RIP Sirtech...) to create this massive world to explore and plunder. In fact, there are even some "secret areas" that are as large as something that offer enough content they'd be sold as $10 DLC add-ons nowadays.
Pros:
- Heaps of content
- Good RPG mechanics
- Fun party-based interactions
- Great theme with well developed lore
- Good NPC conversations with full voice-acting
Cons: Basically it's old
- Slow combat (you can get a mod for this. I recommend it)
- Dated graphics
- Repetitive sound bank
- Controls feel outdated
- Unforgiving - even on easy difficulty, this will be hard. Expect pain. Quick-save often. Learn and improve. This is ultimately a positive for me but presents a steep learning curve.
9/10. I would pay good money to see a HD remaster with some modern luxuries.

I'll try to keep it short (gonna be difficult).
Intro: Played this game about 10+ years ago (could be 15+)... in Russian, and it still was cool when I was so young I had no idea what was going on half the time. I remembered deep char creation, went back to try it.
First day experience: I spend half day creating my party of 6. Every following character took more time. Truth be told, I spent most the time reading and looking up info online on classes, combos, strengths ect, but I can tell you... it is VERY DEEP. Especially because the way it balances the classes isn't "linear"... Classes have tiers, basically meaning more powerful and imba ones are harder to play and are a lot weaker earlier and require more exp per level as well as pumping resources (time and ingame money) into them.
Unique points:
* Classes - As described in "First Day". I think it was 15+ different ones? They partially overlap.
Example#1 - I love the fact that you can have a mage, that can cast everything in the game. But the class is so sh't and useless first half of the game, that it's not an insta-pick unless you want a challange.
Example#2 - Variety of "tank" options... You can either be unkillable, because you have a %-chance to ressurect. OR you can have insanely high health regen, to be hard to bring down in the first place. OR you can have so fat armor that nothing really even scratches you. OR you can be so hard to hit (enemy miss), only option is AoE spells. Every option also has weaknesses in certain ways, which you can also try to mitigate...
* This game enemy scaling is probably amongst the best I've seen in many RPGs. Grinding your character levels and skill early on doesn't make the rest of the game significantly easier, nor does it severely punish you either. I feel like I've significantly leveled up and improved my stats (some of my main attributes are maxed) and yet I still feel going to beginner areas somewhat of a challange.
* Looting - You have loot that is visible on the floor, loot that is in chests/containers and loot that is "invisible" but you require a certain skill to "see" it. [either Ranger in party with it or "Search mode" or certain Active-Spell]
* Strong status effects - Not just "different" versions of DoT damages ( like many RPGs do ) but actual status-effects that impact the combat, some are annoying enough because they're "permanent". Meaning they persist until taken care of with a strong status-specific potion or some other means (but there's enough ways to not feel cheesed either).
* Races and Factions! - Amongst the most amount of interesting races (for me), without them all being "cheesy" as most modern RPGs... Mouse/Hamster people fighting against Rat people, awesome... Fish faced dudes, Robotic aliens, Half slime-insects, giant hairy gorillas... Also finally NO DRAGONS (they've been severely overused and are boring)
* Journal - It has several interesting features.
1) No cluttered useless chit-chat or background info you don't need.
2) Quest hints and info is quite steamlined and slim, basically couple keywords.
3) Doesn't hold your hand and make you feel like a ret'rd by telling you where to go and what to do precisely.
* Inventory man.- this is done brilliantly. I love looting and this game enables it, but at the same time it has some "soft" penalties for being a pack-yak.
Weak points:
* Graphics obviously outdated. Doesn't bother me though.
* So many awesome races existing in the game that you cannot create a character from. Sadly it'd probably break story logic, but hell I want to make a party of slime-insects or Fish-faces!
* I'm not a game dev, but I see oceans of opportunities and "easy" ways to deepen the game and add replayability imo.
* Many items despite different stats, qualities and names have same visual icon. This doesn't bother me, but in a modern game I would address this.
* Game objective and quest log "can" be confusing, but it has a good effect to it [read Unique points.]
* This game has interesting universe, wish there was like a "encyclopedia" to turn back to, to read up on what you've collected or found on different factions, races, events ect.
Conclusion: This is the kind of game, that makes me search for similar games in similar genre, that are as little as 10 years newer. P.S If you find anything that can come close, let me know.

I like games with a lot of replayability. When I think about how much I've replayed this game (which is probably dozens), it would probably count as my favorite game. Considering that to be true, my experience wasn't exactly golden from the start, but I am glad that I did get back into it.
I bought this game a long time ago before it was ever on Steam and I played it once and I didn't quite get the feel for how to run a party composition and I failed to get far in. I ended up setting the game down for a good 4 or 5 years before I picked it back up on a whim.
It may take a bit of trial and error feeling out a good party composition, or one that you can work with. If you have any experience with table top rpgs, you may have an easier time balancing out what you need to have a good experience. Several party compositions work, of course, but you many need more experience to use them as adaptly.
You will always (at least if you're new) need a good melee tank or 2 to absorb the volume of attacks that tend to target the front row, and that can be filled by a fighter, lord or valkyrie well enough, but some classes can really help you get along with what the game gives you
In general, Rangers, Bards, and Gadgeteers are a good boon for a party because of their various strengths for how the game is set up.
Rangers auto search for hidden items that you could run over and prevent you from a surprise penalty on initiative for combat that toggling a manual search does to you, and their ranged attacks scale well for late game.
Bards are useful because they can utilize all the instruments scattered throughout the game that can have some powerful magic effects by spending some stamina. They also can function well enough at a melee spot if you build vitality for a good amount of stamina (needed for instruments) and hit points.
Gadgeteers also benefit from various scattered parts in the game that can be combined to make gadgets that function much like the bard's instruments, very powerful as you progress. Their omnigun also grows more useful as they level with added chance effects that can help weaken enemies and have a growing list of ammunition types. ( % chance blind, unconsciousness and other effects on hit, can use rocks and musket balls and later darts, bolts and arrows)
Magic begins a little sparce for casters, but ramps up toward mid level depending on which class and which schools of magic you spend points on (using magic can also add points in that school). You may want to spend heavily on one element to begin with and between magic usage and increased access as you level, you'll be more free to effectively spend points on other magic later on.
Despite some difficulties when you're new, the game can be intimidating with an imbalanced party, but don't be afraid to play around with it. If you really push through into this game, you'll find exactly how great this game is. You have a lot of freedom with how to proceed and you can make allies with just about any faction. You can attack anyone too, but just make sure that you can survive the consequences (or save first).
Another friendly note: the Rapax Rift/Castle areas can be a deadly in the mid game if you're not ready to take on a high number of exceptionally strong enemies, though you generally get a good taste of you may fair in the swamps. Don't be afraid to flee a combat either, you may be unlucky enough to encounter a strong wandering mob of enemies that hit like trucks.
Anyways - Survival is very rewarding in this game, save often if you see uncertain creatures on the horizon, or just run the other way. Leveling up feels good, and not too many games these days has that level of satisfaction with each level you gain. Don't be afraid to use a guide if you get stuck, I never did, but it can really help if you're not used to this style of rpg. It is a great game if you have the knack or patience to learn its ins and outs. It really was ahead of its time in many ways.

Fallout: New Vegas is the fourth Fallout we should have gotten, but sadly we got the garbage pile that was just Fallout 4 instead. But that's another review for another day. Thanks to mods and the modding community, this game can be changed to make it look like it was developed and released in 2017. To bring this game up to speed with current hardware, I'd recommend getting the following mods from the Nexus website:
Please note that in order to utilize these mods properly, you must use the Fallout New Vegas Script Extender.
Fallout New Vegas is literally the best of the best experience when it comes to open world first person shooters with RPG elements in it. Obsidian literally fixed EVERYTHING that was wrong with Bethesda's release of Fallout 3, and even surpasses Bethesda's latest title, Fallout 4, in many ways. Traits are back from the first two Fallouts and some mods add even the original traits from the first two games. Speech checks are now based on a specific number rather than a percentage chance so that if you want to win speech checks, you HAVE to build your character around charisma a bit. You can't completely ignore charisma anymore by reloading a save, but instead if you want to be able to convince someone, you have to actually level up your speech skill or you don't pass the speech check. Energy weapons actually feel powerful enough that it's now a skill worth investing points into. I could write an essay on why New Vegas surpasses Bethesda's failure of a game that is Fallout 4, but if you buy this game, you'll instantly realize just how much better this game is compared to Bethesda's releases and how this game hearkens back to the development and gameplay style of Fallout 1 and 2. If Fallout 5 turns out to be developed by Obsidian and retains the proper RPG elements that New Vegas is known and loved for, then I will be very happy to buy it day one.

Quick Note:  I am aware that my earlier reviews aren't all that good.  While it's a little too late to do anything about, the least I can do is do better.  So for now on, I'll give a more detailed review on these games.  So hopefully you'll enjoy them more than the others.  Now on to the review...
Fortified is a Tower Defense game mixed with 3rd-Person shooting, and it is developed and published by Clapfoot.  The game takes place in the 1950s during a Martian Invasion.  Humanity is in danger and it's up to four brave people, each with their own set of arsenals, to protect Earth and repel the Invasion.  The game also features a 4-player Co-Op mode, where players can work together to play the game's 12 maps plus the Invasion mode.
I was actually interested in this game, mostly because I grew up playing a ton of tower defence games in Newgrounds, both good and bad.  I also liked how the game's presentation utilizes the setting to make it look and sound like it's a 1950s alien invasion comic.  Although for some reason, I'm getting that Team Fortress 2 vibe while playing this game.  I can't be the only person thinking that, right?
I enjoyed Fortified for what it is, this is a game that makes for a pretty good time killer.  Something to pass the time when you are up for some Martian killing, tower defense-style.  The mechanics of the game has you setting up defenses and repeling the invasion.   Before that, you have to choose which of the four classes will you be playing as: The Captain, The Rocket Scientist, The Agent, and the Spaceman (whom I blame for the invasion).  Each has their own playstyle, structures, and weapons although some of them are shared with other classes.
The main objective is to protect the rocket from a set number of waves in each level.  Depending on which class you play, you need to determine which weapons and structures are best suited for the map you are in.  The exclamation mark circles indicate where the enemies will spawn from, with green arrows indicating the path they take.  This will help you set up defenses where it's needed most.  Most maps have more than one pathway, so be ready to move from point to point to stop the Martians from overwhelming you.
Completing each map will give you EXP, and earning enough will unlock more weapons and structures for the class you used.  In addition, you will earn skill points which can spend to unlock the weapons/structures and their modifiers.  Modifiers adds an ability to the weapon/structure.  Each weapon/structure has two abilities, but you can only choose only one to use in the map, so be sure to choose wisely.
In regards to issues,  Fortified isn't a game that's going to grab you're attention for too long.  There isn't much to do outside Invasion mode and Co-Op mode.  You probably beat the Solo mode within 6-7 hour, probably less if you know what you are doing.  Also, I did experience one game crash, but other than that, the game runs pretty well.
I did enjoy Fortified for what it is, however it's not a game I can fully recomend to those that like the single player experience.  But if you friends that likes these types of games, maybe you'll fun with it.
Rating: B

A game that needed QA. Badly. The core concept has been done before in games like Orcs Must Die, and it was done better there. While the game does have some core elements that could give some fun at first, it quickly starts to lose the shine of its great aesthetic, as repetition becomes the name of the game here. Sure, it's fun to blow things up with a TNT launcher for example, but limited weapons/items to put on the field, and a lack of variety in maps, it won't keep your attention. Multiplayer could have made up for it: as when the game gets into pure chaos: it can be rather fun with friends. But if you don't have friends: good luck. The matchmaking system has no options to it: you're at the mercy of the draw....regardless of whether or not you wanted to play on a higher difficulty or not. You'll have to host....but remember that the players that come may not even be of an equivalent level to you. And even when you get a good party: the game's balance is bad: it does not scale well to more players, and you'll get overrun, very quickly, even if you know what you're doing. Oh, and there's no mute option as well. It's a game that still has potential, but at this current iteration....it's not worth the asking price. It feels like it's come three months too early.

Killer is dead: The Mad Spectacular origins
Humble Bundle strikes again with another free game, this is the first Suda51 game I have played which means that an entirely new folder had to be created in order to fit it in. “The Mad Spectacular” I think describes this game very well considering, well everything that happens in the game.
I will try to give a summary of the story but it turns out it is kind of hard considering the developer’s tendency to write some very strange story threads but I will try. Mondo is a half human half cyborg assassin working for some sort of agency....somewhere that kills monsters and gods with swords....somehow. Then there is something about the moon and something about things coming from the moon to get Mondo for some purpose........
I can’t get my head around the plot, the rules of whatever world Killer is dead is set in do not make any sense, the characters are so alien in logic and often design that there does not seem to be any consistency, there is a Bram Stoker like vampire in the same world as a thinly veiled Alice in wonder land homage. There are six armed women right next to cyber punk augmented super assassins. That is not to say about any of the other things that appear in Killer is Dead. The trouble with this is there does not seem to be any cohesion to the madness, no logic of any kind. It feels like Suda51 just threw anything that he liked into the world without any idea as to making it all fit. Then combine that with the obtuse writing and strange characters and you have a story that, while is compelling and drives you to finish it, makes no sense afterwards as well as rendering the dramatic moments impossible to get emotionally invested in because you are struggling to understand what is going on.
The game play however is really good, a hack and slash by nature you use the right mouse button to attack and space to block and dodge, if you time your dodges right you can rapidly cut up your foe in dazzling style. It is fun and satisfying to get in the rhythm of things striking at the right moments and darting out again. It is fast paced and enjoyable to play well but does not punish you too hard for messing up. You can finish off your opponents with certain final button prompts that will grant you some sort of resource to level up, heal or get ammo. Levels are mission based and linear but the game always throws enough stuff for you to hunt down or kill to make sure it does not get boring and the bosses are fun and challenging.
The game has a comic book art style to it that while looks very beautiful and fairly unique has some issues with shadowing, some levels got so dark from shadow that I could not see what was going on or where I was going. I messed around with the shadowing because the default was so dark, I could not get the game to be lit properly. It was really irritating as I could not always see how beautiful the game was because of the shadowing or bloom.
Game performance was incredibility unstable, sometimes it ran like a dream yet other times there was freezing, frame rate drops and stuttering. Considering that it came out in 2013 this could be excused to an extent as it might not run as well on modern systems. This is an interesting game to tackle for a review. When a game is free and very short, it's odd to choose whether to recommend it or not. the static speaks my name can be completed in about ten minutes. If you're curious enough to play it and are not put off by the subject matter, there's really no reason not to give it a whirl. At the same time, I'm not going around telling people to play it. There are upsides and downsides, but it is lacking and not worth going out of your way for.
Let's first cover the parts that are simple to discuss. The graphics are good. It has a unique art style that I enjoyed. The music is easily forgotten. It is low-key and is fine for the atmosphere, so in context it is okay. The controls are simple and do the job they need to. Since it is a walking simulator, there is no need for anything beyond the movement and examination keys. The sound is fine, and the game runs well. I would like to say more about these things, but there isn't much else to cover for them.
That leads us to the story. The store page already gives the main gist of the game away, and even if it didn't, you'd learn it quickly upon starting to play. You're a man who is about to kill himself. Before doing so, you have some objectives to complete. You can't leave your house, so there isn't much to explore. The rooms that are present have distinctive features and are intriguing for a minute or two, then there is nothing else to do with them. Your interactions are limited. There isn't much to the game before reaching the end.
This is one of those games that falls into the "artsy" category. You know how some people say games aren't games at times, but rather an expression of art and little else? They try to get something across to the players and that's it? I don't subscribe to that way of thinking except on very rare occasions. I certainly call the static speaks my name a video game. However, it only seems to be trying to convey messages rather than doing much else. Since that appears to be the point, I'm fine with that concept. Players should know what they are getting into, though, especially if that is not the kind of thing they would enjoy.
I felt a sense of unease while playing. That's a good thing in this case. The atmosphere seems like it should be bleak, and it feels like I should be questioning what I see. Yet there wasn't enough to it to make me become that engaged. It's difficult for me to describe this because it is a personal thing rather than one I can factually analyze. I wasn't sucked into the game like I was in some walking simulators I've played, and despite the story being open-ended, I didn't care much to look deeper into it. Perhaps it was simply too open-ended for me. With only the barest of explanations, along with not getting much of a look into the protagonist's life, I had no reason to do much beyond finish playing, shrug, and move on.
One thing that I did find disappointing is that the game ends when it looks like it could be much longer. I won't give away the exact reason for this, but it is an idea that has potential. It just didn't go anywhere with the part at the end. If it was a really bad game, I would be glad that it ended quickly. Instead, I felt let down because this small idea barely took off.
I've seen some people claim that the static speaks my name has changed their lives. Certainly plenty of players have enjoyed it. If you think you would be interested in it, give it a try. As for me, it felt like a short story that didn't have enough substance to make it worth recommending. I don't regret playing it, but I also don't see much of a reason to do so.
