West of Loathing is a game that needs no twenty paragraph long review.
The basic premise of the game is that you're going out West to find your fortunes, help people, or just get off your boring farm and do something fun for once.
:
Combat is simplified turn-based. You have a number of "Action Points" that let you do special actions on your turn and they refresh between battles, and once you're out during combat you can either snort some smelling salts or just do basic attacks. It's so easy that you could probably expect a ten year old to grasp it within a minute or so.
There are 3 classes in the game you can be and they all get their own style of fighting. They're your standard archetypes of fighter, mage, and thief. You can also have a "pardner" NPC that helps you out in combat whom can also level up with you. They all fight in their own way as well, so you have some incentive beyond just reading their unique dialog to pick a new one each playthrough.
If you're looking for hardest game ever, look elsewhere. The combat here is easily cheesed once you find the first "grinding" zone near the starter town, which lets you attack a group of enemies forever to grind out XP to level up. Plus, combat items don't end your turn if they're used, so you could stock up on poisons and dynamite to obliterate every enemy in your way.
For people who want a harder game, there is a hard mode that can be unlocked in the prologue. You can also intentionally forgo having a pardner join you in the game if you enjoy having harder combat and less funny dialog.
Levelling up is done either by auto-levelling (Don't do this) or by point buying via accumulated XP. There are several skills you can level up, some of which are unique to which class you pick. Further skills can be picked up in-game by reading skill magazines that you will lose every single time after reading them just once. But fear not: You can easily acquire every skill in the game and still have a few skill books left over.
:
The story is simple, like much of the game. You're out West, you're trying to get to Frisco, and there's baddies and obstacles in the way. However, the main quest is not all there is to do. There's a lot of sidequests to do, each with their own little story to tell, and this is where the game REALLY shines.
The writing is absolutely fantastic. Unless you have no sense of humor, I guarantee that the game will make you laugh quite a few times, and merely sensibly chuckle some other times. Your potential pardners all have unique dialog and their own personal stake in one of several sidequests in the main game. Everything in the game is designed to give you a good laugh and enjoy yourself, so it's wise to go into this game not taking anything too seriously.
Once you reach the end of the game (This takes about 8 hours if you're insistent on doing every single thing possible in the most timely manner, it can be much shorter if you beeline through the main quest) you're allowed to continue adventuring and completing sidequests. However, there ARE multiple endings, of a sort! Depending on which sidequests you complete and how you complete them, the ending cutscene will change! Don't expect some big world shattering difference to occur that rocks you to your core, but at least know that the game will acknowledge that you did indeed bother to fulfill sidequests and change your ending for it.
:
If you like funnyman writing filled with sarcasm and snark and aren't looking for a game that intends to really "challenge" you outside of hard mode, this game is for you. There's plenty of locations to visit and sidequests to do, certainly enough to kill an afternoon or two. You can also get some replay value out of the game via achievements (There is no way to get every single one in one or two playthroughs), hard mode, classes, and selecting a new pardner.
If you end up enjoying the game, I'd also recommend you pay a visit to the Kingdom of Loathing itself. Unlike this game, it does not cost money to play but it still delivers on the humor.

Ok, so I have 30 minutes of playtime. What right do I have to review the game from that, you might think.
I do not have 30 minutes of playtime. I have had 30 minutes of trying to get the game to work properly, before I gave up.
Everything seems top notch, from what I've read and seen from the game. I like the graphics style better than competing rally titles, the sounds are actually good, the stages are varied, narrow and realistic, the car selection is awesome, it has some small, but nice costumisation options, the career mode is extensive and interesting. Just to name some of the good things about this game.
The car handling and physics I cannot say much about, because I'm not able to actually play the game the way it's meant. But from what I can tell, it actually feels much better than Milestone's last effort, WRC4, and it might very well hit the sweet spot between harsh realism and forgiving arcade-style driving. But I wouldn't know for sure, because it has too many game breaking bugs.
I really wanted to like this game, because it has so much good going for it. But it is unplayable:
-Graphics options are a joke, and it's impossible to configure the game to run smoothly without having to disable all the three(!) quality options available, on a system that runs most games at 60 fps on high settings.
-Configuring custom controllers is a nightmare. Want to have multiple controllers or external shifter? Forget it. Want to map some functions to your keyboard? No can do. And my G27 is stuck at 180 degrees no matter what I do. It works in all other games, but not this.
-The menu actually stopped responding a couple of times (in 30 minutes!) and I had to kill the game from task manager.
-The game has no FOV or seat adjustment sliders, neither does it have the option to remove the steering wheel from cockpit view. Triple screen support I don't know, because I have only a single screen.
If Milestone can present a game that actually works, this could be one of the best rally games ever. But in its current state, it's mostly unplayable. If you've been told that the demo doesn't do the game justice, it actually does - the full version is just as bad.
I'm getting a refund.
But I'll gladly buy the game back if Milestone can make it work.

Our script of the video... better watch that and set the fps to 60 for the video.. unlike in the game :(
Script:
Sebastien Loeb Rally Evo is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥on the PC. You can see us playing it here, like this, and this, and here like this and even like this. And most of the time we had a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ experience with it. The effort that went into the development of the pc version must have been close to none. But we found some settings, that worked for us in the end. Time for a PC Master Race Reality Check.
In order to keep input lag as minimal as possible and unlock the framerate, we usually don’t play games with v-sync enabled. Unfortunately Sebastien Loeb Rally Evo becomes a visual mess as soon as players don’t sync their frames. Constant stuttering, lockups, frame drops and spikes get in the way of controlling the cars. As you can see in the footage: the game is almost unplayable like this. It’s such a mess.
So we thought, okay let’s try to enable v-sync and cut frames at 60 then, but guess what? The game continues to stutter regularly. We were facing frustrating circumstances.
Next we tried out the PS4 version with the first patch being installed. We wanted to know which sweetspot developer Milestone chose for the console. After recording and analyzing some footage and noticing some minor input lag we concluded, that the PS4 version ran at 30 frames per second with v-sync enabled. Along the way we encountered some minor frame drops during replays and races at night as well as other technical issues like fading objects at the side of the road and missing sound effects. But after all: the PS4 version was at least working and fun to play. From what we hear the Xbox One version has way more framerate problems. For our testing we were limited to the PC and the PS4 though.
So we went back to the pc port, opened up the barebones graphical options for the game and set the sync to half. On 60Hz displays this option limits the framerate to 30 and voila: We reconstructed a Playstation-like experience on our PC. At least the game was starting to be playable. The stuttering was gone completely, but we were still unhappy with the input lag, that naturally occurs by enabling V-Sync. Here you can see the PC version with and without V-Sync side by side. The in game wheel movement matches our inputs 1:1 without V-Sync.
As a last resort we gave FreeSync a shot and finally prevailed. The inputs are not as good as they could be without any syncing, but as you can see: the input lag is minimal and our Eizo monitor did a good job keeping the jumping framerate in check. Like this we definitely preferred the slightly better looking pc version over the console version.
Apart from getting the game working in a playable fashion we also have some other bad news: Triple monitor setups or Ultrawide resolutions are not supported at all. Playing the game in 4K on the other hand is possible, but it takes a heavy toll on your  framerates. Even on our high end build featuring a Geforce GTX 980 Ti we went as high as 1440p for the maximum resolution. Our racing wheel, the Thrustmaster T500 RS was detected and worked well. It has to be noted that playing SL Rally Evo with a wheel additionally reduces input lag, because players can turn the wheel as fast as they want to. Playing with the pad, the turning animation of the virtual driver has to be finished first.
And that’s it. We put a lot of research and work into this episode, because the game underneath the technical mess is by far the best Milestone has produced to date. We enjoy the driving, the track layouts, the campaign and many different parts of the game. But as it stands we at least have to put up a huge warning sign for this game. Depending on your hardware with the 30fps lock, FreeSync or GSync the PC Master Race still enjoys the best version of the game in the end.

!! This Review will change over playing time. Status: 02/07/2016 !!
Dear rally fan and dear Milestone team:
First impression: much better than expected!
Bad things second:
1. Microstutters appear very often, even if the framerate is constant 60 per second.
2. Wheelsupport is no optimal yet. (Keyboard is not working during a race => only 1 controller is working during a race, so you cannot have for example a G27 wheel and a clubsport shifter together.
3. Many Gravelstages are worse than the Vanilla RBR gravelstages (Mostly Australia and Mexico, Wales is okay for example)! Clearly a lack of time is the reason why the gravelstages are so bad in SLRE (Sebastien Loeb Rally EVO). Road textures are very simple and extremly repetetive and also the the road borders are non existing, looks like a 15 year old game. First impression is that its no fun to drive on those gravelstages.
4. No tripplescreen support yet, but with the current performance it wouldnt work yet either.
5. You have no tire choice in game, like in DIRT Rally! Sadly i hope they will add this!
6. Damage. The damage on highest settings appear earlier after crashes than in DIRT Rally on highest settings, but its still not realistic. Please add a "simulation mode" to the damage settings with close to real strengh settings for the car. A 20-30 km/h hard impact can already rip a wheel off! We want that in SLRE also!
7. Carsetups are done with sliders and no real values. We want Nm, etc.!
To the bright side of the game:
PHYSICS
The physics are very good, even from a simulation freak standpoint. Cars over- and understeer like you expect it, like brakes also. Weight transfer works, but not sure yet if this is a bit damped in this game. Clearly Sebastien Loeb had a very good influence to Milestones affort to make a real sim this time. Is DIRT Rally better in this aspect, or RBR (Richard Burns Rally with and without NGP)?! I have no final conclusion yet but what i experienced to far that the tarmac physics are supperior to the DIRT Rally and also RBR Vanilla physics!! I never expected that to be the case, i must admit!
Gravelphysics appear good too, but i have to investigate a lot more time to validate this first impression.
GRAPHICS
Solid. Cars look nice and some tarmac stages are very beautiful and realistic. Pikes Peak is also very nice and bumpy, like the real one. Much better than DIRT Rally Pikes Peak and also much much better than RBR Pikes Peak MOD ;). Again you see where Sebastien Loeb gave most input! You can clearly see where he put his most time in: Tarmac physics, his Citroen Cars and Pikes Peak! This equals his interests and strenghts. I hope soon the other parts get same attention too!
FORCE FEEDBACK
Quite good, i only have a G27. So i can only compare between different simulations and not judge the full potential of the Force Feedback in SLRE => Better than DIRT Rally and around equal to RBR, but worse then RBR NGP.
GAME SIZE
Many nice and historic cars. Many many hours of fun :). Pikes Peak is great. Tarmac Rallies also. Long realistic and NARROW stages :)
RallyCross is a nice addition and very much fun, i have a smile on my face all the time. I actually have not enjoyed a simulator for a long time this much! Drifting is wonderfull precise and the A.I. is fast, is not breaking too often too early, like in other titles! and also very agressive which i quite like in RallyCross! Its not clean racing like in IRacing, guys! This is meant to be nasty and thats where the fun starts! You can very easily and realisticly turn a A.I car by just clipping this rear end. The cars are not welded to the ground like in DIRT Rally RallyCross! So are you, you can BE turned very easily! So much fun, try it yourself, you wont regret!!
All in all i must say this game has the potential to be the successor or Richard Burns Rally (RBR). I am very impressed by the physics. If they/you fix the obove mentioned problems SLRE might be the next "big thing" in the rally simulator world!
Thanks for reading :)

First, I am a YouTuber and G27 Steering Wheel user I have a 38 minutes video review/parody about this game on my channel.
And I only played about 2 hours to consider a Refund later.
I have about 600 hours on Assetto Corsa, 50 hours on rFactor 2 (recently bought) and about 140 hours on Dirt Rally (main content on my channel at the moment).
About the "Only 2 hours" criticism: For a racing sim I don't think you need too much time to judge the driving feel of a racing title using a wheel, you can definetly feel how the driving feel/physics are the first moment you turn the wheel on any game/sim. About the content, it is just Dirt Rally with more content both on Cars, Stages and events. Still this is a First Impressions Review.
NOT RECOMMENDED TO:
-Those who can't decide between this or Dirt Rally or WRC 5 as a Rally game. Get DiRT Rally.
-Those that want a casual racing experience.
-Those who are not willing to deal with the bugs and can't ignore bad sound/graphics/performance.
-Those who don't have a good gaming PC.
-Those who have a steering wheel currently not supported on the game, mainly high-end gear. Check forum first.
-Those that can't play without a add-on Handbrake or Button Box (No support)
RECOMMENDED TO:
-Those who are willing to deal with the bugs and can ignore bad sound/graphics/performance.
-Those who played hours and hours of Dirt Rally and want more content in general.
-Those who want a realistic rallying experience.
-Those who have a good gaming PC
-Those who have supported wheel. G27 works if "Allow game to adjust" is UNTICKED on the Profiler.
_______________________________________________________________________
Game PRO/CONS
PRO:
- Surprising amount of content on both Rally Stages and Cars from all eras of Rally (More content than Dirt Rally)
- Stages are very narrow just like in real life.
- Game physics and terrain surface/car dynamics are very realistic, definitely a simulation game if you turn off the Assists. Its debatable if this game simulation/driving part is better than Dirt Rally.
- Like Dirt Rally, it simulates the challenges of Rally racing. So it is difficult but rewarding game experience.
- Price is fair if you eliminate the bugs and performance issues. There is a lot of content for the money.
- Progress and Car Unlock systems tied with Reputation and Credits earning. *We need more of credits based unlocks on racing simulations.
CONS:
- Unstable game-breaking performance, framedrops and micro-stutters that adds horrible input lag on controllers and wheels
- Terrible and limited Graphics options, can only change the already limited options outside the game in a Launcher.
- Terrible car sounds design, the sound is rough but the sound positioning is usable.
- Mediocre but believable graphics,
- Unpolished and very stupid amateur bugs, the game ONLY SAVES if you have ENGLISH UK selected on the Windows Control Painel>Region and Language Settings.
-You will get stuck on the Tutorial if you choose it just after making your team because you need to select the type of controls you are using. ALT-F4 is only solution.
- Stupid lack of support for simulation gear for a SIMULATION GAME (Common sense, please Milestone) like high-end Steering Wheels, Handbrake, Button Box, Joystick add-ons.
- Limited usable steering wheel/controllers/keyboard when in-game, can not use the keyboard buttons if using a controller or steering wheel or controller. Meaning if you use a wheel you can not use the keyboard or joysticks to function in conjunction, I can't use my Logitech Extreme 3D PRO Flight Stick as Handbrake like I do in Dirt Rally and other racing sims.
_____________________________________________________________________
At the current state of the game I DO NOT recommend it, a lot of bugs and instabilities in the games performance. However if you are really getting bored with DiRT Rally and just want more rally content with a surprisingly good driving physics then feel free to get this game a try, you can refund it later anyway.
BUT BE WARNED: You must deal with the bugs and annoyances of this game, if you are not a patient guy or gal, then stay FAR AWAY of this game.
The lack of response from the Developers on Milestone is very disrespectful to those that want this game to be at least playable with a stable performance.

It stays true to its prequels, with the complex character and party building and even surpasses it with its itemization and magic-system.
The tactical, phase-based combat is different, due to the 3D engine, but in a good way.
All in all Sir-Tech managed to "modernize" the game without removing the "Wizardry feel" and dumbing it down. This is no small feat, if we look at all kinds of "sequels" and "spiritual successors" in these days.
The game is challenging. Not as hardcore and obscure as the previous games in the series, but it is still no small task to build a capable party and learn the combat system, and successfully finish the game.
It also requires a moderate amount of grinding and save/reloading, but just enough, not to make the game unpalatable.
The artwork is good, it has nicely drawn portraits and a well-designed UI. I also like the stylish, rather wacky 3D graphics, and it looks remarkably good for a 2001 game, on my Win 7 machine, with forced 16Q antialiasing and anisotropic filtering.
The audio is great: A pleasant soundtrack, lots of decent to good voice-acting, and what's truly unique is the different voice-sets for the PCs, which gives them a lot of character.
I find it hard to find some negatives, but here we go:
The combat is very slow out of the box, so using the Wiz8Fast and Wizardry 8 speed mod is mandatory. Also it is possible for PCs and NPCs to get stuck sometimes, plus a few crashes now and then (I had like 5 of them in 100 hours).
I've played over 300 hours of Wizardry 8, a full playthrough requires around 100 hours. If you manage to get this kind of free-time and are interested in an accessible, tactical dungeon-crawler, I can highly recommend it.

I'm a huge fan of Might and Magic, playing every one of them but being one of the few people who like the later games (6, 7 and 8) the best.
I bought Wizardry because when I was younger I remember it being a big deal and I knew it was the same sort of game as Might and Magic. Can't go wrong with that, right?
It turns out that you can. I wrongly assumed that since Wizardry was a little newer than Might and Magic it'd control better, work better. But instead it's like playing a game in molasses.
I'm seven hours in and I feel like I haven't done anything because every combat grinds on for ten minutes while you sit twiddling your thumbs and it auto plays out. It's boring. I understand the character depth and that you've got so many choices in theory beforehand but the actual execution of those choices isn't exciting for me at all.

Finally a semi-playable Wizardry game! Thanks to the 3d presentation, it isn't as confusing to navigate around. However, as with all Sir-Tech games, they take 1 step forward and 2 steps back. The navigation would be better except they didn't use more landmark items to ease confusion, so you still need to draw a map.
Character creation also got a lot better since you don't need to roll for hours on end to get good stats. It's a point buy system with static stats based on Race selection and Class selection. The streamlining of this made it more apparent that the game's level up system was badly done. Stats cap at 100 except by special items and it's very easy to reach 100 for the skills you want. They padded this process by forcing a 3 point limit per stat, per level.
The other major negative is the stat system gives no legimate education on the impact of stat raising. All you are told is high numbers are good and low numbers are bad. No info is given for hit chance, overall effectiveness, what randomizer is used to determine success, .etc Considering this is a D&D knockoff, knowing what your stats mean should almost be mandatory. The manual doesn't answer that either, by the way.
I tapped out from playing farther after encountering the statue trap that sends the player down a pit to fight a bunch of bugs. I didn't die, but that was mostly due to seeing it's a trap and interacting with the statue while the bugs noticed me above the chute. I was stuck in combat even after the chute closed itself. Their own traps were badly designed thanks to the lame detection system for combat.
If one wanted to play a Wizardry game, I would suggest this. That isn't high praise of 8 as much as a signal of how bad these games are.

Upon the release of Grimoire: Heralds of the Winged Exemplar, I had a rekindled urge and desire to play an old school dungeon crawler. I remember always wanting to play these old style RPGs when I was younger but I never had the patience for them. I felt like I could enjoy them more now where as a child, I just felt like the game was unfair and I couldn't understand why. And while I wanted Grimoire, I didn't want to pay that price. And then I found Wizardry 8, a game from a tried and true series and said, what the hell.
I tried 6 and 7 first. I wasn't a fan. Some things don't age well and the aid of nostalgia glasses don't help. They were just too outdated and honestly, the graphics were too pixelated and I had a really hard time reading them. The games literally hurt my eyes to look at. And I thought they were too clunky. I just didn't have a whole lot of fun in the short time that I did play them, so they got returned. But Wizardry 8 however, was a different story.
This game is closing in fast on 20 years old and even though it looks like it (albiet in a charming early 3d way), it sure doesn't feel like it. The frame rate is surprisingly smooth for something of this age. The sound is very high quality and the dungeon layout is beautiful.
The controls are a little odd and the default key layout is strange, but nothing huge to complain about. It's a minor gripe at best.
This game truly holds up after all this time and still runs wonderfully on modern systems. Unlike it's predecessors, Wizardry 8 has aged gracefully. It shows us that modern, phot-realistic graphics do not always make the game.

I've been a long time player of Nexon games, and when I saw Vindictus, I was honestly shocked. From a company known for such a cutesy game like MapleStory, this is a very brutal and fast-paced action game that is surprisingly set in the world of their most famous MMO, Mabinogi.
The character roster was small at first, but it quickly grew into a rather wide array that promotes extended play. Some of the characters are 'clones' of each other at first glance, but don't let this fool you; each hero is different and requires time to master.
While the game dungeons can be played solo, I find that it's a lot more fun to adventure with a party; you receive additional EXP, items, gold, and so on. The party finder system also makes it easy to jump into a group for a dungeon, or create one.
One thing I should note, however, is that this game is very demanding graphics-wise, and is absolutely punishing towards slower hardware. If you don't have a relatively compotent PC, this game will not be kind to you.
Other than that, Vindictus is a great experience that you should not pass up, especially if you enjoy Nexon games.

The best modern Fallout title - second best, if you count Fallout 2.
It is able to masterfully blend features and mechanics from the old Fallout games with the more modern, immersive approach of first/third person action and free roaming. It learns from the mistakes made by Bethesda in Fallout 3 and provides you a wonderfully grim experience.
It is far from being perfect, however. If these games are known for one thing, it would be their flaws. Wonky, unstable and outdated engine; at places, very bare-bone map (regardless of the reasoning); flawed questlines and often broken beyond repair due to silly "mistakes"; VATS unfortunately needed, despite it being garbage and performing horribly.
Despite all of this, like most good games, you're able to overlook these issues. FNV provides such a good experience overall that these flaws are easily outweighed. Hell, it was one of the only games that made me cry during the end of a DLC because of how my hopes were so suddenly crushed.
If you enjoy Fallout's RPG mechanics but doesn't feel comfortable with the old turn-based combat, top view camera and you prefer more of the modern freedom, this game is exactly what you're looking for.

Here's some gameplay from our 2 hour long session yesterday:

An immense amount of fun, extremely satisfying seeing burning alien robots ragdoll into walls after you light them up with rocket fuel, freeze them with weaponized liquid nitrogen, and shotgun them in the chest with your double barrel. A solid challenge even on normal, adapting your strategy and loadout is essential to defeating the martian scum. The game encourages you to change stuff around and figure out a method that works, so if youre getting stomped, try something new.. re-spec your character how ever often you want, sell your structures with no penalty. Its challenging and fun, not needlessly punishing and frustrating.
The art and style is on point and captures the 50s pulp look perfectly. The flailing robot designs are a fantastic homage to the era that inspired them, and they are straight up hilarious to annialate. Having an immense amount of fun so far in the single player campaign, and can't wait to quadruple the destruction and intensity with da homies in co-op!

3rd person co-op tower defense. Yes, it's basically a sci-fi version of Orcs Must Die but (A) it's a great retro-futuristic setting, (B) it has 4 playable characters all with their own unique abilities, and (C) it has some interesting twists on weapons and defenses. I played for a couple hours with my kid and we would have kept going but it was getting too late in the evening. Even on Normal difficulty (there's no "Easy") it was quite a challenge. Once we got to the third stage, we found ourselves getting whupped pretty good until we figured out a few tactics.
One important tactic is to resell and move/mix your defenses around as needed. They don't depreciate so the game encourages this. If you have minions (way way cool) they act as a squad you can issue orders to. Once I discovered that, it made a pretty big difference. Other than that, smart placement of defenses, situational awareness, timing "Super" mode correctly (you get a super boost you can use once or twice per map), and good aim is pretty much all you need.
The game's slick, the graphics are nice, the setting is unique (groovalicious!), and the gunplay, tactics, and mechanics are a ton of fun. The progression system of earning points to spend on upgrades is well paced. You can respec if you want to try spending your points differently, and I think that's essential.
My only gripes: I wish they had more female characters (at least one other), and I wish the game had more levels. Heck, it would be cool if there were a few "adventure" style maps where you'd have to make your way from point A to point B fending off enemies (like in the Sniper games). There are a couple different modes for each map though, so that's cool.  If you have a friend who might be interested in playing this with you, I highly recommend it.

[Full disclosure: My copy of Blitz Breaker was supplied
]
When discussing games of incredible difficulty or challenge, there are typically three schools of thought I subscribe to: Spelunky for roguelikes, Dark Souls for action/RPG, and Super Meat Boy for arcade-like, rapid fire levels. Blitz Breaker comes from the latter school; featuring levels that frequently take less than a minute or two to complete, are full of gimmicks that are introduced over time, and becomes the stuff of patience-testing nightmares near the end. While the controls are incredibly simple and easy to underestimate, the skill, tact and timing needed to execute successful runs through the levels is still quite impressive, even if the game has some bothersome elements that could’ve been avoided.
Your character cannot walk or run; the only methods of locomotion are a meager little jump, dashing in one of the four cardinal directions, and using parts of the environment, like by a magnetized platform or conveyor belts. The catch is that your character doesn’t stop dashing until they bump into a surface which, if the surface is a harmful one, then results in exploding death and returns you to the start of the level to try again. The levels and obstacles are all designed around this control scheme in compact levels that are quick to complete when you know the tricks. To be expected, the game is clever in unveiling new gimmicks (sawblades, cannons, keys etc) and starts off easy until they’re mashed together to really test your skill. These levels, or ‘worlds’, are punctuated by boss battles that are quite punishing, since a death restarts the entire fight from scratch. Levels have a par time and meeting this will reward you with stars, a collectible needed mainly for completionism, but which also unlocks different characters who have no purpose other than a visual one. Extra time towards the par can be gained by collecting coins throughout the level - Later on it feels like every coin must be grabbed to reach the par time unless speedy tricks are used to shave precious seconds. While the first twenty or so minutes will be a relative breeze, before long Blitz Breaker gets real mean and unfortunately rather irksome.
I’m not exclusively talking about the difficulty in terms of level design anymore, since that’s to be expected out of a game like this. Hitboxes interacting between your character and obstacles can be an iffy deal, since a handful of pixels brushing past a spike can result in some dubious deaths. This also is a problem when falling at terminal velocity and then dashing at the last moment; you’ll hear the sound effect of the dash being executed via your input, yet your character will still take a death regardless. It’s hard to tell if this is just the hitboxes not co-operating or if this is a proper bug that never got ironed out. The timer at the top of the screen obstructs the upper section of the level, and this can result in dashing headfirst into spikes hidden behind said timer if you’re not aware, which feels just downright silly. The game also does itself no favors by having a taunting message appear on screen after a death, resulting in annoyed jamming of the jump button in order to get by it as fast as possible and begin a fresh run. This makes fast restarts take a moment too long which can be a deal breaker for a game like this.
The biggest takeaway from Blitz Breaker of all comes not from a design quirk but from player input; in that you will try to dash around as fast as possible and make the same mistakes constantly. Even when there’s a spike wall to your left and a conveyer belt needs to carry you to the next platform, there will be that awful urge to dash that way to try to save time. I cannot count the number of times I’ve dashed straight into a spike wall after breaking a barricade and mashing the button to try and save time instead of just waiting for the correct and safe moment to continue. The game excels at preying upon player impatience, especially if you’re trying to go for every par time and collectible. This is both great game design and comically infuriating, and you’ll certainly have to train yourself to not just dash yourself to oblivion at every waking opportunity.
So even with some bothersome points that can effectively rob a successful run, Blitz Breaker is still a competent little title, with emphasis on little. The game is incredibly affordable and also short if you’re just trying to finish the game, but getting all the collectibles and par times is another story entirely, especially with them being scattered across an infinite-lived Story mode and an Arcade mode with finite lives. The difficulty may be off-putting for some, but for those looking for a new challenging platform in same veins as Super Meat Boy and the like, Blitz Breaker certainly can be recommended.

Introduction
It's come to this. After the 54 reviews I've done I've found good games *cough* Skyrim *cough* and I've found bad games *cough* *cough* Day One: Garry's Incident *cough**cough* But out of all of the bad games that I've reviewed I've never had a game leave this sort of bad taste in my mouth like Jack Orlando did. I'm not saying that Jack Orlando is one of the worst games of all time (That spot is still held by day one) but I felt betrayed. I felt all of my childhood crumble down and fall apart right in front of me and I felt that Jack Orlando was the bomb that fell on the genre that I grew up with. I would also like for everyone to take note that Jack Orlando and another point and click adventure game that I reviewed called "The mystery of the Druids" were released around the same time and I think it was these games that killed the point and click genre. At least with mystery of the druids I enjoyed it because it was so bad it was good. Jack Orlando has barely anything good in it. Everything from the dialogue, the sometimes unresponsive point and clicking or the characters, nearly everything is wrong.
Plot
The plot is that it's set in 1933 and you play as detective Jack Orlando, who used to be a worldwide famous detective, capturing crooks and saving lives and even being awarded a gun by the mayor. However Jack's fame has worn and he barely has anything left. However one night in an alley near Jack's place, Jack passes by the alley and witnesses a murder and Jack is then knocked out. Police find him the next morning and believe he murdered the victim who's revealed to be Major Pete Reynolds of the US army. Jack is then given 48 hours to clear his name and thus is the plot of the game. There isn't really anything necessarily wrong with the plot except that it's quite a cliche plot. Someone's given a limited amount of time to clear their name for a crime they didn't commit, it's been done to death by both video games and movies. Another thing I have to talk about is the pacing of Jack Orlando. What I'm about to say will probably make absolutely no sense. The pacing is confusing. Now if any of u have played at least one point and click game you will know that the basic thing is to do logical things in order to unlock certain areas, conversation topics or items in order to advance. Jack Orlando does that but not well. Another thing that should be basic to point and click games is to lock off dialogue that may spoil later parts of the game. Jack Orlando's locking system must have gotten mixed up somehow. It locks off the things that don't need to be locked off and unlocks the things that should be locked. The developers think that they should lock a bar away which the only reason that bar exists is for one thing, pick up a vase next to the piano and to unlock the bar, you need to give a packet of cigarettes to a bellboy which the game never even hints towards. However the developers decide to not lock away a certain piece of dialogue about a casino from the beginning of the game whereas Jack isn't supposed to have this dialogue until near the end of the second act.
Art style
The art style I have mixed opinions about. This whole game was hand drawn and the backgrounds look really good. They match that sort of noire detective feel that the rest of the game should have done. The character designs are another story. They sort of look like what would happen if u tried to watch an overweight, middle aged man try and fit into a size 2 shirt. They look uncomfortable and they look like they've been rammed into the setting.
Voice acting
The voice acting is for the most part bad as well. Jack sounds like he was drunk half the time he was on set to record his line. Elisabeth sounds like she was voiced by a 7 year old that was pretending to be in her early 20s. The voice actor for Don Scaletti sounds like he's trying way too hard to put on an Italian accent and failing every time he does it. The list goes on.
Characters
If any of you have read either my Harvester review (which I got quite a bit of backlash on) or my mystery of the druids review (on steam), you should know that characters for me tend to be the con of point of click games and I say none stood out. But the thing is with Jack Orlando is that they all stood out just because of how bad the writing for them were and how bad and clumsily the voice actors said their lines. Interpret that information however you want.
Puzzles
Also, Jack Orlando's puzzles are just plain confusing and make no sense. In my Harvester review I said that puzzles in Harvester were "more like petty crimes done by the village idiot." In my mystery of the druids review I said "The puzzles seem straight forward at first but the solution for most of them is extremely ludicrous" With Jack Orlando there are things which shouldn't even have to be puzzles but are and every single puzzle are stretched out and are made way too difficult than they have to be. At the start you need to find your keys to your apartment and Jack, being the typical adventure game hero, never has anything on him the player doesn't tell him to carry. So where is the key? Under the rug at the entrance to the apartment. You might as well have had Jack carrying the key instead of making me put in that extra 5 seconds of gameplay to look under a rug and find the key. There are also tons of items that you can pick up that serve no purpose to the game. I can see that maybe they were trying to make it more difficult to break the usual adventure game trend to trick u that everything has a use but in this one it doesn't but Jack Orlando doesn't do this well.
Soundtrack
The one thing that this game seems to do right and better than any other adventure game is the music. The music is fantastic. It is that perfect music you could imagine being in an old noire detective video game. Type in youtube jack orlando soundtrack and listen to it.
Final verdict
Jack Orlando is a badly put together, unfinished point and click adventure game where puzzles are thrown at the player with no rhyme or reason.

If you're a fan of Rally racing games, I cannot recommend SLRE highly enough.

On the audio side of things, the game doesn't quite hit the mark - the Co-driver is competent enough and delivers the pace-notes admirably, but the engine sounds and other effects aren't the greatest.
The amount of content in the single-player portion of the game is immense and offers dozens of hours of play-time, with a large and well conceived career mode being the main focus.
Again, I can't recommend this game highly enough - it really is a brilliant rally game.
Milestone should be proud of what they've achieved here and SLRE deserves to be recognised as the fantastic game it is.

This game is a solid bargain even at today's full price or higher.
Negatives:
Graphics are badly dated, but this kind-of disappears as you get into the game. They are adequate to show you what is going on so you can choose strategies and tactics.
When starting the game, the screen remains black for an unusually long time. This can lead new players into thinking something is wrong and pushing Esc or other keys to try to "unstick" it. This can ruin the game loading. Just be patient and the game will load reliably every time.
The game is difficult at first. It is possible to fail so badly that only starting over works.
Character creation is deeply involved and not entirely obvious.
Battles take a long time. If you are experiencing the dubious help of "allies" a single battle can take over an hour of real world time. If this is too annoying there are mods or play something else. I have no mod and no trouble with this but some are impatient or want a faster pace. There is nothing wrong with that. Play something else.
Game designers were partially, but only partially successful in removing repetition and tedious aspects. For example vendor inventories need to be kept clear of cheap ammo (by buying and stashing it somewhere) or their inventories get clogged up and they do not offer the better items they will otherwise have as you go up in level. There is no need to grind in the game... but players sometimes do repeat things. After a while that can become not fun... but it is not needed. Conversations with NPCs (non-player characters) and RPCs (recruitable player characters) tend to be a bit tedious but they have bits of key info hidden among the topics.
There is a thing called Expert Skills that can be very important (only opened when an attribute is brought to natural 100) and powerful. This is a great game feature but is poorly documented. Power-Strike, Power-Cast and Eagle Eye are all powerful as well as sometimes other Expert Skills, depending upon the character and party. Only planning the character from the beginning lets one obtain these at all in time to matter. This is interesting and fun; it is only the lack of documentation (in game or manual) that is negative.
Some Expert Skills do not help all of the characters one might think it should. For example, the Expert Skill Power-Cast does not benefit the Bard or Gadgeteer at all, even though their musical instruments and gadgets respectively do cast spells. It can be frustrating taking all the time to give an expert skill that does nothing.
Positives:
There are many ways to design characters and parties. Some are better than others but the variety of right answers is huge.
The difficulty of monsters (expecially at first) makes every choice in character creation and development, as well as tactics and choice of spell or attack during a round really matter. This is fun.
There is not just one way to take on enemies. Spells and/or weapons can be used with multiple widely-varying strategies.
Skill increases are rewarded when those skills are used. It feels natural and fun that you become increasingly effective at whatever you do.
Running and hiding in and fighting from nooks is part of this game. Once you get used to that it is a positive rather than a negative and is fun.
Every character in the game is potentially very strong. There are no weak characters, only weak players in generating and developing them.
Even great players can combine into a weak party. The party is the emphasis for player wisdom in generating the right characters, in the right combinations, and using the right formation so they use what you want them to be good at. I keep saying "right" but there are lots and lots of right answers.
The story is weak and a small part of the game but it is consistent with several choices to explore during replays. The world is  a non-linear one that you can take in different orders (lots of right answers to exploring with various sequences). Numerous items are only in one spot and a few items only appear randomly in some games.
Enemies level approximately as you do, one of the first RPGs to implement this feature and making boring tricks like grinding in one area simply bad ways to play this game. Unlike some games you do not need to rush, however, and there are plenty of rewards for thorough exploration.
The replayability of this game is extremely high, with different parties and styles explored, long after the story branches are all well known. No two games are even vaguely alike, even if you choose similar characters and sequences. Enemies are random and wide in variety, expecially when you change the sequence a bit (almost no wrong answers in doing so).
Even after playing this game 10 or 20 times there is still a lot of depth and new things to learn. If you avoid advice tellng you that you need to play a certain way or that certain characters are weak then tons of possiblities and ways to play are opened up and give very different gaming experiences.
There is no randomness in character creation and development. For a certain class and race you get the same number of attribute and skill points to distribute every time. This is excellent because you can try different things, refine your choices, take or not advice from other players. Your skill as a player in developing your characters matters... a lot.
None of the complexities of the game are needed to enjoy and win it, only a bit of patience and maybe one or two restarts if one is a bit unlucky.

First things first, what you see in the trailer is esentially what you get: this is a simulation of owning a succulent pot along with the responsibilities that come with it, but without the cost of going to a flower shop or handling actual plants. You start with a pot of succulents, water them, weed them, and listen to some pretty good ambience as you do so. And… that's really it. That's pretty much all there is to this game.
So why do I recommend it? The first reason is because sometimes the simplest ideas are the best. This is a concept so easy to understand and "play" (as this is moreso a simulation than a game), and it does it extraordinarily well.
The second reason is also probably the most obvious: it's free. You don't have to pay a dime for anything in this game, as you will get another free succulent once a week. And unless you want succulents on-demand or an additional pot, the microtransactions are entirely optional. You can also unlock another pot by buying Ice Water Games's other game, Eidolon. I haven't played it yet, but if the atmosphere is anything like it is in this game, I'm sure I'll enjoy it. Besides, I'm a sucker for walking sims, haha.
But the final reason I love this game and play it at least once a week is because this my be the most relaxing game I've ever played. Even when I have it open for just five minutes at a time, it's very effective at calming me down when I'm stressing over something. That alone makes it worth the arbitrary disk space for me.
That being said, I can understand why this game isn't for everyone. It's a very slow game, and it's not the kind that you can sit down for an hour and expect to accomplish a large amount of action or change. There are plenty more options that are also free if that's what you're looking for. For those wanting to Zen out, look no further.
In a way, this game is kind of like life; change is only evident over time, the best things in life are free, and life (like the virtual succulents) is fleeting and will be gone before you know it if it's not taken care of. But if you give it the love and care it needs, you can really get the most out of it.

Vindictus is a game that has been developed by devCAT and is published by Nexon... just reading this one name (Nexon of course, not devCAT) has probably made you look away already. The game has initially been released in Korea on the 21st of January 2010, whereas the North American market has only seen its release on the 13th of October 2010. If you believe that nine months later is a long time, let's not forget that the European market has discovered Vindictus on the 5th of October 2011 (so nearly a whole year later) and the Australian gamers have received this game on the 15th of November 2012 (so nearly three years after the initial release of the game in Korea).
This slightly irritating bit aside, let's talk about the game itself that relies on the Source Engine produced by Valve which means that players are (supposedly) capable of interacting with their surroundings but this aspect is limited to destroying props laying around, or using them as improvised weapons. No throwing them around like you would have done so in Half-Life 2 with the Gravity Gun... and indeed I am pointing out this feature because it has been one of the major positive aspects of the Source Engine, and Half-Life 2 has exploited it amazingly in its level design whereas Vindictus simply failed to achieve the same result. Therefore, if Vindictus wanted to rely on the Source Engine to be their main selling argument... maybe, just maybe the developers should have stepped up their game to match Half-Life 2.
The game offers you the "choice" between eleven Classes... which are also characters. It means that, if you want to play a Class, you have to accept (or barely tolerate) the fact that you're gender-locked and aspect-locked. Yes I did say "aspect-locked" because let's be honest, the game doesn't allow you to modify your character. If you want to play that one mountain of muscles capable of swinging a massive pillar around... it will inevitably be a beefy black man. Of course you can change the skin colour, the eyes, the eyebrows, and a few sliders for the bodyshape but all these options are severely limited and don't really allow you to deeply modify your character.
The gameplay now. It is not bad at all if you love beat'm'up games such Phantasy Star Online. It relies on a simple and efficient rule : hit your enemies and do not get hit back. Oh did I say "Phantasy Star Online"? Of course I did, because this game is composed of small levels considered as one-way missions, exploration is not something the players will have to worry about because the action plays out in corridors. The only large place you will ever find is the room of the final boss! And I hope that you love loading screens, because you will see several of them.
The story, since the early days of the game where it barely existed and mattered has evolved into three Seasons but the third one remains incomplete at the moment, and the second season is much shorter than the first (a prologue, ten episodes and an epilogue versus four episodes and an epilogue). So there is something to explain all the fighting, but it quicly becomes secondary once another flaw of the game hits you in the face : it is a korean game, so it involves an unhealthy amount of grinding and a ridiculous RNG that will frustrate you eventually (I should not have to fight a single Boss thirty-two times just to get a single piece of equipment, and I confirm that I did count). And quite frankly, once you reach the third Season you won't care about the story anymore because it becomes ridiculous during the Season 2, Episode 2.
But maybe you'll never get to this point mainly because the first Season of Vindictus is not fun at all, and this is a fact that few players (especially the die-hard lovers of Vincdictus) will never admit. The early missions of the game have terribly aged, and Season 2 is a smelly content that will rather make you drop the game... well, if the many bugs and glitches, plus the neverending lag don't. You see, very often you will face a boss, beat him down until his body is nothing more than a fine paste, and although his health will reach the absolute zero he won't die at all. Thus you end stuck in an instance, unable to leave, and if you dare pressing Alt+F4 to quit out of desperation you shall be rewarded with a penalty for abandoning a bugged dungeon. And what about the lag you might ask? The game relies on a small software called ProudNet to establish connections between players so even there is a server to gather everyone together, instances are actually played via peer-to-peer... which means that one guy playing with a potato-powered connection will inevitably ruin the fun of everyone else. And sometimes the server itself might simply kick you out for no reason, just because it felt like doing so, forcing you to shut down the game and relaunch it in order to log back in.
Now comes the technical aspect of the game. The first time I have launched this game, I clearly remember seeing a poorly textured character because the game has auto-selected the lowest graphic settings available. So I go to the Options menu in order to rectify this little mistake, move the slider all the way to "Maximum" and click "Apply"... and the game suddenly froze. Not just frozen on a frame you see, even the sound bugged out instantly and started playing the same 0.2s of an audio clip in loop as if my computer was about to experience a blue screen of death! So I press Alt+Ctrl+Suppr and properly end the process, then restart the game. Happily my settings have been saved and the game looks fantastic... but then new problems occured. Whenever I clicked a button to go to the character's creation, the sound was severely acting up, producing a loud "clic" that clearly cut off the soundtrack playing in the background. And once I eventually got the chance to play the game and reach the main hub after the tutorial... my FPS went from a mere 60 down to a pityful 19-21 just because of the many players present in the area. I will have you know and take in consideration that my computer is blessed with the power of an Intel i7-6700K plus a Nvidia GTX 1080, combined to 32Gb of RAM and a dedicated soundboard the Asus Xonar Phoebus. This game has been released in 2010, we are in 2017, and you are going to tell me that neither Nexon nor devCAT have fixed a massive memory leak and other performance-related issues in seven years? Nothing in my hardware justifies these massive and sudden FPS drops, plus the stuttering sound whenever there's a loading screen or an action-packed scene going on.
As a matter of fact, I do not recommand this game at all to anyone. And I have not even talked about the Cash Shop that is nothing more than a glorified lotery at every level beginning at 4€ / $4 without any explaination for such high entry price, or the Enhancing & Enchanting systems that can (and often will) break your hard-earned gear regardless of its rarity (reaching the +10 is the most risky thing you will ever do in this game, just staring at it will give you cold sweat). I am not telling you to avoid this game at all cost, because it is a fun game to play... but you will have to look past all the aforementioned flaws in order to get any degree of fun out of it.

I have played this game for 3 years, so do not pay attention to the time counter on Steam, because this was just available after the EU service migration.
Vindictus has certainly one of the unique PvE combat system of all action MMORPG. Every actions such as attacks, dodge and interaction are responding the way they should do. You can not play this type of combat passively, on the contrary, you must pay attention for every actions you make. Thus this game requires your skill a lot, which is so much fun to play.
Overall the semi-realism character design and level design are beautiful, which show off in the latish updates. The equipments look interesting which give you a variety of combination between various type of armor e.g. cloth, light, heavy, plate and importantly avatar sets, which is only available through NX shop or special events.
Now that was the first glance of a shiny game. Of course there is a downside, a major downside to be more exact. But let me gather them bit by bit.
First of all, since the Europe version (XE) is wiped, you are going to play Vindictus on North America Premiere version. This Premiere version is not equivalent to the original Korean version, for some reason. This can be see in the play mechanic of Vella where you can hold shift to go into Cross Stance and release the button to cancel the animation. Okay, this point is only understandable to Vindictus player.
But it is rather disappointing to not get the full potential of the game.
To be honest, this game is not PvP friendly at the beginning. Maybe there was an unbalanced time for people who enjoy PvP content, but do not get the idea of playing this game for PvP. It is not worth it and boring to be clear.
The other thing is the Peer-to-Peer connection to get into raids or battle. This type of connection requires you a decent upload rate to setting up raids or battles. Consequently if you have bad internet connection then you are limited to enjoy the exciting content of the game: raids. Raid is boss battle only which require you, depends on difficulty, a lot of focus and skill. As follows, you will experience lags, stuttering and unresponsive. So it depends on your hoster, because he/she should also have a good connection to carry the party member. The downside is, if you are not fulfil the requirement of the hoster, such as low ATK or ABC (Attack Speed, Balance, Critical Hit) then he is able to kick you out of the board. And this is a disappointing feeling for player to be „left“ out.
Furthermore the loading time is a thing. A feature which is still common in modern game, but the loading time in this game is literally too long! You are waiting roughly 30 seconds to board the actual battle and once you have completed it, take another 30 seconds on top of that? No, how about a random time from 1 minute to never ending battles? Not funny at all.
Rather than that, searching for specific items on the marketplace can give you a random disconnection due to its loading time. Not only that, you also get disconnection in any time. No matter if you are raiding, selling, sitting, chatting or waiting for battle result. Once you get a disconnection, you are out – restart the whole game to come back.
Also you get a 10 minutes IP-lock every time your IP has changed. As a result you are not able to sell or buy items, open boxes, claiming mails, which is annoying in a long term. 10 more minutes will not hinder „hacker“ to delete your precious treasure. You should know how to secure your account.
Finally the major issue on this game is performance. Game performance is THE most essential thing for a good game. Vindictus is not optimized at all. You will never see the 60 fps marker in any raids or battles for a good gaming experience. No matter if you fulfil the system requirement, which is nuts, or you have access the high horse power gaming rig, you never get the 60 fps – okay except for log-in screen or facing walls. To be truth, your fps will be in the low 30 or 20 in raids/battles and crowded city, it is just the fact.
This review contains game experiences so far without going in details to the publisher side Nexon Inc. Of course there are a few issues going on such as blocked country, bots and gold sellers, TirCoins, banned player, cash grab events, where you literally have to buy NX (real money) to get excellent stuff.
Nexon is responsible for this game and it will surely affects your game experience as a result. So keep that in mind.
This game has reached his age and it is not worth to begin with.
So in a nutshell, do yourself a favour and use your limited time in something else. This game is not worth to play.

++ competitive boss fight
+ beautiful character design, level design
- different game version NA Premiere ≠ KR Premiere
- PvP... come on are you kidding me?
-- Peer-to-Peer connection for raids and battles
-- long loading time (boarding boat, searching marketplace, ending battles)
-- disconnection appears randomly (another RNG feature?)
-- 10 minutes IP lock
--- performance is ridiculously trash

Fortified is a tower defense game similar to Orcs Must Die, but with a 50s comic book aesthetic.
The first thing you'll notice is the stylized look of the game. It nails the general atmosphere, including graphics, writing and cheesy dialogue that normally comes with 50s comics.
You'll feel right at home if you've played the Orcs Must Die series. You place defensive structures in between waves, and run around with cool weapons, fending off aliens alongside your turrets and structures.
The combat is very satisfying. You have a selection of cool weapons to choose from. Ranging from a futuristic freeze ray to a classic tommy gun. Each weapon also has a secondary fire, that allows for further versatility when you're attacking enemies. Enemies ragdoll when you kill them, which makes shooting feel very gratifying.
Killing enemies also charges up a Hero meter that allows you to become super powerful, and wreak havoc. They differ depending on what character you're playing as. Some might have infinite ammo and be very fast, while another might fly or freeze nearby enemies.
When you kill enemies, you gain money to spend on structures. These can be built on the ground, or walls to help you keep the hoard back. Traps can either assist in ways like slowing down an enemy, or flat out blow them up. You may also  sell and re-position a trap if you want to make changes in between waves.
As you play through the game, you'll unlock ability points to spend on new structures and weapons for your characters. Each character has a few unique weapons and structures to call their own. My personal gripe with the game is that I want to play and have fun with each different character. Although the fact that they all level up separately, means I need to play earlier, more boring levels and slowly unlock stuff for that new character. It's not a huge problem, as some people might not mind it, and it adds replay value, but it bugs me a bit.
There are 2 game modes to currently choose from. Each can be played solo or up to 4 players. The campaign has 12 levels. Each have a large amount of waves, differing types of enemies and last quite a while, so the replay value is decent. The Invasion mode pits you in what seems to be an infinite number of waves (I say seemingly because I don't see anywhere the game explains it). Each wave also adds a few random modifiers to make things interesting. Like faster enemies, quick Hero recharge times, etc. Pretty good mode to play for fun after you've upgraded your characters.
Overall, I really love the look of the game, and it's a lot of fun. It's definitely something that is more fun with friends, but you can play it solo or with the public just fine as well.
(The graphics options menu has a lot of nice customisable options too)

First of all, this is MEANT to be played in co-op. It is definitely one of the best coop games out there, and I have enjoyed every minute of it with a very good friend of mine, as well as playing it alone. Many of the levels are designed for coop, but has a sort of hot-fix for singleplayer solving etc... Much coop, very fun, such laughter. wow.
The game features puzzles which will test both your brain and timing. In the singleplayer part of the game, many of the puzzle seems to fade into becomming mostly timingskills rather than actual puzzles. Quite easy to figure out, somewhat difficult to execute. In the coop part however, the puzzles require teamwork, timing, space for experimentation and time to think (although timing and executions are still present).
The game is fairly short in single-player, unless you try to accuire every collectible in one run. This is also the case in co-op. My advice; play the coop and take your time to explore and have fun. No need for rushing (unless a challange requires you to do so).
Full controller support is always a plus. Having tested both mouse/keyboard and controller, i find that they are equally pleasing. A matter of preference really. Also the game allows for local-coop with either keyboard or gamepad(s) which is awesome!
The overall movement mechanics really has a flow to it, you feel in control when you dash around the map, aiming your gun og moving at the same time.  Movement on the keyboard however may at times be a bit annoying as you can only move in vertical, horizontal and diagonal with the WASD, this is however nothing that you will not get used to.
the combat system is very easy to get used to, and is actaully pretty straight forward. (point => shoot => kill) it does however feature a lot of custimization later on, which I am not going to spoil. All I can say is, mutiple options are great! it's easy to learn and utilize, especially with mouse/keyboard, which may give the user more aiming freedom (yet again, a matter of preference).
Visuals are pleasing, and the astosphere is great. The theme of the game is present throughout the game, which is nice. The only thing the games actually lacks, is a better storyline. It's pretty straight-forward; Lara must help the good guy defeat the bad guy, solving puzzles and defeating minions. BUT! the story is not the main focus of the game, the gameplay, the levels, the coop is indeed the driving force!
My friend and I had a blast playing it, can't recommend it enough for some couch-gaming!

Far Cry 2 is loaded with tons of horrible gameplay mechanics, but if you're very patient, you can appreciate the rest of what the game has to offer. What sticks out to me is the story. It's not amazing by any means, but it offers a much more grounded experience than that of 3 or 4. There is no unbelievable, larger than life villain for the player to hate. Instead, it's an arms dealer you've been contracted to kill, who isn't all he seems to be. What's most unique about the game is that you're not a good guy, you're a mercenary. You do bad things for money and it really doesn't matter who it affects. Whether you like a character or not, you may find yourself paying them a visit with a loaded gun. Even when you do help innocent people, it's almost always in your own self interest. This immorality combined with the inability to make any meaningful choices is actually very refreshing when most other games on the market settle for hamfisted good and bad options. You don't choose who you are in Far Cry 2.

This is the best computer role-playing-game I've ever played. It's like one of those old-timey DOS RPGs that you always say you're going to go back and play, except when you finally do it's so abstruse and clunky and old-fashioned that you end up dying in the first encounter, or unable to figure out how to get out of the first town, so you quit after 20 minutes.
It's like that, except it's actually accessible and playable, with an interface that you understand how to use just by looking at it. It still has all the good stuff about those old RPGs that everyone raves about: worldbuilding, a boatload of secrets and mysteries to unravel, multiple ways to solve problems, skill checks out the wazoo, bad graphics, exciting loot, a million viable ways you can build your character, and a rewarding tactical turn-based combat system. It's also the funniest game I've ever played, which is a low bar, but WoL grabs that brass ring and races past the finish line with it faster than Superman can mix this metaphor.
If you like computer role-playing games you should play West of Loathing.
One erratum (9/22/17): If you want the rewarding tactical turn-based combat, make sure you equip the hard hat. Otherwise the battles are pretty trivial. If you do put the hard hat on, make sure you select the option to distribute your XP manually instead of letting the game allocate it for you. The game would still be fantastic and well worth the price of admission if you just want to breeze through the combat and explore the world, but for me personally the challenging combat and the decisions I had to make when building my character added an extra layer of enjoyment to the game.

Where to begin with this game?
This game had some strengths, but some serious weaknesses that I just couldn't overlook.
I really liked the game mechanics  they are a lot different than the other heavy hitting Hack and Slashers out there. The controls are rather simple, and most of the executable moves are over the top, and visually, very satisfying to watch. Graphic wise, the game does pass. It uses a  unique anime style that embraces silhouettes and darker color pallet that give the game intense feel to it, but I wouldn't necessarily say it has good graphics.
I also really enjoyed the music. It has an old school funk jazz beat  to it that really goes well with the anime look. It reminded me a lot of cowboy bebop.
Unfortunately, in spite of this games good attributes, I found this game extremely cringy. Some of the voice acting made me dive for the mute button, but then again, high pitched screeches are really common in anime, so it could just be me.
The storyline in this game is simply confusing. None of it makes sense. There are so many obvious plot holes and established narrative ignored that nearly every cut scene you catch yourself asking "Why am I playing this?"
I also found a lot of the mini missions to be really creepy. They are interactive date sims where the object is to check out girls with X-ray glasses  while they are not looking. (I swear I'm not making this up.) This had to be thought up by a thirteen year old, or someone very lonely.
Overall this weeaboo adventure was way too weird for me. If you are looking for a good game, this is not it,
get Mass Effect instead….

Tracks are also great, they are using lots of elevation changes, scenery is quite diverse and dangerous too. And for all the purists there they are narrow as hell. But thankfully Pikes Peak lets you breathe freely.

Career mode is pretty large and it returns to the formula of multitude of small events in different classes seen in WRC 2 and RIDE. "Loeb Experience" is nice addition too.
In sum, Sebastien Loeb Rally EVO joins the pantheon of my favorite rally games along with Colin McRae Rally 2.0, Dirt Rally, Richard Burns Rally and Mobil 1 Rally Championship. Milestone finally delivers.

There's a good game undereath the lack of audio quality, and at times, visual polish.
The physics can feel clunky at times, but if DiRT Rally didn't exist then this would be the best rally game of recent times.
When Milestone learn that rally needs great sounds to properly portray the spirit of the sport, as well as smooth physics, then SLRE could be a serious contender for best rally game. They also need to better optimise their games to run on both consoles and PC, because right now they're pretty bad.
The content cannot be faulted. Although some of the car models are inaccurate, the sheer variety of both cars and events are second to none in rally games. They've done a great job there, but maybe focussed a little too much on quanitity over quality.
Until these things are addressed, (which haven't been since their first WRC title), DiRT Rally will remain at the top for quality, but that doesn't mean you should skip this title.

I saw this game years ago at gamestop and thought it looked lame. I was never big on party based games. Several months later I decided to quit WoW and started thinking about other games to play. I found the demo for this and was hooked. Its the first party RPG I've seen where its possible to get through the game with any party combination if you're determined.
The first party I ran with was a fighter, rogue, ranger, mage, bishop, and a second fighter. A rather dry party but it got the job done. I've started several other play throughs but life keeps getting in the way. The bard class is excellent as you can level the music skill up outside of combat. The bards instruments focus on dealing damage and debuffing the enemy. The gadgeteer is the opposite where his creations focus on buffing the party and his weapon upgrades with every level. There are several other classes, all classes bring something unique to the table.
The world is narrow but big. My current play time of 1.8 hours only counts my steam played time, not my GOG or CD playtime. For $10 you will easily get your money's worth out of this game. There are secrets dungeons and unmarked quests to explore. While you can only have 6 PCs that you made in your party, 2 NPCs can join you. Keep in mind the more characters you have in your party, the less exp each of them gets as it is divided up.
My biggest issues with the game are 1. Combat can take a while at higher levels and 2. The mobs level up with you at times. Of course you do get some rather powerful weapons and abilities at higher levels. You can feel your characters getting stronger and they do unlock new abilities with each level up. Theres a great sense of progression with the game.
I would highly recommend this game. Since I first played it I have looked for games like it. Etrian Odyssey is to grindy for my taste but I like the map making system. Other games the grinding is ok but the map system is horrible. This is one of the few games that I cant find anything like it to play afterwards except for one of the spinoffs that came out for ps2 but that still doesn't have the same feel.

This game is an absolute beast.
I debated on getting this game for a long while. I finally broke down and got it in a bundle and I'm so very glad that I did. I somehow missed this game when it was current, so I don't have any nostalgia blinders. I did grow up in the 80s/90s though, so I'm pretty well versed in the various eras of ugly video games and older graphics don't bother me. Still, this one looked like it might have been just too dated to be fun. The screenshots tend to look horrible so I hesitated.
I'm so glad my misgivings were wrong. The graphics are actually not even that bad once you have a little time to adapt. I find the visuals quite passable now (though they are dated for sure, lets be clear on that).
One thing I noticed that kept being repeated while I was researching this game is that even today, nothing compares to Wizardry 8 or carries the torch. Its true. This RPG really is in a class by itself and if there is anything that really does its job, I have never seen it - spiritual successor or otherwise.
The character creation system is complex. There are a lot of races and classes to choose from and you can have up to 6 in your party, with 2 extra slots to recruit optional NPCs later. The leveling system gives the player a lot of control in each character's development and skills can also be raised through use, which is nice.
Combat is turn based and you can issue commands to each party member before rounds. You can also turn continuous combat off and on (even mid-fight) to speed things up if desired. Formation also matters a lot but you can change it up during combat if a group of enemies attacks you from behind (being surrounded can be very dangerous though!).
For a game this old, the voice acting is surprisingly good as well.
Another thing that's impressive about this game, is how sophisticated and polished the interface truly is. There are a couple of things that are kind of annoying when you're trying to do things quickly (such as mass potion brewing/stack splitting) and the inventory can be a bit of a pain sometimes but even so, the interface of this game is probably one of the best designed I have ever seen.
This game is still worth playing, later. If you like party based RPGs this one is highly recommended.

I've been playing this game since 2011 and continue to play it today (casually). It's important to keep that in mind throughout the rest of the review since I'll be wording things from a Casual player's perspective.
THE GOOD
• Great, shiny graphics (but due to its age, don't expect to be blown away).
• Very solid, satisfying melee combat, second to none that I've seen. You can almost feel each hit, each slice, each stab.
• The characters are numerous and play differently, making for great replayability.
• Raids are so much fun
THE BAD
• Graphics can be overproduced at times, leading so slow performance even with a good PC
• Lower-level quests are mind-numbingly dull with the same trash mobs over and over, in the same rooms over and over (only in lower levels)
• The story content  is not worth the amount of time you'll spend walking back and forth in town between NPCs (only in lower levels)
• player base seems to be shrinking at an alarming rate. Only Veterans seem to log in anymore
THE IMPORTANT NOTE
The next fact is neither Good nor Bad: There is a large range between Casual and Veteran players. This is understandable; Casuals don't want to put in all the time to get the best gear, and Veterans do not want to Raid with dead-weight. For the latest and most stat-heavy content, you will likely not be welcomed onto a Veteran boat if you are not a Veteran. However, Veterans are more than happy to Raid with you on older content.
Nexon has made many improvements to the game since I started playing. Story-based drops are now guaranteed, you can purchase rare materials with Seals (gained over time doing Raids) and different difficulties are available for each Raid to tailor to your skill level and equipment. Content-wise, the game is at it's best right now.
However, since the Steam Recommendation is based on whether or not I'd suggest it to new players, the answer is No. The lower-level grind is too dull, and the small player base may be indicative of a Conclusion sometime soon.
That being said, I'll continue to play it as a filthy Casual. :)
